16179-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Number fifty-five of The Great Round World, dated November 25, 1897, calls its week exciting for Cuban matters. A magazine article by Mr. Taylor, saying Spain could not settle the Cuban question and America ought to interfere, had stirred Madrid papers to anger. Senator Salvani wrote hotly that Taylor, when minister to Spain, had seemed eager for friendship and had declared there was no fear of American action.

The children's paper retells the quarrel in plain language, letting young readers follow diplomacy, pride, and press debate across the Atlantic. Each side's words get a fair, short hearing. The issue captures how the Cuban question heated up in American and Spanish opinion just before war.
17563-king-s-cutters-and-smugglers-1700-:
E. Keble Chatterton, author of books on sailing ships and the British navy, published this history of revenue cutters and smugglers in London in 1912, with thirty-three pictures and a coloured frontispiece. A revenue cruiser chasing a smuggling lugger opens the plates, with a note that the cruiser had to hoist revenue colours before firing, day or night. The period covered runs from 1700 to 1855.

Chapters trace the earliest smugglers, the growth of smuggling, smugglers' methods, the Hawkhurst gang, revenue cruisers, cutters and sloops, preventive organisation, and cutters' equipment. Readers get a sea history of cat and mouse along Britain's coasts, told by a writer who knew ships. It suits readers of maritime history and of Georgian crime.
21350-roister-doister-written-probably-a:
Nicholas Udall, master of Eton and then Westminster School, wrote Ralph Roister Doister before 1553. Edward Arber edited this reprint in 1869 from the unique copy at Eton College. The play is counted the earliest surviving English comedy. Its hero is a boastful fool who believes himself irresistible to women.

Matthew Merrygreek, the witty parasite, eggs Roister on to court Dame Custance, who is betrothed to Gawyn Goodluck. A love letter read with the pauses in the wrong places turns praise into insult, the play's most famous joke. Udall built his schoolboy comedy on Roman models, and English drama's comic line starts here.
29653-conestoga-wagons-in-braddock-s-cam:
Don H. Berkebile, on the exhibits staff of the Smithsonian Institution, wrote this paper on Conestoga wagons in Braddock's campaign of 1755, as paper nine from the Museum of History and Technology. More than two hundred years had passed, he notes, since the Pennsylvania farm wagon first drew notice through army service in the French and Indian War. By early May, fifteen hundred pack horses stood at Fort Cumberland.

Braddock reached Frederick, Maryland, on April 21, to find only twenty-five wagons had come in. Berkebile traces how these early wagons, forerunners of the post-Revolutionary Conestoga freighter and the prairie schooner, carried an army. Readers of military and transport history will find a precise, vivid study of wagons at war.
4803-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
Motley's Rise of the Dutch Republic reaches Philip the Second in the Netherlands in 1555 in this third volume, dated 1855. Chapter one opens with abdication of Charles resolved upon, Brussels in the sixteenth century, and the hall of the palace described. Portraits of prominent individuals present at the ceremony, formalities of abdication, and universal emotion follow, with remarks on the character and career of Charles.

His retirement at Juste closes the chapter's scope, after a scene of high ceremony and public feeling. On October 25, 1555, the estates of the Netherlands were assembled in the great hall, to witness an emperor laying down power before his son. Motley lingers on the hall, the persons present, and the emotion of the moment, before turning to Philip's reign. Readers get the abdication itself, the hinge on which the whole history turns, in Motley's ceremonial opening.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: Andrew Johnson, tailor's apprentice who never spent a day in school, fills this sixth volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. Taught the alphabet by a fellow workman, Johnson learned to read, worked as a journeyman tailor, and rose to the presidency. The volume prints his messages and papers after Lincoln's death. Richardson preserves Johnson's record of peace and restoration.
a-general-history-and-collection-of-voya: Volume nine of Robert Kerr's voyages continues early English voyages to India after the East India Company. Its chapters follow the eighth voyage of 1611 by Captain John Saris through the Moluccas to Japan. Arrival at Brando and further observations complete the voyage. Kerr's volume keeps the English record of Asian trade in systematic form.
ady-candle-in-the-dark-1655:
Thomas Ady's Candle in the Dark, published in 1655, is a direct attack on the witch-hunters of his day. Ady was a physician in Kent who had watched trials rest on dreams, spite, and forced confessions. His title promises a small light against a great darkness of error.

He argues that witchcraft prosecutions rest on false testimony and melancholy, the sickness of mind his age mistook for sorcery. Scripture, rightly read, gives no warrant, he says, for hanging old women on such evidence. Ady's lonely protest helped prepare the later English turn against the witch trials.
agrippa-fourth-book-occult-philosophy-16:
Robert Turner puts a pack of rite texts in English in the Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy set, out in London in 1655. The lead text bears Agrippa's name, though sages doubt he writ it. It teaches how to call and bind souls by name, hour, and rite. With it stand Agrippa's Geomancy, the craft of fate by earth marks, and two more famed texts of the art.

Peter de Abano's craft and the Arbatel, a book of bright souls, fill the set. Turner gave English mages their chief store of rite. The book is a grimoire shelf in one.
alan-of-lille-de-fide-catholica-1855:
Alan of Lille was the universal doctor of the twelfth-century schools. He wrote De Fide Catholica contra Haereticos, On the Catholic Faith Against the Heretics, in four books around 1200. The text here is drawn from the Migne Patrologia Latina, volume 210, in its 1855 reprint, and it is in Latin. Alan aimed his book at the Cathars, the Waldensians, the Jews, and the Muslims in turn.

He tries a bold method: to argue from reason and from texts his foes accept, since they scorn his own authorities. The work is the first systematic anti-heretical summa of the schools. Alan's wide reading fills it with authorities marshaled like troops. It shows the classroom arming itself for the age of the Inquisition.
alexander-letter-aristotle-india-1555:
The Letter of Alexander to Aristotle purports to be Alexander the Great's own report on the marvels of India. This text follows the edition of 1555. No one now credits Alexander with it, but the Middle Ages believed every word, and copied it for a thousand years.

The letter describes dog-headed men, headless folk, and giant ants that dig gold. Rivers of fire and trees that speak crowd the march eastward. Such tales seeded the whole medieval monster-race tradition. Mapmakers placed these peoples at the world's edge for centuries. Antiquity's tallest travel tales live here, the cornerstone of a long, strange geography of wonder.
arbatel-of-magick-turner-1655:
Robert Turner's 1655 English translation made the Arbatel of Magick open to English readers for the first time. The Arbatel, whose Latin title means On the Magic of the Ancients, is a Renaissance handbook of spiritual wisdom. Its author is unknown, and its tone is prayerful rather than dark.

The book teaches the Olympic spirits, planetary powers said to govern the ages of the world in long turns. Its short aphorisms join magic to humility, charity, and trust in God, warning the reader against greed and pride. Protestant readers prized the Arbatel as godly magic, and it shaped English occult practice for centuries.
arxiv-2509-00855:
Tengzhou Zhang, with two co-authors, Zhizhen Chen and Zi Cai, reveals nontrivial quantum phases at infinite temperature, a regime usually expected to wash out quantum order. Using unbiased quantum Monte Carlo simulation, they study a hybrid model of hard-core bosons whose hopping is mediated by the density of soft-core bond bosons that can absorb entropy indefinitely.

Zhang and his co-authors show a Bose-Einstein condensate, a collective quantum state, can persist in three dimensions even as temperature approaches the infinite limit. In two dimensions, the quasi-superfluid is depleted by bond boson fluctuations, which instead enhance conductivity of the hard-core bosons in the normal phase. A generalization to a fermionic model is also discussed.
arxiv-2509-01055:
Large language models learn better reasoning when training rewards can be checked, but that training often stops at a single reply with no tools. Dongfu Jiang, with eleven co-authors, presents VerlTool, a shared framework for training agents that act over many turns and use tools such as code runs, search, databases, and vision.

Earlier tool training code was built task by task, which made it slow and hard to extend. VerlTool uses standard interfaces for tools, stays aligned with the VeRL library, and runs steps out of sync to cut waiting time, nearly doubling speed. Tests across six task types show strong results. The team offers the system as a base others can build on.
arxiv-2509-01155:
Huyuan Chen and Bobo Hua study finite-energy solutions of Kazdan-Warner type equations set on a two-dimensional lattice graph, a grid of points with links. Such equations link a function's spread to an exponential term, and their solutions help describe curved surfaces and field models. A point source term sits at the origin of the grid.

When a sign in the equation is positive, Chen and Hua prove a continuous family of finite-energy solutions exists for some parameter values. That result settles an open problem about the related Liouville equation. When the sign is negative and a second value passes a stated threshold, they show the solutions form a layered structure and they identify the extremal, or edge, solution.
arxiv-2509-01355:
Jose Carmona Tapia, with three co-authors, studies a class of quasilinear equations. In these, the main term depends on the solution's slope in a power-law way. The equation includes a natural growth term tied to the gradient. A reaction term changes sign. Solutions are sought inside a smooth bounded region, with value zero on its border.

The reaction function is positive between two zeros. The authors find an area condition on the two functions. That condition is both needed and enough for a solution of a stated size to exist. They also show how the gradient term shapes existence. The more negative one function is, the stronger its smoothing effect. For any fixed parameter, a suitable choice can always restore solutions. Growth terms thus rescue hard problems.
arxiv-2509-01455:
A deployed language model must know when to stay silent, not just what to say, since a confident wrong answer can do harm. Markus Oehri, with eight co-authors, presents UniCR, a framework that turns mixed uncertainty signals into one calibrated probability that an answer is right. Signals include sequence likelihoods, self-consistency spread, retrieval fit, and feedback from tools or verifiers.

A light calibration head, tuned with temperature scaling and proper scoring rules, produces that probability, and a refusal rule then enforces a user-set error budget. Distribution-free guarantees come from conformal risk control. For long answers, confidence is aligned with atomic factuality scores drawn from retrieved evidence, cutting confident hallucinations while keeping coverage. Tests span short questions, code with execution checks, and retrieval-based long-form tasks.
arxiv-2509-01755:
Subhadip Paul leads five co-authors on a sound based method to gauge damage in blood samples. Anemia, a lack of healthy red cells, needs fast and accurate tests, above all for at-risk groups. When red cells break open, called lysis, two values matter: how much has broken and how much oxygen the blood holds. The team uses photoacoustics, where light pulses make sound waves that reveal blood traits.

Lab tests on human blood are matched with computer models of light and sound spread. Two pairs of light colors prove best for reading cell share, damage level, and oxygen level at once. Accuracy stays above ninety percent across a wide damage range in their checks. More work is needed before the method can serve in live patients.
arxiv-2509-01955:
Yu Jiang leads twelve co-authors in a catalog of molecular clumps traced by a carbon monoxide isotope across the Milky Way. Clumps are dense gas lumps where stars may form, mapped by the MWISP survey. A global detection scheme paired with a clump finding algorithm extracts tens of thousands of clumps. The data cube spans a huge sky area at high resolution.

A hierarchical distance method resolves the classic near far ambiguity for nearly all clumps. Most clumps prove gravitationally bound and hold nearly all the catalog mass. Scaling laws across surveys follow universal power patterns. Clumps tied to masers, natural microwave lasers, show shifted traits that betray active star formation. The catalogs ground future work on clumps and galactic change.
arxiv-2509-02055:
Yang Zhang leads nine co-authors with Align-Then-stEer, a light method to adapt vision-language-action robot models to new tasks. Such models learn broad manipulation skill from large mixed data sets. New robot bodies or tasks shift the action distribution, forcing costly fine-tuning. Their framework first aligns action spaces inside a unified latent space.

A variational autoencoder with a reverse divergence penalty embeds new actions into modes of the pretrained distribution. Guidance during generation then steers outputs toward the target domain. Tests span simulated and real cross body and cross task settings. Average multi task success rises notably in simulation, with a striking gain in the real cross body case. The plug-in design keeps adaptation data and compute low.
arxiv-2509-02155:
Sharad Barde, Ganesh Mundhe, Mayur Kshirsagar, and A N Bhavale compute characteristic polynomials and energies for the ABS matrix of select graph classes. The ABS matrix encodes atom bond sum connectivity, a degree based index from chemical graph theory. Its entry for linked vertices depends on the degrees of both endpoints through a square root formula. Non-linked pairs get zero.

For specific graph families, the authors derive the full characteristic polynomial of that matrix. Eigenvalues follow from those polynomials directly. ABS energy, the sum of absolute eigenvalues, is then computed for each class. Such spectral data link graph structure to molecular property models. The results add closed forms where numeric computation was the norm.
arxiv-2509-02355:
Caterina Fuster-Barcelo, Gonzalo R. Rios-Munoz, and Arrate Munoz-Barrutia report a 2025 education study on redesigning a biomedical image processing course inside a health machine learning master's programme. The redesign ran over two academic years.

Students coded together in real time with Google Colab and logged experiments with Weights and Biases, a tracking tool. Rubric-guided peer review, where classmates grade against shared criteria, added structured feedback. Compared with an earlier cohort, final project scores spread out more and carried higher entropy, suggesting fairer separation between strong and weak work. Surveys also showed deeper engagement. The authors argue that tool-supported teamwork plus clear review rules can improve both learning and fairness in STEM classes.
arxiv-2509-02555:
Rio Akizuki and six co-authors present a 2025 machine learning paper on cheaper ways to tune model merging, a technique that blends several trained models into one. Merging works well only with good hyperparameter settings, but testing settings on large models is expensive.

The authors build surrogate benchmarks: fast predictive models trained on collected samples that estimate a merged model's score from its settings alone. Two search spaces are defined for the settings. Tests show the surrogates predict merged performance well and reproduce how optimisation algorithms behave over time. Researchers can therefore develop and compare tuning algorithms at low cost before spending on full merges. The approach targets a practical bottleneck as merged language models grow larger.
arxiv-2509-02755:
David Beers and Gillian Grindstaff wrote a 2025 topology paper on merge trees, structures that record how connected components of a filtered space merge over time. Two distances compete: a fast bottleneck distance on barcodes, and a richer interleaving distance that is hard to compute.

As raw maps, the two distances differ, because many merge trees share one barcode. The authors instead compare the intrinsic metrics, distances measured by shortest path length inside merge tree space itself. They prove those intrinsic versions coincide, settling a conjecture. Both distances therefore induce the same length geometry. In practice, where a path between trees is known, the cheap bottleneck distance can stand in for the interleaving distance, which is generally hard even to approximate.
arxiv-2509-03055:
Jonathan A. Mavroforas and Anthony H. Dooley wrote a 2025 exposition of rough path methods for decision problems under randomness. Rough path theory describes wiggly driving signals by more than their values alone, which makes many stochastic problems behave in a stable, path-by-path way. No single earlier treatment covered control, filtering, and stopping together.

Optimal control steers a system at lowest cost, filtering estimates a hidden state from noisy data, and optimal stopping picks the best moment to act. The authors gather the needed theory from Lyons, Gubinelli, and others into one self-contained account. They fill in proofs that were missing or sketchy elsewhere. A central verification theorem links candidate control solutions to the governing Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. Open challenges for rougher signals are flagged at the end.
arxiv-2509-03155: M. Balakhnev and V. Sokolov wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on the Schwarz-KdV equation, from the famous Korteweg-de Vries wave family. Each integrable equation, meaning one open to exact solution methods, carries a family of linked systems. Some are continuous, some discrete, some between. The authors list those companions for this case. They then generalize it to a vector version with several parts at once. They note such versions exist here as a striking fact, with no known proof of why.
arxiv-2509-03255:
I. Diachkov and 7 co-authors built a tungsten collimator prototype in 2025 using three-dimensional metal printing. In X-ray imaging, scattered photons blur the picture, so an anti-scatter grid filters them out before they reach the detector. A cleaner image can mean lower radiation doses for patients.

The part was made by laser powder bed fusion, which melts metal powder layer by layer with a laser, in a geometry that converges toward the X-ray source. Tests checked whether the grid improves detection of markers in the image. Results were positive, with clear gains in marker visibility. The advantage stood out most when the team added artificial obstacles that imitate harsher imaging conditions. The work supports printed tungsten as a route to better medical X-ray grids.
arxiv-2509-03555:
A 2025 physics paper by Everardo Rivera-Oliva gives another formula for Clebsch-Gordan coefficients. Those coefficients are numbers used in quantum mechanics to combine two angular momenta into one total. Standard derivations lean on a Gram-Schmidt procedure, a step-by-step orthogonalisation method, to build the combined states.

Rivera-Oliva instead applies angular momentum ladder operators, tools that raise or lower angular momentum one step at a time. Repeated raising reconstructs each subspace of the total angular momentum basis. Notably, the raising operator rebuilds even subspaces whose total angular momentum is not maximal, where older routes needed the Gram-Schmidt procedure. The resulting formula offers an alternative computation route. It complements, rather than replaces, the formulas already in the literature.
arxiv-2509-03755:
John Augustine and five co-authors work on downloading data from an external source across an asynchronous network of unreliable peers in a 2025 computer science paper. Their model links many peers in a peer-to-peer network, with one trusted source holding a bit array. Peers can message each other cheaply or query the source at higher cost, and some fraction may fail mid-run.

The Download problem asks every healthy peer to learn the whole array while minimising source queries. Earlier work assumed synchronous communication, where rounds tick in lockstep. This study tackles asynchronous timing, where messages arrive with unpredictable delays. For crash failures, deterministic protocols are query-optimal and tolerate any fault fraction below one. For Byzantine failures, where faulty peers can lie, a lower bound is extended to randomised protocols at high fault rates. Below it, a randomised protocol with near-optimal query cost exists.
arxiv-2509-03855:
Zhouyi Zhou and eight co-authors set out to push Linux toward deterministic sub-microsecond response times through interrupt isolation in a 2025 research paper. Real-time workloads suffer when interrupts fight for cores and timer handling adds overhead. Ordinary Linux, even with real-time patches, struggles to answer events within half a microsecond reliably.

Their approach centralises and cuts timer interrupt interference across cores. A dedicated interface lets the system invoke timer handling only when chosen, while non-critical cross-core interrupts are suppressed. Jitter and response latency fall significantly as a result. Experiments run on a multicore ARM platform. It consistently achieves response times below half a microsecond, beating conventional PREEMPT-RT Linux setups. The authors present interrupt isolation as a lightweight strategy for deterministic real-time work on a general-purpose system.
arxiv-2509-03955: In a 2025 research paper, Dmitri Liventsev and four co-authors describe an upgrade to LABM, a beam monitoring device at the SuperKEKB accelerator. Beam monitoring is crucial for reaching high collision rates, the output that drives a collider's science. LABM watches beamstrahlung, the radiation a charged particle beam emits when it speeds up inside the other beam's electromagnetic field. Observing that radiation reveals beam conditions without touching the beams themselves. The paper describes the 2023 upgrade of the device.
arxiv-2509-04655:
Specialised language models can give unreliable answers when a question falls outside their training area. Ayush Gupta, lead author with five co-authors, propose an inference-time detector for such out-of-domain inputs in a 2025 paper. Their method builds on inductive conformal anomaly detection, a statistical framework with controlled false alarm rates.

The new measure uses dropout tolerance, based on the idea that in-domain inputs withstand random neuron dropout better than unfamiliar ones. Tests on medical models show better detection than baseline methods. The approach aims to flag risky inputs before a specialised model answers them confidently.
arxiv-2509-04955:
Simulating quantum circuits on classical computers remains essential while quantum hardware stays noisy and limited. Guolong Zhong, lead author with two co-authors, present a parallelisation solution for a chemistry simulator package in a 2025 paper. Their work speeds up a full-amplitude simulator on both CPU and GPU systems.

Three optimisations drive the gains: batch-buffered overlap processing, dependency-aware gate contraction, and staggered multi-gate parallelism. Each one splits the work in a smarter way. Benchmarks across circuit types show the package beating leading open-source tools in their tests. The authors argue the results show hybrid-level parallelism can handle large-scale quantum simulation efficiently and portably on high-performance systems.
arxiv-2509-05055:
Ramsey numbers measure how large a tournament must be before it must contain a given directed pattern. Domagoj Bradač, lead author with three co-authors, prove linear bounds for a broad family of digraphs in a 2025 combinatorics paper. The family is acyclic digraphs with bounded degree and a local edge structure called graded bandwidth.

Vertices split into layers, and edges jump forward by only a limited number of layers. Under those conditions the authors bound the oriented Ramsey number by a constant multiple of the vertex count. The result unifies earlier theorems on bounded height, bounded bandwidth, and tree blow-ups, and covers oriented grids and hypercubes.
arxiv-2509-05155:
An overdetermined problem is one where extra boundary conditions force the domain to be a ball. Hongjie Dong and one co-author prove such a Serrin-type result for Lipschitz domains in a 2025 analysis paper. The unknown function vanishes outside the domain and satisfies a weak equation mixing a surface measure on the boundary with a volume term inside.

They show the domain satisfies that system if and only if it is a ball. Their approach offers an alternative proof for Lipschitz domains and answers an open question from earlier work. A generalisation of the method to the anisotropic setting is also discussed.
arxiv-2509-05255:
Uniform bounds for solutions of a hard equation on curved spaces are proven by Hussein Cheikh Ali and Saikat Mazumdar in a 2025 analysis paper. The Hardy-Sobolev equation mixes a curved-space diffusion term with a singular weight that blows up at one chosen point of the manifold.

Working on closed spaces of dimension three or more, the authors assume a sign condition tying a coefficient function to the space's scalar curvature at the special point. Those conditions were known to be sharp for a single bubble-shaped solution in higher dimensions. Under them, all positive solutions stay uniformly bounded, with no prior cap on energy or size assumed. Such bounds are a key step toward knowing when solutions exist.
arxiv-2509-05355:
Drone swarms for disaster response need command structures that change with the mission, Ahmed R. Sadik and three co-authors argue in a 2025 paper. Fixed designs, centralised or otherwise, struggle when conditions shift, wasting energy and dropping connections.

Their architecture lets a large language model choose among centralised, hierarchical, and holonic layouts, which differ in how much control sits at the top. The choice uses live mission facts such as task complexity, swarm size, and link stability. In extensive simulations the adaptive design beat static models on growth to larger swarms, energy use, and staying connected. The authors present the approach as a resilient option for real disaster work.
arxiv-2509-05655:
Forces switch a two-dimensional lattice material between unusual quantum phases, Rahul Ghosh maps in a solo 2025 condensed matter paper. The model generalises the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain to a square lattice, with uneven hopping between neighbours, longer-range hopping, and a staggered on-site energy.

Without interactions it hosts either a quadratic band touching or protected Dirac points, depending on the chosen settings. A self-consistent Hartree-Fock analysis finds that weak to moderate interactions can break time-reversal symmetry and stabilise a quantum anomalous Hall insulator with a small bond-order twist. Another nematic Dirac semimetal phase strengthens with asymmetric hopping and offset potential. The phase map guides searches for interaction-made order.
arxiv-2509-05755:
Coding assistants that run tools on a user's machine can be hijacked through those tools, Yuchong Xie and nine co-authors demonstrate in a 2025 security assessment. Six popular real-world coding agents are red-teamed, the first systematic study of tool-invocation risk in this class of software.

In a first phase the team leaks system prompts through a general flaw that exfiltrates them via harmless-looking tool arguments. In a second phase they inject instructions through tool descriptions and return values, achieving remote code execution. Payloads adapt using the leaked information. Their method succeeded on most agent and model pairs in emulation and on real agents, with execution reached everywhere tested. Practical defences close the report.
arxiv-2509-06055:
Radical transparency runs into mathematical walls, argue Faruk Alpay and Hamdi Alakkad in a 2025 paper built from logic and order theory. A disclosure policy that must report on itself faces self-reference, and the authors ask what that costs. Their treatment is logic-first: ethics questions are turned into fixed-point and diagonalization results.

The results stack up. An impossibility theorem bars any expressive system from defining a total, consistent transparency predicate for its own statements. Lawvere's argument makes self-referential equilibria inevitable. And Knaster-Tarski theory guarantees extremal fixed points, with the least one minimizing a formal risk measure. Partial transparency can stay consistent through Kripkean truth, while Löb's theorem flags self-endorsement risks and a recursion result captures Goodhart's law under full disclosure. The conclusion is a calculus for partial, principled disclosure.
arxiv-2509-06155:
One model that generates video and its soundtrack together is introduced in a 2025 paper led by Duomin Wang with nine co-authors. UniVerse-1 targets coordinated ambient sound and speech, in the style of leading closed systems. Instead of training from scratch, the team stitches together pretrained video and music generation experts, fusing corresponding blocks deeply.

An online annotation pipeline labels training data during training itself, keeping sound and picture aligned in time and avoiding the damage stale text labels cause. After fine-tuning on thousands of hours of audio-video material, the model produces well-coordinated ambient sound and strongly aligned speech. A new benchmark, Verse-Bench, supports systematic evaluation, and the model and code are released publicly.
arxiv-2509-06355:
A video game becomes a laboratory for long-horizon strategy in DECOY, a 2025 simulator from Yunzhe Wang and two co-authors. Full-fidelity multi-agent environments are expensive, so DECOY abstracts Counter-Strike: Global Offensive into movement decisions on waypoints, skipping aim and shooting mechanics while keeping terrain fidelity. Neural models trained on real tournament data reconstruct what happens between moves.

Replays generated from human match data inside DECOY closely match the original games, by the authors' evaluations. The discretized design preserves strategic depth, the level at which positioning and timing decide rounds, while running cheaply enough for planning research. The environment is released publicly for multi-agent planning and behavior generation studies.
arxiv-2509-06555:
Light that refuses to spread out as it travels is reported by Nilo Mata-Cervera and four co-authors in a 2025 optics paper. Diffraction normally widens any beam, and tighter beams spread faster. Engineered non-spreading waves exist, but in practice they eventually give way to diffraction.

Inside optical vortices, swirling beams of light, the authors find a natural structure called a skyrmion that avoids diffraction entirely. It stays confined at scales smaller than the wavelength of light itself, which ordinary waves cannot do. In experiments, the structure traveled a distance more than a thousand times larger than expected for its tiny width without spreading. Because this form occurs naturally rather than by careful engineering, the authors suggest it could open new directions for applications that need light held in a very narrow channel.
arxiv-2509-06655:
A corkscrew swimmer moving through fluids that only flow under enough force is described by Farshad Nazari and colleagues in a 2025 fluid mechanics paper. Yield stress fluids, like gels and pastes, act solid until pushed past a threshold. That behavior changes how a rotating helix can travel.

Three stages appear. First, the swimmer must overcome the material's yield strain just to rotate. That alone is not enough: net motion begins only when viscous forces are strong enough to deform the material plastically some distance away. Once moving, yield stress slows the swimmer at small helix pitch angles but, surprisingly, speeds it up at large pitch angles, where it dominates the flow. Pictures of the flow show motion tightly confined near the swimmer, unlike in ordinary fluids.
arxiv-2509-06855:
Finding the right passage in a huge particle physics literature is rebuilt around document structure by James McGreivy and three co-authors in a 2025 information systems paper. Retrieval-augmented generation matches text chunks by meaning, but facts spread across segments lose their context. Large collaborations produce exactly such sprawling corpora.

The first system, SciTreeRAG, exploits the hierarchical organization of physics articles, building a tree of the corpus so retrieved contexts stay focused and rich. The second, SciGraphRAG, goes further: language models convert the unstructured corpus into a knowledge graph, and retrieval then follows cross-document relationships that chunk matching misses. Both are demonstrated as proofs of concept on the LHCb experiment's publications from CERN. Structured knowledge of this kind could speed methodological and editorial review inside collaborations, and help outsiders analyze open data reliably.
arxiv-2509-06955:
Dark matter that is too fuzzy or too warm is ruled out by the growth of supermassive black holes in a 2025 astrophysics paper by John Ellis and three co-authors. A semi-analytic model of galaxy and black hole evolution inside the standard cosmology reproduces the observed relation between stellar mass and black hole mass, both before and after JWST. Alternative dark matter would suppress the small halos that the fit relies on.

Fuzzy dark matter and warm dark matter both delay the formation of small galactic halos, which play important roles in matching high-redshift black hole data. Comparing the predicted mass relation under each alternative, the authors disfavor fuzzy fields lighter than a stated bound and warm particles lighter than another bound, each at ninety-five percent confidence. Early black hole growth thus becomes a laboratory for dark matter physics, complementing direct searches.
arxiv-2509-07055:
Tomás González and 3 co-authors propose sequentially auditing differential privacy in a 2025 paper. Differential privacy is a formal guarantee that a mechanism's output reveals little about any single. Auditing whether a black-box mechanism actually satisfies that guarantee is major, but earlier batch auditing methods are limited by fixed sample size.

Their practical sequential test processes streams of a mechanism's outputs, providing anytime-valid inference while controlling type one error. Experiments show the test detects violations with sample sizes orders of magnitude smaller than current methods, reducing the number from tens of thousands to a few hundred examples across diverse real-life mechanisms. Notably, it identifies privacy violations in a differentially private training algorithm in under one training run, unlike prior methods needing full model training.
arxiv-2509-07455:
Detailed images of retinal blood vessels help doctors diagnose eye disease early, but the best imaging method is costly and motion-sensitive. Pooya Khosravi and 5 co-authors present XOCT in a 2025 research paper. XOCT is a deep learning system that translates ordinary retinal scans into angiography-style images, which show blood flow vessel by vessel. Earlier translators often blurred the fine, dense vessel details doctors need.

The system learns from layer-by-layer projections of the retina, so each layer gets its own supervision signal. A multi-scale fusion module then rebuilds vessels at several sizes at once. On a public dataset of five hundred eyes, XOCT improved the translated projections most used in clinical review. Better translation could widen access to vessel imaging on cheaper, common scanners.
arxiv-2509-07555:
Yi Liu and 4 co-authors tackle a failure mode of knowledge editing in language models in a 2025 paper. Knowledge editing updates a model's facts without retraining, often by retrieval-augmented generation, where edited facts are stored and fetched at question time. Such methods handle simple edits well but stumble on multi-hop questions, which chain several facts, because the system skips the relevant edited fact, a problem named edit skipping.

Their method, IRAKE, adds guided decomposition: the question is broken into steps guided by single edited facts and by whole edited cases. That guidance aligns the model's problem-solving granularity with the stored facts, so the right edit is actually used. Experiments show IRAKE reduces edit-skipping failures and beats leading methods on multi-hop question answering after edits. Reliable updating matters as model knowledge ages quickly in a fast-changing world.
arxiv-2509-07655:
Angelos Zacharia and 2 co-authors design collaborative exploration for a marsupial robot team in a 2025 paper. A marsupial team pairs a ground robot that carries an aerial robot, releasing it when flight helps. Exploration of unknown, confined, or large spaces is crucial for such robots, yet communication between them is limited, so shared maps must stay small.

A graph-based path planner guides exploration and deploys the drone where its expected gain clearly beats the ground robot's, such as open halls or spots the ground unit cannot reach. A task-driven map compression strategy shares volumetric maps at chosen resolutions while preserving exploration-critical detail, even at high compression rates. Simulation and real-world experiments validate the approach. Efficient teamwork like this suits search, inspection, and disaster response where bandwidth is scarce.
arxiv-2509-07855:
Quantum simulations of electrons and other fermions may run on shallower circuits thanks to a 2025 paper by D. E. Fisher and 4 co-authors. Mapping fermionic behaviour onto qubits often stretches circuits too deep for today's noisy hardware. The authors add Majorana swap networks, rearrangement patterns that bring interacting particles next to each other inside the computation.

Two compilation strategies cut both circuit depth and the number of two-qubit gates. One cyclic method organises all two-particle interactions using far fewer swaps than a naive approach would need. Shorter circuits lose less information to noise, so variational algorithms that estimate energies of molecules and materials become more practical on near-term quantum machines.
arxiv-2509-08055:
X-rays from the most luminous quasars at cosmic noon are catalogued by C. Degli Agosti and 27 co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper, the twelfth in the WISSH quasar project. The sample holds eighty-five hyper-luminous broad-line objects seen when the universe was a few billion years old. Their nuclear emission reveals how fast their central black holes were feeding.

Spectral analysis covers about half the sample, hardness ratios handle sixteen more, and the rest get estimated intrinsic luminosities, with only eight sources undetected. Relations between X-ray output and other bands are compared against the general active galaxy population. Extreme quasars test whether the same feeding physics scales up, or whether the most luminous objects play by different rules.
arxiv-2509-08255:
Fine-tuning teaches a language model a new task and quietly erases old skills, a failure Wei Huang and 2 co-authors attack with pruning in a 2025 machine learning paper. Their investigation finds a key factor: how much the task vector, the weight change produced by fine-tuning, overlaps the pretrained parameters. Heavy overlap in the wrong places tracks with catastrophic forgetting.

The proposed forgetting-aware pruning metric uses the ratio between task vector and pretrained weights to decide what to prune, balancing new-task performance against retained knowledge. Pruning is usually about shrinking models; here it becomes a memory protection strategy. Organisations fine-tune foundation models constantly, and a cheap guard against forgetting preserves the broad competence they paid to obtain.
arxiv-2509-08555:
Kevin Pack and 2 co-authors benchmark optimization methods for calibrating quantum devices in this 2025 paper. Calibration means tuning a device so it runs as intended. The team works in simulation that mimics real lab conditions.

Algorithms such as Nelder-Mead and CMA-ES, a leading evolution based method, are compared on simple and complex control pulses. Simple pulses have few settings, while complex pulses have many. Across all tests, CMA-ES performs best, and the authors recommend it for automated bring-up and tuning. Labs building quantum hardware gain a clear guide for choosing an optimizer.
arxiv-2509-08655:
The freshwater polyp hydra regrows its whole body plan, and the actin fibers on its skin form patterns with visible defects. Sabyasachi Mukherjee and Anirban Sain model that morphogenesis in a 2025 research paper. Fluorescent imaging has shown nematic-like actin arrangements, with aster-like defects at the head and tentacle tips. Whether those defects actually drive tentacle growth was unclear.

The authors treat the outer tissue as a viscoelastic, growing fluid membrane. Simulations include membrane growth and actin polymerization, the assembly of actin into bundles. One specific head defect, they find, plays no positive role in starting tentacles. Actin reorganization at tentacle bases and tips fits other defect arrangements. The team proposes that active actin polymerization, plus tissue fluidity, helps grow the tubular tentacles. The work links a physical fiber pattern to a classic puzzle in animal development.
arxiv-2509-08955:
Spin glasses remember patterns over time without any spatial order, a paradox first framed fifty years ago. Jingjin Song and 13 co-authors report a way to watch that memory form, in a 2025 research paper. Their probe is resonant magnetic X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy, a technique reading speckle patterns in scattered X-rays. Hidden in that speckle's four-spin correlations is the spin-orientation memory itself.

The team applied the method to a classic copper-manganese alloy above its spin-glass transition. They tracked the critical slowing of spin fluctuations across timescales from seconds to hours. The way the correlation time diverges with temperature follows the same law used for viscous structural glasses. That universality hints at deep kinship between magnetic and ordinary glasses. The method also opens studies of spin ices and quantum spin liquids, where direct memory probes have been missing.
arxiv-2509-09155:
Synthetic speech in Spanish can now be cloned from seconds of audio, while detectors remain trained mostly on English and Chinese. Maria Risques and 3 co-authors introduce HISPASpoof in a 2025 research paper. HISPASpoof is the first large-scale Spanish dataset built to detect synthetic speech and identify its source. It gathers real speech from public corpora across six accents.

Synthetic speech in the dataset comes from six zero-shot text-to-speech systems. The team evaluated five representative detection methods. Detectors trained on English failed to generalize to Spanish. Training on HISPASpoof improved detection substantially. The dataset also supports attribution: identifying which system generated a fake. With Spanish spoken by hundreds of millions, the forensic gap the dataset fills is a global one. It gives researchers a benchmark for building voice security that does not stop at the English-speaking world.
arxiv-2509-09255:
Geonsun Lee and 11 co-authors introduce Sensible Agent, a framework for unobtrusive interaction with proactive AR agents in a 2025 paper. Proactive augmented reality agents offer context aware help, but voice prompts can be disruptive or socially awkward. Delivery style matters as much as content.

The framework adapts both what help to offer and how to deliver it, using real time multimodal sensing. An expert workshop and an annotation study inform the design. Egocentric cameras and large multimodal models infer context and suggest minimally intrusive delivery modes. A prototype on an XR headset is tested in AR and VR. Perceived effort falls versus voice baselines, with high usability.
arxiv-2509-09655:
Sanjay Basu and 6 co-authors present a reinforcement learning method for Medicaid care management in a 2025 health paper. Offline learning must improve decisions from past records without risky live trial and error. Their procedure tunes a separate safety threshold for each protected subgroup, aiming to cut harm while levelling a chosen fairness target, either coverage or harm, across groups.

Records came from a real population health program serving Medicaid members, with identities removed. Rivals included plain imitation of past behaviour and a global conformal safety method. The new approach matched those baselines on estimated value while scoring better on fairness. Uncertainty ranges and subgroup gap tests are reported throughout, supporting a claim of safer, more even decision support.
arxiv-2509-10155:
Andrey Yu. Konyaev, writing alone, completes a classification problem in differential geometry in this 2025 paper. The subject is Nijenhuis operators, mathematical objects that arise in the study of integrable systems. Near certain points, one asks whether such an operator can be put into a simple standard form, a question called linearization.

An earlier paper had settled nearly every two-dimensional case in the analytic setting. One algebra, known as b1,alpha, resisted the general method. Konyaev solves that remaining case here, finishing the two-dimensional problem. Along the way, the work connects to classic results on straightening vector fields and to the maps that track how solutions return after one loop.
arxiv-2509-10255:
Ka-Hou Leong and Avery Meiksin model a glowing ring around the first galaxies in this 2025 astrophysics paper. During cosmic dawn, X-rays from early stellar systems should have warmed the gas between galaxies, mostly evenly. The brightest sources, though, would heat a distinct warm ring around themselves, leaving a readable mark in the 21-centimeter radio signal.

Using a new time-dependent three-dimensional ray-tracing code, the pair follows one star-forming galaxy in a heavy dark-matter halo at redshift twelve. They vary the X-ray spectra, star formation strength, and the galaxy's extended halo. Their verdict: spotting the ring would take a few thousand hours with the SKA1-Low telescope, or about a thousand with SKA2-Low, unless the galaxy is an unusually bright starburst.
arxiv-2509-10455:
Jared Siegel and nine co-authors combine three kinds of observations to show galaxies blowing their gas out more violently than simulations expect, in this 2025 astrophysics paper. Feedback from black holes and stars reshapes where matter sits, but neither simulations nor observations agreed on how strongly. The team joins new kinetic Sunyaev-Zeldovich measurements from DESI and ACT, X-ray gas masses from eROSITA, and lensing-based halo masses.

Across group and cluster halos over much of cosmic history, gas has been expelled beyond several times the halo's characteristic radius more efficiently than most leading simulations predict. The flagship FLAMINGO simulation misses both the X-ray gas fractions and the combined signal badly. Its most extreme variant, with rarer but stronger black-hole outbursts, matches the data, suggesting real feedback is burstier than modelers assumed.
arxiv-2509-11055:
Hyunbae Park and five co-authors published this 2025 astrophysics paper. It asks what tiny clumps of dark matter might do to a faint radio signal from the early universe. The signal comes from hydrogen gas before the first stars lit up. Astronomers call those early times the Dark Ages and Cosmic Dawn.

The team ran computer simulations of how early matter gathered and flowed. They worked out how small-scale clumping changes the signal's average strength across the whole sky. The effect traces matter packed into regions far smaller than a galaxy. That makes the signal a possible new test of what dark matter is. During Cosmic Dawn the effect is harder to pick out. Starlight shapes the signal then as well.
arxiv-2509-11355:
Robin Narsingh Ranabhat and 3 co-authors teach image networks to look at shapes instead of textures in this 2025 paper. Convolutional networks classify images well but break under common corruptions, such as noise and weather effects, that people shrug off. A known cause is their habit of leaning on fine texture rather than the outline of the whole object.

Two training penalties push back. One asks the network's features to agree between a photo and a blurred, low-frequency copy of it, starving texture cues. The other uses supervised contrastive learning to organize features around class-consistent, shape-bearing patterns. On the corrupted CIFAR-10 benchmark, both methods improved robustness while leaving clean accuracy intact, suggesting loss design alone can steer networks toward sturdier vision.
arxiv-2509-11755:
Paul Templier and 3 co-authors let robot controllers grow up in a 2025 paper inspired by animal growth. Animals' bodies change a lot early in life, altering how they move, while robots are often trained under fixed body settings. The authors mimic growth by varying actuator strength over a robot's training lifetime.

Their curriculum, SMOL, varies torque to imitate how power-to-weight ratio shifts during growth and ageing. Placed inside a quality-diversity method that collects many distinct good behaviors, it raised both scores and behavioral diversity across control cases. Agents used helpful early physics to find skills that later served as stepping stones at final body strength. A human-inspired variant modeled nonlinear shifts like puberty, based on human power output studies.
arxiv-2509-11855:
Virgile Mahaut and six co-authors extract fragmentation functions with record precision. This 2025 particle physics paper treats dihadron fragmentation functions. They give the odds that an energetic parton showers into a specific pion pair. Pinning them down sharpens collider predictions and proton spin studies.

Data from the BELLE experiment anchor the analysis. Three upgrades mark it. Perturbative calculations reach next-to-next-to-leading order. Monte Carlo generators only estimate flavor contributions, where data are blind. Two fitting strategies run in parallel. One uses a traditional physics-informed functional form. The other parametrizes the functions with a neural network. The network approach paves the way for more robust, flexible determinations.
arxiv-2509-11955:
Space and time can be treated together, in one block, rather than step by step. Christian Köthe and one co-author take that stance in 2025 for convection-diffusion equations. These equations mix spreading with transport. Trouble starts when transport wins and the solution forms sharp layers.

The authors fold the flow term into a total time derivative. That move lets standard stability and error tools for space-time finite elements carry over. Their least-squares form defines the discrete adjoint. From it they pull local error markers. These markers steer an adaptive mesh. The mesh refines where the solution needs detail. It does not lean on added stabilizing terms. The schemes are always uniquely solvable. Numerical tests back the theory. Even steady cases with unbounded speeds are handled, through a careful choice of function spaces.
arxiv-2509-12355:
Topological order is a deep pattern of long-range entanglement, yet the usual test, entropy scaling, can be fooled by junk contributions. Sergi Mas-Mendoza and three co-authors propose a graphical test in 2025 built on the ZX calculus, a diagram language for quantum processes.

Feed the method a split of a state into two regions, and it returns a contour diagram that shows long-range links only when the state is truly long-range entangled. The toric code and color code pass with different counts of nonlocal nodes, which separates their orders, while trivial states show none. The count survives changes of boundary and ground state mixture.
arxiv-2509-12855:
James Grant, Michael Kunzinger and three co-authors study meeting points along time-like paths in rough space-time in 2025. Smooth space-time has a clear rule for when paths refocus. Rough settings need new forms that still match the smooth case.

Four forms are set out and compared: one-sided, paired, out-of-reach, and final. All agree with the classic form when space is smooth and well behaved. Uses include a time-like form of the Rauch bound. A link to a recent Cartan and Hadamard result is also proved. An added part treats curve distance in full, a tool used all through the work.
arxiv-2509-13055:
Youngkyoung Kim and 5 co-authors automate code generation for semiconductor equipment control in a 2025 paper. Semiconductor manufacturing and testing rely on highly specialized equipment and domain-certain programming languages. The Algorithmic Pattern Generator language is critical for precise hardware control but is hard to program, with low-level syntax and a steep learning curve.

Large language models generate high-level code from natural language well, yet their effectiveness on low-level equipment languages remains limited. The authors propose Progressive Knowledge Enhancement, a multi-stage prompting framework that progressively extracts and activates latent knowledge within a model, guiding it from simple to complex examples without broad fine-tuning. On an industrial dataset, the method greatly outperformed standard prompting and surpassed leading methods in generating correct code, with higher exact match scores.
arxiv-2509-13155:
Augusto Facundes, Thiago Dorini and two co-authors map in 2025 which faces of silver chromate stay stable under real air and heat. The crystal draws interest for light-driven cleaning, but skill hinges on which faces show. Lab vacuum views miss real gas pressure effects.

Quantum calc and heat theory are joined across many faces and caps. Free energy is tracked as oxygen and silver supply shifts. Cluster linkage at the surface proves decisive for stability. Shape builds predict how crystals reshape as settings change. Exposed faces in balance shapes are named. The frame guides face-aware design for this and kin oxides.
arxiv-2509-13255:
Mattia Soldan, Fabian Caba Heilbron and three co-authors encode dense video frames cheaply in 2025 with ResidualViT. Dense tasks like grounding and audio description need many frames. Full feature cost at high frame rates blocks wide use.

Learnable residual links keep frame traits consistent in time. A token cut drops repeat data while reusing a pre-trained base. A light distillation mimics base frame traits at low cost. Four tasks and five sets show cost cuts up to three-fifths and speed gains past twofold. Accuracy stays close to the full base model.
arxiv-2509-13355:
Dietmar Offenhuber examines man-made data and the concept of ground truth in a 2025 paper. Man-made data are used for privacy protection, training data making, or convenient access to quasi-real-life data in any shape or volume. They mimic real-world readings but do not refer to external features of the world.

That lack of a representational relationship does not prevent researchers from using man-made data as training data and as ground truth repositories. It is claimed that unrealistic data can even lead to better model results than real-life data, by compensating for known biases, preventing overfitting, supporting generalization, and improving robustness to outliers. Injecting noisy or implausible data can be beneficial. Ground truth thus becomes a self-referential affair, complicating the usual assumption that representational quality determines data fidelity.
arxiv-2509-13555:
Aiden Harbick and four co-authors model a materials problem in a 2025 superconductivity paper. Hydrides are hydrogen-rich patches that form in niobium cavities used to accelerate particles. Surface hydrides are known to cause Q-disease, a sharp loss of cavity performance. Past work found ways to remove them.

Using time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory, the team extends the picture to hydrides below the surface. They show these hidden hydrides cause the high-field Q-slope. That is a different performance drop at strong fields. Its sudden onset marks a switch from a vortex-free state to one where magnetic vortices penetrate. Controlling hydride size and depth through impurity doping, they argue, can eliminate the effect.
arxiv-2509-13655:
Shi-jing Zha, Suo Qiu, Sagawa, and Xian-Rong Zhou study charge symmetry breaking in a 2025 nuclear physics paper. Mirror hypernuclei are nuclei that swap protons and neutrons. Each also carries one lambda particle. Tiny energy gaps between the mirrors reveal where the strong force treats the two nucleon types differently.

The team models these systems with a deformed Skyrme Hartree-Fock approach. Pairing correlations and an explicit symmetry-breaking term complete the model. Their results match observations across the light mass range studied. Deformation means the nucleus stretches out of a spherical shape. It mattered noticeably for the binding energy gaps in the mass eight and nine mirror pairs. Spherical models would miss that detail.
arxiv-2509-13755:
Zhaoyang Chu and nine co-authors ask whether code language models can be made to forget in a 2025 software security paper. Such models memorize sensitive training data and can repeat confidential code word for word when prompted. Fixes such as deduplication or differential privacy require retraining the whole model, which deployed systems can rarely afford.

The team studies machine unlearning, editing a trained model after the fact. They curated fifty thousand high-risk memorized samples as targets and compared two gradient-ascent unlearning methods. Their variant, CodeEraser, erases only the sensitive segments inside code while protecting the surrounding structure and function. Across three model families it removed targeted memorization effectively and cheaply while keeping the models useful.
arxiv-2509-13855:
Shamsiiat Abdurakhmanova and Alex Jung learn Gaussian mixture models across a network in a 2025 machine learning paper. A mixture model explains data as a blend of bell curves. In distributed settings, each node holds different, scarce data. That data cannot simply be pooled. Privacy is one reason. The local samples also disagree with each other.

Their method uses a given similarity graph between nodes. The graph guides how parameters are shared. Each node leans on neighbors with similar data. Its raw records stay at home. Aggregation stays flexible rather than forcing one global model. In low-sample, mixed regimes, the graph-regularized models beat both central and purely local training. The graph, it turns out, carries real statistical value.
arxiv-2509-14355:
Dawn Lawrie and six co-authors overview the TREC 2024 NeuCLIR track in 2025, a shared test of search across languages. Neural methods may change how well users find news and technical writing written in another language. The track builds the collections to find out.

Collections cover Chinese, Persian and Russian news, plus Chinese academic abstracts. Four task types run from cross language search to multilingual search and report generation. Five teams plus the coordinators submitted several hundred runs across eight tasks. Results and task designs are reported for each type. Shared collections matter because cross language search cannot improve on private data alone. Later teams can rerun the same tests and compare fairly.
arxiv-2509-14555:
The XRISM collaboration, with Marc Audard as lead among one hundred thirty-five authors, reports in 2025 that a super Eddington X-ray binary wind blows slower than expected. Radiation pressure in such systems should unbind disc material at extreme speed. Those winds may feed back on whole galaxies when scaled up.

New high resolution X-ray spectra from the XRISM mission resolve the wind in layered, stratified components. Measured speeds fall short of the extreme values theory predicted for Eddington winds. Kinetic power estimates therefore drop as well. Slower stratified winds change how much energy accretion discs return to their surroundings. The result tempers feedback models that assumed the fastest, most powerful outflow the theory allowed.
arxiv-2509-14655:
Preeti Kumari, P. Muthukumar and Jaydeb Sarkar give a new norm bound in 2025 for composition operators on the Hardy space, a key space of analytic functions. Such an operator plugs one function into another. Littlewood theorem, a classic result, shows the operator is bounded and gives a norm bound.

The trio give a fresh proof of boundedness that leads to a tighter bound. Their bound beats the classic Littlewood bound for these operators. Norm bounds are not mere bookkeeping: they cap how much an operator can boost a function, which sets stability in uses from signal work to control. Even in a textbook space, classic constants can be tightened by a cleaner proof.
arxiv-2509-14755:
Ahmed Sheta and four co-authors use latent diffusion models in 2025 to add training data for spotting smell linked objects in historic artworks. Smell cues, such as flowers, food or pipes, are rich in culture but hard to label. Fine grained classes leave labels sparse and classes badly skewed.

Synthetic images from diffusion models top up the scarce true labels. More than one augmentation plan is tested for detection scores. Adding well picked synthetic data lifted detection in their tests. The large pretraining inside diffusion models lends visual know how that a small heritage set cannot give on its own. Digital humanities gains a hands on recipe: make targeted synthetic cases where archives are too thin to train a detector.
arxiv-2509-14855:
Michael Tatarjitzky and Boaz Rafaely present AmbiDrop, a speech enhancement method that works with any microphone array layout, in a 2025 audio processing paper. Multichannel enhancement uses spatial clues to make speech clearer, but most learned systems are tied to one fixed array shape. Change the layout, and performance often collapses.

AmbiDrop first converts recordings from any array into the Ambisonics format, which describes sound fields with spherical harmonics. A neural network trains on simulated Ambisonics data, with random channel dropout added so it tolerates encoding errors from unfamiliar layouts. On arrays seen in training, it matches a standard baseline. On unseen arrays, the baseline degrades while AmbiDrop keeps improving clarity and quality scores, showing strong generalization for real-world use.
arxiv-2509-15055:
Kieran Wood develops a new formalism for perturbing massive gravity theories around any background spacetime in a solo 2025 gravitation paper. Massive gravity gives the graviton a small mass, and its ghost-free version is notoriously awkward to expand around general backgrounds. Earlier metric-based approaches ran into complications that obscured the theory's healthy structure.

Wood starts from the vielbein formulation, then switches back to metric variables once the expansion is organized. The switch sidesteps many earlier difficulties and makes the ghost-free interaction structure transparent. The method extends naturally to higher perturbation orders and to several interacting metrics. Applied to proportional, cosmological, and black hole backgrounds, it recovers and extends known linear results. As a final demonstration, the cubic multi-gravity potential around a generic background is derived for the first time.
arxiv-2509-15155:
Seyed Kamyar Seyed Ghasemipour and four co-authors let robot foundation models improve themselves through practice in a 2025 robotics paper. Models pre-trained on web-scale data usually reach robot control only through imitation of human demonstrations. Language models gained a second wind from reinforcement learning after pre-training, and the authors borrow that recipe for embodied systems.

Stage one fine-tunes the model with both behavior cloning and a steps-to-go prediction objective, teaching it to estimate how far a task is from done. Stage two turns that estimate into a shaped reward and a success detector. A fleet of robots can then practice downstream tasks autonomously with minimal human supervision, learning from their own attempts. Experiments on real and simulated robots show the two stages together significantly outperform imitation alone.
arxiv-2509-15355:
Salmoli Ghosh and six co-authors review what powers kiloparsec-scale outflows in radio-quiet active galaxies in a 2025 astronomy paper. Radio-quiet nuclei were long thought jetless, yet many show radio emission spanning thousands of light-years. The review synthesizes the team's polarimetric findings on the origin, drivers, and impact of that emission in Seyfert and LINER galaxies.

Multi-band observations with the Very Large Array trace magnetic field geometry and dynamics in the outflows. Low-power jets plow into their surroundings, slowing and disrupting while locally regulating star formation, a feedback channel in supposedly quiet systems. Several radio properties scale with black hole mass just as in radio-loud galaxies, suggesting the two classes differ mainly in jet power. A composite picture emerges, with disk and black hole jointly driving collimated and wide-angle winds.
arxiv-2509-15555:
Rasil Baidar, Sasa Maric, and Robert Abbas build a guard against attacks on connected devices. The spread of smart devices and fast mobile links has widened the surface for floods, malware, and new attacks. Their guard joins three neural parts: one reads local patterns, one reads order over time, and one flags odd items by how poorly it rebuilds them.

Training runs across edge devices, so raw data never leaves each site. On a known test set, the fused model scores near the top on both catching attacks and balanced error checks. It answers in a tiny slice of a second per sample, well inside fast network budgets. The team also weigh how the guard explains itself and handles drift.
arxiv-2509-15855:
David Wolpert and Jan Korbel ask what it means to say a physical system computes. Computers built by humans clearly compute: their parts map cleanly to inputs, outputs, and inner logical steps. Natural systems said to compute, like the brain, were not designed. For them, which parts play those roles is not clear in advance.

The pair first survey many dynamic systems whose computing traits have been studied. They then build a broad frame for naming which computations a given system emulates. Any system able to compute can, in principle, be matched to an abstract machine doing the same work. Their frame makes that matching precise. The paper opens a theory of natural computation.
arxiv-2509-15955:
Zhangqi Jiang leads a team that learns from multi view data when some views are missing. Many data sets describe each item several ways, and gaps are common. Graph based semi supervised methods spread labels along similarity graphs. Missing items were usually flagged and ignored. The team argue ignored items break local clusters, warping the fused graph and hurting accuracy.

Their method fights back with an adversarial fusion scheme that learns a robust shared graph. Stacking all similarity tables into a tensor lets them rebuild the missing structure from high order patterns, using a low rank model. Anchors cut the compute cost. An alternating solver with a reduced gradient method fits the parts. Tests target semi supervised classification with missing views.
arxiv-2509-16155:
New sky surveys hint that dark energy may change over time and may even cross into a strange phantom state. Raphaël Kou and Antony Lewis test a simpler story: one unified dark fluid that acts as both dark matter and dark energy. Their fluid has no sound speed and no uneven stress, yet it matches the same growth history of the universe.

Fits to data from space and ground surveys come close to the standard evolving model, without any phantom part. Growth of cosmic structure also looks much the same. Telling the two stories apart will be hard, even for the next wave of surveys.
arxiv-2509-16355:
A sunflower in set theory is a family of sets that all overlap in exactly the same core. Patrick Bennett and Amanda Priestley study a random process that builds a set family one piece at a time, always picking at random among pieces that would not complete a forbidden sunflower. The question is how large the family grows before it gets stuck.

To answer it, they extend tools from an earlier random process study by Bennett and a co-author. The analysis tracks the random growth with care. Such processes reveal how big a structure can get while dodging a fixed pattern, a theme across combinatorics.
arxiv-2509-16455:
A powerful recipe for writing hard probability laws with matrices gains a clear probabilistic meaning in this study. Davide Gabrielli and Federica Iacovissi show that any law the matrix product recipe can express has an exact match. It is a mixture of product laws. The mixing rule is a Markov bridge, a path pinned at both ends. The enlarged state space makes the two views match.

A constructive method finds the mixture form for any given law. Known laws for driven particle systems drop out as examples. The bridge picture unifies results that were built case by case and may guide new ones.
arxiv-2509-16555:
Shiyin Kuang and co-authors study a sharp change in how electrons spread in a 2025 physics paper. In some disordered materials, states can shift from spread out to trapped in place. The team focus on materials with chiral symmetry and a weak form of topology. They ask what kind of transition these systems show.

They mix lattice simulations with theory that tracks change across scales. Their checks cover a class not fully mapped before. The usual scaling picture does not fit all of their data. Still, theory shows the mark of weak topology in uneven scaling across directions. The work suggests new tests are needed to settle how these phases behave.
arxiv-2509-16655:
Serena Wang and co-authors study pay in bug bounty programs in a 2025 paper. Firms offer cash to outsiders who find and report security flaws. Little was known about how raise sizes shape what gets found. The team analyze data from one of the world's largest programs, run by Google.

After rewards rose, more high-value flaws came in. Skilled hunters supplied much more work in response. The rise both drew new top hunters and pulled veterans back to the program. The split between new and old hunters is traced in detail. Firms can use the findings to set pay that draws real skill.
arxiv-2509-17255:
Thorsten Hellert, Drew Bertwistle, Simon C. Leemann, Antonin Sulc, and Marco Venturini report a first for large science facilities in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their system lets a language model run multi-stage physics experiments on a working particle accelerator. The test bed was the Advanced Light Source, a production synchrotron that serves many research teams.

Given plain-language prompts, the system drafts a plan, fetches past data, resolves control channels, and writes the needed scripts. It then works the machine within strict safety limits and studies the results. On a sample machine-physics task, prep time fell by a huge factor next to hand scripting by an expert. Plan-first design, bounded tool access, and full records make each run open to audit. The authors offer the design as a template for other big facilities.
arxiv-2509-17355:
Ckristian Duran, Nanako Kimura, Zolboo Byambadorj, and Tetsuya Iizuka built a spiking neural chip in a 2025 arXiv paper. Large neural networks cost too much power for small edge devices. Spiking networks promise low power, above all in analog form, but they suffer from noise and weak wiring options.

The team's design is a field-programmable spiking network in CMOS, built for reservoir computing. Each neuron is a leaky integrate-and-fire circuit with its own voltage-controlled oscillator. Weighted links between neurons can be rewired through an on-chip FPGA frame, so the reservoir can take many shapes. The chip ran the FORCE learning rule, memory tests, and a standard time-series task in both simulation and real measurements. It stays compact and uses very little energy per spike, with no analog-to-digital converters needed for readout.
arxiv-2509-17555:
Ohood Aldalbahi and Miryana Grigorova extend a risk integral used in finance and insurance. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies Choquet integrals distorted at random, with respect to a capacity rather than a plain probability. The distortion itself is now random and known only through coarser information, a sub-algebra of events.

The pair establish core traits of these integrals, including comonotonic additivity under stated conditions. They then prove a representation result: conditional risk measures that respect first-order stochastic dominance and add over comonotonic risks are exactly these integrals. When the random distortions are concave, the matching dominance notion becomes the stop-loss order. Examples extend known tools such as Value at Risk and Average Value at Risk. The work gives risk theory a richer, information-aware family of measures.
arxiv-2509-17655:
Jordi Tuneu, Eva Santos, and Peter Filip explain a seasonal puzzle in cosmic muon counts. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that single muons vary with the seasons in a well-understood way, tracking temperature in the upper air. Multi-muon events, though, swing the opposite way, and no past study has explained that reversed rhythm.

Working with the NOvA Near Detector, the team gives the first quantitative account of the phase and size of that variation. They also explain how the effect scales across event multiplicities. Their tool is the FLUKA Monte Carlo code, with a realistic detector model, atmospheric profiles, and underground muon propagation. Results are checked against the latest CORSIKA simulations with modern hadronic models. The findings refresh how seasonal muon flux is modeled and set constraints for experiments that count muons year-round.
arxiv-2509-17755:
Fizza Rubab and six co-authors teach neural fields to integrate, again and again. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies neural representations of repeated antiderivatives taken straight from a function. The idea mirrors summed-area tables, a workhorse of image processing, but those tables live on grids, which shuts them out of continuous neural models.

The team introduces and compares a range of methods for repeated integration, some adapted from prior work and some new. Tests span several input dimensions and integration orders, grading both reconstruction quality and downstream use in filtering and rendering. The results show which designs hold accuracy as integrals stack up. Beyond the scores, the work lets classical cumulative operators move into modern neural systems. It also offers lessons for the broader task of learning operators that involve calculus, not just pointwise maps.
arxiv-2509-17855:
Robert Litschko and 4 co-authors build word lists that show how a dialect spells its words. Their 2025 study uses Bavarian, a German dialect with no fixed spelling rules. Large language models are rarely tested on such local speech, so their skill there is unclear.

A new frame, DiaLemma, builds the lists from plain text in one tongue only. Human checks gave a large set of German-Bavarian word pairs as ground truth. Nine top models were then tested on word sense and form. They did best on nouns and close word pairs, and worst at telling a true match from a bent form.
arxiv-2509-18055:
Yuki Isobe leads a large team that reads the chemical mix of far-off galaxies with the Webb telescope. Their 2025 paper uses a deep survey called JADES, with hundreds of young galaxies from early cosmic time. Stacked light from those galaxies shows the gases that stars had forged by then.

Carbon ran low next to oxygen, while neon sat close to it. The mix points to yields from huge stars that blew up fast. Silicon ran lower than star-based hopes, which hints that much of it sticks to dust grains. Iron and other traits add to the tale of fast early growth.
arxiv-2509-18155:
Aaron Pim and Tristan Pryer build a fast stand-in for proton dose sums in cancer care. Their 2025 paper deals with a clash: exact Monte Carlo dose maths are trusted, but slow. Care plans that must adapt or weigh risk need many dose sums, fast.

Their neural stand-in adds Monte Carlo dropout, which also gives a doubt score per point. Tests move from a one-dim toy case to bone-water setups and a full 3D water case. Doubt splits into model doubt and input doubt, each with its own zone of weight. Speed gains over Monte Carlo were large, with doubt kept in hand.
arxiv-2509-18255:
Subham Dutta Chowdhury and 3 co-authors bound charge flow terms in a simple low-energy transport model. Their 2025 paper works on the Drude-Kadanoff-Martin model, set by three terms: a relax time, a spread rate, and a charge squeeze trait. Sharp bounds tie those terms to the base scales of any lattice model below it.

Their main tool bounds a response function for charge density. At top energies, the model clashes with how lattice spectra fade, so it cannot hold there. At low energies, they bound the mean free path from below. That bound yields a known rule on when a plain Drude peak can form.
arxiv-2509-18955:
Jérôme Taupin and two co-authors improve how independent agents learn to act in games when they cannot talk to each other. In many-agent settings each player sees only its own rewards, so learning must be fully distributed. Perturbation-based methods handle this by letting agents try small random changes and keep what pays. The authors add tweaks drawn from practical observation of how these methods behave.

The changes keep the known convergence guarantees: agents still settle into states that maximize the average reward, and do better when truly optimal states exist. The methods also become robust when random noise is added to the rewards, with similar guarantees. A final idea lets the size of the random changes shrink over time. That mirrors simulated annealing, the classic trick of cooling a search so it settles.
arxiv-2509-19555:
A safety filter keeps a robot or vehicle from drifting into danger, but most filters assume the danger zone is fixed in advance. Sankalp Agrawal and four co-authors let the danger zone change at run time. Their filter works inside a learned world model, where scenes are stored as compact codes. A user-supplied image can define what counts as unsafe, and similarity in code space measures closeness to trouble.

A calibration step sets how near the system may approach that trouble. Training happens inside the world model's imagination, so any seen image can stand in as a test constraint.
