He studies their one dimensional modules, which are the simplest building blocks. The question is which of them appear inside simple finite dimensional modules of the larger algebra.

Meereboer gives a complete classification of those one dimensional modules. He also determines the branching rules, which say how big modules split when viewed through the smaller structure. The main result shows certain projections respect the based structure on both sides. To prove it, he builds a crystal basis theory at a limiting value. The results match the integral forms of canonical bases.
arxiv-2510-17755:
Brenden W. Hamilton and three co-authors test computer methods on a puzzling change in cerium metal. Cerium can collapse in volume while keeping the same crystal structure. Its electrons shift between local and shared states during the change. Two rival stories, named Mott and Kondo, explain that shift differently.

The team compared many density functional methods at three levels of theory. Density functional methods approximate electron behavior to predict material properties. They squeezed the metal in simulations across the phase boundary at zero temperature. Methods that matched experiments best were checked for their predicted mechanism. The comparison shows how method choices shape the physical story.
arxiv-2510-17955:
Ilay Kamai and three co-authors explain how gas giant planets can form close to a star in a double-star system. Giants are usually thought to need the zone past the water snow line to build cores fast. In tight binaries, the partner star also cuts off stable orbits, which can rule that zone out.

The team scans a large catalog of binary systems and picks out giants in that awkward spot. They compare metal content and orbit shapes, model how snow lines move, and fit planet positions against the tidal cutoff. Their channel accounts for where such giants sit and predicts more cases.
arxiv-2510-18455:
Liyang He and his four co-authors build a framework for testing retrieval-augmented generation systems inside online games. Such systems answer questions by first looking up source material, but games change constantly: content updates arrive, and player interests shift with them. No standard benchmark captured both kinds of change, and any automatic benchmark still needs questions that feel like real player questions.

Their framework, ChronoPlay, tracks the two moving parts with a dual update mechanism. Its question engine draws on official sources for factual accuracy and on player community material for authentic wording. Applying the framework to three different games produced the first changing benchmark of its kind for gaming. The results show how retrieval systems cope when both the game world and its audience keep moving under them.
arxiv-2510-18555:
Felix Auer and his four co-authors tackle a shortcut used in planning energy systems. Full year-long simulations are too heavy, so planners compress time into a few representative periods. That compression breaks the order between periods, which distorts anything that carries over time, such as stored energy or machines that must stay on once started.

Their fix uses a Markov transition matrix, a table of probabilities for moving from one representative period to the next, to reconnect the periods through expected values. Unlike earlier matrix methods, theirs adds no new variables or constraints; it simply rewrites the rules at period boundaries, and it can handle linked time steps and on-off decisions. On a standard reliability test system, the method cut the typical operational error sharply when period transitions were not near-diagonal, at almost no extra computing cost.
arxiv-2510-18755:
Valentina Casarino, Paolo Ciatti, and Peter Sjögren prove a delicate endpoint result. The field is harmonic analysis. They work with the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. It is a family of smoothing operators tied to Gaussian noise. The setting is nonsymmetric. The natural measure does not double nicely there. The quantity at stake counts jumps. It tracks how often smoothed versions of a function jump as scale varies.

The authors show the jump measure defines a weak type one-one operator. The order is two, and the invariant measure is used. The result refines their own earlier work at the endpoint. For the related variation measure, the claim held above order two. It failed exactly at order two. The jump version survives at that point. It is a rare such result for a nonsymmetric semigroup. The space there is nondoubling.
arxiv-2510-18955:
Jiaru Li, Christopher E O'Connor, and Frederic A Rasio test whether flybys of planetesimals can break the resonant chains seen in young exoplanet systems. Many compact systems seem to form locked in mean-motion resonances, then break out of that neat pattern over roughly one hundred million years.

With body simulations and analytic estimates, the authors track how passing planetesimals from a distant store disturb those chains. A store with enough total mass can do the job, and the disrupted systems often go unstable to close encounters later. The scenario gives one concrete route from ordered chains to messy systems.
arxiv-2510-19055:
Brandon James Carone and two co-authors introduce MUSE, a benchmark that tests music perception and relational reasoning in audio language models. Current evaluations can hide basic weaknesses, since a model may name instruments yet fail to hear how musical parts relate to each other.

Ten tasks probe core listening skills in four leading models, compared against a human baseline of two hundred people. One model handles basic perception well, while others score near chance, and step-by-step prompting helps inconsistently. The wide gap with human experts shows how far machine listening still has to go.
arxiv-2510-19255:
Mingrui Zhao and seven co-authors survey four-dimensional content. Such content is three-dimensional geometry that moves over time. It can also interact. Neural fields and motion learning have sped the field up fast. Three-dimensional generative tools helped too. The right representation decides what a system can capture.

The survey does not list every paper. It picks representative works instead. Each choice shows a strength and a challenge. Data and application conditions shape both. Readers get a map of trade-offs. The map serves builders of dynamic scenes in graphics and vision.
arxiv-2510-19555:
Simone Alghisi and four co-authors take apart why vision-language models fail at counting objects in images. Rather than only reporting benchmark scores, they probe seven leading models under controlled conditions. The models prove sensitive to how many objects appear, what type they are, how they are arranged, and whether distractors are present.

A layer-by-layer analysis locates many errors in the final step, where the last layer's representation is mapped into the output. Retraining only that output layer lifted counting accuracy by up to twenty-one percent. The same fix brought consistent gains on real-world datasets, suggesting a cheap, targeted repair for a common weakness of these models.
arxiv-2510-19855:
Manish Kumar presents two quantum algorithms for nonlinear reaction-diffusion equations, the kind that describe how substances spread and react. Both rest on cut-off Chebyshev polynomial fits, applied to the linearized problem. The first uses matrix powers. The second repurposes the quantum spectral method.

The main step is to derive when the Carleman embedding matrix can be diagonalized. That matrix encodes the nonlinearity, so the step is vital for both algorithms. A stepwise routine does the job. The second algorithm's gate cost compares well with the best known method for this problem. Kumar is candid about two gaps: no bound yet on a key Carleman matrix quantity, and one step that rests on a conjecture about a trig equation. He offers workarounds for most practical cases.
arxiv-2510-19955:
Márcus Vinícius Lobo Costa and four co-authors test how well vision transformers, trained with contrast-based objectives, learn features of 3D shapes from many 2D views. Recognizing 3D objects from images usually demands wide labeled data. Convolutional networks can miss global shape relationships. The study pairs state-of-the-art backbones with supervised and self-supervised contrastive losses.

On downstream multi-view tasks, the transformer-plus-contrastive pairing performed strongly. A supervised contrast-based model reached about ninety-one percent accuracy on the ModelNet10 benchmark. The authors credit the transformer's grasp of overall shape. Contrastive training then refines that grasp into sharper local distinctions. Because the work is empirical, it rests on wide evaluation rather than theory to make its case.
arxiv-2510-20155:
Penghao Wang and six co-authors introduce PartNeXt, a dataset for understanding three-dimensional objects through their parts. Knowing an object parts supports work in vision, graphics, and robotics, but the older PartNet dataset relies on untextured shapes and expert labeling that is hard to scale. PartNeXt contains over twenty-three thousand high-quality textured models with fine-grained, hierarchical part labels across fifty categories.

Benchmarks on the dataset cover class-agnostic part segmentation and a new task of part-centered question answering for 3D language models. Leading segmentation methods still struggle with fine and leaf-level parts, and the question task exposes wide gaps in open-vocabulary part grounding. Training one model on PartNeXt instead of PartNet brings substantial gains.
arxiv-2510-20355:
Daniel Grieser and Jørgen Olsen Lye analyze geodesics that pass through a thin neck on a family of surfaces that degenerates toward a cuspidal singularity. Two classes of paths cross the waist where the neck is thinnest: those hitting it almost vertically and those hitting it at a clearly oblique angle. Each class behaves in a striking and different way as the neck shrinks.

Nearly vertical geodesics show a surprising focusing effect, with certain exit directions preferred for a generic limiting singularity. Oblique geodesics instead wind around the neck more and more as the parameter tends to zero, and the authors give a precise quantitative description of that winding. Numerical solutions illustrate both effects, and the proof uses a two-scale blow-up analysis.
arxiv-2510-20655:
Manuel Palma Banos, Joel D Kress, Rigoberto Hernandez, and Galen T Craven offer a data driven way to recover the hidden reaction steps behind a set of changing chemical amounts over time. Knowing the steps and their rates is a core need in chemistry, yet complex networks make the steps hard to guess from data alone.

Their method, called SISR, searches a space of possible reaction schemes guided by the rule that atoms must balance in each step. It pairs a smooth search over rates with a genetic search over scheme forms to find a compact fit. On test networks, both simple and tangled, the method recovers the true steps and rates well, even when the data carry noise.
arxiv-2510-20955:
Jeff Pflueger and one co-author approximate safety feedback for mobile robots without a safety oracle, using model predictive control inside a simulator. Safe control methods usually assume direct safety checks or hand labeled safety data, both costly and often inaccurate.

Modern simulators capture complex interactions and carry implicit safety limits that are hard to write down by hand. By rolling out candidate actions in simulation and scoring the outcomes, the method builds a stand in safety function. Robots can then screen actions before acting in the real world, a useful route when explicit constraints resist modeling.
arxiv-2510-21155:
Dandan Liang and five co-authors tackle slow workers, called stragglers, in split federated learning, where training is shared between edge devices and a central server. The server normally must wait for fresh outputs from clients, so one slow device can hold up the whole round of training.

Their method, named MU-SplitFed, lets the server keep updating on its own for several steps during each client round, loosening the strict wait. They work in a zeroth-order setting, which avoids computing gradients directly, and they prove a convergence rate that improves as the number of extra server steps grows. Experiments show steadier performance than standard methods when stragglers are present.
arxiv-2510-21355:
Mukul Dwivedi and Andreas Rupp build a numerical method for a fractional wave equation. The equation models waves in plasmas and shallow water. It generalizes a classic model by swapping its smoothing term for a fractional version. A dial in the equation covers several regimes. One setting gives the classic case, and another gives a Benjamin-Ono type case.

Their scheme uses a Fourier spectral method in space. A special time stepper handles the stiff wave part exactly. The domain is flat and wraps around at the edges. The authors prove that the space scheme preserves discrete versions of mass, momentum, and energy. They also show the approximations converge to the single true strong solution. Error bounds are sharp in space and fourth order in time. Computer tests confirm the accuracy and the conservation behavior.
arxiv-2510-21455:
Jorge Díez and four co-authors propose explaining a recommender system's picks by predicting the photo a user herself would take of the item. On travel and review sites, users post pictures alongside ratings, and the authors treat those pictures as arguments: the shot a person chooses shows what she valued about the place.

They build a formal framework that estimates the chance a given user would have taken a given photo of a given item. A recommender armed with that model can justify a suggestion by showing the user the view she would likely have captured, which should raise trust. Companies also gain a picture of which product features customers highlight. Restaurant reviews with photos from six cities of different sizes, drawn from TripAdvisor, illustrate the approach.
arxiv-2510-21655:
Michał Czakon, Kilian Erhard Minguez, and Felix Eschment supply the final missing piece for approximating quantum chromodynamics amplitudes when one gluon carries almost no energy. In that soft limit, amplitudes simplify dramatically. Precision calculations with heavy quarks need more than the leading behavior. They also need the first correction suppressed by the gluon's small energy.

Their main result is a soft operator acting on the color and spin data of the hard particles. It produces the correction while keeping every particle on its mass shell. It also conserves momentum exactly. The authors give a complete formula for the subleading term in a second limit. There, a light quark and antiquark fly out nearly parallel. The one-loop soft approximation requires that limit. Curiously, the collinear answer runs through a high-energy limit, tying two corners of scattering theory together.
arxiv-2510-21755:
Virgile Troude and Didier Sornette find a new engine for the heavy tails and power laws that haunt physics, biology, and social systems. The classic explanation, Kesten processes, multiplies a quantity by random factors and adds noise, producing power laws when growth briefly turns supercritical and excursions run away before fading.

In several dimensions, they uncover a different lever: the eigenvectors of random non-normal matrices lean on each other instead of standing perpendicular, and that leaning amplifies fluctuations at every step. The amplification effectively raises the growth exponent and fattens the tail, and it strengthens with dimension until it dominates the classic mechanism. Polymer chains stretching in turbulent flow, where velocity gradients intermittently yank molecules long, illustrate the effect in a real system.
arxiv-2510-21955:
Ranadeep Roy and Yuan-Ming Lu map a quantum spin Hall insulator under disorder. Such a material conducts along its edges while its interior stays insulating. The team asks what happens when its neat crystal order is scrambled into an amorphous tangle. Topological phases were once thought to need tidy lattices. Recent work has questioned that view.

Roy and Lu use a standard model of the effect. They chart the phase diagram as disorder and a mass setting vary. A real-space recipe supplies the topological marker. Disorder can kill the topological phase. It can also create one from a plain phase. Strangest of all, it can do both in sequence. A topological state fades under weak disorder, then returns as disorder grows. Edge-state reasoning and transport calculations back the map. The work widens where engineers might hunt for robust quantum materials.
arxiv-2510-22055:
V Venktesh, Deepali Prabhu, and Avishek Anand build a testbed for checking numerical claims in the wild. Numbers lend a fake air of authority. False claims dressed in figures can do outsized harm, yet automatic fact-checkers have mostly practiced on tidy, artificial examples rather than the messy figures people actually share.

A human checker first splits a claim into its numerical pieces, gathers evidence for each. Only then rules, and the benchmark is designed to force machines through the same honest search. Earlier collections leaned on rough automated splitting and weak web search, which gathered off-target evidence and let future information leak into the past. The new benchmark aims for a realistic retrieval setting, so systems trained on it practice the evidence gathering that real verification demands.
arxiv-2510-22155:
Hindy Drillick and Shalin Parekh follow a random walker lost in a landscape that itself keeps changing randomly over time. In such space-time random media, the walker's likely position after a long run spreads in a bell curve near the center. The interesting question is how far out into the tail that Gaussian calm survives before the randomness of the environment takes over.

Working in every spatial dimension, the pair identifies a critical wandering radius up to which the rescaled fluctuations stay Gaussian under the frozen view of one environment. That radius grows almost linearly with time in dimension one, nearly linearly with a logarithmic discount in dimension two, and flatly linearly in dimension three and above. Centering the observation window away from the start is allowed, which recovers older results at the origin as a special case and extends them into the far tail.
arxiv-2510-22355:
J Abuhlail and co-author A Alfaraj study weak separation rules for a special kind of lattice equipped with a Zariski like topology. Such spaces meet the weakest separation rule but sit far from the Hausdorff rule, so finer grades matter. The pair ask when these lattices meet several grades between those poles.

They give picture based tests for each grade and supply families of examples and counterexamples. Their main use is for spectra built from prime, maximal, and minimal ideals of commutative rings and semirings. The results sort out which weak separation grades those spectra can reach.
arxiv-2510-22455:
Brandon James Carone and two co-authors test whether large multimodal models truly hear music or mostly read symbols. Claims of musical understanding often mix listening with score reading, so the team separates the two. They benchmark three leading models on syncopation scoring, transposition detection, and chord quality, using both audio and MIDI inputs.

Models scored near perfect on MIDI but dropped sharply on audio, and extra examples or step by step reasoning helped little. One model, Gemini Pro, led in most settings, while a logic aided method stayed fragile on sound. The work maps a clear gap between reading music and listening to it.
arxiv-2510-22755:
Rotating dense matter may force certain mesons into a shared state. Mesons are particles made of a quark pair. Kshitish Kumar Pradhan, Dushmanta Sahu, and Raghunath Sahoo study rho mesons in 2025. Their setting is hot, dense hadronic matter in rotation. Such matter appears in heavy ion collisions.

When the meson chemical potential nears its mass, condensation can occur. Condensation means many particles share one state. Rotation couples to the meson spin. That coupling aligns the shared state along the spin axis. The result is a distinct polarization pattern. The authors suggest rapidly spinning neutron stars may host this phase.
arxiv-2510-23055:
Manjeshwar Aniruddh Mallya, Alessio Ferrari, Mohammad Amin Zadenoori, and Jacek Dabrowski evaluate large language models for turning online user feedback into software requirements. App reviews hold useful signals, but volume and noise make manual review hard. Models promise to classify feedback and even draft formal requirements, yet solid evidence for those uses is still thin.

The authors test models on classification and specification tasks with thorough, replicable checks. Their study weighs where models beat older techniques and where they still falter. Software teams get grounded guidance on automating feedback review without trusting model output blindly.
arxiv-2510-23255:
Yuto Nakajima and Takayuki Watanabe study the shape of limit sets formed by iterated function systems whose maps change at each step. When rules shift, even at random, the limit shape is poorly known next to the fixed case of Mandelbrot and Hata.

The authors build a framework based on simplices and homology that makes the shape of such limit sets open to strict proof. They then apply the abstract theory to concrete randomly generated systems. Knowing these shapes extends fractal geometry to the more realistic setting where rules vary over time.
arxiv-2510-23455:
Khoa Nguyen and five co-authors propose SGFusion, a federated learning algorithm that uses the geography of mobile users. Devices are mapped onto geographical zones, and one model is trained per zone, adapting to local data and behavior. Zones are not independent, though: nearby users often behave alike.

The authors model correlations among zones as a hierarchical random graph fitted by Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. At each step, a zone fuses its gradient with gradients from related zones. Geography-aware fusion should beat both one global model and isolated local models for mobile services.
arxiv-2510-23555:
João C. G. Henriques and four co-authors explore tiny magnetic chains built from nanographenes, carbon flakes only a few atoms wide. These flakes carry spin, and linking them in a row lets physicists replay famous one-dimensional magnetism models with unusual control. Earlier work used related flakes to realize the Haldane phase, a landmark state of spin-1 chains.

The team studies chains where the links alternate in strength, using a simulation method called the density matrix renormalization group. They map where the Haldane phase ends and a dimerized phase begins, including a new edge state carrying spin one. Two real materials stand out as candidates: an extended Clar's goblet molecule and a passivated four-unit triangulene. The authors also show how a tunneling spectroscopy test could tell the two phases apart in the lab.
arxiv-2510-23655:
Anahita Eslami-Rad and two co-authors build the basic geometry of profinite diffeological spaces. Such a space gets its smooth structure by pulling back from manifolds of finite size through a system of projection maps. The class is wide: it covers limits of manifolds, solution sets of differential relations, and spaces matched by tube-like approximations.

On these spaces the authors set up tangent and cotangent spaces, forms, metrics of Riemannian type, and connections. They then add operators, Laplacians, symplectic forms, and momentum maps, and they compare the de Rham and singular versions of cohomology. Parts of this toolkit existed before, scattered across separate settings and half-built. By joining them into one account, the study gives workers a single frame for doing geometry on these limit spaces.
arxiv-2510-23755:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports a measurement of Higgs boson production together with a top quark pair, using multilepton events at the Large Hadron Collider. The data cover proton-proton collisions at thirteen trillion electronvolts, totaling an integrated luminosity of 140 inverse femtobarns. Six final states, sorted by the number and flavor of charged leptons, are fitted together to pull out the rare signal and pin down backgrounds.

The measured rate comes out at about sixty-three percent of the Standard Model prediction, with an observed significance of 3.3 sigma against an expected 5.3 sigma. The team also measures the rate in slices of the Higgs boson's transverse momentum and extracts joint results with single-top-plus-Higgs production. A further analysis probes whether the top-Higgs coupling mixes CP-even and CP-odd parts. The results fit the Standard Model picture, and large mixing angles are ruled out at the stated confidence level.
arxiv-2510-23855:
Carmine Autieri and a co-author work out how spin-momentum locking changes in altermagnets once relativity enters through spin-orbit coupling. In the simpler non-relativistic picture, an altermagnet's spin direction is tied to the electron's momentum in a fixed pattern. Spin-orbit coupling adds antisymmetric exchange, which cants the spins, so the three spin components lock in different ways.

The authors call the result relativistic spin-momentum locking and compute it for two materials. In orthorhombic YVO3 it mixes s-wave and two d-wave parts. In hexagonal MnTe the dominant component starts as a bulk g-wave. The Néel vector breaks a sixfold symmetry and demotes it to d-wave, joined by other d and s parts. Though the canted components are tiny in real space, they carry notable weight in momentum space. That weight feeds measurable properties such as the spin-Hall conductivity.
arxiv-2510-24455:
Nikola Bogdanovic and two co-authors investigate how ideals in a polynomial ring factor into atoms under ideal multiplication. They study the monoid of nonzero ideals of a multivariate polynomial ring, building on recent advances in factorization theory for unit cancellative monoids. Extending techniques from a 2022 paper by Geroldinger and Khadam, they construct new families of atoms in this ideal monoid.

The authors also analyze the submonoid of nonzero monomial ideals, deriving its arithmetic properties and computing sets of lengths for specific classes of ideals. Sets of lengths record the possible numbers of factors in a factorization, a central measure in factorization theory. The results deepen the study of ideal monoids in classical algebra.
arxiv-2510-24555:
Dinesh Kumar Keshari and two co-authors study a domain in complex space tied to the structured singular value, a tool for judging robustness of feedback control systems. The domain, associated with three by three matrices, lives in seven dimensional complex space, with a five dimensional sibling also considered. The authors characterize the main domain and its closure using realization formulas.

Neither the domain nor its closure is circular or convex, yet both are simply connected, and the closure is shown to be polynomially and linearly convex by a new proof. The team also establishes necessary conditions for a Schwarz lemma on these synthesis domains, a step toward function theory for control relevant domains.
arxiv-2510-24755:
Baptiste Chevalier, Shimpei Yamaguchi, Wojciech Roga, and Masahiro Takeoka give a new Monte Carlo way to solve hard pick tasks. Such tasks pick the best mix from many picks, and the score rule may be a black box. Their way probes the score rule at random points to gauge its broad traits.

A greedy step, borrowed from sparse sense work, then builds the best pick from those traits. The trick is to fit the broad traits with no over fit to the probes. In code tests, the method held its own next to a known heat based search. Math in the work backs why it can work, and its dials can be set to the compute at hand.
arxiv-2510-25055:
Nourah M Salem, Elizabeth White, Michael Bada, and Lawrence Hunter test if chat models can spot gaps in what health science knows, from the texts of the field. A gap may be stated in plain words, or it may just be implied by what a work leaves out. Past work most oft caught the plain kind.

Their tests span near fifteen hundred texts in four sets, with both closed and open models, at part and whole text scales. For the implied kind, they add a scheme that builds a case in steps and sorts would be gaps into bins for a check. Finds are used to show where models do well and where they fail. Gap reads can steer new work.
arxiv-2510-25155:
Yatao Zhang, Ye Hong, Song Gao, and Martin Raubal map how town systems and traffic shape each other, in both ways, across thirty towns on six land masses. How towns grow and how folks move are tied in loops, yet cause in both ways at once is hard to pull from mere links. Their frame joins two tools to get at it.

One tool weights town reads by space and time; the other traces how one run can foretell the other when crossed. Town form and use swayed traffic more than town make up did, though make up linked more tight. In most towns, the town to traffic sway beat the back sway. Long run back sway still showed.
arxiv-2510-25455:
Alexey Petukhov verifies a countable separation property for associative algebras. His 2025 mathematics paper starts with a specific algebra case. The algebra has a simple module with trivial endomorphisms. That module also has a trivial annihilator there. He proves a list of nonzero elements exists. Every two-sided ideal contains at least one listed element.

Based on that result, he treats free associative algebras. Those algebras may have finite or countable generator sets. The field underneath can be any field whatsoever. The countable separation property was studied by Dixmier earlier. Prior work focused only on Noetherian algebras, however. Free associative algebras are far from Noetherian in structure. That distance makes the new result more striking. It extends separation ideas to a wilder algebra class. Readers in ring theory may value the extension. The proof connects module conditions to ideal structure.
arxiv-2510-25955:
Xiaoyu Yang leads seven co-authors in a self supervised framework that learns both speech and general audio in one model. Self supervised learning trains on raw data without labels, using parts of the signal as targets. Most prior models specialize in either speech or sound events, which leaves a gap between the two domains.

Their system, SPEAR, distills knowledge from a speech focused teacher and a general audio teacher into one student model. Continuous teacher outputs are turned into discrete tokens through multi codebook quantization, which splits the code into several parts. The student predicts both token sets from masked input, with a token mixing step for complex scenes. Results set a new best on the SUPERB speech benchmark in their tests.
arxiv-2510-26355:
Guo-Hong Du, with five co-authors, measures two key numbers for the late universe without leaning on the standard model of cosmology. One number is the Hubble constant, the present rate at which space expands. The other is a curvature value that tells whether space is flat. Both are disputed, since different data sets give answers that do not quite agree.

Du and the team use an inverse distance ladder, a chain of distance measures built from strong lensing, old stars, gamma ray bursts, and new survey data. Their best mix gives an expansion rate near seventy-two, close to local measures, and a curvature near zero. That points to a flat universe, and it eases the long clash over the expansion rate.
arxiv-2510-26455:
Szabolcs Borsányi, with six co-authors, maps how quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force, changes with density. Drawing that map at high density is hard because lattice simulations hit a complex action problem. The team works at imaginary values of a key density measure, where simulations still run, and watches strangeness, a trait tied to strange quarks.

Borsányi and the team find that at the chiral transition, the point where quark behaviour shifts, two strangeness measures stay constant as density varies, if a neutrality condition holds. They use those constants as stand-ins for the transition line and extend them to real density with high-order expansions. Results reach a density measure of four hundred mega-electronvolts and match both known transition results and a gas model of hadrons. Beyond five hundred, the line starts to part from the freeze-out line, as expected.
arxiv-2510-26955:
Joshua Pughe-Sanford leads six co-authors in a theory of how sense neurons sort a changing world. The group treats incoming signals as paths from a noisy, high-dimensional system. Each neuron, they argue, learns coherent sets, meaning groups of states whose paths stay close together for a short time, and then tags new inputs by group.

Math based on the stochastic Koopman operator, a tool that tracks how patterns evolve, shows how a neuron could do this job. For a standard noisy process, the key pattern reduces to a single weighted sum a neuron can compute. Some neurons would flag shared futures, others shared pasts. The scheme also offers a fresh account of why neural responses often cut off negative values.
arxiv-2510-27055:
Michal Zawalski, Meriem Boubdir, Klaudia Balazy, Besmira Nushi, and Pablo Ribalta offer a practical test for whether a dataset leaked into a language model training set. Such contamination inflates benchmark scores and hides true skill, yet training corpora are often secret. Their method, CoDeC, watches how in-context examples, meaning sample items placed in the prompt, change model confidence.

For unseen data, examples usually raise confidence, but for memorized data they can lower it by disrupting recalled patterns. Scores from this contrast separate seen and unseen datasets cleanly in experiments. Tests also find strong signs of memorization in open-weight models with undisclosed training data. The method is automated and works across models and datasets, easing routine benchmark checks.
arxiv-2510-27355:
Zijian Wang and Chang Xu give language models a smarter way to shop among their own thoughts, in a 2025 paper. A model can branch its reasoning into a tree of paths, then pick the best ending. Blind branching wastes effort on weak paths. Their framework, ThoughtProbe, scores each branch early using the model's inner signals.

A small classifier reads those hidden signals and ranks the branches. Compute goes to the high scorers first. When the tree is done, all branch answers form a pool. A pooling step then weighs each answer by the scores of the branches behind it. The best-backed answer wins. On several arithmetic reasoning tests, the method found and picked good paths far more often than plain search.
arxiv-2510-27455:
Prosenjit Roy and Itai Shafrir study waves on domains that stretch to infinity in this 2025 paper. The domains are cylindrical: bounded across, endless along several directions. On them sit elliptic operators, equations for spread and vibration, with mixed boundary rules, part fixed and part free. The question is what happens to the eigenvalues, the natural tones, as the domain grows.

They show the tones settle toward a pattern set by simpler problems. Those simpler problems live on a domain endless in just one direction. The eigenfunctions, the shapes of the tones, settle in a matching way. The work continues an earlier study in the same line. It gives a clean way to predict tones for long tubes and channels from one-direction models.
arxiv-2510-27555:
Redouane Douaifia, Salem Abdelmalek, and Mokhtar Kirane study math models of three linked substances that spread and react over time in 2025. Such models are called reaction-diffusion systems, where spread and chemical change act at once. The team adds a rule that caps total mass and a new sum rule that links the three parts.

Under those rules, the team proves that smooth solutions exist for all time in any space size. The proof holds for a wide range of edge rules, even when growth terms are strong. With a bit more assumed, values stay bounded over time. A test case with three species that prey and compete shows the method at work.
arxiv-2511-00055:
Leonhard Duda, Khadijeh Alibabaei, and Elena Vollmer compare centralized and federated learning for segmenting thermal urban traits in drone imagery. Federated learning trains a shared model across participants who keep their data local, bypassing privacy and technical barriers to central storage. Their real-world scenario uses unmanned aerial vehicle thermal images, where cities' heat traits are the target.

Practical implementation and effectiveness of the federated route are measured against the centralized baseline. Remote sensing readers get evidence on whether privacy-preserving training costs accuracy in this setting. Thermal splitting supports urban heat studies, so a workable federated option could unlock data owners otherwise cannot share.
arxiv-2511-00155:
Sascha Desmettre, Devika Khurana, and Amira Meddah develop a hybrid exact scheme for simulating first-passage times of jump-diffusion processes with time-dependent thresholds. First-passage time, when a process first hits a barrier, is central in finance and risk modeling. Exact simulation exists for constant thresholds, applying exact diffusion simulation between jumps, and an adaptation to moving thresholds was proposed in a more general setting.

They show that adaptation applies to jump-diffusion models by establishing a formal correspondence. Probability and finance readers get exact, bias-free simulation where thresholds move, as with time-varying barriers in options or default models. Moving thresholds are realistic, and exactness avoids discretization error.
arxiv-2511-00255:
Biologists sort beetles by laying them on trays and photographing each tray, which leaves thousands of images to process by hand. Fangxun Liu and a large team built BeetleFlow, a three-stage pipeline that handles the pile automatically. Stage one finds each beetle on a tray, stage two sorts and crops each insect, and stage three outlines body parts in fine detail.

Detection pairs a transformer-based finder with a vision-language model in repeated rounds. For the outlining stage, the team hand-labeled hundreds of beetle images and tuned two segmentation models. The pipeline turns a slow manual chore into a fast step that can speed up ecology research.
arxiv-2511-00555:
Dianye Huang, Nassir Navab, and Zhongliang Jiang help robot policies recover when a task starts going wrong. Diffusion policies with action chunking are strong at imitation learning for manipulation, but they can overfit to proprioceptive cues, the robot's own joint signals, at the expense of vision. When an early step fails, say a missed grasp on a drawer handle, the policy may have no way back.

Their dual-branch design separates the senses. A visual branch tracks task progress, while a fused branch merges vision and proprioception for precise motion. If an intermediate goal fails, control switches to visual-branch action chunks that return the robot to a known state for another try. A deep Koopman module strengthens temporal structure in the visual stream, and test-time loss signals guide chunk blending. Gains appear in both simulated and real tasks.
arxiv-2511-00755:
Volodymyr Kuznietsov and four co-authors simulate particle number fluctuations near a phase transition critical point, hunting signals that heavy-ion collision experiments chase. Their tool is particle dynamics of a classic Lennard-Jones fluid in its crossover region. They extend earlier work to third- and fourth-order cumulants, statistics that capture skew and sharpness of fluctuations, in both position and momentum acceptance, plus integrated correlations.

Near the critical point, the higher cumulants settle as fast as second-order ones but suffer stronger finite-size effects. Interactions push cumulants far from the ideal-gas base case, and kurtosis turns strongly negative on the crossover side. A proton-identification efficiency cut, like the one real experiments apply, dilutes that strong signal sharply. The study sets expectations for the RHIC beam energy scan program.
arxiv-2511-01455:
Fausto Colantoni and Mirko D'Ovidio study a variant of Brownian motion, the random wandering used to model particles and prices alike. In their version, called elastic Brownian motion, the moving point is not stopped when it reaches the edge of its region. Instead, it restarts from a random position inside the region and keeps going.

The authors pin down the process in three ways: through its stochastic differential equation, its generator, and a direct description of its paths. They also work out the long-run probability distribution and a spectral representation. The final section turns to harmonic functions on the upper half-space to study the trace process left at the boundary.
arxiv-2511-01555:
Nathan LeRoy and six colleagues built software tooling for a data-format problem in genomics. Experiments in epigenomics produce sets of genomic intervals. These are stretches of DNA flagged by a measurement. But every dataset defines its own regions. That clashes with machine learning methods that need a fixed vocabulary of tokens, the way language models use tokens for words.

Their library, gtars-tokenizers, maps any interval set onto a predefined universe of regions, tokenizing a genome the way text is tokenized. Written in Rust with bindings for Python, R, the command line, and WebAssembly, it offers two overlap algorithms and plugs into Hugging Face-style workflows for PyTorch and TensorFlow. Benchmarks put it at top efficiency on large datasets, removing hand-rolled preprocessing.
arxiv-2511-01755:
Rong Li and nine colleagues release 3EED, a benchmark for finding objects described in words inside three-dimensional scenes, the skill an embodied agent needs to act on instructions in the open world. Existing benchmarks were mostly indoor, single-platform, and small; 3EED spans vehicles, drones, and quadruped robots outdoors, with camera and LiDAR data.

The dataset holds over 128,000 objects and 22,000 human-validated referring expressions across diverse outdoor scenes, roughly ten times larger than its predecessors. A scalable annotation pipeline pairs vision-language model prompting with human verification. The authors add platform-aware normalization and cross-modal alignment methods, and set protocols for in-domain and cross-platform testing. Results expose significant performance gaps between platforms, marking generalizable 3D grounding as an open problem the benchmark is meant to drive.
arxiv-2511-02055:
Sameer Wagh and ten co-authors propose a new way to organise the market for AI training data. Today's data economy, they argue, concentrates power because data is extracted without control, privacy, or fair payment. Their system, Private Map-Secure Reduce, extends the classic MapReduce computing pattern to a decentralised network where computation travels to the data instead of the other way round.

Cryptographic checks are meant to guarantee privacy, support price discovery, and align incentives between data holders and model builders. The team demonstrates recommender system audits, an ensemble of six language models reaching strong accuracy on a broad knowledge test, and analytics spread over hundreds of nodes. They present the design as infrastructure for a fairer data economy.
arxiv-2511-02155:
Ryuichi Takahashi, Kunihito Ioka, Masato Shirasaki, and Ken Osato report the first measurement linking two independent tracers of cosmic gas. Fast radio bursts are delayed by free electrons along their path, an effect called the dispersion measure. Meanwhile, hot gas leaves a shadow on the cosmic microwave background through the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect. One quantity tracks electron density, the other thermal pressure, so together they can separate how dense the gas is from how hot it is.

Using 133 localised radio bursts and microwave maps from the Planck satellite and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope, the team detected a positive correlation. It spans a wide range of angular scales. The Planck-based signal was about twice the size predicted by the standard cosmology and reached four standard deviations of significance. Assuming the gas has one uniform temperature, the amplitude implies electrons near twenty million degrees on average.
arxiv-2511-02355:
Akshat Pathrikar asks how a surrounding halo of dark matter would change the observable behaviour of a black hole. Real astrophysical black holes rarely sit in empty space, so their vibrations, radiation, and shadows may carry the halo's fingerprint. The study works with a Schwarzschild-like black hole immersed in a specific Dehnen-type dark matter halo profile, and examines perturbations of three kinds: scalar, electromagnetic, and gravitational.

Quasinormal modes, the characteristic tones of the ringing black hole, are computed with a WKB method sharpened by Padé approximants. Particle motion and photon trajectories are traced, and observations of the black hole's shadow are used to constrain the halo's parameters. The paper also examines greybody factors, which filter the Hawking radiation escaping to distant observers, completing a combined picture of how a dark matter environment could show itself.
arxiv-2511-02455:
Yuhan Liu, Varun Nagaraj Rao, Sohyeon Hwang, Janet Vertesi, and Andrés Monroy-Hernández sketch an alternative future for app-based delivery work, in the form of an open protocol. Today's platform delivery economy concentrates power in the platform, hides decision-making from workers, and misaligns what the system optimises against what couriers need. Their proposal, OpenCourier, is a blueprint for a decentralised network of community-owned delivery platforms that interoperate through shared rules rather than a single company's servers.

The vision paper lays out the network's components and layers and walks through hypothetical scenarios showing how orders, workers, and community platforms would interact in practice. No system is built or tested. The stated goal is to provoke discussion and steer future work toward delivery arrangements that are more equitable, transparent, and centred on workers, with lessons for the wider gig economy.
arxiv-2511-02655:
Supercomputers now mix many kinds of chips, so science code must run well on varied hardware. Johansell Villalobos, Josef Ruzicka, and Silvio Rizzi tested four software frameworks that promise such portability in a 2025 paper. They built two small test programs, an N-body simulation and a grid simulation, and ran each across all four frameworks.

Tests ran on one node of the Polaris supercomputer with four NVIDIA A100 graphics cards. Speed differed a lot by framework. OCCA ran small test cases fastest, though its reduction tools may limit larger runs. OpenMP lagged on the grid case, likely due to slow data sharing between nodes. The authors call for better reductions, memory handling, and larger scaling studies.
arxiv-2511-02855:
Francis Atta Howard and Kinvi Kangni study the link between two algebraic structures from quantum theory: the Spin one-half group and a quasi-boson form of the SU(1,1) group. Their 2025 paper explores how spin particles can be decomposed through this connection. The quasi-boson structure turns out to carry a left invariant Haar measure, a standard way to integrate over a group.

The authors then work out the spherical Fourier transform for that structure. In a special case, when Planck's constant is set to one, this transform becomes a Kangni-type transform, a known variant in harmonic analysis. They also bring in the universal enveloping algebra, which packages the group's operations. The results add detail to the bridge between spin algebra and boson-like systems.
arxiv-2511-02955:
Jialin Zhang asks how many entropy readings it takes to pin down a probability distribution when the labels do not matter. His 2025 paper uses generalized Shannon entropy, a family of disorder measures indexed by an order parameter. The question is when a finite set of these readings identifies a finite distribution up to reordering its entries.

For an alphabet of size K, he proves that K minus one distinct positive orders are enough, and that fewer will not do when no repeats are assumed. If the distribution's repeat pattern is known, with s distinct values, then s minus one orders suffice and are again necessary. The results give a label-free base for inference on unordered spaces, and support goodness-of-fit tests across different alphabets.
arxiv-2511-03555:
Zheshi Zheng, Yuanyuan Li, Peter X K Song, and Jiming Jiang revisit their small-area method against the real outcome of the 2024 United States presidential election. Small area estimation borrows strength across regions to sharpen thin local polls. Using poll data gathered one week before election day, the model called every state where polling existed.

Beyond accuracy, the team stresses honest uncertainty. A new measure, the probability of an incorrect call, gets estimated by a conformal method after the standard bootstrap proved too weak. Sensitivity checks then probe pollster bias, finding swing states especially exposed. The post-election audit offers a rare case where a forecasting method can be graded against full ground truth.
arxiv-2511-03655:
Mikel Antonana, Joseba Makazaga, and Ander Murua show that a carefully vectorized implicit integrator can beat famous explicit ones at high precision. Symplectic integrators preserve the energy geometry of Hamiltonian systems over long runs. Implicit versions were long thought too costly, despite their higher order.

Their sixteen-order, eight-stage method packs its math into wide vector instructions that process several values at once, hidden from the user. Head-to-head runs on several Hamiltonian systems in double precision show it outpacing top explicit symplectic rivals where accuracy demands are strict. Long orbit and molecular simulations live in that strict regime, so a faster high-order workhorse could shorten many research computations.
arxiv-2511-04155:
Olav Finne Praesteng Larsen, Massimiliano Ruocco, Michail Spitieris, Abdulmajid Murad, and Martina Ragosta test generative models of aircraft landing trajectories. The models are trained at a busy airport, and the question is whether they can transfer to airports with little data. Trajectory data underpin traffic management tools, yet secondary and regional airports often lack enough records for learning or large simulations.

Diffusion and flow-matching models pretrained on Zurich landings were fine-tuned on Dublin data in amounts from none to all. Diffusion models matched competitive performance with only five percent of local data and reached baseline level near twenty percent, beating scratch training throughout. Flow-based variants gained less evenly, marking diffusion transfer as the strongest route.
arxiv-2511-04355:
Amir Molzam Sharifloo, Maedeh Heydari, Parsa Kazerooni, Daniel Maninger, and Mira Mezini ask where language models still fail at code generation, beyond what leaderboards show. Rankings say little about which tasks models consistently miss, yet those failures are exactly what developers need to see to improve the next generation.

Tasks from four popular benchmarks were screened for ones major models most likely fail. Static complexity of solution code was checked as an explanation, then one hundred fourteen stubborn tasks were inspected systematically. Four recurring weakness patterns emerged, alongside common complications inside benchmark tasks that trigger failure. The analysis separates model shortcomings from benchmark artefacts, a distinction raw scores blur.
arxiv-2511-04455:
Guillaume Etter surveys brain-inspired learning in artificial intelligence in this solo review. Deep learning already borrows key features from real neural networks, such as layered units and attentional designs. Yet its error signals travel in ways no brain could use, and it struggles to learn step by step.

Etter reviews recent neuroscience findings that could supply more plausible learning rules. Synaptic plasticity, how real connections change with use, remains only partly understood. The survey maps where brain ideas have already powered progress in perception and cognition. It also marks open gaps where biology may guide the next round of AI design.
arxiv-2511-04655:
Ellis Brown leads five authors urging benchmark designers to train on their own test set. Multimodal models can ace vision benchmarks without seeing the images at all. Language priors and skewed answer patterns hand out free points.

Blind tests show what a model already gets for free, not what it could learn. Their Test-set Stress-Test cross-validates a text-only model on the test set's own questions. It yields a benchmark score plus a bias score for each question. A random forest on crafted features adds a fast, readable audit. The method exposes shortcuts before a benchmark ships.
arxiv-2511-05655:
Michele De Leo and colleagues warn that the Milky Way's rotating bar can fake the signs of past galaxy mergers. Astronomers rebuild the galaxy's history from clumps of stars in orbital data, read as remains of swallowed galaxies. The bar, a long rotating structure at the galaxy's center, can trap stars and create clumps of its own.

Using precise star data and a custom orbit tool, the team found clear overdensities in several orbital spaces. Checking showed the bar's resonances caused them, not mergers. Trapped stars pile up locally in ways that mimic real substructure. The authors give a fast way to spot resonant loci and judge how much of a clump the bar explains.
arxiv-2511-05755:
Ivano Lodato, Aditya Iyer, and Isaac To tackle causal questions when a data table has a whole row of gaps. In such tables some chances are undefined because the missing entries arose from random sampling zeros. The usual fixes, dropping rows or filling in guesses, can quietly bias estimates of treatment effects.

Instead, the authors treat the unknown chances as free dials. They write the causal query as a formula in those dials, then push the formula to its extremes under basic probability rules. The result is a sharp range that must contain the true value, under weak assumptions about how much data is missing. The method works whatever caused the gaps, giving rigorous bounds for causal inference with holes.
arxiv-2511-05955:
Surbhi Madan and co-authors predict where people in a conversation are looking, using the scene and faces plus context. Gaze reveals attention, engagement, and confidence, so reading it matters for social AI. Their model, CSGaze, treats facial and scene information as complementary inputs rather than rivals.

A fine-grained attention step centers on the main speaker, which sharpens the model's grasp of group gaze patterns. On three gaze data sets the method matched leading approaches. The attention scores double as explanations, showing what drove each prediction. Tests on unseen data sets showed the model carries to new scenes. The authors argue context, often ignored, is what makes social gaze predictable.
arxiv-2511-06055:
Animesh Karnewar leads a team shrinking text-to-video generation until it runs on a phone chip. Their system, Neodragon, makes two-second clips at portrait resolution directly on a Qualcomm neural processor in under seven seconds. Existing transformer video models are built for servers, not mobile hardware.

Four tricks do the shrinking. A distilled text encoder replaces a giant one at a fraction of the size. A distilled decoder swaps in without disturbing the latent space. Unimportant denoiser blocks are pruned and the loss recovered by a two-stage distillation. Step distillation cuts how many evaluations generation needs. Paired with a compact image generator and an upscaler, the full system stays lean in parameters, memory, and run time.
arxiv-2511-06155:
Kamyar Amini connects two counting functions that arise in the quantum K-theory of Grassmannians and of their cotangent bundles. These I-functions encode deep geometric information, but relating the two versions directly is not obvious. Amini defines a K-theoretic operation on classes, called balancing, to build the bridge.

Balancing lifts the I-function of a Grassmannian to the I-function of its cotangent bundle, with a clear geometric meaning. A matching operation on difference operators behaves compatibly for the functions studied, including those of projective spaces. For general Grassmannians, the procedure also recovers the Bethe-Ansatz equations of the cotangent bundle, guided by the abelian and non-abelian correspondence.
arxiv-2511-06355:
Yang Hwan Ahn builds a unified theory of flavor, where particle masses and mixing patterns follow from consistency demands rather than free choices. The setting is a string-derived supergravity with the Standard Model gauge group joined by modular and extra abelian symmetries, gravity included from the start. Anomaly cancellation and gauge coupling unification act as the ruling constraints.

Mixed anomalies cancel in detail, with pieces from Kähler transformations matched by rotations of gauginos and the gravitino. The surviving conditions then pin down quark and lepton flavor structures, set the symmetry-breaking scale, and predict a definite axion mass. Seesaw and supersymmetry-breaking scales come out near ten tera-electronvolts, and the framework also addresses the axion quality problem.
arxiv-2511-06455:
Milena Trajanoska, Riste Stojanov, and Dimitar Trajanov use language model agents to stitch together databases that companies keep in separate silos. Split storage breeds inefficiency and blocks data from working together. Knowledge graphs offer a meeting point, if the tables can first be mapped onto shared vocabulary.

A team of specialized language model agents lays a semantic layer over relational tables, matching tables and columns to Schema.org terms. Existing vocabularies guide the agents as they link structured data across systems. The approach reached mapping accuracy above ninety percent across several domains in the authors' evaluation, suggesting a practical route from scattered tables to one connected knowledge graph.
arxiv-2511-06555:
Nsibiet Udo and Praise Adeyemo link companion matrices to permutation matrices through algebra. Each such matrix is built from the coefficients of one polynomial. Their objects are binomial ideals arranged in a symmetric family inside the coordinate ring of affine space. Reducing the ones tied to those ideals, under fixed monomial orders, produces a surprise.

The reduced ones come out as permutation matrices, and they obey clean rules from group theory among themselves. The paper traces what those reductions mean for lattice ideals, which encode how exponents relate. It also describes the groups these maps generate, tying matrix reduction, combinatorics, and group structure into one picture.
arxiv-2511-06755:
Said Laaroua checks whether the reference frame used for supernova redshifts could be biasing the measured expansion rate of the universe. Distances from Type Ia supernovae anchor the Hubble constant, and converting redshifts from our moving solar system to the cosmic microwave background frame leaves a residual pattern across the sky. If mishandled, that pattern could masquerade as cosmology.

Using more than fifteen hundred Pantheon+ supernovae with full covariance weighting, the analysis recovered the expected tiny monopole and a dipole lined up with the microwave background dipole within a degree. Pushed through the covariance matrix, the residual shifts the Hubble constant negligibly, at most about two percent of the size of the current tension.
arxiv-2511-06855:
Ya-jin Zhou reviews how the angular patterns of particles produced by photon collisions reveal the physics behind them. When photons strike nuclei or each other, the outgoing particles show azimuthal modulations, wave-like patterns in their emission angles. These patterns diagnose the linear polarization of the photons, soft radiation effects, and quantum interference at femtometer scales.

The review covers ultra-peripheral heavy-ion collisions, where tests at STAR, ALICE, and CMS match theory well, including a striking double-slit interference effect between the two nuclei. It also covers electron-positron colliders, where pion pair production lets physicists extract amplitude phases. Those phases feed into calculations of hadronic light-by-light scattering, a key uncertainty in the muon's anomalous magnetic moment.
arxiv-2511-07055:
Katharina Beckh, Sven Heuser, and Stefan Rüping formulate a task they call complete evidence extraction. Decision support systems often justify an output with a short sufficient snippet, but regulatory compliance and medical billing demand all the input tokens that support a decision, not just enough of them. Working in medical coding, the authors ask how fully automated systems can recover that full evidence.

Their approach exploits the Rashomon effect: many other models perform equally well while attending to different evidence. Aggregating token-level attributions from an ensemble of language models therefore recovers evidence any single model misses. On a dataset with human-labeled evidence, ensembles of only three models already beat the best single model, greatly raising evidence recall for only a small extra token overhead.
arxiv-2511-08355:
Thomas Moorcroft, Alberto Amo, Francois Copie, and Stephane Randoux show that discrete time change changes how a weakly touching lattice thermalizes. With usual Hamiltonian evolution, energy saving fixes the final heat from the starting state. Grids driven in discrete unitary steps, realized in light based circuits and fibre pulse systems, follow varied rules because extra temporal periodicity enters the dynamics.

Model runs show weak nonlinearities drive every band toward equal modal occupation, an infinite heat state with a chemical potential, regardless of the starting mode pattern or band structure. Engineering the step timing opens resonant Floquet channels that speed equilibration. Discrete time therefore reshapes weak wave turbulence in a fundamental way.
arxiv-2511-08855:
Maud Lemercier and twelve co-authors detect chemical modifications on RNA without ever training on a modified example. Nanopore sequencers read native RNA molecules directly, and modifications disturb the ionic current in ways that standard tools, tied to known contexts and labeled data, often miss.

The method turns detection into anomaly hunting. For each read, the signature transform extracts sturdy features from the raw current near a site, and an anomaly score compares them with nearest neighbors in a reference set of unmodified reads. Scores become p-values at read and site level. On heavily modified bacterial ribosomal RNA the method recovers known sites across many modification types. Applied to dengue virus transcripts it flags a new methylation site, confirmed by targeted lab assays, and it also runs on mammalian messenger RNA.
arxiv-2511-08955:
Qinyi Zhang and four co-authors build the first broad benchmark for predicting how material microstructures evolve, a simulation task at the heart of materials design. Deep learning stand-ins promise to replace slow standard solvers. But studies so far compare models in clashing ways, prize raw accuracy over physical faithfulness, and ignore how errors compound over time.

MicroEvoEval tests fourteen models, both microstructure specialists and general spatio-temporal designs, across four tasks with datasets arranged for short and long horizons. Scoring adds structure-keeping metrics for physical fidelity, alongside accuracy and cost. Modern designs such as VMamba come out ahead on long-term stability and physical fidelity. They also run far faster, by about an order of magnitude. The authors argue full-picture testing is not optional. They point to these designs as the way forward for stand-in modeling in data-driven materials work.
arxiv-2511-09055:
Xingchi Chen and nine co-authors clear haze from ultra-high-definition photographs by treating dehazing as a flow. Prior-based methods adapt poorly to new scenes, while deep networks strain at 4K resolutions and often distort colors, so the team recasts the task with flow matching and a haze-aware vector field.

The cleanup proceeds as a continuous flow, giving an adaptive nonlinear color transformation learned from data, and the method plugs into many backbone networks rather than one fixed architecture. A learnable three-dimensional lookup table compresses the haze transformation into a precomputed mapping for fast inference. A fourth-order Runge-Kutta solver then integrates the flow step by step, suppressing artifacts. Across experiments the method beats seven state-of-the-art rivals, gaining about two decibels of PSNR with better dense-haze handling and color fidelity.
arxiv-2511-09255:
Junjie Miao and Minghui Xu compute fractal dimensions for Moran sets, a flexible generalization of self-similar sets. Instead of one fixed construction rule, Moran sets allow the pattern to change from stage to stage. The paper focuses on the Assouad and quasi-Assouad dimensions, which capture worst-case local scaling.

For Moran sets whose contraction ratios stay bounded away from zero, the authors give exact formulae for the quasi-Assouad dimension. Without that assumption they prove upper and lower bounds instead. To recover exact answers they define quasi-normal and normal Moran sets and derive formulae for those classes. The results sharpen how the dimension of irregular fractals can be pinned down.
arxiv-2511-09555:
Hao Shi and seven co-authors give robots a cleaner spatial sense by keeping meaning and geometry in separate channels. Point-based perception loses fine detail through sparse sampling, while image methods entangle semantics with noisy depth, corrupting both. Their framework, SpatialActor, disentangles the two explicitly for robotic manipulation.

A semantic-guided geometric module fuses noisy measured depth with expert priors chosen under semantic guidance. A spatial transformer then uses low-level spatial cues for accurate two-dimensional to three-dimensional mapping and feature interaction. Across more than fifty simulated and real tasks, SpatialActor sets state-of-the-art results on RLBench in the authors' tests. It also improves markedly under noisy conditions and generalizes better from few examples to new tasks.
arxiv-2511-09755:
Yinan Liu and nine co-authors report a materials result on type II silicon clathrate, a cage-like form of silicon prized as a possible direct bandgap material for light-based electronics. Earlier samples were held back by heavy doping and defects, and nobody had tested whether hydrogen could clean them up the way it does for ordinary silicon. The team used a remote plasma treatment to drive hydrogen into the crystal framework.

After treatment, measurements showed sodium donor states falling nearly tenfold, the lowest doping level yet reported for these clathrates. Light emission grew fortyfold, its main peak shifted toward the natural band edge, and a new peak appeared near 930 nanometers. The gains survived heating to 400 degrees, which points toward silicon-based light emitters.
arxiv-2511-09955:
Uday Bhaskar and five co-authors use vision-language models to label training data for fast object detectors aimed at autonomous driving. The big models detect objects with no task training, but they are slow and sometimes hallucinate, while hand labeling is prohibitively costly. Their pipeline has the vision-language model write pseudo-labels, then trains real-time YOLO detectors on them.

The key idea is per-object co-teaching: two YOLO models train side by side. Each filters out individual unreliable boxes from a batch using the other model's per-object losses, instead of discarding whole images. On the KITTI driving data set, detection quality jumped well past a baseline model while staying real-time. Adding just ten percent true labels pushed results higher still, with similar gains on two other data sets.
arxiv-2511-10155:
Tomasz Paterek and Arseni Goussev generalize quantum backflow, the odd effect where a quantum particle's probability flows backward against its momentum. Observation has stayed out of reach because the standard effect is tiny, under four percent, and it demands wave packets with a clean momentum direction, hard to prepare and verify under noise. Their formulation works for arbitrary momentum distributions instead.

General backflow is defined as probability flow exceeding what the momentum distribution alone predicts. The standard limit falls out as a special case, but the general excess can reach nearly thirteen percent, more than three times the old bound. The authors extend the idea to the related reentry phenomenon, give explicit example states, and argue the larger effect opens a realistic path to experimental observation.
arxiv-2511-10455:
Baoyi Zeng, Marc-Antoine Martinod, and Denis Defrère improve a key calibration step in nulling interferometry. That technique cancels starlight so faint planets can be seen. The quantity to recover is the null depth, and noise plus instrument flaws make its calibration slow and tricky. Their approach pairs a physical simulator with neural posterior estimation, a machine learning form of Bayesian inference.

The simulator folds in real observational data so the model learns conditions like those at the Large Binocular Telescope Interferometer. On synthetic and real data the model matched the accuracy of the conventional self-calibration method, reaching errors of a few parts in ten thousand. It also cut retrieval time to about a quarter of the usual cost, making the approach practical for other interferometers.
arxiv-2511-10655:
Andrew Kiruluta and Priscilla Burity extend their Spectral Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning framework, a system that reasons over knowledge graphs using spectral methods rather than attention. This second report adds three improvements grounded in meaning that all happen before the core reasoning stage runs.

First, transformer embeddings merge nodes that mean the same thing, cutting redundancy. Second, pretrained inference classifiers check edges at the sentence level, filtering weak claims. Third, linking with outside knowledge graphs such as ConceptNet and Wikidata fills in missing context. On the ProofWriter, EntailmentBank, and CLUTRR benchmarks, the changes brought steady accuracy gains, better handling of attack cases, and less inference noise, while keeping the system clear and scalable.
arxiv-2511-10755:
Luchang Niu, Saleem Iqbal, Yang Xu, and Robert W. Boyd calculate how far entangled photon pairs can travel through turbulent air before their quantum link weakens, a design question for free-space quantum communication. Working with the extended Huygens-Fresnel principle and a Kolmogorov turbulence model, they derive the joint state of the signal and idler photons after separate turbulent paths.

Expressed in the position basis, the state shows spatial correlations surviving the turbulence even as purity is lost, with the correlations turning from quantum to classical in character. Most usefully, they find a finite range of propagation distances over which the angle and orbital angular momentum entanglement is maximized. That window offers concrete guidance for building quantum links spanning several kilometers of atmosphere.
arxiv-2511-10855:
Tom Yuviler and Dana Drachsler-Cohen present ExPairT-LLM, an exact learning algorithm for choosing the best program among several that a language model generates. Existing selectors can fail by treating two different programs as equivalent, or by trusting the model to predict outputs correctly for every possible input.

ExPairT-LLM instead asks the model two simpler kinds of questions: pairwise membership and pairwise equivalence queries about candidate programs. The answers feed a tournament that identifies the correct program and tolerates some mistakes by the model along the way. On four popular code datasets, its success rate beat the state-of-the-art selection algorithm by about thirteen points on average and up to about twenty-seven. It also lifted the performance of models doing complex reasoning by about twenty-four points.
arxiv-2511-11055:
Michael Schwarz and Julian Erhard present a static checker that can prove a program has no data races, the bugs where two threads touch the same memory at once. Sound checkers must rule out every clash, not just likely ones. Their tool builds on digests, short summaries of a thread's past that were first made to tune how much thread history an analysis tracks.

They recast the rules for when clashes cannot run in parallel as digests inside a formal thread model. Built into the Goblint analyzer, the method solved more than five times as many tasks correctly as lock-only reasoning on a standard benchmark suite.
arxiv-2511-11155: Luca Benatti proves that the isocapacitary notions of mass all agree with each other. Mass here is a geometric measure of how much a space contains, judged through capacity, a notion of size based on energy. The family includes Huisken's isoperimetric mass and Jauregui's isocapacitary mass. Showing the definitions coincide means results proved for one form carry over to the others, which settles which notion workers in this area should treat as standard.
arxiv-2511-11355:
Ryan Cecil and Lucas Mentch introduce model class selection, a generalization of the recent idea of selecting a set of near-optimal models rather than one winner. Classical selection picks a single model by a fixed criterion, while set selection keeps every model that is plausibly optimal. Their step up asks which whole collections of models, among several rival collections, contain at least one optimal model.

Under mild conditions, data-splitting methods are shown to solve the problem in general. That yields a formal way to test whether simpler, interpretable model classes can match complex black-box methods on a given data set. Simulated and real-data experiments illustrate the approach across cases.
arxiv-2511-11755:
Isadora Cristina and six co-authors introduce Brazil Data Commons, a platform that gathers Brazil's scattered public datasets into one searchable, linkable place. Fragmented sources, inconsistent standards, and weak interoperability have long blocked research and evidence-based policy in the country.

Built on shared ontologies and the wider Data Commons approach, the platform lets users discover, integrate, and visualize information across domains through friendly interfaces and flexible access. Brazilian data is placed in a global context rather than left in isolated portals. Democratizing access is the stated aim: journalists, researchers, officials, and citizens should all be able to ask data-driven questions without first becoming data engineers.
arxiv-2511-11855:
Andrew Krapivin and three co-authors settle a decomposition problem open since 1997. Erdős and Pyber posed the line of work then. The task is to split a uniform hypergraph's edges into complete multipartite pieces. Each vertex should belong to few of the pieces. The graph case goes back to a forty-year-old question of Chung, Erdős, and Spencer.

An explicit partition bound is proved for the general case. A corollary improves the maximum share size in binary secret sharing on uniform hypergraphs. That earlier bound rested on work of Nechiporuk from 1969. Long-standing extremal questions rarely close in full. This one now does, with a cryptographic side benefit attached.
arxiv-2511-12055:
Jiachun Zheng and three co-authors propose DataInNet, a neural network design for solving partial differential equations, the equations that describe many physical systems. Standard physics-based networks can struggle when solutions change fast or have high frequency parts. DataInNet instead builds known data, such as sources and boundary conditions, into the network itself.

One subnetwork fuses those different kinds of data, while a second learns the physical detail the data do not capture. Because the design rules out solutions that break known constraints, the search space shrinks. Tests include the Helmholtz equation and high frequency cases, where the method reports very low errors.
arxiv-2511-12155:
Thong Bach and three co-authors explain why safety training for large language models can stay incomplete. During training, the learning signal weakens for later parts of a reply, so safety lessons may not fully change what the model prefers near the end of its answers. That gap leaves room for attacks.

The team defines tokens the base model favors over the aligned model as signs of incomplete learning. Their fix adds adaptive penalties and teacher guidance aimed at those undertrained regions. Across Llama and Qwen families, attack success falls sharply in their tests, while general ability is kept. The work gives both a cause and a practical remedy.
arxiv-2511-12355:
Sonu Kumar and nine co-authors report a strong link between electric and magnetic response in a crystal with the chemical formula PrMgAl11O19, studied at very low temperatures. The material is a non-Kramers hexaaluminate, and its dielectric response follows a quantum paraelectric form when no field is applied. A broad anomaly appears near a few kelvin.

That anomaly tracks the multi-hump pattern of the magnetic heat capacity as the field changes, evidence of robust magnetoelectric coupling. The inverse permittivity scales in a simple way with the squared magnetization, matching a Landau theory term. Heat also expands the crystal in a field-sensitive way, tying the coupling to the low-lying energy levels of the praseodymium ions.
arxiv-2511-12455:
Xiantao Fan and six co-authors build a generative model to reconstruct wall-pressure patterns in turbulent boundary layers over space and time. Those pressure fluctuations drive noise and vibration in underwater and aerospace systems. Simple models miss their full complexity, detailed simulations are too costly at high flow speeds, and sensors usually give only point readings.

Their framework couples a patchwise conditional neural field with a latent diffusion model, working piece by piece across the surface. It takes sparse sensor readings and a cheap mean-pressure summary as input, can adapt to new sensor layouts without retraining, and produces ensembles with calibrated uncertainty. Validation shows accurate recovery of the fields and their key spectra.
arxiv-2511-12555: Hassan Oubba studies two kinds of derivation-like maps. They act on the generalized quaternion algebra over a commutative ring. That algebra is viewed as a Lie superalgebra. The maps are super-biderivations and local superderivations. The second kind acts like a derivation at each point, one point at a time. The main result is short to state. On these algebras, every local superderivation is in fact a superderivation.
arxiv-2511-12655:
Jiajun Chen and twenty-five co-authors report transport experiments on one-dimensional moiré superlattices, patterns formed when layered materials are stacked with a slight mismatch.
