They prove any dimensionally consistent change keeps the symmetry size, and test the method on the classic Michaelis-Menten equations.
arxiv-2512-13555:
Daniel Galicer, Julián Haddad, and Joaquín Singer extend the Busemann-Petty problem from geometry. The classic question asks whether smaller central slices of a symmetric convex body force a smaller total volume. A later form by Zvavitch asks the same when size is measured by two arbitrary densities.

The authors widen that result in three ways at once. They allow slices of any codimension, not just flat cuts of one step down. They loosen the growth rule on the density ratio, and they allow a distinct pair of densities for each body. They also give an isomorphic form, where the constant depends on a star body's distance to a class of intersection bodies, plus cases past work missed.
arxiv-2512-13655:
Richard J. Young compares tools that remove refusal behavior from large language models, a process called abliteration. Safety training teaches models to refuse harmful queries, but that refusal can block legitimate security and cognitive research. Abliteration aims to remove refusal in a surgical way, by orthogonalizing key directions.

Young tests four tools, Heretic, DECCP, ErisForge, and FailSpy, across sixteen instruction-tuned models of 7B to 14B size. Single-pass methods kept skills best on the tested subset, with small GSM8K drops for ErisForge and DECCP. Math reasoning was the most sensitive skill overall, with GSM8K change from +1.51 points to -18.81 points by tool and model. The study gives selection criteria for users of these tools.
arxiv-2512-14055:
Nicholas Lawson and William Bialek revisit whether noisy gene expression can still carry optimal information. Gene expression is famously noisy, yet control systems seem tuned to extract as much information as possible from few molecules. Their simple model has one transcription factor controlling a large number of target genes.

They include only physically required noise: random arrival of transcription factors at targets, and counting noise in mRNA synthesis and degradation. With a limited total mRNA budget, information capacity about factor concentration is maximized by spreading resources across the largest possible number of target genes. The optimal input distribution skews toward smaller concentrations. In some limits, optimal transmission coincides with noisy individual expression levels, and the parameter dependence is sloppy, allowing wide variation.
arxiv-2512-14155:
Precious Ogbonda Amadi and five coauthors study a single trapped ion in a 2025 paper on Fisher information. The ion sits in a Paul trap, which holds charged particles with electric fields, plus an optical lattice that adds a repeating light based potential.

The team tracks Fisher information, Shannon entropy, and their combined complexity for the ground and first excited motion states. In the simple harmonic case, the combined measure stays fixed while the other two shift with the effective frequency. That balance breaks once a quartic correction makes the wavefunctions non Gaussian. The change grows with the lattice strength and is stronger for the excited state, giving a clear baseline for later work.
arxiv-2512-14255:
Long My, Shao Hen Chiew, Jing Hao Chai, and Hui Khoon Ng present information efficient decoding for surface codes in a 2025 paper. Surface codes are a leading route to fault tolerant quantum computing, but they create a data backlog problem during certain logical gates.

Those gates need real time decoding of syndrome data, the error signals from the quantum chip, to choose the right frame for the gate. That sets a minimum data rate between the quantum processor and the classical decoder, which can be hard to reach. The authors give two decoders that use far fewer syndrome bits. The count scales with the width of the code patch, not its area, easing the link demands.
arxiv-2512-14455:
Flavio Pineda and Luis O. Pimentel model the early universe in a version of Higgs inflation extended with an extra field, the scalaron. The two fields mix as inflation proceeds, so the path of the system through field space can bend. The authors solve the background and small-ripple equations numerically to see what patterns that bending leaves behind.

Everything hinges on one coupling strength. Near a value around a tenth, a brief turn swaps energy between two kinds of ripple and stamps local features onto the spectrum. With much weaker coupling the spectrum stays smooth, but one ripple type survives to the end of inflation.
arxiv-2512-14555: Matthew Antrobus, writing in algebra, gives an exact test for when a certain Lie algebra built from a finite p-group is solvable, meaning its iterated commutators eventually vanish. The algebra is the first Hochschild cohomology of the group algebra, taken for an odd prime p. His criterion is read off a directed graph constructed directly from the group, and it yields nontrivial information about the structure of these Lie algebras.
arxiv-2512-14655:
Iman Ahmadabadi and five coauthors test a functional called pxcLDA in a 2025 paper. The functional sits inside a density based theory of electrons coupled to light. It aims to describe the electron density of many electron systems, from weak to strong light matter coupling, without treating photons in full.

Earlier work derived the functional and tested it on one electron systems. Here the team sets a key factor by comparing with two trusted reference methods. Across atoms and molecules, pxcLDA matches the cavity changed densities given by those references well. The factor moves toward one as system size or collective coupling grows, which reflects exchange driven behavior. The authors call the method a practical route for real electron systems.
arxiv-2512-15055:
Yifei Bian and six coauthors measure fast, tiny deformations of large structures with a camera that sees changes, not frames. Bridges and towers flex at high frequency under complex loads, but normal high speed cameras cost much and fail in harsh light. Event cameras, which report only the pixels that change, offer a way around both limits.

Their method sticks blinking LED markers on the structure. First it filters noise from the event stream, using the blinking pattern and links in space and time. Then it separates events caused by motion from events caused by blinking, so fast moving markers can be tracked cleanly. A single event camera then measures the planar deformation. Tests confirm the method measures high frequency planar deformation accurately, a cheap route to watching big structures flex.
arxiv-2512-15355:
Feihu Liu and a coauthor build a computing framework around MacMahon's Omega operator, a tool from partition analysis. MacMahon set out partition analysis in his book Combinatory Analysis. It solves problems about sets of linear equations and bounds in whole numbers, counting the solutions with generating functions. The Omega operator is the engine that throws out terms that cannot occur.

The study develops a basic method for doing this analysis by machine, making the operator's use routine. As test cases, the authors give shorter computations for Han's formula, the k-gon partitions problem, and a two dimensional problem. They also turn the method on a further hard problem. The work serves readers who count partitions and lattice points, by making a classic but tricky technique workable.
arxiv-2512-15555:
Alejandra Melo and co authors argue for spectroscopic alerts as a new discovery channel in a 2025 white paper. Wide field surveys such as LSST, Roman, and Euclid will soon produce up to a billion photometric alerts per year. Yet judging what a changing object really is often needs spectroscopy, and global follow up can take only about ten thousand to a hundred thousand spectra a year.

Spectroscopic alerts would flip the order: real time notices triggered when a spectrum itself changes in a notable way. The paper lays out the science cases this enables and the instrument needs behind it. It calls for a wide field, highly multiplexed facility built for the 2040s.
arxiv-2512-15855:
Georges Obied and Mario Reig study charged black holes in the 1/N expansion in a 2025 paper. In theories with many colors of quarks coupled to gravity, black holes lose charge only by emitting baryons, a process suppressed by a huge combinatorial factor. That bottleneck changes how charged black holes end their lives.

Above a critical charge, black holes approach extremality as they evaporate, then stall there for exponentially long times without any symmetry protecting them. Much later they grow a cloud of deconfined quarks, a quark corona, linked to the horizon by unbreakable strings. As an application, primordial black holes as light as one gram could survive to today, reopening dark matter parameter space.
arxiv-2512-15955:
Alexios Veskoukis and Dimitris Kalles examine regulated predictors in published decision tree models in a 2025 paper. Decision trees are prized because readers can follow them, and papers using them usually list their inputs openly. Many of those predictors, such as age, diagnosis codes, and location, fall under privacy law, a link rarely checked.

The authors compile a corpus of decision tree studies, assign each reported input to a regulated data class, and link each category to passages in European Union and United States privacy laws. Many inputs prove regulated, with the largest shares in health care and clear gaps across fields. The evidence supports privacy saving methods and oversight checks in machine learning practice.
arxiv-2512-16155:
F Abbate and a large team describe a prized hunt in an arXiv paper uploaded in 2025. A pulsar orbiting Sagittarius A star, the supermassive black hole at our galaxy's center, would be a dream laboratory. Its timing would show relativistic effects far stronger than in any known binary, and its signals would probe the gas and magnetic fields near the black hole.

Many searches of the galactic center have run, yet only seven pulsars are known within a projected 100 parsecs of the black hole. A larger hidden population is likely, veiled by the messy environment. The authors update the science case since the last SKA planning book and set out observing strategies for the upgraded SKA design. They forecast what the new telescopes should reveal once observations begin.
arxiv-2512-16255:
Chrysanthi Kosyfaki and three co-authors mine movement data in a paper published on arXiv in 2025, which carries an arXiv admin note about text overlap with an earlier paper. Transport firms aggregate trips to spot how passengers flow between regions over time. Patterns can hide at many scales of space and time, so a single fixed view misses trends.

The authors define origin, destination, and time patterns, and give a bottom-up algorithm that enumerates them all. Clever pruning cuts the search space and cost sharply. They add constrained and top-k pattern variants for different applications, plus a fast approximate method for patterns of a given size. Tests on three real data sets showed the methods work efficiently and surfaced interesting flow patterns. The tools suit any field that tracks movement, from transit planning to logistics.
arxiv-2512-16455:
Ignacio Heredia leads a large European team in presenting a research platform in an arXiv paper released in 2025. Artificial intelligence tools built for industry fit open science poorly, where the FAIR principles demand data and models stay findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. AI4EOSC answers that gap inside the European Open Science Cloud.

The platform federates computing and storage from many research infrastructures behind one environment for building, training, and serving models. A development platform, a serverless AI-as-a-service layer, and a federated orchestration model form its modular design. FAIR-by-design rules enforce standard metadata and provenance tracking through the deployment pipeline, following W3C PROV. Community installations across varied cloud providers show the system deploying smoothly, cutting manual work for researchers while raising reproducibility.
arxiv-2512-16655:
Xinqun Mei, Guofang Wang, and Liangjun Weng open a new problem in convex geometry. The problem concerns capillary bodies. Such bodies sit in a half-space and meet its wall at a fixed angle, like a droplet on a surface. The authors define a k-th capillary area measure for such bodies.

With that tool they pose a Christoffel-Minkowski problem. Find a capillary body whose given area measure matches a prescribed one. The task turns into a Hessian-type equation. It carries a Robin edge rule on a spherical cap. Under a natural condition on the data, they prove a smooth convex body exists. They also prove it is the only one. The result adds a boundary case to a classic theory.
arxiv-2512-17055:
Brian Nelson and Behrouz Farhang-Boroujeny design packet detectors for filter bank ultra-wideband radio, where a huge bandwidth is split into parallel moderate-rate channels. That split avoids converters that must sample at the full 500 megahertz or more.

Starting from a single-processor design, they build a detector on the Rao score test that exploits the signal structure through a cascade channelizer, the single-radio-band detector. It needs fast sampling, so they extend it to a multi-radio-band version on parallel slower processors. Simulations show both versions perform alike in typical channels. An over-the-air demo across 1.28 gigahertz found reliable detection at signal-to-noise ratios as low as minus 40 decibels.
arxiv-2512-17155:
Yixuan Cheng and coauthors define Bidirectional Technologies, tools built to serve aerospace and climate needs at once. Both fields share challenges, and global agendas such as the UN 2030 Agenda and Space2030 already cast space work as climate help, yet joint design stays rare.

A broad literature review sorts shared challenges into four groups: life support, energy systems, monitoring and exploratory systems, and novel technologies, in Earth and space settings alike. Traits that mark successful joint tools are drawn out, then turned into starter recommendations for policymakers and engineers. The pitch is resource thrift: one technology line advancing two urgent agendas.
arxiv-2512-17455:
Ronnie de Souza Santos and four co-authors investigate a new threat to software surveys: paid respondents who let a chatbot invent their answers. Surveys are a core way to learn how real programmers work, so fake answers poison real conclusions. The team studied two surveys run in 2025 on the Prolific platform and hunted for planted text.

They found 49 answers bearing the fingerprints of synthetic writing: same-shaped paragraphs, uniform phrasing, and shallow attempts to sound personal. Human review plus an AI detector service backed the call. Such polished fakes, they warn, strike at every layer of a survey's trust. They name data authenticity as a fresh test every survey must pass, and urge checks that mix software screening with human judgment.
arxiv-2512-17755:
Lara Janiurek and Viv Kendon smooth a stuttering quantum walk into flowing equations. A quantum walk spreads a particle by repeated coin flips and steps; the lazy version adds a third option, stay put. Zooming out from single steps to a continuous flow is routine for two-state walks, but the lazy three-state walk, noise included, had no clean continuum form.

The pair derive it, using a three-state coin and two flavors of noise. Without noise, the flow matches a Dirac-style equation: left and right movers stream ballistically, mixing locally, with rest as an internal state. Noise on the coin alone dims internal coherence while the stream stays quantum. Noise on position kills long-range interference and turns the walk classical fast. The map clarifies how rest states steer quantum transport.
arxiv-2512-18055:
Neda Novakova and four coauthors present BlockSets, a chart method for groups whose members are big. Most set charts shrink members to tiny labels or dots, which fails when each member is a long text, an image, or a chart of its own. BlockSets lays members out on a grid and wraps each group in a blocky outline.

Math solvers search for neat layouts, and when a group cannot stay in one piece, the method splits it and marks the split for the reader. Stacked outlines are ordered so every group can still be traced. On every real data set the team tried, a valid stacking turned up.
arxiv-2512-18155:
Aresh Dadlani and coauthors study how fresh data stays in sensor networks when an attacker is actively making it stale. The measure is the age of information: how old the newest received update is. Attackers who jam or slow updates push that age up.

They model a two source M/G/1/1 queue in which one source is hostile, injecting negative arrivals as a Poisson process and slowing service, with the attack bounded in rate and duration. Using moment generating functions, they derive closed form formulas for the average and peak age for any number of sources. A worst case attack model and stochastic dominance arguments then give firm bounds on the age. Computer checks confirm the formulas and show how much harm a resource limited attacker can do.
arxiv-2512-18755:
Jianyi Zhang and three co-authors attack language model safety with a psychology trick: the mere exposure effect, where repeated contact makes things feel safer. Their automated framework, MEEA, posted to arXiv in December 2025, tests whether chatbots can be worn down gradually. It assumes nothing about the model's internals, working as a black box.

MEEA builds chains of prompts that grow slowly in toxicity and tunes them with simulated annealing guided by similarity, toxicity, and success. Across closed and open models, including GPT-4, Claude-3.5, and DeepSeek-R1, it beats seven baseline attacks, improving success rates by over 20 percent on average. Ablations confirm both the annealing and the exposure mechanism matter. The deeper finding is uncomfortable: a model's safety boundary is not fixed, it drifts with conversation history, so defenses must watch whole interactions.
arxiv-2512-19155:
Yin Jun Phua asks whether theories of consciousness can be tested on artificial agents. Three camps dominate the debate: global workspace theory, integrated information theory, and higher-order theories. Each names a different signature of conscious processing, and brains do not allow clean removal of one part at a time.

Phua builds agents that carry each mechanism, then cuts parts out and watches what breaks. One lesion wiped out self-monitoring while task skill stayed intact, like a synthetic blindsight. Shrinking the workspace degraded access in graded steps. The patterns suggest the three theories may describe stacked layers of one system rather than rivals.
arxiv-2512-19255:
Zetao Xie, Zehai Pang, and Yi Yang merge two quantum optics traditions: parametric light processes and free-electron photon interactions. Electrons passing near light fields can shape quantum states of light, yet they had never been placed inside a driven nonlinear system. The authors build the theory for that meeting.

In their setup, a degenerate parametric process creates Bogoliubov quasiparticles that electrons can couple to through two detuned channels. Each side can amplify the other. Seeding with squeezed vacuum gives gain-only or loss-only electron spectra and heralded squeezed states. With plain vacuum, selecting electron sidebands carves out high-fidelity Schrödinger cat states of light.
arxiv-2512-19355:
Simon Ståhlberg and Hector Geffner bring first-order logic to goal-conditioned reinforcement learning. Logic languages already describe planning problems compactly and express policies that transfer across instances. The hard case is a big training world where random wandering never reaches the goal, so plain trial and error starves.

Hindsight replay helps by relabeling a failed run as a success for the goal it did reach. The authors go further: states and goals become sets of logical atoms, and goals can be full states, subsets of the stated goal, or partial variants. Those choices make each trajectory teach more, and policies learn faster and generalize better across states and goals.
arxiv-2512-19555:
Hrachya Babujian, Angela Foerster, and Michael Karowski compute structure functions for deep inelastic scattering at tiny momentum fractions, inside integrable models. Structure functions tell how a struck target's innards share momentum. Small-x behavior is a classic strong-coupling puzzle. Integrable models offer rare exact handles on such questions.

For the O(N) sigma model and the SU(N) chiral Gross-Neveu model, both asymptotically free, they find a universal falloff. It is set by the inverse of x times a squared logarithm, confirming a Balog-Weisz conjecture. A second model family, including sine-Gordon, instead shows plain power behavior. The sine-Gordon case, they suggest, may matter for real QCD.
arxiv-2512-19755:
Gabriele Fioretto and three co-authors model thin sheets that pull on themselves in uneven ways. Their framework extends classic plate theory to sheets with a favored direction. The sheets may have uneven fiber reinforcement. They may also contract through their thickness as they act. A step-by-step expansion yields the balance laws for such plates. In them, target curves fight with the limits that shape imposes.

The showcase use is why cells line up on curved ground. On a tube-shaped base, the model predicts a sharp switch in the favored angle. Cells go from crosswise to lengthwise, by way of a slanted pose. The switch is set by how hard cells pull against the curve of the base. Round and oval bases give other patterns, and the model matches lab results. A last case treats the buckling of active rings.
arxiv-2512-19955:
Wu-zhong Guo, Song He, and Tao Liu ask how entanglement should be counted across time. The usual count compares two regions split in space. Their frame handles regions split in time as well. It merges the spacetime density matrix method with the replica method. That makes Rényi and entanglement entropies well defined for any spacetime interval. The intervals may be spacelike or timelike.

The frame is applied to two quench types. Global quenches are prepared by boundary states. Local quenches come from operator insertions. In both, the team gets closed-form entropies for general setups. Timelike entanglement acts unlike its spacelike kin. After a global quench it stays fixed in time. It hangs only on the time gap, and it carries a set imaginary part. A quasiparticle picture explains the pattern. A sum rule that links the two kinds holds in both quench types.
arxiv-2512-20455:
K Nobleson and the Indian Pulsar Timing Array collaboration dissect the noise in their second data release. Timing twenty-seven millisecond pulsars precisely enough to sense gravitational waves means knowing every jitter in the data. The team models stochastic noise pulsar by pulsar, using Bayesian inference to select models and estimate parameters.

Short-benchmark pulsars mostly show clean Gaussian residuals with no red noise, one exception aside. Three famous pulsars prefer the most complicated models, with both achromatic and chromatic red noise. A few long-benchmark pulsars still show non-Gaussian leftovers, suggesting more advanced noise models are needed. Cutting data near solar conjunctions shifts some estimates, exposing solar-wind bias. The overall budget agrees with the first release, with tighter constraints throughout.
arxiv-2512-20655:
Yuting Hu and co-authors release a dataset meant to drag AI into the chip fab. As circuit features shrink below the wavelength of light, mask optimization by optical proximity correction and inverse lithography becomes indispensable yet painfully slow. Deep learning could accelerate it, but training data built from synthetic layouts, ignoring cell hierarchy and neighbourhood context, transfers poorly to real manufacturing.

MaskOpt is built from real designs at the forty-five-nanometre node, with over one hundred thousand metal-layer tiles and even more via-layer tiles. Tiles are clipped at standard-cell placements and offered at several context sizes, since neighbouring shapes bend the optics. Benchmarks of leading models expose distinct trade-offs, and ablations confirm that context and cell awareness both matter for accurate masks.
arxiv-2512-21255:
Nele Callebaut, Blanca Hergueta, Ruben Monten, and Matteo Selle stress-test the holographic dictionary with dirt in the bulk. Their arena is a three-dimensional gravity model whose black holes include the backreaction of a scalar field, so matter is not a perturbation but part of the solution. Holography relates deformations of the boundary field theory to changes imposed at the bulk's edge, and the famed T-Tbar deformation is the benchmark example, usually matching a simple cut-off recipe.

With matter present, the two deformations divorce. The authors compute both in full. Deforming the boundary theory corresponds to mixed boundary conditions on the metric. The bulk's cut-off prescription yields a deforming operator containing T-Tbar plus extra irrelevant terms. Energy spectra computed from both sides agree once the scalar source's flow is included. Holographers inherit a corrected entry in the map, proof that matter reshapes famed dualities.
arxiv-2512-21455:
Sean Campbell, Courtney C. White, Amanda M. Alexander, and William Ott study how randomness in timing affects genetic switches. A bistable circuit rests in either of two states, and cells need such switches to stay put until a real signal flips them. Protein production takes time, and its noisy steps make the delay before a regulator is ready spread out rather than fixed.

Across a variety of bistable circuits, the authors show that more noise in the delay makes the resting states far more stable. The average time before a circuit flips on its own grows dramatically. They explain the effect with stochastic hybrid models, whose fast-switching limit recovers the distributed-delay model, and by extending a simple three-state model of bistability. The result hints at how evolution tuned biological switches and guides engineers building synthetic ones.
arxiv-2512-21555:
Qi Hu, Jiangchao Liu, Xin Yu, Lin Zhang, and Edward Jiang present XTrace, a system for tracing Android apps while they run in the hands of real users. Some defects, nicknamed ghost bugs, appear only in specific production situations. Static logs and after-the-fact crash reports cannot catch the context needed to diagnose them.

XTrace introduces non-invasive proxying, avoiding any rewrite of the virtual machine's data structures. It builds on the Android ART runtime's built-in instrumentation, optimized for speed and stability. The framework was evaluated inside a ByteDance app with hundreds of millions of daily users. Large online A/B tests showed no significant effect on crash or unresponsiveness rates. Overhead stayed tiny, under seven milliseconds at startup and almost nothing per method call, across Android 5.0 to 15. In production, XTrace helped diagnose over eleven severe crashes, speeding root-cause hunting by over ninety percent.
arxiv-2512-21755:
Himanshu Chandrakar studies the three-cut complexes of hexagonal grid graphs, continuing a line of work on the topology of graph-based complexes. A k-cut complex is built from the subsets of vertices whose removal disconnects the graph in a controlled way. A complex is shellable when its largest pieces can be ordered so each new piece attaches cleanly to the earlier ones, which makes its shape easy to compute.

Chandrakar proves the three-cut complexes of all hexagonal grid graphs are shellable, by constructing an explicit shelling order from reverse lexicographic ordering. From that shelling he counts the spanning facets exactly, with a closed formula. The count implies the complex has the homotopy type of a wedge of that many spheres, all of one dimension that grows with the grid. General results already implied these facts abstractly; the contribution is the explicit construction.
arxiv-2512-22055:
Stability theory for gradient methods leans on smoothness assumptions, Lipschitz gradients and controlled Hessians, that ReLU networks violate by construction. Ronald Katende isolates a minimal obstruction. No uniform smoothness-based stability proxy can hold globally for ReLU networks, even where training looks stable in practice.

A concrete counterexample shows the classical bounds failing outright. Katende then identifies a minimal generalized derivative condition under which such statements can be meaningfully restored. The note warns that smooth approximations of ReLU can actively mislead. It motivates frameworks built for nonsmooth models from the start. The point matters for anyone who proves things about training.
arxiv-2512-22155:
Leonardo Lopes wrote this dissertation on anomalous transport, the unusual flow of charge in materials, aiming at a solid-state version of the Chiral Magnetic Effect from high-energy physics. The stage is a flat honeycomb lattice, like graphene but altered. Usual graphene cannot host the effect because its two sublattices are symmetric, which prevents the mass gap needed for well-defined pseudo-chiral states.

Lopes builds a low-energy model of a honeycomb lattice with sublattice symmetry deliberately broken, opening a band gap and giving quasiparticles a pseudo-chirality based on which sublattice they favor. A time-reversal breaking term unbalances the two valleys, mimicking the chiral chemical potential of relativistic systems. Commutator calculations confirm total angular momentum, including an emergent lattice spin part, stays conserved, validating the model's consistency.
arxiv-2512-22255:
Abhranil Chandra and six co-authors report a counterintuitive recipe for teaching reasoning: train a model on chains of thought that end in wrong answers. Synthetic reasoning traces from stronger models improved performance even when every trace's final answer was incorrect, sometimes beating training on human-annotated data. The authors test two explanations for why distribution shape can matter more than correctness.

First, synthetic text sits closer to the model's own distribution, making it easier to learn from; paraphrasing human traces toward the model's style confirmed this by improving results. Second, wrong traces are often only partly flawed and still contain valid steps. Tests spanned mathematics, algorithmic reasoning, and code generation across MATH, GSM8K, Countdown, and MBPP, using models from several families.
arxiv-2512-22355:
Adelle M. Wright and Benjamin J. Faber test whether a fusion reactor shaped as a quasi-symmetric stellarator can reach its intended calm operating regime. Stellarators confine plasma with twisted magnetic fields. One reactor strategy runs a strong field at lower plasma pressure to dodge destructive instabilities, and the authors examine a reactor-scale quasi-axisymmetric design with a flattened core pressure profile.

Macroscopic and neoclassical checks look favorable for the low-pressure regime. But linear and nonlinear simulations with the GENE code show an abrupt transition into a regime of highly damaging transport at low local plasma pressure. The authors characterize both regimes and the confinement transition between them. The findings carry broad warnings for stellarator optimization and for quasi-symmetric design strategies generally.
arxiv-2512-22455:
Jiacheng Li and six co-authors give LoRA, the popular low-rank fine-tuning method, a temporary dose of nonlinearity. LoRA adapts large models cheaply by training small linear adapters, but that linearity caps its expressive power compared with full training. Their strategy, AFA-LoRA, installs an activation function that starts out nonlinear and anneals toward linear as training proceeds.

Early in training the adapter enjoys the stronger representational capacity of a nonlinear map. By the end it has settled into the linear form that lets LoRA adapters merge seamlessly into the base model. The team implemented the method across supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and speculative decoding. Results show a reduced performance gap between LoRA and full-parameter training, keeping the practical mergeability that made LoRA attractive.
arxiv-2512-22555:
Fynn Jerome Aschmoneit and Bastiaan Cockx generalize a classic geometry problem: two cylinders crossing at right angles. When both cylinders pass fully through each other, their overlap is the Steinmetz solid, whose volume and surface area have known formulas. Real engineering parts, though, often meet only partway, with an arbitrary intersection depth, and that partial case had no exact treatment.

The authors derive general integral expressions for the intersection volume and surface area as explicit functions of intersection depth. Alongside the exact forms, they fit empirical approximation functions that evaluate in closed form with relative errors below fifteen percent across the full depth range. Quasi-Monte Carlo simulations validate both the analytical and approximate solutions, giving designers a usable tool for manufacturing and simulation work.
arxiv-2512-22755:
Hayato Morimura works on the basics of the wrapped Fukaya category, a structure in symplectic geometry that groups Lagrangian submanifolds of a Liouville sector into a category. The category is usually built from an axiomatic package called an abstract wrapped Floer setup. Morimura proposes a leaner set of axioms, dropping choices that prove needless and removing the factorization axiom from the setup.

With the simplified axioms in place, the author reformulates a standing conjecture about the category and then proves it. The claim is that the wrapped Fukaya category is exactly what results from localizing an infinity-category along its continuation maps, meaning those maps become invertible and nothing else is forced. Proving the conjecture amounts to comparing the two axiom systems side by side and showing they produce the same category.
arxiv-2512-23055:
Jamie Alnasir presents E6BJA, a software reimagining of the classic flight computer, the circular slide rule pilots have used for decades to plan flights. Mechanical whiz-wheels and electronic calculators remain valuable teaching tools, but their fixed shapes and narrow designs fit poorly with how pilots now work on phones and computers. E6BJA runs natively on iOS, Android, and Windows, with a web version alongside.

The software reproduces the standard calculations and extends them with better atmospheric modeling, carburetor icing risk estimates, and weight-and-balance tools tailored to common training aircraft. Every calculator carries an embedded short essay explaining its assumptions, variables, and equations, so the tool teaches while it computes. Comparisons with mechanical and electronic flight computers claim gains in accuracy, fewer errors, and teaching value. Trade-offs of native multi-platform development are discussed as part of the design story.
arxiv-2512-23255:
Masaya Takabe and co-authors improve a lightweight way of storing images: representing a picture as a sum of two-dimensional Gaussian blobs. Two-dimensional Gaussian splatting compresses well and decodes in real time, but with few Gaussians the reconstructions blur object boundaries, because nothing tells the blobs where edges are. Their framework feeds contour information into the representation from the start.

Segmentation priors divide the image into object regions. During rasterization each Gaussian is confined to its own region. That stops colors from bleeding across boundaries and keeps edges crisp even under heavy compression. A warm-up scheme steadies the early training and improves convergence. On synthetic color charts and the DAVIS video dataset, the method reconstructed edges more faithfully than existing two-dimensional splatting approaches, with the clearest gains when the Gaussian count was very small. Rendering stays fast and memory use stays low throughout.
arxiv-2512-23455:
Bao-Jun Cai, Bao-An Li, and Yu-Gang Ma review how short-range correlations between nucleons change what we can say about neutron stars. In dense nuclear matter, pairs of nucleons briefly interact at very short distances, which pushes some of them to high momenta and reshapes the matter's momentum distribution. That microscopic detail feeds directly into the equation of state, the rule linking pressure and density inside a star.

The review traces how these correlations alter the kinetic part of the equation of state and its symmetry energy, then follows the effects outward to star properties. Mass-radius relations, tidal deformability, cooling thresholds, and the boundary between core and crust. It closes with open questions and the observations that could test the picture.
arxiv-2512-23755:
Sheo Yon Jhin and Noseong Park try to read the human mood inside a time series without looking at any outside information. Forecasters often add news or social media feeds to capture the psychology that moves financial and economic data, but those feeds are expensive and cumbersome. Their framework, HINTS, instead extracts human factors from the forecasting residuals themselves, the part of the data the base model failed to explain.

The extraction is guided by the Friedkin-Johnsen model of opinion dynamics, which describes how social influence, memory, and personal bias evolve, used here as a structural bias for self-supervised learning. The recovered factors feed a leading forecasting model as an attention map. Across nine real-world and benchmark data sets, forecasts improved consistently, and case studies showed the extracted factors lining up semantically with real events. The work appears at an AAAI 2026 workshop.
arxiv-2512-23855:
Corbin Pacheco and Nausheen Shah ask whether the mathematics of entanglement can be tested where particles actually collide. Bell inequalities expose quantum clashes, but transplanting them into particle physics needs care, because measurements there are dictated by interactions, not by free choices of detector settings. The authors propose Bell-type inequalities as operator-level tests in flavor space.

They construct flavor operators tied to mass identification, flavor change, and charged-current weak mixing, all arising from Standard Model interactions, and treat those interactions as alternative measurement settings in a thought experiment. For entangled two-particle states, the operators produce correlations that violate Bell-type bounds, ruling out non-contextual local descriptions under the stated assumptions. The violations spring from the operators' algebraic structure, not from kinematics or exotic dynamics. The article closes by sorting out how the predicted patterns might be probed in data, and where the reasoning stops.
arxiv-2512-24255:
Jiping Yu and six colleagues ask how oblivious memory would help trusted processors. Trusted hardware lets parties compute jointly while keeping data private. Privacy comes at a cost. Data-oblivious algorithms hide access patterns, but they run slowly. Graph analytics are important and especially exposed to access-pattern attacks.

Oblivious memory built into the processor hides accesses from adversaries. The authors co-design storage layouts and algorithms around it. Their prototype runs a hundred times faster than baselines. The memory needed is only about per-core cache size. Existing processors could add it with negligible overhead. The insight is architectural. A small, well-placed hardware feature can remove a large software penalty. Private graph analytics on untrusted infrastructure is the target use.
arxiv-2512-24555:
Xueyan Li and four colleagues teach vision-language models to write memes. Meme humor needs more than captioning an image. Context, template conventions, and subjective taste all matter. Their framework, HUMOR, guides a model through layered reasoning. It first identifies the template's intent. Then it explores diverse reasoning paths under different contexts. Finally it anchors on one high-quality, context-specific path.

Subjective humor needs a second ingredient. A pairwise reward model is trained inside groups of memes sharing one template. It proxies human preference even with noisy labels. Group-wise reinforcement learning then optimizes against that reward. A trust region guarantee keeps improvement monotonic. Experiments show stronger reasoning diversity across several base models. Preference alignment grew more reliable, and meme quality rose. The authors frame the recipe as general. Open-ended, human-aligned generation can be steered by comparison inside coherent groups.
arxiv-2512-24755:
Sungwoo Kang offers a diagnostic framework for deciding when combining sensor streams helps industrial monitoring and when it hurts. Fusion is the default for mixed thermal, sensor, and other data, yet no systematic check existed for cases where fusion lowers detection quality. The three-step procedure measures single-modality gaps, inspects gate weights, and corrupts each modality in turn.

Formal criteria then route a system toward a suitable fusion strategy before deployment. Validation spans three datasets with two different routing outcomes, including an industrial thermal and sensor set. Plant monitoring readers get a pre-deployment test instead of blind trust in fusion.
arxiv-2512-24855:
Gabriel Rabelo-Soares, Reinaldo Francener, and Gabriel Ramos compute proton entropies that capture full phase-space structure in deep inelastic scattering. Multiplicity there has been linked to entanglement entropy, but that definition is over-time only. They instead build the Wehrl entropy from the gluon Husimi distribution, a positive phase-space account found by smearing the Wigner distribution.

A gluon light-front spectator model, with wave functions inspired by soft-wall holographic QCD and settings fixed by global parton fits, supplies distributions and parton densities. Readers in hadron physics get entropy measures that respect transverse structure as well as over-time momentum, at small momentum fraction.
arxiv-2601-00055:
Sumit K Sarbadhicary leads nineteen co-authors, including the PHANGS Collaboration, in cataloging red supergiants, the huge cool stars that end their lives as supernovae. Their 2026 survey uses Hubble and Webb telescope images to search nineteen nearby galaxies, far beyond the Local Group where most earlier work stopped. Ground and older space instruments lacked the sharpness and sensitivity to do this systematically at such distances.

Selecting stars by predicted colors and brightness, the team assembles the largest single-survey red supergiant release yet, covering stars above about ten solar masses. The stars cluster in spiral arms and central starburst rings, as expected for young populations. Their density tracks local star formation closely and total stellar mass only weakly, and the team derives how many such stars form per unit mass of young stars. The catalog should help trace future supernova sites and date stellar populations.
arxiv-2601-00255:
Abdallah Daddi-Moussa-Ider leads four coauthors in solving how a tiny twirl stirs fluid inside a wedge. Microfluidic devices often confine flow in wedge shaped spaces. At low Reynolds number, motion is smooth and reversible. Flow from a point force in a wedge was solved long ago. Flow from a point torque, a rotlet, was still missing.

The team derives that missing response in full. A Fourier style transform and a classic field form do the work. Resulting flow maps show clear structure and key traits. Shape of the wedge and torque direction both matter. From the solution they build a mobility tensor. It links applied torque to particle motion. Broken symmetry in the wedge adds a surprise. A twisted particle also drifts sideways as it spins. Device designers gain exact tools for such motion.
arxiv-2601-00555:
Abu Hanif Muhammad Syarubany, Farhan Zaki Rahmani, and Trio Widianto describe a shopping robot in a 2026 paper. The robot works indoors and takes orders in plain speech. As it moves, it builds a light map of the place. The map notes signs at each fork and which way each shop lies. Printed tags on the walls give the robot fixed points to line up on.

A large language model reads each order and picks the robot's next move. At each fork it picks a way to turn, and whether to enter a shop. A control program then runs the move with set motion skills. Those skills dodge blocks, line up on tags, enter shops, and grasp goods. The team tested the stack in a computer model of a store. They also tested it in a real hall. The robot ran whole tasks, from order to goods in hand.
arxiv-2601-00655:
Kasra Fouladi and Hamta Rahmani train models that are not only accurate but also explainable in ways that respect expert knowledge. Their framework, Interpretability-Guided Bi-objective Optimization, encodes a hierarchy of feature importance as a directed acyclic graph, built using a central-limit-theorem-based construction. Feature importance over time is measured with temporal integrated gradients.

A relative importance score then tracks how much of a model's total attribution each feature carries, and a geometric projection combines the accuracy gradient with the interpretability gradient during training. The authors prove convergence to Pareto-stationary points, where neither objective can improve without harming the other. They also sketch an oracle design for a known weakness in the gradient computation, left for future work.
arxiv-2601-00855:
Joseph Oche Agada and eight co-authors present, in 2026, a hybrid AI method to pin down crystal structures with defects. A crystal's traits flow from both its neat lattice and its local flaws. Labs read structure from diffraction patterns, the spots made when rays scatter off the lattice. The classic fit method can get stuck at a near miss.

Their frame first codes each pattern down to a small set of numbers, with a learned coder. The coder is built to respect scale rules and physical sense. A search method then roams that small space, plus the raw one, for the best fit. The test case is a crystal named Ho2Ti2O7, of the pyrochlore family. Scores from a standard package serve as the bench mark. The authors compare coder-aided search, plain search, and the classic fit. The frame aims to find better structures in less time.
arxiv-2601-01055:
Ernest Fokoué builds a theory of ensemble learning in which each new model leans on the two that came just before it. Most classic methods, such as boosting, add one model at a time with no memory of earlier steps beyond a running sum. The Fibonacci-style update studied here gives the ensemble a memory, so past structure shapes each new step.

The paper sets out a family of update rules, covering Fibonacci, tribonacci, and higher-order versions, plus smooth time limits written as differential equations. Fokoué proves when these flows settle, when they stay stable, and how well they should do on new data. Tests with three classic smoothers show gains over fixed weighting. The work closes a trilogy that grew from Fibonacci weighting into a full theory of learning systems that evolve over time.
arxiv-2601-01255:
Sergeev and 4 co-authors lay out a plan for turning a major matroid theorem into computer-checked form. Seymour's breakdown theorem explains how regular matroids, a broad class of structures in combinatorics, can be built from simpler pieces. Formalizing it in the Lean proof tool needs careful planning first.

The blueprint shows how order and dependence run through the whole proof. It covers representations with entries limited to minus one, zero, and one, and shows regularity survives joining pieces in three basic ways. Special cases like graphic and cographic matroids are included. The document serves both as a work plan and as a readable map.
arxiv-2601-01355:
Jiang and Zhao study how lone wave packets, called solitons, can be pumped through a patterned material in set steps. Such motion links to topology, the branch of math that tracks features that resist smooth change. By adding interactions between sites, not just on each site, they find motion can be guided further than linear theory predicts.

The work also upends a common belief about speed. Going slower does not always help, because weak instability sets a lower bound on how fast the pattern must change. When several solitons move together, their interactions weaken the usual robustness. Still, the results widen design choices for controlled transport.
arxiv-2601-01555: Sababheh and Moradi give fresh limits on how large certain inner products can be in Hilbert spaces. Those are the general spaces where length and angle still make sense. Their short paper states that the results improve earlier bounds in the same line of work. They also apply the new bounds to two standard measures for operators. Those measures are the numerical radius and the operator norm.
arxiv-2601-01655:
Emiliya Khidirova and Oktay Karakus present UniCrop, a reusable pipeline that prepares farm data for yield forecasts. Good forecasts need satellite images, weather, soil, and land shape data together, yet each crop or region usually demands fresh hand work. UniCrop automates gathering, cleaning, and aligning those sources for any place, crop, and time window set by the user.

The pipeline draws more than two hundred variables from six data sources, then trims them to a compact set that keeps signal while cutting overlap. On 557 rice field records, fifteen chosen features fed four standard models. A blended ensemble beat the best single model, and code plus guides are shared openly.
arxiv-2601-02055:
Blast aluminium with an ultrafast laser pulse and its lattice disorders before it heats. Fernando Rodriguez Diaz and Kasra Amini capture that non-thermal regime. Their tool is high-repetition ultrafast electron diffraction. It runs at energies beyond earlier setups. The reachable momentum range widens.

The team watches ten Bragg peaks and six diffuse signals. The mean-square atomic displacement jumps promptly. Energy rushes from excited electrons to the lattice. Relaxation then depends strongly on diffraction order. Low orders settle fast. High orders linger near a plateau. Equilibration, it seems, runs on several timescales at once. Residual oscillations reveal a coherent acoustic breathing mode. It sits near zero point one nine two terahertz. The mode supports selective, non-thermal energy redistribution.
arxiv-2601-02155:
Waves rippling through the Sun's photosphere carry energy upward. The telescope itself can distort the measured spectrum, though. M. Berretti and eight co-authors use high-resolution observations of a magnetic pore. The data come from the Dunn Solar Telescope. They ask how much of the reported wave behavior is instrument rather than Sun.

Deliberately degrading the detail shifted the dominant wave band. It moved from five millihertz down to three. Stray light from the neighboring quiet Sun polluted the pore's signal. Its true cycles were masked. The implication is uncomfortable. Wave energy estimates from lower-detail instruments may be deeply underestimated. The study sets a baseline for reading the sharper views from DKIST and MUSE.
arxiv-2601-02455:
Xinyu Wang and six co authors improve post training quantization for speech recognition models, the compression step that shrinks a trained model to three or four bits per weight without retraining. When layers are quantized one by one, each layer sees inputs already distorted by the layers before it. An earlier compensation method used one coefficient for the whole model, mixing the global setting with differences between layers.

Their method, FADE, builds a separate coefficient for each layer from the layer's rounding distortion and a calibrated solver response. With no training and no per model search, and adds nothing at run time. Across seven Whisper, Moonshine, and Qwen ASR models and four English benchmarks, FADE lowered word error rates in most settings compared with the fixed earlier method. Gains were largest where three bit models had collapsed, which the authors frame as damage control rather than usable accuracy.
arxiv-2601-02755:
Federico Camia and Rongvoram Nivesvivat find infinitely many boundary operators hiding in the Brownian loop soup, a random collection of loops that models fluctuating interfaces. They work in the subcritical phase and expand the two point function that gives the probability that Brownian loops separate two marked points on the upper half plane. The expansion is in conformal blocks, the building pieces of a two dimensional conformal field theory.

The operators that emerge are primary operators of a theory with central charge at most one, and their conformal dimensions are non negative integers, an unusually tidy spectrum. Comparing the expansion term by term with loop probabilities gives the even dimension operators a concrete meaning. Each inserts multiple outer boundaries of Brownian loops at points on the real axis, tying abstract field theory data to visible geometric events.
arxiv-2601-03555:
Yuxuan Jiang and Francis Ferraro address a training problem for tool-using language agents: when a long task fails, which step deserves the blame? Reward models that judge whole processes often give noisy signals because they lack clear rubrics. Their framework, SCRIBE, adds mid-level supervision between grand planning and single actions.

SCRIBE matches each subgoal to a skill prototype from a curated library, turning open-ended judging into a structured check against a defined rubric. That routing cut reward variance and steadied training. Across reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, the method reached state-of-the-art results. More reliable step-level feedback could make agents safer to train for real jobs, where one bad tool call in a long chain can undo everything else.
arxiv-2601-03655:
Jinsong Zhou and nine co-authors present VideoMemory, a framework for keeping characters and settings consistent across a long generated video. Today's models make fine short clips but often change a character's face or lose props when scenes cut or time passes. VideoMemory plans the story first, then generates each shot with help from a Dynamic Memory Bank.

That bank stores visual and written descriptors for characters, props, and backgrounds, updating after every shot as the story changes them. A multi-agent system breaks the script into shots, retrieves the right memories, and synthesizes frames and video from them. The team built a fifty-four item test set, described in the work, for this long-form setting. Consistent long video is a key step toward AI-made narrative film.
arxiv-2601-03855:
Chong-Wei Wang and four co-authors present MPM-QIR, a quantum circuit framework that stores and compresses images by matching measurement probabilities to pixel brightness. A variational quantum circuit learns the image, with pixel positions encoded through an ordered mapping to the flattened pixel list, so no extra coordinate qubits are needed. Compression efficiency then ties directly to how complex the circuit is.

A bidirectional convolutional design creates long-range entanglement at shallow depth, capturing global image structure with fewer parameters. Under one shared testing protocol, the method reached strong reconstruction quality, above the thirty decibel level, at lower parameter compression ratios than rivals across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 benchmarks. Leaner image representations matter for quantum hardware, where every parameter and qubit is precious.
arxiv-2601-04055:
Prith Sharma and Austin Z. Henley argue that prompts for language models should be tuned section by section, not as one block. Prompt quality strongly affects reliability, above all for smaller open models that lean on clear structure. Whole-block tuning makes errors hard to locate and lets prompts bloat.

Their method, Modular Prompt Optimization, splits a prompt into fixed parts such as role, context, task, limits, and output format. A critic model writes local textual feedback for each part, and updates are merged with duplicates removed. Tested on ARC-Challenge and MMLU with two small instruction models, the method beats both an untuned structured prompt and the TextGrad baseline. Gains come without changing model weights or the prompt layout.
arxiv-2601-04455:
Chuan Meng and five co-authors ask whether the tools that rank search results can also judge them, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Relevance judgments — human-style labels of whether a passage answers a query — are increasingly predicted by large language models at great expense. Yet re-rankers, built to order results by relevance, are solving a near-identical problem, and reusing them could save duplicated effort.

The team adapts eight re-rankers from three families two ways: reading their generated true-or-false tokens as verdicts, or thresholding their scores into labels. On five years of TREC deep learning track data, the repurposed judges beat a leading language-model judge in around half the cases. They also caught a bias worth knowing: re-ranker judges favour results from their own and related re-rankers, a self-preference that any evaluation built on them must correct for.
arxiv-2601-04555:
Shogo Nakayama and Masahiro Okuda soften a hard cutoff that wastes training data, in a 2026 arXiv paper on semi-supervised contrastive learning. The standard recipe assigns a guessed label only when the model's top predicted probability clears a fixed threshold, then learns contrastively from the survivors. Everything under the bar — often most of the unlabelled data, especially early — is simply thrown away.

Their loss instead estimates each sample's confidence from the entropy of its predicted distribution, a smooth measure of how decided the model is, and weights samples accordingly. Guessed labels can then be used even for previously excluded samples, and the contrastive objective accounts for the confidence of both the anchor and its positive partner. Across their experiments, classification accuracy improved and learning stayed more stable when labelled data were scarce — the regime where throwing data away hurts most.
arxiv-2601-04655:
Yves Noat, Alain Mauger, and William Sacks present a theory of how cuprate superconductors condense, centred on excitations they call pairons, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Cuprates, the copper oxides that superconduct at record temperatures, still lack an agreed mechanism. In the authors' picture, the condensate couples strongly to excited pair states. the gap depends on energy in a way set by an effective spin exchange energy, with no retardation of the kind phonon theories assume.

Fitting tunnelling spectra extracts the model's two parameters, the condensation energy per pair and the antinodal gap. A derived formula for the critical temperature then predicts sharply: across all dopings, the critical temperature is proportional to the condensation energy, not to the gap — the reverse of conventional superconductors. The factor is traced to pair excitations obeying Bose statistics above a small mini-gap, and the authors argue one mechanism runs along the whole dome.
arxiv-2601-04855:
Francesco Ferrini and 7 co-authors rethink how graph neural networks cope when node features go missing in a 2026 paper. Missing data is routine in healthcare and sensor networks, yet most studies test only mild cases: sparse high-dimensional features and data missing completely at random. The authors prove that high sparsity itself limits information loss, making every model look robust and comparisons meaningless.

To fix evaluation, they introduce new synthetic test settings and propose a robust solution for harder missing-feature regimes. Honest benchmarks matter because a model that seems safe on easy tests may fail on real patients or sensors. Their work gives practitioners a clearer picture of when graph models can be trusted with incomplete data.
arxiv-2601-05055:
Francesca Chadha-Day reviews axion superradiance in a 2026 paper, a process where light fields grow explosively around spinning objects. A rotating black hole or neutron star can amplify a light bosonic field, much as a whirling system feeds energy into a wave, while its own spin drains away. Axions, hypothetical light particles proposed for dark matter, are the prime target of this mechanism.

Because the growth depletes spin, finding a highly spinning black hole would rule out axions in a certain mass range. The constraints hold even when the particle barely interacts with ordinary matter, making superradiance a strong way to hunt for new physics. Chadha-Day also stresses the care needed in drawing those conclusions, since astrophysical details can weaken a naive bound.
arxiv-2601-05155:
Gonzague Radureau's 2026 paper puts machine learning to work on a hard branch of astro-physics. The branch tracks how hot, fast plasma trades light with the space it fills. Light made by the plasma can be drunk in by it too. That trade sits at the heart of how stuff falls onto black holes and how jets shoot out. A code named HADES runs such tasks, with a light trade model fit for stuff that is half clear and half murk.

For all its truth, the code eats huge sums of machine time. Radureau homes in on one of its two chief costs: the part that tracks light band by band. A learned stand-in, trained on past runs, could swap that part for a swift guess. Such cuts would let labs run more takes, at more fine grain, near black holes.
arxiv-2601-05255:
Sai Khadloya and 3 co-authors present CourtNav, a voice-guided navigator for long legal documents, in a 2026 paper. Court work rests on close reading of records, charge sheets, pleadings, annexures, and orders. Those files often run to hundreds of pages. Staff support is limited, so reading everything during a hearing is impractical, and finding one paragraph can stall a courtroom.

CourtNav maps a judge's spoken command, such as going to a paragraph or highlighting a contradiction in cross-examination, directly to a highlighted passage within seconds. It transcribes the command and routes it through a grammar-first classifier backed by a language model. Anchor-accurate navigation could return hearing time to argument and judgement instead of page hunting.
arxiv-2601-05455:
Sahil Wadhwa and 6 co-authors introduce ART, a 2026 method for checking claims in a way people can inspect and challenge. Large language models can judge claims, but their reasoning is often hidden, which is a problem in high-stakes settings. ART instead grows a tree of arguments from a root claim.

Child arguments support or attack their parent. Strength is decided bottom-up through pairwise contests between children, judged by a separate model, until a final verdict emerges. Tests on several datasets, with different argument generators and comparison strategies, show the structured approach beating strong baselines. The authors present ART as a clearer and more reliable route to claim verification.
arxiv-2601-05555:
Patrick Loic Foalem and 3 co-authors report, in a 2026 study, the first large-scale look at Policy-as-Code adoption in open-source projects. Policy-as-Code writes governance, compliance, and security rules as code inside a system. Despite wide tool adoption, little was known about how projects actually use these tools.

The authors analyzed 399 GitHub repositories using nine popular tools, mixing usage statistics with close reading of policy files. A model-assisted classification, checked by experts, produced a taxonomy of five categories and fifteen subcategories. Adoption was diverse, often early-stage, and oriented toward governance, configuration control, and documentation. Strong co-use of some tool pairs appeared. The taxonomy should help practitioners and tool builders improve interoperability.
arxiv-2601-05955:
Yuliang Chen and 7 co-authors present FaST-PT in 2026, an approach for federated domain generalization with lower communication and computation costs. Federated learning trains across distributed clients without centralizing data, but models still fail on unseen domains, and data differ sharply between clients. Their approach attacks both problems together.

A lightweight multimodal style transfer method transforms image embeddings under text supervision, expanding the training distribution and softening domain shift. A dual-prompt module splits prompts into global parts, capturing shared knowledge, and domain parts, capturing local specifics. A prompt generation component then blends suitable prompts per sample. Across four cross-domain benchmarks, the authors report performance above leading federated generalization methods, with ablations backing each component.
arxiv-2601-06055:
How MacBook chargers changed over generations is the subject of a 2026 study by Zeyi Liao and 2 co-authors. Apple moved from MagSafe to USB-C, then back to MagSafe 3. Each switch reflects a mix of new technology, user convenience, and cost.

The study follows these charging systems from launch to obsolescence. Old chargers become electronic waste when ports change, which carries environmental costs. Manufacturers and consumers both feel economic effects, from redesign spending to buying replacements. The authors argue future transitions should be planned so innovation does not come at the expense of ecological health or household budgets. Their analysis names the factors that drive charger evolution and its wider effects.
arxiv-2601-06355:
When two gas clouds crash head-on, stars form in bursts. Tabassum S. Tanvir and 1 co-author ran the first such crash tests that track single stars and all their push-back in a 2026 study. Crash speed, field lines, and light from young stars all play a role.

The crash sped up star birth and moved its start to an early time. Yet the share of gas turned to stars stayed much the same in all runs. Slow crashes let gas pile into long strands, with star birth that kept a steady pace. Fast crashes squeezed gas hard, lit a bright burst, then saw push-back tear the cloud apart. Field lines that ran with the crash path made fewer, weightier stars. Lines across the path held gas back, and stars came out small and spread wide.
arxiv-2601-06455:
Jananan Arulseelan introduces pseudofinite W*-probability spaces in a 2026 mathematics paper. These operator algebra objects are defined through model theory: they behave, in the language of continuous logic, exactly like ultraproducts of finite-dimensional von Neumann algebras carrying arbitrary faithful states. The matrix algebra case gives what the author calls pseudofinite factors.

Arulseelan proves these are indeed factors and can never be of the most exotic type classification. Explicit families built like the classic Powers factors realize a range of type III factors, sharing their universal theories with the corresponding Powers factors, which makes those theories uncomputable. Pseudofinite factors are also shown to be full. A striking consequence: hyperfinite type III factors are never pseudofinite.
arxiv-2601-06655:
George Pasparakis and six co-authors guess shock states of stuff with far less data in 2026. A shock curve lists the states a stuff reaches when hit by a shock. Each point on that curve has cost a pricey run on a large machine.

Their frame is a chance-based curve fit bound by the laws of shocks. It learns from just a few runs and fills in the rest of the curve. A chance form of a Taylor sum builds the fit at its core. Jump rules at the shock front shape the fit so it stays true to the laws. The fit thus honors heat laws, not just the dots on a graph. Labs that study blasts and impacts can stretch small budgets much more. The way is built for work where each run costs a great deal.
arxiv-2601-07255: A team led by A. von Ungern-Sternberg Schwark posted a 2026 arXiv paper on a crystal called SmNiC2. The team asks how two states of the crystal act on each other. One is a wave in the charge of the crystal. The other is a state where the crystal acts as a magnet. A link through the shake of atoms in the grid ties the two states. The team probes the crystal with X-ray scattering. They add Raman spectroscopy, which reads shifts in light bounced off the crystal.
arxiv-2601-07655:
Lea Enzi and Stefan Thonhauser ask when an insured person should report a claim at all. Their 2026 preprint studies optimal claim reporting inside a bonus-malus insurance system. In such a system, reporting a claim moves the customer to a higher-premium class. Staying claim-free for a set period moves them down to cheaper premiums. Small claims may therefore cost more than they pay.

The authors model the contract as two regimes with transitions between them. The customer must weigh a payout now against years of higher premiums. Solving for the optimal rule gives a threshold for when reporting pays. The analysis serves actuaries who design bonus-malus schemes. It also explains rational customer behavior that insurers observe, such as hiding small accidents.
arxiv-2601-08055:
Daniil Karuzin, Zhiyu Dong, and Leonid Levitov study paired electrons in flat, curved electronic bands. Their 2026 arXiv paper starts from odd superconductivity found in rhombohedral graphene. They ask what bound states form when bands carry Berry curvature, a geometric twist in electron motion.

The authors solve a two-body problem and find chiral bound states with nonzero angular momentum. These are not the usual round s-wave pairs. With a Fermi sea present, the same forces lead to chiral pairing and several superconducting phases. Those phases break time-reversal symmetry, so the work links band geometry to new kinds of superconductivity.
arxiv-2601-08155:
Inpyo Song and four co-authors tackle explainable video anomaly detection with spatial grounding. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that anomaly detection matters for safety-critical uses. Yet many systems give explanations that cannot be checked against the video itself.

The gap grows in scenes with many interacting entities. Existing methods often produce incomplete or visually misaligned descriptions there, which lowers trust. The team proposes instance-aligned captions, where each caption ties to a specific object in the scene. Aligned captions let users verify what the system claims it saw. That verifiability is the point: an explanation should point at evidence, not float free.
arxiv-2601-08955:
Youwei Liu and four co-authors teach agents to look ahead in a fake world before they act. A world model is a learned sim of how a place changes when an agent acts. With it, an agent can plan with no risk to the real place. Past use was short: one step, or a fixed span of steps, no more.

Their method is called Imagine-then-Plan. The agent shifts its look span to fit the task at hand. Hard tasks get a long look. Easy tasks get a short one. A reader who builds agents gets a plan rule that bends with need. It may lift task scores while it keeps sim cost in check.
arxiv-2601-09455:
André Artelt, Martin Olsen, and Kevin Tierney study how hard it is to compute certain explanations of model decisions. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats counterfactual and semi-factual explanations in explainable AI. A counterfactual says what change would flip a decision; a semi-factual says what could change while the decision stays.

Clear explanations are essential when models are used in high-stakes settings. The authors bring complexity theory to the question, asking which explanation tasks are tractable at all. Hardness results draw a map of where explanation tools can be fast and where they cannot. That map helps practitioners pick explanation types their systems can actually deliver.
arxiv-2601-10255:
Jorge Olmos-Trigo sets an exact rule for how small grains bend light when a field is near. Such grains are named nanoparticles. Past rules bound how they can take and scatter light. Those rules are firm for plain and mixed grains. Magneto optical grains had no such rule.

These grains shift how light acts when a field is on. Olmos-Trigo works out the exact law for them. It covers grains with a line of symmetry. It holds for any light and any field. The law sets hard caps on what such grains can do. That guides the design of light tools at tiny scale.
arxiv-2601-10355:
Zhihao Xu and co authors mine text for fake tool use paths to train agents. An agent must learn to call tools in long chats. Real paths of such calls are hard to get. They are vast in kind and cost much to mark by hand. That gap slows agent work.

The team made a text based path to forge them. Plain text holds rich tales of tool use. From those tales, they forge paths that act like real runs. The paths span many tasks and tools. Models can then train on the forged paths. The aim is agents that learn tool use at scale.
arxiv-2601-10455:
Ruochen Li and co authors rethink how surgical plans by AI are graded. A plan for surgery must mix sight, long chains of thought, and craft facts. It is not clear that grades today test that mix well. A bad grade can pass a bad plan, or fail a sound one.

The team set a goal based test. A plan is right if it meets the goal of each phase. Goals are set by pro rules for each step of the craft. The tool is named SurgGoal. It checks if the goal is met, not if the words match a key. That is a more true test for safe use.
arxiv-2601-10655:
Carlo Cafaro and James Schneeloch take a symmetry-based look at quantum search. The continuous-time form of Grover's search uses a fixed Hamiltonian, an energy rule that steers the system. The search path stays inside a flat plane spanned by the start and target states. Within that plane, the motion has a clean shape.

The authors note a sharp limit: the search fails when start and target states are orthogonal, at right angles in state space. They frame the dynamics through Schrödinger's equation between such states. The view clarifies why some searches stall before they start. It gives quantum algorithm designers a geometric check on when Hamiltonian search can work.
arxiv-2601-10755:
Richard Evan Schwartz writes a personal, hands-on account of Boy's surface. Boy's surface is a famous immersed copy of the projective plane in three-dimensional space. It twists through itself in ways that defy easy mental pictures. Schwartz admits his own past tries to grasp it faded fast. The image would form, then slip away without a trace.

His paper is a fresh attempt to build the surface and hold it steady. The tone is that of a working geometer thinking aloud. Readers get both the construction and an honest record of struggle with a classic object. It suits anyone who has met a math shape that refuses to sit still in the mind.
arxiv-2601-11155:
Harald Garcke, Kei Fong Lam, Robert Nurnberg, and Andrea Signori model protocell growth. Their 2026 preprint uses a Mullins-Sekerka model with reactions. Protocells are simple cell-like drops from before true life. How they grew and split is a core puzzle of early life.

With reactions in play, drops can grow in the model. A grown drop can lose stability and then divide. The cycle of grow, split, grow can then repeat. Such cycles give chemical compartments, tiny walled spaces for reactions. Living systems rely on such compartments to stay organized. The team tests stability of the cycle and runs numeric trials. That checks when the grow-and-divide loop can hold up.
arxiv-2601-11255:
Yuling Shi and six coauthors improve search-based answers to hard questions. Their 2026 preprint is on multi-hop question answering with RAG. Multi-hop questions need facts chained across more than one source. Retrieval-augmented generation pulls texts in to help a model answer.

Most current methods let the model guide its own search path. The model plans each step and writes the next query. That self-guidance can break the chain of thought midway. Poor splits of the question let errors grow from step to step. The team's tree-based reasoning aims to hold the chain firm. A tree can keep more than one path in play at once.
arxiv-2601-11355:
Jagadis Nayak, Aviad Frydman, and Gopi Daptary join two exotic materials. Their 2026 preprint links a topological insulator to a disordered superconductor. The insulator is BiSbTeSe2, a known surface-current material. The superconductor is amorphous indium oxide, a messy film.

The pair forms a hybrid interface for the tests. Resistance and temperature runs show superconducting signs at low heat. The signs persist when the oxide sits in an insulating state. That hints that superconducting links survive the disorder. The effect is called proximity-induced superconductivity in the work. Such hybrids probe how surface states and pairing interact. They may guide designs for fault-tolerant quantum parts.
arxiv-2601-11555:
Triloki Nath, Manohar Choudhary, and Ram Pandey extend the Heron problem. Their 2026 preprint defines a generalized k, m Heron problem. The classical Heron problem seeks a shortest total path. A point must touch given sets with least summed distance.

The new form uses k feasible sets and m target sets. All sets are nonempty, closed, and convex in n-space. The task seeks an optimal configuration among them all. Optimality conditions state when a configuration cannot improve. An algorithm computes the optimum under those conditions. Heron-type tasks arise in facility siting and path design. More sets make the model fit real networks better.
arxiv-2601-11755:
Wenjing Chen, Yixin Chen, and Victoria G. Crawford study fair picks from large sets. In many tasks, data split by kind into groups that do not overlap. A good pick must stay fair or balanced across those groups, not just score well as a whole.

They build methods with two goals at once for this cover task. One goal is a good score, and the other is to meet the group rules well. Such two-goal methods are called bicriteria in the field. The work gives a way to trade a bit of one goal to gain much in the other, with proof of the bounds.
arxiv-2601-12055:
Lina Meyer, Felix Wissel, Tobias Knopp, and their co-authors set key choices for a label-free image cleaner in an automatic way. The cleaner, deep image prior, needs no training set. Its skill rests on net form and on when to stop its steps.

Tuning those choices by hand for each new image is slow. Their tool moves choices from past, like images to new ones. The test case is fluorescence microscopy, used in cell labs. Fast auto-tuning could let the cleaner run on large image batches.  Auto picks could also cut hand work for lab staff.
arxiv-2601-12155:
Xiang Gao, Xinmu Wang, Yuanpeng Liu, and their co-authors rebuild 3D objects from images with help from topology. Rebuilding is ill-posed, since shape, look, and topology can each be read in many ways from flat views. High-genus objects, with many holes, are the hard case.

They add persistent homology priors to inverse rendering. Those priors pin the hole count and shape class while views fit the rest. A firm topology prior can stop smooth but wrong rebuilds. The work targets meshes for design and scans.  High genus shapes test the prior more than plain shapes.
arxiv-2601-12355:
Beicheng Xu and four co authors aim to make machine learning easier for non experts. A key task is to pick a good algorithm and tune its settings. That joint task is known as the CASH problem. Tools that solve it can spare users a long trial and error search.
