One classic tool is Bayesian optimization, but it can start cold with no good first guesses. Large language models can help here, since they bring prior sense of what may work. The team blends the two in a method called LB-MCTS. The mix is meant to make the search both fast and well guided from the start.
arxiv-2601-12855:
Yao Dong, Xin-Yao Huang, and Guo-Feng Zhang demonstrate nonreciprocal light transmission in an optomechanical system. Nonreciprocity means light passes one way but not the reverse. Their platform is driven by three mode parametric interactions. It handles both intense classical fields and weak quantum signals.

The platform is modular and reconfigurable. Each three mode optomechanical system serves as a fundamental building block. A single block already achieves nonreciprocity for classical fields. One way light control is key for isolators and circulators in photonics. Extending it to quantum signals serves quantum networks. Blocks that combine could build larger nonreciprocal devices on demand.
arxiv-2601-12955:
Premashis Kumar, Massimiliano Esposito, and Timur Aslyamov sort the ways a classic chemical model can go unstable. The model is the Brusselator, a toy system of two chemicals that react and spread. Their form of it is nonideal and keeps honest books on heat and energy. It adds the push and pull between molecules in both the spread and the reactions.

They then recheck a known scheme that sorts such instabilities into types. For each type, they ask if it can occur in this stricter model, and what it looks like. Push from entropy and pull from energy trade off to pick the winner. Spots, stripes, and waves in real chemicals start from such instabilities. A model that keeps its physics honest gives forecasts users can trust more.
arxiv-2601-13355:
Tawfiq Ammari and Samantha Gilgan study how folks with misophonia meet tech that can set off their traits. Misophonia is a state where set sounds, or cues tied to them, spark strong ill feels. It is still poorly known in clinics, yet it can shape a whole day.

The team ran sixteen semi structured talks with folks in the United States who live with it. They ask how such folks use, shun, or bend tech that boosts their trigger sounds. Shun is a key act, a form of non use by design. For tech teams, the finds call for sound picks and mute paths that do not force a hard pick of all or none.
arxiv-2601-13455:
Mohamed Moussadek Maiza builds a deformation theory that turns quasi Poisson forms into Poisson forms, and links it to 2D field theory. A deformation eases one math form into a next by a smooth path. His path starts with Hamiltonian quasi Poisson manifolds, a loose form used in gauge work.

It ends with Hamiltonian Poisson manifolds, the firm form, with worn cases let in. The theory also spans singular cases that spring from symplectic implosion, a cut down of a gauge space. Maiza shows the imploded cross section of a double deforms to the implosion of a cotangent form. Such bridges let tools proved on one side cross to the next.
arxiv-2601-13855: Jan Moser works on Jacob's ladders, a tool tied to the zeta function and prime counts, in work that assumes the Riemann hypothesis. The focus is the Ingham integral from 1932 and the point where its remainder term meets the Fermat-Wiles theorem. Moser proves that some increments of the integral exist with special traits. They yield new functionals and new forms of that famed theorem. The paper also adds fresh puzzles on sets of integrals.
arxiv-2601-14055:
Andrea Protani and co-authors locate brain tumors in multi-modal MRI with a new graph method in 2026. Modern vision backbones for 3D medical imaging process dense voxel grids. They use parameter-heavy encoder-decoder structures to rebuild space in detail. That design spends many parameters on spatial reconstruction rather than feature learning.

Their SVGFormer is a decoder-free pipeline for the task. A content-aware grouping stage partitions the volume into a semantic graph of supervoxels. Supervoxels are small, like-minded chunks of the scan. A graph neural network then reasons over that graph to find the tumor. Leaner models could scan faster while keeping accuracy.
arxiv-2601-14255:
Sangbeom Lim, Seoung Wug Oh, Jiahui Huang, and their co-authors present VideoMaMa in this 2026 paper. The topic is video matting, the task of cutting a subject out of each frame with soft, exact edges. The output is an alpha matte, a map of how clear each pixel is. Good matting models are hard to train for real-world clips.

The main block is a lack of labeled data. VideoMaMa starts from coarse segmentation masks, rough maps of where the subject is. It turns them into pixel-exact mattes. To do so, it draws on pretrained video diffusion models, which bring strong prior knowledge of how real scenes look and move.
arxiv-2601-14555:
Botong Ou and Baijian Yang work on Internet of Things security in this 2026 paper. IoT connectivity keeps expanding and brings quality-of-life gains around the world. It also introduces growing privacy and security concerns. One root problem is a lack of clear definition for managing shared and protected access to IoT sensors.

Without that definition, channels open by which devices can be compromised and sensitive data leaked. The authors present a WebAssembly based portable and secure sensor interface. WebAssembly gives a sandboxed, portable runtime for sensor access code. Readers get an interface design meant to let many apps share sensors without opening the door to leaks.
arxiv-2601-14755:
Lei Xie, Peilan Wang, and Guanxiong Shen study secure wireless links in this 2026 paper. They investigate movable antennas as a way to enhance physical layer security. The setting is a MIMOME system: multiple-input, multiple-output, with a multiple-antenna eavesdropper. Movable antennas can shift position to favor the true receiver over the eavesdropper.

The scenario is practical. The transmitter has imperfect eavesdropper channel state information. It knows only the instantaneous line-of-sight component, plus the statistical properties of the non-line-of-sight component. In plain terms, secrecy must hold with partial knowledge of the spy's channel. The work is a design, not a test on live air. It shows what can be kept safe when facts are thin. Readers get a security design that works under that honest limit.
arxiv-2601-14955:
Hanqi Jin, Gaoming Yang, and co-authors study how shoppers behave on e-commerce sites. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with recommendation, the art of guessing what a user wants next. A shopper may click, save, add to cart, or buy an item.

Each act means something different. The shifts between acts say a lot about intent and changing taste. The authors build a model that tracks these behavior sequences. A graph attention network in the model is made fully aware of the shifts between one small act and the very next act.
arxiv-2601-15055:
Isaac Baglin, Xiatian Zhu, and Simon Hadfield attack federated learning from a fresh angle. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with deep leakage, where a foe rebuilds private data from shared model updates. Most defenses try to block that rebuild.

The usual guards add noise, scramble data, or encrypt it. Yet they can still leak broad facts, such as class mixes or feature patterns. Strong denoising attacks often break them in the end. The authors present SpooFL here, a novel spoofing approach that takes a quite different path from pure blocking alone.
arxiv-2601-15255:
Prithak Bhattarai, Andrew Brandt, and a large collaboration lay out the design of a new accelerator experiment. Their 2026 arXiv white paper presents DAMSA, short for Dark Messenger Searches at an Accelerator. The experiment uses a short baseline at an accelerator site.

DAMSA hunts for short-lived processes in particle physics. Its targets include signs of a dark sector, a hidden family of particles. It also seeks well-motivated signals inside the standard model itself. As a conceptual design paper, the text sets out the detector, the main goals, and the physics case.
arxiv-2601-15355:
Anuj Bathla, Subrat Kumar Pradhan, and a large team photograph electric current inside a diamond transistor. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with field-effect transistors built on hydrogen-terminated diamond, layered with hexagonal boron nitride. Seeing the current's path helps engineers judge the device.

The team uses wide-field quantum diamond microscopy for the image. Nitrogen-vacancy centers inside the substrate act as tiny magnetic sensors. Their readings map the magnetic field of the flowing current. From that map, the team reconstructs how current moves through the transistor while it runs live in the lab.
arxiv-2601-15455:
Patrycja Balik, Szymon Jędras, and Piotr Polesiuk revisit a landmark algorithm from programming language theory. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the 1991 work of Jouvelot and Gifford. That work gave an algebraic way to reconstruct types and effects in a program.

A type-and-effect system tracks what a program returns and what side effects it may cause. The 1991 algorithm is a milestone in that area. It has inspired much later work in static analysis. The authors offer remarks on its algebraic structure, clarifying the firm foundations the classic 1991 algorithm rests firmly on.
arxiv-2601-15755:
Tristan Williams, Franziska Weeber, Sebastian Padó, and Alan Akbik critique how aligned language models are judged in a 2026 arXiv paper. Models are often steered to match the opinions of demographic groups. Most checks compare marginal response distributions. Each survey item is treated on its own. Matching item-by-item averages is essential, the authors grant. It may still miss deeper structure.

Real populations hold latent patterns that tie answers together. Cultural values theories describe exactly those patterns. A model can match every single item yet miss the whole worldview. The authors build a framework to test representativeness beyond marginals. For anyone using models as stand-ins for public opinion, that deeper check is the difference between a poll and a caricature.
arxiv-2601-15955:
Stacey Alberts and a large team present mid-infrared survey data in a 2026 arXiv paper. The data are part of JADES Data Release 5. They come from JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument, MIRI, in coordinated parallel observations. The fields are GOODS-S and GOODS-N. Medium to ultra-deep mid-infrared imaging is reframing views of the early universe, the authors note. It reveals ultra-red dusty galaxies and quiet, quiescent ones.

The view extends to the epoch of reionization and the first galaxies. Mid-infrared light shows what near-infrared views miss. Dusty systems hide at shorter wavelengths. Coordinated parallels gather data while another instrument leads, doubling the science per hour. Data release papers document these sets so the whole community can use them well.
arxiv-2601-16355:
Suhong Moon and four coauthors study self, joint work and frame shifts in groups. Their 2026 preprint mixes real folk and fake folk in group games. Games are of the social trap type, where self gain clashes with group gain. Human acts rest on both clear thought and self and frame cues. The team asks if large models fake those human acts well.

They test model acts next to real acts in the same games. Like acts would back use of models as test folk. Split acts would mark where fakes break from real thought. The work helps teams judge sims of group life. It ties self cues to joint work scores.
arxiv-2601-16755:
Rohit Gheyi and a team of five co-authors hunt build flaws that hide in rare setups. Big software can switch parts on or off by flags. Some mixes of flags break the build at compile time. Tests oft miss those rare mixes. Their 2026 preprint pairs big AI models with this hunt.

The models scan code with its flag rules in view. They flag mixes that are apt to break. They then draft fixes for the breaks they find. This could save teams from late, costly build shocks. It suits cars, phones, and cloud tools with many flag paths.
arxiv-2601-16955:
Roman Poletukhin, Marcel Kollovieh, Eike Eberhard, and Stephan Günnemann build 3D molecules from stiff parts. Most AI builders place atoms one by one. Drug work oft thinks in chunks, not lone atoms. Their 2026 preprint treats chunks as stiff blocks. Each block keeps its shape as the build goes on. Flows then place the blocks in 3D space.

Their frame grows from frame-based work on proteins. It now serves plain molecules of all sorts. Block builds keep known good chunks whole. That speeds the hunt for new drugs and stuff. Labs can screen block-built forms for worth.
arxiv-2601-17355:
Yi Lyu, Shichun Yu, and Joe Catudal present Safeguard, a security layer for software defined networks. Such networks let apps set and change policy at line speed. Data can drive those changes as needs shift. That speed is a gain, but it holds a risk. Bad or odd data can push policy too far. Over-correction can cause harm no one meant.

Safeguard puts security controls at the network layer itself. Controls watch for shifts that go past safe bounds. The goal is fast change without loss of grip. Network teams gain a guard that moves at the same pace as policy. The work fits a world where networks re-shape themselves in real time.
arxiv-2601-17455:
Sagar Mahapatra and co-authors study a disordered crystal with a long chemical name, BaCu one-third Ta two-thirds O3. Copper ions carry spin one-half. They share a pseudo-cubic lattice with tantalum at random. X-ray tools map the local disorder in detail. They show tight structural limits on magnetic exchange paths. No magnetic order or spin freezing shows down to 0.1 kelvin.

That calm points to emergent random spin singlets. Spins pair up in random bonds rather than one set pattern. Such states test theories of quantum magnetism. They may host traits sought for new materials. The work shows how disorder can create order of a new kind. It guides hunts for like states in kin compounds.
arxiv-2601-17555:
Justin Downes, Sam Saltwick, and Anthony Chen use image salience to compress satellite photos. Satellites gather hundreds of terabytes of images each day. Storage and bandwidth costs climb with that flood. Most users care about small regions of each image. The rest can be stored with less detail. The authors preprocess images by salience to guide compression.

Saliency marks the parts viewers and tasks need most. Sharp storage there, lean storage elsewhere, saves space. Savings let archives keep more scenes in reach. They also speed image transfer to field teams. The industrial paper targets real pipelines. It weighs quality where it counts, not pixels in the abstract.
arxiv-2601-17655:
A. Madhav Sai Kumar and co-authors study instabilities in drying colloidal films. When suspensions dry, particles deposit in complex patterns. Cracks and delamination often spoil the film. The team tests sessile droplets with silica nanoparticles. They vary particle surface charge and substrate wettability together. Both traits shape how the drop dries.

They track evaporation dynamics and final deposit shape. Crack patterns are part of the record. Coupled effects matter because real coatings vary both at once. Paints, inks, and printed films all face these flaws. Knowing which mix cracks worst guides better formulas. The study gives makers a map of charge and surface effects.
arxiv-2601-17855:
Zixi Chen and co-authors name a hidden waste in how large language models are served. Their 2026 preprint reports that over forty percent of compute power can be lost to load imbalance. The loss is not a hardware limit. Serving systems run workers in lockstep, and each step waits for the slowest worker. Workloads differ and shift, so stragglers keep appearing while fast workers sit idle and draw power.

The authors propose a universal load balancing rule and apply it to model serving. A better split of work across workers cuts the idle time. The gain is free capacity in data centers that are already built. At the scale of modern AI services, that saving is large in both cost and energy.
arxiv-2601-17955:
Chandranathan Anandavijayan and Pallavi Bhat test a new story for how magnetic turbulence dies away. Their 2026 preprint studies systems where magnetic energy rules. Such turbulence shows a robust flow of energy toward large scales, even with no net magnetic helicity. That flow clashes with the standard picture of cascades to small scales. Recent work points to magnetic reconnection, the snapping and rejoining of field lines, as the driver.

The team probes that claim with two tools. They track how the spectrum evolves, and they study the current sheets where reconnection happens. Both tests check whether reconnection sets the pace of decay. The answer matters for plasmas in space, stars, and fusion devices.
arxiv-2601-18055: Christian Koke studies what happens when one term of an operator family is scaled up without bound. His 2026 preprint follows operators of the form A plus beta times B as beta tends to infinity. The family converges toward an effective operator defined on the kernel of B. The result shows how a strong constraint term forces the whole system onto a smaller space.
arxiv-2601-18155:
Aman Desai, Amelia Lovison, and Paul Jackson present a method to rebuild a fleeting bound state of two top quarks. Their 2026 preprint deals with toponium. Results from the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider point to a top-antitop bound state near the threshold where pairs are born. The state decays almost at once, so its traces are faint. The authors use Recursive Jigsaw Reconstruction to piece the state back together from its decay products.

Jigsaw methods split a messy event into frames that can each be read more clearly. Rebuilding toponium tests our grasp of the heaviest known particle. It also opens a new window on how quarks bind at extreme mass.
arxiv-2601-18255:
Fei Meng studies how language models can keep learning without losing what they know. His 2026 preprint addresses continual learning. The core tension is between stability, holding old knowledge, and plasticity, picking up new tasks. Experience replay is a standard guard against catastrophic forgetting: old examples are mixed back into training. Yet its effects across the many skills of a large model remain underexplored, as Meng notes.

The title promises more than retention. It speaks of orchestrating structural safety alongside plasticity. That framing treats forgetting as a design problem, not just a data one. The study serves anyone who must update a deployed model over time.
arxiv-2601-18355:
Mauro Bonafini, Van Phu Cuong Le, and Riccardo Molinarolo study wave math in a space whose walls move with time. A wave in a fixed box is hard enough. Here the box can grow or shrink as the wave runs, and the wave must die at the walls at all times. The team asks when such a setup still has a sound answer that maths can trust.

They give two paths to the same end. One builds the answer step by step in small time hops. The next bends the rules with a soft fine that fades as the hops shrink. Both paths land on a weak but real answer under mild rules on how the walls may move. Work like this backs models of waves in tanks, tubes, and rooms that change shape in use.
arxiv-2601-18455:
Yihan Chen, Jialin He, and Tianying Xie work on a count task in the maths of large sparse sets. Take a set of points with a rule for which groups of points count as a full set. The set is called full when each new group you add breaks a banned shape. The task asks for the least count of groups a full set can hold.

The banned shape here is a tight knot of four points with all links among them, in a three-way form of the graph world. The team pin down that least count, or bind it tight, for the case at hand. Counts like these map the edge between sparse and dense. They show how thin a set can be while it still blocks the banned shape at each step.
arxiv-2601-18555:
Roberto Di Via and four colleagues teach a tool to find key points on hip scans in two kinds of image. Care for a hip fault rests in part on angles staff read off X-ray shots. Those angles flag a fault where the hip ball and its socket clash. But the full size and span of the clash need a three-dim view, which a deep scan can give.

A tool that finds the same points in both kinds of shot would let staff blend the two views. The X-ray gives the quick angles. The deep scan gives the span. The team test if their marks hold up when the kind of shot swaps. A firm cross test could cut hand work and make hip calls more even across clinics. It could also help plan cuts with both views in hand.
arxiv-2601-18955:
Ryan Flynn and Anders W. Sandvik study magnetism in two thin layers twisted against each other. When two sheets sit at a slight twist, a moiré pattern forms and the pull between the layers waxes and wanes across the sheet. That uneven pull can breed patchy magnetic textures.

The pair use a simple model of spins on the two layers, called a bilayer Ising model. The twist, or a slight strain in one sheet, sets the pattern of the pull. Their simple setup lets them map how the textures form without the clutter of a full material model.
arxiv-2601-19255:
Haoting Zhang and Shekhar Jain turn expert rules into anomaly detectors for supply chains. Spotting odd time series early lets managers act before shortages or gluts grow. Classic detectors learn from data alone and often flag patterns that clash with business sense, while hand review cannot scale to millions of products.

Their method uses language models to learn logic rules from human experts, then applies those rules at scale. The blend keeps the judgment of experts and the reach of software. Supply chains are the test case, but any field with scarce experts faces the same trade.
arxiv-2601-20255:
Yueyang Wang and four colleagues propose HE-SNR, a way to guide the mid-training of large language models for software tasks. SWE-bench is the standard test of model skill on real coding problems. The skills it tests are mostly built during mid-training, then drawn out by later fine-tuning.

The authors argue that good metrics to steer mid-training are missing. Their approach uses entropy to uncover latent logic in training data, and a signal-to-noise view to judge its value. Better mid-training guidance could raise coding skill without simply adding more data or compute.
arxiv-2601-20355:
Yue Liang and four colleagues present CURVE, a framework for scene understanding that resists spurious correlations. Scene graphs describe an image as objects and relations, a structured view that helps reasoning. But models overfit to patterns that happen to hold in training data, which harms them on new distributions.

CURVE is inspired by causality and joins variational uncertainty modeling with uncertainty-guided structural regularization. The design suppresses relations that vary a lot between environments, keeping those that look stable. More robust scene graphs would help robots and image systems act sensibly in places unlike their training data.
arxiv-2601-20455:
Thomas Eiter, Robert Lasarzik, and Marcel Śliwiński prove a new existence result for energy-variational solutions of evolution equations. Their result covers a general class of partial differential equations that change in time. Compared with earlier work on this solution concept, the advance is twofold, concerning weaker demands on the regularity weight and energies with merely linear growth.

They also discuss selection criteria for choosing among solutions. Applications include fluid dynamics systems such as the Euler-Korteweg system and binormal curvature flow. Broader existence results let modelers use this flexible solution concept for more physical systems. In plain terms, more flows now have a proof that a path through time exists at all. That is the ground on which the rest of the field stands.
arxiv-2601-20555:
Wadhah Zai El Amri and Nicolás Navarro-Guerrero present Vibro-Sense, a way for robot hands to feel touch through vibration. Rich contact sensing is crucial for manipulation, yet traditional tactile skins are expensive and hard to integrate. Their alternative localizes touch and tracks its path using vibro-acoustic signals.

Seven low-cost piezoelectric microphones are fitted to the hand. An audio spectrogram transformer decodes the vibration patterns made during physical contact. Cheap whole-hand touch could give warehouse and service robots the feedback they need to handle objects gently, without costly skins. The mics are cheap parts, not custom lab gear.
arxiv-2601-20655:
June Chen and four colleagues present OnePiece, a large distributed inference system with RDMA networking for AI-generated content workflows. AI generation now produces high-quality creative work across many domains. Yet existing systems waste throughput, resources, and scalability when many multi-stage jobs run at once.

OnePiece is optimized for those staged workflows, where the output of one model feeds the next. RDMA networking moves data between machines with low delay. Faster shared infrastructure would lower the cost of image, video, and media generation services as demand grows. The aim is more work done on the same racks of chips, with less time lost in line.
arxiv-2601-20855:
Sebastiano Monti and four co-authors test how well AI models plan far ahead. Their 2026 paper presents SokoBench, a benchmark for long-horizon planning and reasoning. The name nods to Sokoban, the classic box-pushing puzzle. Large language models have been tested hard on complex reasoning. Their long-horizon planning, though, has not been studied as closely. The team set out to assess it in a systematic way.

The benchmark targets state-of-the-art large reasoning models. Long-horizon tasks need many steps that stay consistent to the end. One early error can ruin the whole plan. SokoBench measures where models break down as plans lengthen. That gives developers a clear view of a weak spot. Better planning tests are a step toward agents that can carry out long jobs alone.
arxiv-2601-21155:
Oleksandr Tomalak and five co-authors extract a key nucleon property from antineutrino scattering data. Their 2026 paper concerns the nucleon axial-vector form factor. That form factor, called G_A, governs how leptons interact weakly with protons and neutrons. Processes it shapes include elastic antineutrino-nucleon scattering and muon capture by the proton. Knowing G_A precisely is critical for neutrino physics. Experiments worth billions depend on it.

The authors apply radiative corrections to the scattering data. Such corrections account for photons emitted during the interaction. Ignoring them biases the extracted form factor. From the corrected data they also derive the axial radius of the nucleon. That radius measures the size of the nucleon's weak charge. The work sharpens inputs for neutrino oscillation experiments. It is careful phenomenology in service of big detectors.
arxiv-2601-21455:
Yizhou Min, Yizhou Lu, Lanqi Li, Zhen Zhang, and Jiaye Teng question a standard way of grading uncertainty forecasts. Conformal prediction gives intervals with a promised coverage rate. Shorter intervals are usually judged better, since they look sharper while keeping the promise.

The authors show that interval length can be gamed. A trick they name the prejudicial trick makes intervals look shorter while coverage stays valid on paper. The catch is that the gain is not real sharpness. Their warning matters because these intervals guide medical, financial, and safety choices, where fake precision can do real harm.
arxiv-2601-21755:
Younoussa Sow, Nicolas Anquetil, Léandre Brault, and Stéphane Ducasse migrate a legacy language extension to modern Fortran by model transformations. Old Fortran still runs vital industrial code. Moving it to the two thousand eight standard is hard, and house extensions make it harder.

Extensions like Esope carry semantics rooted in old limits and domain logic that no manual records well. The authors transform models of the code rather than rewriting by hand. Automated transformation preserves meaning while updating the form. The approach offers industry a safer path to modernize code that plants and labs still depend on daily.
arxiv-2601-21955:
Fariba Afrin Irany explores whether generative language models can classify hospital patients from their records. Electronic health records hold vast amounts of unstructured clinical narrative. Those notes could support disease characterization, finding patient cohorts, and clinical decision support, if machines could read them well.

Long, specialized clinical text is hard to model, labeled examples are limited, and disease classes are heavily imbalanced. Irany's 2026 preprint presents a GPT-based architecture that moves from generative modeling to clinical classification of these notes. Success would help hospitals surface at-risk patients. It would help them build research cohorts. No armies of manual chart reviewers would be needed. Still, the stakes demand careful checks before any clinical use.
arxiv-2601-22055:
Yaxin Du and co-authors build a question answering system for long, mixed documents. Retrieval-augmented generation answers questions over long documents, but it stays brittle when text, tables, and figures are interleaved across many pages. Flat chunking, the usual preparation, breaks the document's native structure.

Chunks cut loose from their tables and figures become fragments that are hard to interpret alone. The team's 2026 preprint proposes a reader built on dual evolving graphs, structures that track both the document's layout and its meaning as reading proceeds. Reports, manuals, and papers are inherently multimodal, so a reader that respects that structure could answer with far fewer confident mistakes.
arxiv-2601-22355:
Binshuai Wang and Peng Wei add two new yardsticks for how far a data spread sits from a bell curve. Their 2026 preprint works in the frame of optimal transport, which prices the cost of reshaping one spread into another. They use the cone shape of that space to define an angle and a gap.

The angle tells how off-bell the spread leans; the gap gives its distance to the best bell fit. Both rest on the mean and spread of the data. Such tools help analysts judge when bell-based methods are safe. They give a clean, geometric read on shape.
arxiv-2601-22855:
Cécile Mailler and Zoé Varin study a math model of ants finding the shortest path to food. In the model, ants wander a graph between a nest and a food source, two marked points. They cannot talk to each other; they only leave scent trails as they explore.

The authors analyze this process on a family of graphs built from triangles in series and parallel. Such models show how simple local rules can solve a global search problem. The results inform both biology and the design of search algorithms that copy ant behavior.
arxiv-2601-22955:
M. Schubert and four co-authors study a cold gas of magnetic atoms squeezed into thin shapes. The atoms pull on each other over long range, and not equally in all directions. In such low-dimensional setups, the gas can form either solitons, lone stable waves, or quantum droplets, self-bound drops.

In one dimension the switch between those states can be abrupt or smooth, depending on conditions. The authors map how the crossover plays out in one and two dimensions. These gases are clean labs for studying matter that holds itself together.
arxiv-2601-23055:
Marek Kosiek and Krzysztof Rudol describe the spectrum of the bidual of a uniform algebra. A uniform algebra is a closed family of functions with a strong form of convergence. Its bidual is a larger algebra built by applying a duality step twice, and its spectrum is the set of its basic evaluation-like points.

They show that this spectrum is a quotient of the hyper-Stonean envelope of the original spectrum. The result links abstract algebra structure with topology. Such descriptions help analysts understand how function spaces behave under duality.
arxiv-2601-23155:
Powei Chang and a large team select training data for language models using information theory. Picking examples that maximize the log-determinant of Fisher information is attractive, because that objective is submodular. Submodularity lets greedy algorithms provably reach a large share of the best possible gain under a size budget.

Their SPICE method adds penalized conflict handling to that selection. The goal is efficient training: fewer, better-chosen examples for the same final quality. Careful data choice can cut the cost of instruction tuning sharply. A cardinality budget keeps selection honest: the method must choose a fixed-size set, not quietly use more data.
arxiv-2601-23255:
Ye Yu and four co-authors attack large audio-language models through spoken stories. These models take raw speech as input for assistants, education, and clinical triage. Moving from text to audio opens a new class of weaknesses that is still poorly mapped.

Their jailbreak converts text to audio and hides disallowed directives inside a narrative stream. A story format can slip instructions past filters tuned for plain text commands. The study tells builders that voice interfaces need their own safety testing. Narrative-style audio is the delivery vehicle, wrapping disallowed directives in story form to evade text-oriented safeguards.
arxiv-2602-00155: Robyn L. Munoz and coauthors present aurel, a free Python package for auto relativity math. It tracks what depends on what, with a cache that suits the tangled math of general relativity. One side adds tensor math to SymPy for work with symbols. The other side works out curvature and matter kinematics from space and matter data by finite difference methods. Inputs can be math formulas or data from standard relativity simulations, with helpers to read common codes.
arxiv-2602-00255: Richard Cleve and Alex May give new lower bounds on entanglement cost in non-local quantum computation. Their two techniques, based on controllable correlation and controllable entanglement, can be evaluated for any unitary. For Haar random two qubit unitaries they typically give non trivial bounds. They also bound most common two qubit gates, including CNOT, DCNOT, square root of SWAP, and the XX interaction, none previously bounded. For CNOT, one technique gives a tight bound, fully settling its entanglement cost.
arxiv-2602-00455: Xiangdi Huang and team establish the global existence of strong solutions to the 2D and 3D compressible Navier-Stokes-Korteweg system with arbitrarily large initial data on the torus. That system, derived by Dunn and Serrin, is widely used for modeling capillarity in compressible fluids. Through an original modified Nash-Moser type iteration, the authors establish a critical new estimate linking effective velocity to the lower bound of the density. That estimate is crucial for deriving a positive lower bound on density.
arxiv-2602-00755: Ujwal Kumar and colleagues present Constitutional Evolution, a way to find behavioural norms in multi-agent language-model systems. Fixed rules for single models fail amid emergent social dynamics, so they test norms in a grid-world test under survival pressure. Welfare is scored by a Societal Stability Score combining output, survival, and conflict. Evolved rules from genetic programming with multi-island search reach 0.556, end conflict, and find that minimal talk beats verbose teamwork. Cooperative norms, the authors show, can be found rather than set.
arxiv-2602-01055: Bo Deng and co-authors set the base mark for a 2026 ultrasound base-model contest with 27 sub-jobs. Ultrasound scans vary a lot by body part and by scan setup, and most past tools serve one job only, so they fail as broad clinic models. Their one-net plan pairs an EfficientNet-B4 base with a pyramid net, routing broad jobs to high sense cues and dense jobs to fine place cues. Tests show the plan works well and gives later work a firm mark to beat.
arxiv-2602-01255: Junior da Silva Bessa and co-authors prove smoothness results for minimizers in the thin obstacle problem inside Orlicz spaces. They show minimizers stay Lipschitz smooth and their slopes stay Holder smooth, leaning on De Giorgi's classic smoothness toolkit. As a side gain, their proofs chart the shape of minimizers' zero sets. The work widens classic smoothness lore to Orlicz growth, where power-law rules no longer rule.
arxiv-2602-01755: Luis Varona studies bandwidth for graphs, where a graph has bandwidth at most k when adjacent labels differ by at most k. Dynamic programs take time and space like n to the power k, polynomial for small k but superexponential as k grows. Varona recasts it as bipartite matching for k at least about half of n. Using Hall's theorem he builds one running in time like n to the power n minus k plus one, with linear space. That gives polynomial whenever k or n minus k stays small.
arxiv-2602-01955: Yuchen Yang and colleagues study rotating Bose gases at the lowest Landau level, where an extended strip initial state shows interaction driven instability. In the low density limit, mean field Gross Pitaevskii theory fails, so the team uses exact diagonalisation. Behavior traces to weakly interacting repulsively bound few body clusters, with signatures in observable values oscillating at frequencies of few body bound states. A semiclassical cluster theory predicts cloud width growing as a power law in log time. This slow thermalisation of bound clusters forms quantum many body scars.
arxiv-2602-02155: Yamaan Attwa and colleagues sharpen a lower bound for multicolour Ramsey numbers by swapping the random graph inside an earlier construction. Earlier work by Conlon and Ferber, then Wigderson and Sawin, improved the asymptotic bounds using blowups of an unbalanced binomial random graph. This short note uses a random sphere graph instead. That model was recently applied by Ma, Shen, and Xie to two-colour off-diagonal bounds. The substitution yields an exponential improvement, showing that sphere-graph geometry buys real power in this extremal setting.
arxiv-2602-02455:
Han Bao and 5 co-authors build a benchmark for what happens when users give AI agents flawed instructions, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Real inputs often hide intent, omit parameters, assume false facts, or stay ambiguous. Text-only tests miss the execution risks that follow when an agent can act over multiple turns.

Drift-Bench evaluates agents through multi-turn clarification in state-oriented and service-oriented environments. A taxonomy of cooperative breakdowns, grounded in classical communication theory, organizes the fault types. A persona-driven user simulator and the Rise evaluation protocol run the interactions. Experiments show substantial performance drops under input faults. Clarification success varied widely across personas and fault types. The benchmark gives agent builders a diagnostic tool for failures that could otherwise become unsafe executions.
arxiv-2602-02555:
Bizhe Bai and 3 co-authors push language model exploration by shaking the model's parameters instead of its outputs, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often reweights solution traces the model already produces, hitting a ceiling at large sampling budgets. Action-space noise breaks the flow of long reasoning chains.

Their method perturbs policy parameters before each rollout, yielding trajectory-level exploration that stays steady within an attempt. Truncated importance sampling corrects the mismatch this creates between sampling and updates. A lightweight scheduler, driven by semantic diversity and normalized self-certainty, replaces costly divergence-based noise control. Built on a widely used group tuning method, the approach widened the effective reasoning frontier across math benchmarks and model families. Gains were largest at big sampling budgets, and the method stacks with other exploration methods.
arxiv-2602-03155:
Can chatbots be designed to be virtuous? Matthew P. Lad and a pair of co-authors investigate that question during 2026. Criticism of large language models' societal impact has grown with the models themselves. Responsible AI work has focused mainly on reducing harm. The authors instead bring wisdom traditions into design, applying a virtue-guided technology design method to language models.

The team catalogs new design patterns meant to guide chatbots toward virtue, then tests them in interviews with technologists. The testers liked the patterns for making models more accurate and sturdier, safer, open to wider access and control, and less wasteful. They also warned the patterns might invite jailbreaking, stretch one fix across too many cases, and prove hard to put in place. Their overall verdict was favorable, with the trade-offs named plainly.
arxiv-2602-03455:
Tesshu Hanaka and 2 co-authors study how many autonomous agents can share one network without a central controller. Their 2026 paper introduces multi-agent routing under crossing costs on mixed graphs. Instead of forbidding conflicts outright, the model charges a cost for head-on encounters, measured by how many agents traverse an edge in opposite directions.

Framed as a congestion game, the setting always admits a pure Nash equilibrium, an outcome no agent wants to leave alone. Equilibria are computable in polynomial time under mild conditions, though the general case is PLS-complete. Minimizing total crossing cost is NP-hard, so the authors design parameterized algorithms for structured instances, offering a foundation for decentralized, risk-aware coordination.
arxiv-2602-03555:
Segmenting organs in medical scans needs many hand-labeled images, which clinics rarely have. Chang Liu and 3 co-authors compare data augmentation strategies for that low-data setting in a 2026 paper. They test four inter-image methods, CutMix, CarveMix, ObjectAug, and AnatoMix, which build new training images by mixing separate patients' scans.

On two organ segmentation datasets, three of the four methods improve the average Dice score over a strong nnU-Net baseline with no augmentation. The simple CutMix wins, gaining nearly five points, even though its pasted composites look intuitively wrong to a human eye. Adding traditional within-image augmentation improves results further. The authors release their implementation as a benchmark for future work.
arxiv-2602-03655:
Giovanni Luca Marchetti and 4 co-authors use a clean puzzle to watch deep learning happen: multiplying a sequence of group elements in order. Their 2026 paper defines the sequential group composition task, where a network receives group elements encoded as vectors and must output their cumulative product. The task is order-sensitive and beyond any linear model.

The analysis separates the roles of sequence length, encoding statistics, and group structure. Two-layer networks from tiny initializations absorb one irreducible representation after another, in an order set by the encoding's Fourier statistics. Perfect learning that way needs width exponential in sequence length. Deeper designs exploit associativity instead: recurrent networks compose stepwise, and multilayer networks compose pairs in parallel with logarithmic depth.
arxiv-2602-03755:
Deep learning libraries are huge and buggy, and the fuzzers that hunt their bugs cry wolf without precise API specifications. Facundo Molina and 4 co-authors use machine learning to supply the missing judgment in a 2026 paper. Their hypothesis is that tensor shapes, abstracting away the actual numbers, capture the constraints an API places on its inputs.

Classifiers train on inputs labeled by observed runtime outcomes, learning which shapes each API accepts. Over 183 TensorFlow and PyTorch APIs, the classifiers generalize to unseen inputs with accuracy above ninety percent. Plugging them into ACETest, a state-of-the-art bug finder, more than doubles its pass rate, from about twenty-nine to about sixty-one percent. Learned input classification, they argue, is how library testing scales.
arxiv-2602-03855:
Le Minh Triet Tran and 5 co-authors bring classical optimization guarantees into learned solvers for inverse problems in a 2026 paper. Deep unrolling and meta-learning perform well in practice but offer little control over descent or curvature, which limits how robust they are. Their method instead learns inside the majorization-minimization scheme, a classical method with built-in descent guarantees.

Rather than learning a whole optimizer, the model learns a shaped curvature majorant that governs each step. A small recurrent network sets it, constrained to valid conditions. For cosine-similarity losses they derive explicit curvature bounds; otherwise, Hessian-vector products estimate the local curvature on their own. On EEG source imaging, the method improves accuracy, stability, and cross-dataset reach over unrolled and meta-learned baselines.
arxiv-2602-04055:
A sharp turn in the inflationary path can amplify ripples enormously. I. Dalianis and 2 co-authors describe that simple mechanism in a 2026 cosmology paper. In two-field inflation, the universe's expansion can proceed in two stages along different field directions, the second at much lower energy.

Fluctuations leaving the horizon during the rapid turn between stages grow by several orders of magnitude. The result is a peak in the power spectrum of primordial fluctuations. Such a peak can seed significant numbers of primordial black holes and secondary gravitational waves. The mechanism is intuitive and fits even simple two-field models, making it easy to explore.
arxiv-2602-04155:
Fairness across groups can be framed as negotiation. Jiwoo Han and 2 co-authors recast fair learning as a bargaining problem among groups sharing one predictor. Their 2026 paper shows familiar robust methods, like minimizing worst-group loss, in fact match classical bargaining solutions with distinct fairness principles.

Their proposal, maximin relative improvement, scores each group by the share of its possible gain that it actually gets. That yields the Kalai-Smorodinsky solution, prized for scale invariance and monotonicity. Absolute losses mislead when groups differ in how well they can be forecast. Finite-sample guarantees under mild conditions complete the case.
arxiv-2602-04455:
Marco Klann, Sven-Olaf Moch, and Kay Schönwald report a 2026 calculation in particle physics. Their subject is heavy-quark production in deep-inelastic scattering, where a high-energy probe strikes a target and reveals its inner structure.

The authors compute mathematical summaries called Mellin moments for two structure functions. They work at next-to-leading order in quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons. Their formulas keep the full effect of the heavy quark's mass. The results match known limits and earlier parametrizations, which are fitted descriptions of the same quantities. The setup also prepares a path toward still more precise calculations at the next order.
arxiv-2602-04755:
Xinyu Zhou and 4 co-authors teach language models to say they do not know in a 2026 paper on temporal question answering. Models rarely abstain, instead producing fluent but misleading answers. Time-sensitive questions expose this, since facts from different periods get conflated.

The authors frame abstention as a teachable skill. Their pipeline couples chain-of-thought supervision with reinforcement learning guided by abstention-aware rewards. A small model so trained beat a leading commercial model on exact match scores for both easy and hard temporal questions. Its detection of unanswerable questions also improved sharply over supervised fine-tuning alone. Yet analysis warned that both training styles can induce overconfidence, so reasoning and abstention need joint care.
arxiv-2602-04855:
Suchismita Roy, Alexander A. Fisher, and Jason Xu make epidemic model fitting tractable in a 2026 biostatistics paper. Stochastic compartmental models describe disease spread well, but fitting them to surveillance counts is hard when missing data make the exact likelihood impossible to compute.

Working within dynamical survival analysis, the authors develop a closed-form likelihood for counts seen at discrete times. The method replaces the population hazard with a large-population limit while keeping a count-valued stochastic model. Simulations showed estimates on par with recent exact but costly methods in partly seen settings. The approach extends to models with personal variation, such as frailty models. Case studies on Ebola and COVID-19 data, plus a network model, show its range.
arxiv-2602-04955:
Simulating quantum many-body systems is a long-standing challenge, because the state of such a system grows exponentially with its size. The work is by Belal Abouraya and 3 co-authors. Tensor networks, especially matrix product states, compress the state by tracking only its entanglement pattern. Even so, following a system whose rules change over time is costly.

The authors add a simple upgrade: average Hamiltonians, which fold the time dependence into a better effective rule for each step. The change lifts the method from first-order to second-order accuracy, so error shrinks much faster as steps shrink. They test it on chains of nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, a candidate platform for quantum devices. For a few centers, average error dropped by a factor of about a thousand at moderate step sizes.
arxiv-2602-05055:
Whether neutrinos are their own antiparticles stays one of particle physics' open questions. D Delepine and A Yebra propose a new way to watch in this 2026 paper, using neutrinos of about a billion electron volts from solar flares and supernovae. The mechanism is resonant spin-flavor precession, where magnetic fields flip a neutrino's spin and flavor at once.

At these higher levels the resonance moves to kinder spots. The Sun's tachocline and convection zone host it for flare neutrinos. For supernova neutrinos, the outer envelope rather than the core hosts it, dodging limits set by the 1987 supernova. The authors work out how the flipping would shift catch rates in coherent neutrino-nucleus scattering and neutrino-electron scattering, with patterns of its own for Dirac versus Majorana neutrinos. The scheme could also probe magnetic moments far below current reach.
arxiv-2602-05255:
Quantum Monte Carlo simulations spend much of their time recomputing determinants and Pfaffians of large matrices. Ao Chen and Christopher Roth attack that bottleneck in this 2026 computational physics paper with lrux, a software package built on the JAX framework. Successive wavefunction evaluations usually differ by a low-rank update, and exploiting that fact drops the cost of each evaluation dramatically.

The package implements determinant and Pfaffian updates for both, plus delayed-update strategies that swap arithmetic for less memory traffic on modern accelerators. It plugs natively into JAX's just-in-time compilation, vectorization, and automatic differentiation, and handles real and complex numbers. Benchmarks on graphics processors showed speedups up to about a thousand times at large matrix sizes. Designed as a drop-in component, lrux targets the many quantum Monte Carlo workflows whose inner loop is antisymmetric wavefunction evaluation.
arxiv-2602-05555:
Robots that assemble parts must judge the exact position and rotation of tools and components, a task called 6D pose estimation. Panagiotis Sapoutzoglou, Orestis Vaggelis, and 3 co-authors introduce IndustryShapes, an RGB-D benchmark data set built from industrial assembly settings rather than tidy lab tabletops. It covers five new object types with hard properties, in scenes that range from single objects to repeated instances of the same part.

The data set is split into a classic set, with thousands of images and annotated poses, and an extended set that adds data types for model-free and sequence-based methods. They benchmark leading methods for pose estimation, detection, and segmentation on it. Scores leave clear room for improvement, which is the point: the set is meant to expose the gap between lab results and factory floors.
arxiv-2602-05955:
Dwarf spheroidal galaxies are mostly dark matter with little background glow, which makes them clean places to hunt for dark matter annihilation signals. A large collaboration reports an improved search using the HAWC gamma ray observatory, a water Cherenkov detector at high altitude. The team looks for gamma rays from heavy dark matter particles annihilating into standard model products.

Compared with earlier HAWC studies, event reconstruction improved and hadronic contamination fell, raising sensitivity. The search also widened: more dwarf galaxies, more annihilation channels, and more data per galaxy. No evidence of a dark matter signal was detected. The team therefore places upper limits on the annihilation cross section across a wide heavy mass range. Null results still matter here, since they rule out territory that models of heavy dark matter might otherwise claim. The analysis is a step in the long indirect detection program that complements collider and direct searches.
arxiv-2602-06055:
When people label text for hate speech or toxicity, majority and minority groups often disagree in steady patterns. Dimitris Tsirmpas and John Pavlopoulos study how to measure that split, called polarization, and tie it to real groups. Standard agreement scores can hide these gaps.

Earlier polarization tools had two flaws. Some split cannot be tied to any group, and opposite splits can cancel out when labels are pooled. The pair built a new measure plus a test for whether a group link is real, and released free software for it. On four data sets, gender and race explained many of the gaps.
arxiv-2602-06155:
Picture-making diffusion models build an image step by step from a random seed, and Kuntian Chen and 5 co-authors ask when the final meaning becomes readable along the way. They call this semantic accessibility. With a fixed sampling method, each seed fixes one path and one final image.

The team trained simple probe classifiers at several points along the path to guess the final label or trait. On four image data sets, the label could be guessed above chance even from the starting noise. Paths ending in confident classifications carried much more early meaning than shaky ones. The measures give a concrete timeline for when sense emerges during generation.
arxiv-2602-06355:
Tuning a text-to-image model with human preferences needs pairs of better and worse pictures, and making those pairs is slow and noisy. Sanjana Reddy and 3 co-authors present Di3PO, a way to build pairs that differ only in a chosen region. The rest of the picture stays fixed, so training signal points exactly at the flaw.

Standard preference tuning often wastes effort on irrelevant pixel differences between pairs. Di3PO isolates the targeted area for improvement while the surrounding context holds steady. The team demonstrates the method on text rendering, a known weak spot where diffusion models garble letters. Their approach improved results over plain fine-tuning and standard preference optimization baselines.
arxiv-2602-06655:
Ethereum is secured by nearly a million validators, and Zeta Avarikioti, Ray Neiheiser, Krzysztof Pietrzak, and Michelle X. Yeo study the bottleneck this creates. Before a block is final, the validators' signatures must be gathered and shared, and that step is a big reason finality takes about fifteen minutes. The authors also show the current gathering scheme has flaws that attackers can use to shift stake toward dishonest nodes.

Their protocol, Wonderboom, collects signatures at million scale within a single short slot, about thirty-two times faster than the present setup, with stronger security guarantees. To test it, they built the first simulator that can model such a protocol at full scale. Even in the worst case, Wonderboom gathered and verified more than two million signatures inside one slot.
arxiv-2602-06755:
Anton Tishchenko and seven co-authors study a smart surface that can serve radar sensing and wireless communication at the same time, and test it indoors at everyday Wi-Fi-like frequencies. The surface, a multi-functional reconfigurable intelligent surface, steers signals to track users in real time. The paper covers how its settings are generated and how a clustering algorithm, backed by a Kalman filter, follows moving users.

The team built a channel model in line with 3GPP standards, describing how radar and radio signals reflect and scatter in this setup, and backed it with indoor measurements. Signals reached nearly everywhere indoors, even without a direct line of sight. In a 5G test, the surface cut throughput swings sharply and raised total rate, by creating a virtual direct path that steadied the connection for a moving user.
arxiv-2602-07155:
Instanton bundles are geometric objects with deep roots in physics, and extending them to new spaces tests how general the theory runs.  Ozhan Genc and one co-author study H-instanton bundles on an infinite family of smooth 3D toric varieties with Picard number two.

The paper supplies two other monad descriptions that generalize the classic ones on projective three-space, classifies bundles whose second Chern class sits in a single degree. Proves existence for all admissible classes when the setting is at most three.  Algebraic geometers get new cases and tools for instantons on threefolds beyond the familiar cases.
arxiv-2602-07355:
Online matching with edges arriving one by one is a classic problem. Degree three is where the best possible ratio was known but not known to be achievable.  Kanstantsin Pashkovich and one co-author close that gap for fractional matchings.

They supply an online method whose competitive ratio reaches the known upper bound of about 0. 5914 for graphs of maximum degree three, complementing the earlier impossibility result.  They also show no online method for integral matchings can reach the same standard.  Algorithm builders get a tight result: the bound is not just a barrier but a target that can be hit.
arxiv-2602-07655:
Discrete breathers are localized, time-periodic vibrations that live inside a lattice bandgap. Their action near a semi-Dirac point, where bands cross linearly one way and quadratically the other, was not mapped.  Andrew Hofstrand studies breathers in a non-linear honeycomb lattice near that point.

In two opposing limits, near continuum and anti-continuum, the breathers show hybrid structure: central cores on few lattice sites plus decaying tails approximated by exact separable solutions of an effective long-wave theory.  The breathers stay dynamically stable over a wide setting range before an instability transition, and Floquet analysis covers extended non-linear waves as well.  Nonlinear lattice teams get a stability map for breathers at a distinctive band crossing.
arxiv-2602-08555:
Fluid moving through a thin, perforated layer behaves differently as flow speeds rise, and the Reynolds number marks the change. Maria Anguiano and two co-authors study a generalized Newtonian fluid in a thin porous medium pierced by tiny cylinders. Their arXiv paper uses homogenization theory to find where inertia starts to matter.

When the Reynolds number scales at or below one over the layer thickness, inertia drops out of the limit and linear or nonlinear Darcy laws link velocity to pressure gradient. Above that critical scale, inertia is expected to enter the homogenized problem. The authors also propose a numerical method for the critical nonlinear Darcy laws and test it on examples. Readers get a sharp threshold for effective flow in thin porous media.
arxiv-2602-08655:
Offline reinforcement learning promises policies learned from static data, but over-rating unseen actions can wreck it, especially on fractured, sparse data. Sarthak Wanjari proposes Geometric Pessimism, a frame that adds density-based penalties from nearest-neighbor distances in state-action embedding space to standard expectile learning. His arXiv paper targets the efficiency-versus-rigor trade that dogs existing methods.

Penalties are precomputed, so caution enters through reward shaping at negligible training cost. On a standard robot benchmark, the method beats its base algorithm by over eighteen points on unstable replay tasks and cuts seed variance fourfold. On a sepsis critical-care dataset, it improves over clinician agreement where the base method collapses to imitation. Readers get a safe, cheap guard against out-of-distribution optimism.
arxiv-2602-08855:
Graph neural networks can fail in a strange way: a test case only slightly different from training data suddenly flips to a wrong answer. Yang Qiu and two co-authors call this Minimal Shift Flip and study it through sharpness-aware minimization, which measures how steep and fragile the loss landscape is around a solution.

They define a Local Robust Radius, the smallest nudge that flips a prediction, and link it to generalization in theory. Training, they find, steadily shrinks that radius, sharpening the landscape. Their fix, an energy-driven augmentation scheme called E2A, breeds fake out-of-distribution samples to widen the margin, and benchmarks show steadier generalization.
arxiv-2602-08955:
In February 2024, Lyft promised drivers a minimum share of each fare and showed them more about per-ride pay. Rubing Li and two co-authors use the staggered rollout as a natural experiment, studying over 47 million trips across six months with difference-in-differences methods and a geographic border design. The question: who gains when guarantees meet transparency?

Driver engagement rose substantially, with distinct contributions from the guarantee and from transparency itself. Hours, utilization, completed trips, and hourly and per-trip earnings all climbed, most for drivers with lower prior pay and shakier income. Extra supply also lifted demand. Yet the authors also find signs that transparency can spark strategic driver behavior.
arxiv-2602-09055:
Sijia Li and two co-authors solve a wave-scattering problem: a time-harmonic acoustic plane wave striking an elastic body with an unbounded periodic surface. The infinite domain is first reduced to a single periodic cell, then cut down with a perfectly matched layer that absorbs outgoing waves. Matching transparent boundary rules for acoustic and elastic waves are built together, proving the cut-down problem is well-posed and converges exponentially.

A finite-element method solves the cut-down problem, and because the body's non-smooth surface creates singularities, the authors derive a residual-based error estimate and an adaptive algorithm that refines where needed. Numerical examples confirm the adaptive scheme works, offering a reliable tool for periodic acoustic-elastic design.
arxiv-2602-09155:
Most patients with low-grade tubular adenomas never develop colorectal cancer, but some do, and telling them apart early would sharpen surveillance. Ahmed Rahu and six co-authors test whether convolutional neural networks can spot subtle histological clues in whole-slide images of low-grade adenomas that predict long-term cancer risk. Standard microscopy, they note, may miss faint architectural or cellular signs of malignant potential.

The study applies deep learning to digitized slides, comprehensively and objectively, seeking features tied to future progression even without known high-risk syndromes. If such signals prove reliable, low-risk patients could be sorted into tailored follow-up and prevention plans, rather than one-size-fits-all screening intervals. The work addresses a critical unmet need in colorectal cancer prevention.
arxiv-2602-09255:
Mobile robots working long shifts need memory that backs planning, recall, and thought over open-ended orders at many levels of detail. Mingfeng Yuan and five co-authors present STaR, an agentic framework that builds a task-agnostic, multimodal long-term memory. It preserves fine object attributes, spatial relations, and dynamic events, then retrieves from it with a scalable task-conditioned algorithm based on the information bottleneck.

Tested on NaVQA campus scenes and WH-VQA, a warehouse benchmark with many look-alike objects built in Isaac Sim, STaR beats strong baselines with better win rates and far smaller position error. Deployment on a real Husky wheeled robot indoors and outdoors confirms robust long-horizon reasoning and practical utility for navigation.
arxiv-2602-09455:
Affine maximizer auctions generalize the classic Vickrey-Clarke-Groves design, guaranteeing truthful bidding and voluntary taking part. Their fixed payment form, however, limits expressiveness when bidders' values move together. Haoran Sun and three co-authors propose link-aware affine auctions in their 2026 paper, adding a payment term that tracks links while preserving truthfulness. Finding the best such auction becomes a constrained tuning problem under the taking-part constraint.

Theory shows classic designs can fall arbitrarily short of optimal revenue in some linked settings, while the link-aware version can reach it. A practical two-stage training algorithm tunes the design, with results on the target function's continuity and a general bound on taking-part breaches. Trials across varied distributions find near-optimal designs with improved revenue and only slight taking-part breaches.
arxiv-2602-09655:
Erik L. André and two co-authors study Bayesian quantum setting guessing when the process holding unknown physics amounts can be used only few times. Their 2026 paper compares plan classes. Usual side-by-side and in-line plans sit beside general plans that may involve open causal order, plus hybrid tuned greedy plans using classic feed between quantum plans to tune the next round.

Within each class, the central question is the best plan: input state, control steps, reading, and guessers. Using higher-order frame, the authors develop a method searching for the best answer, with a number build based on semi coding. Benchmarks against current exact answers show the method strong and precise. Cases from single to multi-setting guessing show tuned greedy plans sometimes matching general plans, and sometimes a strict ladder between all classes.
arxiv-2602-09955:
The Doppler effect shifts a signal's frequency when source and receiver move, and modern wireless systems live with that shift everywhere. A 2026 chapter by Lie-Liang Yang offers a rigorous, wide-ranging analysis for electromagnetic and acoustic signals alike. It covers land mobile links, Internet of Things networks, machine-type links, radar, and satellite navigation and sensing.

The chapter works through motion profiles from steady movement and constant acceleration to general motion. It weighs classical kinematics, special and general relativity, air dynamics, and the medium itself as factors shaping the shift. The aim is a firm theoretical base for both general readers and specialists working on integrated sensing and communications.
arxiv-2602-10255:
Modular networks like critical infrastructures combine dense modules, such as cities, with sparse interconnections, and random disruption drives them through two critical transitions. A 2026 paper led by Yael Kfir-Cohen, with four co-authors, studies those transitions in modular multiplex networks against single-layer modular networks. Modules are arranged either as a Random Regular network or a two-dimensional square lattice, and the systems show diverse transition behaviors, some continuous and some abrupt.

Notably, one realistic model displays two separate first-order transitions in one system. For the modular Random Regular multiplex, the spatial transition's scaling behavior reveals signatures of a mixed-order transition, and the critical threshold where modules disconnect is determined analytically. The results highlight how modular organization and interdependence shape network vulnerability under failure.
arxiv-2602-10655:
Muhammad Yousaf and four co-authors assess vision-language models for underwater robot perception in a 2026 paper. Autonomous underwater robots face low visibility and harsh water, and labeled training data are scarce and noisy. Perception modules built on such data risk untrustworthy conduct in exactly the settings where robots must work alone.

Vision-language models promise an alternative: they transfer to unseen objects and stay robust in noise by thinking from context. The paper tests their results and doubt in underwater settings, where the gap between promise and deployment matters most. The assessment gives engineers evidence about when these models can be trusted beneath the surface and where they still falter.
arxiv-2602-10755:
Llibert Aresté Saló and three co-authors simulate neutron star mergers beyond general relativity in a 2026 paper. They present the first fully uneven evolutions of binary neutron star mergers in Einstein-scalar-Gauss-Bonnet gravity. A moving-punctures approach handles both linear and quadratic couplings between the scalar field and the Gauss-Bonnet stable.

The simulations uncover new post-merger phenomena. Scalar effects enhance the prompt collapse of a long-lived hyper-massive remnant, and in some cases the remnant develops a scalar configuration through distinct scalarisation instabilities. The study opens exploration of beyond-Einstein effects amplified by the uneven fluid motion of merging neutron stars, with implications for gravitational-wave signatures of modified gravity.
arxiv-2602-10955:
Garazi Retegui and three co-authors study prior smoothing in multivariate disease mapping in a 2026 paper. When incidence or mortality for multiple diseases is recorded across areal units, dependence across diseases is expected. Layered models pair a Poisson count model with spatial random effects specified as a prior, smoothing rate estimates across areas.

The writings often compares smoothing induced by a given prior against observed tested risks. The contribution extends prior research on smoothing in univariate areal models to the multivariate setting, examining three other prior choices. The contribution helps disease mappers understand how much smoothing each prior imposes when diseases share geography. Maps should then reflect real spatial patterns rather than prior artifacts.
arxiv-2602-11155:
Non-reciprocal lattices trap waves at edges in ways that depend sharply on edges. Kazuma Saito and four co-authors study a 1D non-reciprocal lattice where a tunable impurity bond bridges the edges. That bridge opens an middle regime with scale-free placing.

Adding quasiperiodic disorder breaks that regime. Depending on edge terms, the system falls into the non-Hermitian skin effect or an extended regime instead. The work shows that edge coupling and quasiperiodicity jointly decide placing in non-Hermitian systems, a point that matters for designing non-reciprocal devices and interpreting their spectra. The result matters for device design, where edge conduct can decide function.
arxiv-2602-11355:
Boolean-Catalan numbers count a refined family of combinatorial objects. Miklos Bona, writing alone, offers Boolean-Narayana numbers as a refinement of that family. He gives an explicit formula for the new numbers.

He also proves unimodality, log-concavity, and real-roots-only results for their sequences, plus a three-term recurrence for their generating polynomials. The paper is short and self-contained, offering a new sequence family with clean structural properties. Combinatorialists gain a refined counting tool whose sequences behave as nicely as the Catalan-like families they extend. The sequences thus join a small set of refined families with proven shape properties.
arxiv-2602-11455:
Multimodal thinking with verifiable rewards works, but how vision enters thinking was murky. Zhengbo Jiao and six co-authors find through cross-modal focus that only a small fraction of tokens show strong visual-textual coupling. Those high-connectivity tokens anchor thinking in the image, while most tokens follow linguistic patterns.

During reinforcement training, credit naturally concentrates on those anchors, sharpening their visual grounding over time. Their Anchor-Token Reinforcement Learning frame selectively reinforces high-connectivity tokens via graph grouping of focus topology. With tiny overhead, a mid-size model surpasses a far larger instruct rival on a maths-vision benchmark, with gains across science, video, and general tasks. Training only low-connectivity tokens degrades results severely, confirming anchors matter.
arxiv-2602-11655:
Edge devices must spot malware in real time with tight limits on compute and memory. The models best at pattern recognition are too heavy to run there. Locally trained models go stale as threats evolve and fail to transfer across domains. Christian Rondanini and four co-authors build a continuous learning system around small transformer models on each device, fine-tuned incrementally on local traffic.

Only tiny LoRA adapter modules are shared through a light coordinator and redistributed. Devices thus learn from each other without exchanging raw data. Tests on two public Internet-of-Things security datasets, under multi-round learning that mimics evolving threats, show accuracy gains up to 20 to 25 percent over isolated fine-tuning. Loss and F1 stay stable across rounds. Each adapter adds under 1 percent to model size, roughly under 2 megabytes.
arxiv-2602-11955:
Optimal domains ask how far an operator's natural home can be stretched. Setareh Eskandari and one co-author study bounded Volterra integration operators between Hardy spaces of the unit ball, mapping the largest domain on which each operator stays bounded. They show that domain always strictly contains the starting Hardy space, so the operator reaches further than its textbook home.

The intersection of all such optimal domains tells a sharper story. When the target exponent is no larger than the source, the intersection equals the starting space exactly. When the target exceeds the source, the intersection is genuinely larger: a tent space of holomorphic functions. The disk version of the problem was recently solved for equal exponents, and this paper extends the picture to the ball with unequal exponents.
arxiv-2602-12055:
Planning flights for large drone fleets in shared, changing airspace must respect temporary no-fly zones, varied vehicle profiles, and strict drop deadlines. Amath Sow and seven co-authors propose DTAPP-IICR, a delivery-time aware prioritized planner with stepwise and iterative conflict resolution. Missions are first ranked by urgency, then roundtrip paths are computed with a novel four-dimensional single-agent planner that handles varied drones. It enforces temporal no-fly zones strictly and treats inter-agent conflicts as soft constraints.

A repeated large local search, guided by a geometric conflict graph, then resolves remaining conflicts, while safe path pruning speeds the 3D search. On benchmarks with timed no-fly zones, the method nears 100 percent success with fleets up to 1,000 drones and gains up to 50 percent runtime reduction from pruning. It beats batch enhanced conflict-based search in the traffic management context.
arxiv-2602-12155:
Tuning an image model after training usually means copying expert examples or ranking pairs, and both routes have flaws. Copying cannot fix drift into unseen states, while ranking needs costly pairs or reward models. Yeyao Ma led this work with four co-authors, turning the tuning problem into imitation learning with an adversarial twist.

Their method, called FAIL, pits model output against expert output without explicit rewards or pair labels. One version uses smooth solvers for low-noise gradients, while a second black-box version suits discrete or tight compute settings. Tuning FLUX on just 13,000 expert demos gave strong prompt and beauty scores, and the same frame also steadied reward-based training against reward hacking.
arxiv-2602-12355:
Tidal disruption events, where a star is torn apart by a black hole, sometimes show early bumps before the main flare. Patrik Milán Veres works alone here. He builds the first sample of precursor tidal disruption events from the literature plus new candidates. The goal is to learn what those bumps reveal about optical emission. Precursors could be key signatures, yet they had never been studied as a group.

The sample falls mainly into three subclasses. These are repeating events, fast events, and events in active galactic nuclei. Precursor timing relative to the main peak correlates positively with central black hole mass. The author suggests precursors arise when incoming stellar debris hits a disk or leftover material from an earlier disruption. In active nuclei, a stable pre-existing disk may play that role. Precursors thus mark repeating partial disruptions in once-quiet galaxies.
arxiv-2602-12455:
Convex functions have clean optimisation theory, but many real functions are only quasi-convex or e-convex, and a unified notion would help. M. H. Alizadeh led this work with one co-author, F. Lara, studying e-quasiconvex functions, a new generalised notion that encompasses both quasiconvex and e-convex functions, including all Lipschitz functions. Extending standard quasiconvex properties to this wider class is the paper's first task.

From those extensions, the team gives sufficient conditions for the solution set to be non-empty and compact. This holds when minimising an e-quasiconvex function, using generalised asymptotic functions, even when minimisers form a nonconvex set. In the differentiable case, they prove sufficiency of KKT optimality conditions when constraint functions are e-quasiconvex. Several nonconvex, non-quasiconvex examples illustrate the new results, showing the wider class is not empty of interest.
arxiv-2602-12655:
Zebrafish growth from 2 weeks to 12 months after fertilisation offers a window on vertebrate growth, but live imaging across that span is hard. Cunyou Bao led this work with eight co-authors, showing in vivo dynamic optical coherence tomography imaging of zebrafish growth, mixed with polarisation-sensitive OCT, OCT angiography, and histology checks.

Two dynamic OCT methods were used: log intensity variance and late OCT correlation decay speed, tracking occupancy of moving scatterers and their motion speeds. Skin stripes show high dynamic OCT signals that vary among pigment-cell types, and mixed dynamic and polarisation-sensitive OCT captures stripe maturation. Dynamic OCT and angiography also visualised vessel growth, giving a multi-contrast live picture of zebrafish growth.
arxiv-2602-12755:
Diffusion models can fill in missing X-ray views, but most tests use synthetic images, leaving a real-world question open. Nelas Thomsen and three co-authors ask whether mismatch in training data or in the imaging model breaks the method on genuine scans. They scanned a physical phantom shaped like the classic Shepp-Logan test object, then trained diffusion priors on synthetic sets with varying degrees of mismatch.

Severe mismatch caused collapse and invented features, yet diverse priors matched or beat narrow, well-matched ones. Errors in the imaging model pulled samples off track and caused artefacts, though a gradual weighting schedule eased the damage and saved compute.
