Optimizers such as AdamW apply uniform learning rates and weight decay across all groups, ignoring that different layers and modules optimize very differently. Their optimizer uses self-attention to adjust those settings on the fly.

A lightweight transformer encoder reads statistical features from each group, such as gradient norms, momentum norms, and correlations, and outputs modulation factors for learning rate and weight decay. The attention module is trained with a meta-learning objective. It combines gradient alignment, loss decrease, and generalization gap. An uncertainty weighting scheme is added, extended with task-specific priorities. Across five tasks, from time series forecasting to sentiment analysis, MetaAdamW beat standard AdamW every time.
arxiv-2605-04155:
Zhenyu Xiao, Hao-Kai Zhang, and Shuo Liu uncover a quantum Mpemba effect in the generation of quantum magic, the nonstabilizerness that makes quantum states hard to simulate classically. The Mpemba effect is the counterintuitive phenomenon where a state that starts apparently farther from a target can reach it faster. Here the target property is magic itself, quantified by the stabilizer Rényi entropy in symmetric random circuits started from tilted product states.

States with lower initial magic can generate magic faster than states with higher initial magic. The acceleration is not fixed by the conserved-charge distribution alone: two families with identical initial magic and charge distribution show qualitatively different growth depending on the spatial structure within each charge sector. Analogous effects appear in SU(2)-symmetric circuits and under nonintegrable Hamiltonian dynamics, so the phenomenon is tied neither to Abelian symmetry nor to circuit randomness.
arxiv-2605-04255:
Alessandro Micheli and three co-authors tackle optimal transport, the problem of moving mass at least cost. Here the data live on curved spaces such as spheres or rotation groups. Flat geometry can distort distances and averages on such spaces, and past methods split useful features between different approaches.

Their framework combines smoothed transport, defined in the curved geometry itself, with a neural model that can evaluate the transport for new points without re-solving the problem. They construct transport estimates from one learned function and prove supporting results for fixed smoothing, aiming to make curved-space transport both principled and reusable.
arxiv-2605-04355:
Mustafa Sakhaia and three co-authors extend a self-driving system with event cameras, sensors that report brightness changes almost instantly instead of taking full frames. Normal cameras and laser scanners can blur or lag in fast scenes and harsh lighting, which threatens safe decisions.

Their design adds event data as a third input stream beside images and laser data, fused through a token-based method inside a transformer model. On standard simulated driving benchmarks, the agent reached full route completion with a competitive driving score. The authors argue event vision is a promising route to more robust driving under hard conditions.
arxiv-2605-04655:
Ishtiaque Ahmed, Leila Musavian, and Haris Pervaiz study a reconfigurable wireless antenna system. It serves two kinds of users at once. One kind is conventional bit-based users. The other is semantic communication users, who transmit meaning rather than exact bits. Pinching antennas, created by pressing a dielectric waveguide at chosen points, can form direct line-of-sight links cheaply.

Most past work gave every antenna equal power. Here the radiation of each antenna is adjusted by changing its spacing from the waveguide, which sets its coupling strength. The authors optimise the system to maximise semantic spectral efficiency. Bit users must still get their required quality of service. The design also respects interference cancellation order and minimum spacing between antennas.
arxiv-2605-05055:
Bac Trinh-Nguyen and four co-authors build an adaptive framework for locating devices outdoors from the angles at which their signals arrive, aimed at 5G and 6G networks. Good location services matter for transport, factories, and smart cities, but training data collection effort varies widely by site. Angle-based methods are known to be robust, yet one training recipe does not fit every data size.

Their framework offers two learning strategies, one for large and one for small training sets, tested on a real massive-antenna outdoor dataset. For large data, a hierarchical method first separates line-of-sight from blocked regions, then refines position within each. The design aims at high accuracy with realistic collection effort.
arxiv-2605-05155:
Xu and seven colleagues ask how beautiful a 3D scene looks, not just how accurate it is. 3D Gaussian Splatting renders immersive scenes from Gaussian primitives, and creators need to know whether the result is visually compelling. Existing evaluations stress reconstruction fidelity and realism, largely ignoring composition, harmony, and appeal. Two gaps cause this: no general dataset carries aesthetic annotations for splatted scenes, and the primitive representation itself resists high-level feature capture. Aes3D closes both gaps at once.

The framework offers Aesthetic3D, the first dataset for 3D scene aesthetic assessment, built on a new annotation strategy, plus Aes3DGSNet, a light model that predicts scene-level aesthetic scores straight from Gaussian primitives. Skipping multi-view rendering cuts cost and hardware needs. Experiments show strong performance at low weight, setting a first benchmark for judging beauty in neural-rendered scenes.
arxiv-2605-05255:
Stuart Edris, Amy McGovern, and Jason Hickey test how well drought and flash drought in Africa can be predicted weeks to seasons ahead using a digital twin framework for Earth research. African droughts hit hard because many regions depend on local farming, yet global machine learning weather models have rarely been checked for skill focused on Africa. Their model, DroughtFormer, adapts a CrossFormer network inside that framework.

DroughtFormer draws on reanalysis and satellite data and respects dry air mass and moisture conservation while predicting soil moisture, vegetation health, and related surface measures. It showed significant skill on most variables, though precipitation and flash drought indices proved harder to predict accurately.
arxiv-2605-05355:
Philip Kaaret and Brian Ramsey review the young field of astrophysical X-ray polarimetry, which measures the polarisation of high-energy light from space. Adding polarisation fraction and angle to the usual measurements reveals new information about accretion flows and magnetic fields in extreme astrophysical systems. That extra geometry is hard to obtain any other way.

The review first covers the physical processes that produce polarised X-rays in astrophysical settings. It then explains the physical principles used to measure X-ray polarisation in practice. Finally, it surveys the detectors that have already flown and those under construction, giving newcomers a map of the instruments defining this observational window.
arxiv-2605-05855:
The suggested prompts that open a chat with an AI assistant are usually chosen from what users already clicked, a loop that drifts toward the popular and generic. Yiqing Wu and six co-authors break that loop by modeling active expression instead. Users signal intent not only by clicking starters but by what they write and share elsewhere.

The authors argue this passive-active gap traps recommender systems in an echo chamber worsened by sparse data. Modeling active expression lets starters track how conversational intent actually evolves in the open world. The result should be suggestions that start better conversations, not just familiar ones.
arxiv-2605-06155:
Ponaki Das and Sainkupar Marwein Mawiong complete the classification of certain minimal finite topological spaces with ten points. Earlier work by Cianci and Ottina proved a homotopically trivial but non contractible finite space needs at least nine points, and classified the nine point cases. The ten point classification was left open, and this paper closes it with a new structural tool, the notion of a naked pair.

The authors show minimal spaces with at most ten points have no naked pairs, which turns minimality into simple conditions on how the space's three levels connect. Case analysis, aided by an exhaustive computer enumeration, gives the full count. No such space exists with one or two middle points, exactly six exist with three middle points, and exactly four with four middle points.
arxiv-2605-06355:
Ignacio Peis, Pablo Olmos, and Jes Frellsen reinterpret order agnostic autoregressive models through the lens of missing data. Such models generate in any order and perform strongly, but incomplete data, the norm in real records, had barely been studied for them. The authors first show standard training on complete data quietly performs imputation under a missing completely at random assumption, which explains robust filling in even at high missingness rates.

They then give the first principled framework for training these models directly on incomplete data under general missingness mechanisms. The same machinery supports active information acquisition, choosing which missing variable to measure next for a downstream task. Their model, MO-ARM, beat established imputation baselines across a suite of real world benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-06555:
Benjamin Aram Berendsohn and Marek Sokołowski study dynamic forests where edges only get deleted. The task is maintaining sums of vertex weights, either over a whole tree component or over a rooted subtree, while weights also update. Standard structures answer in logarithmic time and even allow insertions, so the question is whether deletion-only work can go faster.

For tree sums they give a structure with near-constant time per operation, constant time for unweighted forests, and an asymptotically optimal algorithm in a group model. For subtree sums they prove tight bounds across several variants. The results sharpen what decremental data structures can achieve.
arxiv-2605-06755:
Ismam Nur Swapnil and five co-authors introduce PrePO, a method that cheapens reinforcement learning fine-tuning of language models by skipping predictable optimizer steps. Repeatedly updating a policy on the same rollout batch costs a backward pass per step. PrePO watches two real optimizer transitions, estimates a farther point on the same trajectory, jumps partway there, evaluates the true objective, and applies a corrective update.

Its cost stays fixed no matter how many virtual steps it approximates. Analysis gives error bounds for common optimizers and shows accurate endpoint estimates preserve normal convergence behavior. Experiments reach matched performance in fewer steps and less time, and the same trick also works in supervised fine-tuning.
arxiv-2605-06955:
Victor Livernoche, Jie Zan, and Reihaneh Rabbany improve anomaly detection on table-shaped data using denoising score matching. The method learns a data distribution by training a network to undo added noise, and unusual points stand out afterward. Choosing how much noise to add is the hard part, especially with no labeled anomalies for tuning.

Their scheme sets noise per feature from kurtosis, a measure of a distribution's shape, adapting to sparse and dense regions. A carefully trained single-scale model proves surprisingly strong on standard benchmarks. With a light filtering rule added, it also performs well when the training data itself contain anomalies.
arxiv-2605-07755:
Jiwan Chung and two co-authors argue that the theory of state tracking in recurrent networks has asked the wrong question. Research focused on expressivity, whether an architecture could in principle realize a set of symbolic transition rules. Equally decisive, they claim, is error control: how hidden-state errors drift along the directions that separate one symbolic state from another.

They prove that affine recurrent networks, a class covering state-space models and linear attention, cannot correct errors along state-separating directions once they preserve state representations. Practical trackers therefore learn only finite-horizon solutions, readable while accumulated spread stays small against the initial separation. On group state-tracking tasks the predicted breakdown point, where a distinguishability ratio crosses the decoder's threshold, matched where accuracy actually collapsed.
arxiv-2605-07855:
Jin Wook Lee and three co-authors measure how well AI review agents handle scientific peer review of statistical data analyses. They also probe where their ability is jagged: strong in one place, weak in another. The test bed is seventy-two student projects fitting partially observed Markov process models, drawn from a University of Michigan graduate course, with reports, code, and human peer reviews openly available.

Four AI agents, all built on Claude Code with different instruction files, were compared with the human reviewers. The agents caught plausible technical errors and invalid inference methods that humans missed, but were weaker on interpretive errors, narrative coherence, and domain-informed critique. Changing the instructions shifted which weaknesses the agents emphasized without removing the jagged pattern.
arxiv-2605-08055:
Konrad Wilke and colleagues simulate defects inside mixed-halide perovskites, materials used in solar cells and light emitters. Mixing bromine and iodine can improve stability, but moving defects can still degrade the material over time. The team asks whether arranging the halides in layers can steer that motion.

Large molecular dynamics runs with a reactive force field show strongly directional diffusion. Defects move easily along the layers but are blocked across them. For cesium defects the cause is directional strain and tilted octahedra, while halide motion also depends on local bonding choices. Layered ordering thus offers a design lever for longer-lived perovskite devices.
arxiv-2605-08255:
Yuchu Liu, Rui Zhu, Jingwei Xiong, and Haixu Tang ask a simple question. Can a language model predict polymer properties from scientific prose alone? Two samples of the same polymer can behave in unlike ways. It depends on how they were made, processed, and tested. Yet standard property models read only the chemical structure. They throw that context away.

Their PolyLM framework predicts physical and mechanical performance from full-text literature. It keeps the synthesis routes that authors describe in words. It also keeps processing histories and test conditions. To train it, the team curated a large dataset drawn from the literature. The study tests how far plain language can stand in for structured materials data.
arxiv-2605-08555:
J. Andres Montoya studies the power of pebble automata through the lens of entropy and space complexity. The work compares three classic resource classes: logarithmic space, its nondeterministic version, and the closure of context free languages under thrifty reductions. Montoya presents a claimed proof that the nondeterministic class differs from that closure.

As presented, the separation would also imply that logarithmic space differs from polynomial time, a far stronger outcome. Because such separations touch famous open questions in complexity theory, readers should treat the argument as a claim to be checked by the community, not settled fact. The short paper rewards careful scrutiny of each step in the proof.
arxiv-2605-09055:
Quilee Simeon, Justin M Wei, and Yile Fan describe Octopus, a system that lets an AI agent take control of hardware it has never met before. Normally each new device needs its own drivers and hand-built software, repeated for every platform.

Octopus instead gives a coding agent shell access and a set of plain instructions. In five stages the agent lists the hardware, works out what each device can do, builds typed tools for it, and switches the result on as a live service. A background program then watches the setup and repairs known kinds of failure. The same instructions worked across four hosts with no edits by hand.
arxiv-2605-09155:
Benjamin Castle, Ishai Dan-Cohen, and Assaf Hasson study whether a curve can be recovered from a related group built out of its points. To a smooth curve they attach a generalized Jacobian, a group that extends the classic tool for studying curves, using a chosen point and a divisor. Their 2026 paper asks how much of the original data survives inside a certain subset of that group.

The three authors show the curve, the point, and the divisor can all be retrieved from that subset, apart from a twist by a symmetry of the field. The result settles a conjecture of Booher and Voloch. For finite fields, the same data can also be read from special functions tied to extensions of the curve's function field.
arxiv-2605-09755:
Chenakkod and Dereziński sped up the power method, the classic tool for pulling top principal components from data by low-rank approximation. When the target rank is large, matrix multiplication costs dominate. Their framework accelerates the method with fast sketching, a randomized linear algebra technique that compresses matrices before the heavy multiplications.

The result is simple, provably efficient methods for singular value decomposition, low-rank factorization, and Nyström approximation, with strong test scores on benchmarks. The key new idea is regularized spectral approximation, a property of fast sketching that extends power-method guarantees more flexibly than older proofs. Sketching, the paper shows, can carry the power method further at lower cost.
arxiv-2605-09955:
Belay and eight co-authors argue that rater disagreement is information, not noise, in subjective language tasks like sentiment, emotion and hate-speech labelling. Top-vote counting, the usual fix, erases smaller-group views, while modelling every rater one by one is costly and rarely tried across tasks. Their alternative groups raters by how much they agree, then models the clusters.

Across 40 data sets in 18 languages, agreement-based clustering used the full range of views and beat both majority voting and individual annotator modelling on sorting scores. Among aggregation styles, multi-label and multitask approaches handled clustered annotators better than ensembles or top vote. The data set is public, and the method offers a cheaper way to keep minority readings alive in training data.
arxiv-2605-10155:
Deepanshu and four colleagues present NyayaAI, an AI legal assistant for India, where legal information stays hard to reach because legal language is complex and documentation is vast. The system pairs large language models with retrieval-augmented generation grounded in a curated Indian legal base of constitutional provisions, statutes, case law and judicial precedents. A multi-agent design run through the Mastra TypeScript framework has a main agent working with research, summarisation, case-retrieval and drafting specialists.

A compliance module checks every response before delivery. Domain classification reached seventy percent precision in tests, retrieval precision seventy-four percent, and overall response accuracy seventy-two percent. The authors present these figures as evidence that structured multi-agent language-model systems can meaningfully improve legal access and workflow efficiency for lawyers, law students and general users, with code released publicly.
arxiv-2605-10255:
Linus Ekstrøm, Hao Wang, and Sebastian Schmitt compare two ways of encoding a practical quantum problem. Their 2026 paper studies electric-vehicle fleet management, where charging schedules and customer trip assignments must be decided together under tight constraints such as battery limits, trip overlaps, and grid power bounds.

A conventional binary, or qubit, encoding uses one qubit per vehicle-trip pair. An integer, or qudit, encoding uses one qudit per trip whose value names the assigned vehicle directly. Both allow exactly the same feasible solutions, yet the qudit form shrinks the required Hilbert-space dimension exponentially. Solving many random constrained instances with qudit-based QAOA, the authors found similar or better optimization at much lower resource cost and shorter simulation runtime.
arxiv-2605-10555:
Kai Pan and Rong Hou redesign enterprise tool APIs for AI agents. Language model agents now run enterprise software, yet the APIs they invoke still target human interfaces. Traditional CRUD APIs expect callers to know exact parameters, return raw data, and lack rules for self-run execution. Their 2026 paper presents the Agent-First Tool API paradigm.

The paradigm treats tool APIs as goal protocols, not form endpoints. It introduces three parts. First, a Six-Verb Semantic Protocol structures each tool call as a reasoning loop. Second, a Normalized Tool Contract adds confidence scores, evidence sources, and next actions to each response. Third, a dual-layer governance pipeline combines capability and object permissions with live risk step-up and approval workflows. Tested in a live SaaS system with 85 tools across 6 domains, Agent-First APIs reduce unclear-goal failures, enable error fixes, and enforce strong access control without control layers.
arxiv-2605-10655:
Venugopalan Iyengar introduces BCJR-QAT, a differentiable relaxation bringing quantization-aware training to trellis-coded weight quantization for language models. BCJR-QAT swaps the argmax for the BCJR forward-backward sum-product algorithm at a temperature. It produces a soft codeword, the Boltzmann mean over paths, exactly differentiable, recovering the hard QTIP code as temperature nears zero.

Contributions include a fused Triton kernel making BCJR tractable on one consumer graphics processor with a large speedup at full precision parity. A drift-budget theory of when BCJR-QAT can escape the QTIP post-training basin was verified across four experiments. A good Llama-3.2-1B result at 2 bits per weight under forward-KL distillation rounds out the set. With the right schedule, skipping the high-temperature phase to avoid a diagnosed overshoot, single-layer BCJR-QAT beats QTIP post-training on WikiText-2. Layer gains beat the sum of single-layer gains.
arxiv-2605-11055:
Caleb Robinson and eleven colleagues release the first global agricultural field-boundary map at ten-meter resolution, covering 2024 and 2025. Fields are the natural unit for planting, managing, regulating, and reporting crops, yet global remote-sensing products have stayed pixel-level, with field data limited to European registries or single countries.

A U-Net segmentation model trained on the Fields of the World dataset and applied to cloud-free Sentinel-2 mosaics yields 3.17 billion field polygons across 241 countries and territories. Validation against ground truth in 24 countries gives mean pixel recall of 0.85, with full-country F1 scores up to 0.89. A companion 500-meter uncertainty layer marks where reference data run thin. Agricultural planners get a globally consistent field layer for the first time.
arxiv-2605-11155:
Ashish Gurung and eight colleagues test whether differentiating human tutor roles by student need improves hybrid human-AI tutoring. Hybrid tutoring can beat AI-only tutoring, but early evidence suggests lower-performing students benefit more, raising the question of how to support both groups.

Using within-grade median state test scores, 635 students in grades 5 through 8 received proactive human-initiated support if below median or reactive on-demand support if at or above. A difference-in-discontinuities design compares fall AI-only tutoring against spring proactive-reactive tutoring, isolating the policy effect around the cutoff. Results show human-AI tutoring beats AI alone by a clear overall margin. Tutoring designers get evidence that differentiated human roles beat one-size-fits-all support.
arxiv-2605-11755: Jiaqi Han and five colleagues make image generation far faster by cutting sampling to a single step. Their W-Flow framework first traces a path from a simple reference distribution to the target data through a Wasserstein gradient flow. It then trains a generator to compress that whole path into one step. On ImageNet at 256 by 256 it set a new one-step record at 1.29 FID and sampled about 100 times faster than comparable multi-step diffusion models.
arxiv-2605-12055: Hardy and Sebastian Padó test whether language models encode knowledge of grammar rule breaks. Using sparse coders to split mixed-meaning activations into single-meaning units, they derived a score for units lighting up more for broken than well-formed inputs. They then applied a joint disproof system with three jointly checked tests. Results failed twice over: tests were never jointly met, and no units were shared across all groups, giving limited support for unified grammar break finders.
arxiv-2605-12155: Kaspar Schmerling, Andreas Kugi, and Andreas Deutschmann-Olek propose an optimal control plan to sharpen impulse estimation in linear Gaussian systems. Using optimal estimation for such systems, they turn the task of cutting disturbance uncertainty into a control problem over time-varying system settings. The method shapes estimation spreads through parametric modulation, gaining the most information at the known impulse time. Unlike standard squeezing plans with periodic modulation, which weaken impulse inference, optimal driving cuts estimation variance by up to half on nanomechanical resonators and levitated nanoparticles.
arxiv-2605-12255: Toru Takahashi argues that clashing answers from evidence reflect non-identifiability, not broken thinking. He sorts the puzzle on two levels. At theta-level, the same model yields different answers as settings differ. At W-level, repeat use of a setting biases data contact and updates, so the model splits. He defines a profile of Reference, Exploration, Stabilization, and Horizon, showing how outputs split for the same sight. Disputes project onto bases: concrete versus abstract, outward sharing, and order versus freedom, from limits on math, sight, and teamwork.
arxiv-2605-12955: Zarei seeks a small-scale origin for collapse models, in which gravity destabilises superpositions of mass distributions and forces wave-function collapse. Using the quantum Boltzmann equation for a fermion in a spatial superposition under graviton emission, he ties superposition stability to separation, mass and coupling and derives the decoherence rate. The account bridges quantum field theory and collapse models and bears on tests of gravity-driven collapse, including dissipative continuous spontaneous localisation models.
arxiv-2605-13455: Shashwat Kumar and eight colleagues present a Bayesian framework for tracking synapses, the tiny junctions between neurons, in living brain tissue over time. Imaging of glowing tagged receptors suffers from low signal, shot noise, tissue motion, shifting glow and blur. Their template model treats synapses as shifting brightness points moving under tissue warping. The Bayesian solution maps synapse spots, cleans and sharpens images, infers glow strengths, corrects motion, and gives confidence regions. They show it on simulated data and on two weeks of mouse microscopy data.
arxiv-2605-13655: Tomasz Adamowicz and Iván Caamaño study Hardy spaces of quasiregular mappings on the unit ball under growth and multiplicity rules. Averaged derivatives are used to study edge limit and maximal functions and to mark Hardy spaces for finite-count maps. They also study links among quasiregular maps, mean slopes, BMO spaces and Carleson sizes, plus the role of map counts. Results apply to second-order oval PDEs and A-harmonic rules, growing Astala-Koskela and Nolder results to such maps.
arxiv-2605-14055: Chowdhury and four co-authors offer PEML, parameter-efficient multi-task learning with optimized continuous prompts. Tuning one large language model for many tasks saves data through shared features and saves resources versus one model per task. Existing efficient methods fall short for multi-task use: LoRA tunes the model itself while slighting prompt tuning, and Prefix Tuning optimizes prompts only through a simple architecture. PEML instead optimizes continuous prompts for the multi-task setting, aiming to serve many tasks from a single model.
arxiv-2605-14355: Peng and colleagues introduce Herculean, a benchmark that tests whether AI agents can carry out whole professional finance workflows rather than isolated tasks. It spans four workflows, trading, hedging, market insight and auditing, each run as a separate skill with its own state and success criteria. Across thirty combinations of agent design and underlying model, rankings shift with the workflow. Each design also fails in different ways. Agent skill, they conclude, is an interaction between design and task demand, not a fixed property of the model.
arxiv-2605-14755: Liu and Luo settle two conjectures of Kang, Nikiforov, and Yuan on the p-spectral radius of k-chromatic r-graphs. For an r-uniform hypergraph, the p-spectral radius maximises a polyform over the unit p-norm sphere. The complete k-chromatic r-graph with equal-as-possible colour classes is conjectured to be the unique maximiser, with a stated bound. The case r equal to three was known. This paper resolves all cases r of at least four, giving an anti-Wilf-type spectral certificate.
arxiv-2605-14955: Shuo Li and Yuan Song bound how many distinct rational power factors a finite word can hold. A rational power repeats a block several times, then adds a prefix of that block. Earlier work capped ordinary repeated powers, but rational powers had gone unstudied. The pair proves the count stays below one eighth of the squared length, plus a linear term. Their proof turns word patterns into a constrained extremal problem using graphs and word equations.
arxiv-2605-15055: Quanhao Li and nine others propose DiffusionOPD, a multi-task training method for diffusion text-to-image models based on online policy distillation. Joint multi-task training suffers interference and imbalance, while cascaded training forgets earlier tasks. DiffusionOPD trains one teacher per task. It then distills them into a single student along the student's own rollouts. The authors lift the framework to continuous-state processes with a closed-form per-step objective, reporting lower-variance gradients and consistent wins over multi-reward and cascade baselines.
arxiv-2605-15155: Zhengxi Lu and ten others present SDAR, self-distilled agentic reinforcement learning for long-horizon language-model agents. Trajectory-level rewards give only coarse supervision, and naive on-policy self-distillation shakes multi-turn agents. SDAR keeps RL as the backbone and adds distillation as a gated auxiliary goal, strengthening distillation on teacher-endorsed positive-gap tokens while easing negative teacher rejections. Across Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 models on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA, SDAR beats GRPO by 7 to 10 percent.
arxiv-2605-15255: G. Alencar and V. H. U. Borralho study the Dymnikova regular black hole inside unimodular gravity, where the vacuum sector drives regularization. Letting a measured break of energy-momentum conservation lets the cosmological term emerge on its own as a radial function. The space-time first reads as a charged setup from curved field theory, with charge and magnet sources derived. The same geometry then follows from standard Maxwell electrodynamics in that gravity, with a regular charge field and zero far-away charge.
arxiv-2605-15355: Sanja Karilanova, Subhrakanti Dey, and Ayça Özçelikkale address federated learning of spiking neural networks when edge devices sample at different temporal resolutions. Parameters learned at one rate need not transfer to another, so naive shared averaging falters. Their framework studies how neuron parameters from other rates should be merged at aggregation. Across the SHD and DVS-Gesture benchmarks under varied heterogeneity, the new adaptation methods a lot recover accuracy lost to time mismatch, letting each client train at its local rate.
arxiv-2605-15455: Sheer Karny, Anthony Baez, and Pat Pataranutaporn ask whether showing people a language model's inner workings helps them judge shifting behavior in long chats. Their display turns activation patterns into scores for six traits, shown as a sunburst chart, a drift panel, and attention cues. In a trial with 246 people, the moving display improved prediction and judgment, curbed overconfidence, and beat a still version without losing ease of use.
arxiv-2605-15555: Sakiko Obuchi, Ingyin Zaw, Kazuhiro Hada, Kohei Ichikawa, and Joseph D. Gelfand report a parsec-scale jet in a distant radio-loud quasar accreting above the Eddington limit, resolved by very-long-baseline interferometry at three frequencies. The well-collimated jet stretches about 745 parsecs, making it the most distant known resolved jet of its kind. Its speed and viewing angle suggest a relativistic outflow that is not strongly boosted, pointing to a distinct high-redshift population with implications for feedback in early galaxies.
arxiv-2605-15655: Mozib Bin Awal and Prabwal Phukon track critical slowing in black-hole phase transitions in anti-de Sitter spacetime. They stretch a free-energy landscape frame to spinning black holes. Near the critical point, entropy dynamics slow down sharply. The lowest Fokker-Planck eigenvalue backs the slowdown. Along temperature, pressure, and spin paths, in both directions, rest time follows one scaling law with exponent minus two-thirds. The same exponent fits charged, spinning, and regular black holes, hinting at universal dynamical conduct.
arxiv-2605-15855: Renye Yan and nine colleagues argue that running reinforcement learning over the full denoising path of diffusion models wastes effort and weakens preference fit. Early shapes are unstable and far from the final reward, so rewards lag and actions mismatch. Late gains stall, and further training overfits fine details, boosting reward hacking. Their AdaScope plug-in finds the time to intervene by tracking shape change and meaning match, then halts once denoising settles and reward gains stall. Against top rivals, AdaScope lifts performance by 66 percent while cutting cost by 59 percent.
arxiv-2605-16355: Yan and four others present Density-Sampled Gaussians, a 3D model that samples Gaussian centers from a learnable density over an octree. Unlike fixed grids, it jointly optimizes spatial density and Gaussian attributes under rendering supervision, concentrating primitives where geometry is most complex. A new render loss gradient serves as a differentiable analogue of densification and pruning heuristics. For generation, VecSeq re-indexing anchors latent tokens to a deterministic Sobol sequence, turning set generation into sequence modelling with state-of-the-art single-image-to-3D quality.
arxiv-2605-16555: In 2026, Wu and four colleagues build MedASR, a compact open-source speech model for medical dictation. It has only 105 million parameters, yet aims to be small, fast, and accurate. It tackles scarce clinical training data, long-form transcription, and streaming-style decoding through a sliding window. In their evaluation it cut word errors by 58% relative to Whisper Large-v3 on an eye-gaze test set. Clinics gain a transparent backbone for documentation instead of a closed proprietary system.
arxiv-2605-16655: The CMS Collaboration searches for pairs of additional Higgs bosons produced from an off-shell Z boson in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, with both particles decaying to tau-lepton pairs. Using 138 inverse femtobarns collected by the CMS detector at the LHC, the team finds no deviation from Standard Model background. They set exclusion limits on the Type-X two-Higgs-doublet model alignment scenario. The results rule out previously unexplored parameter regions and complement earlier searches.
arxiv-2605-16755: Min and Gomes present PermFlow, a flow-matching framework for learning permutations, which matter for sorting, ranking, and matching. Existing differentiable methods based on entropy-regularized Sinkhorn collapse to a single softened solution under ambiguity. PermFlow works directly on the affine subspace of matrices with unit row and column sums, using a closed-form projector that preserves constraints along every trajectory. A nearest-target coupling routes distinct noisy starts to distinct valid permutations. The model recovers both valid permutations under ambiguity and scores highly on unambiguous inputs.
arxiv-2605-16955: Thelen and Mauerer present DQI-Kit, a software tool that encodes constrained optimisation problems into Max-LINSAT for decoded quantum interferometry. Hard optimisation with quantum methods usually forces domain goals and constraints into formats a chosen algorithm accepts, adding overhead that can threaten quantum advantage. Their tool offers a unified, open interface for auto encoding, letting users describe common work goals and constraints, and estimates DQI performance on resulting cases. An initial analysis of the transforms discusses inefficiencies and fixes.
arxiv-2605-17255: Long and colleagues present CAM-Bench, a Lean 4 benchmark of 1,000 proof targets in applied mathematics, covering optimization, numerical linear algebra and numerical analysis. Tasks come from textbook exercises and lean on local terms and notation. A context-rebuilding pipeline restores that local setting for each task. Each item ships with its raw exercise, restored context, plain statement and Lean target. Models are scored on tracking local givens and sustaining long proofs.
arxiv-2605-17555: Khilar introduces PFlow-T, a generative model whose forward process runs entirely on persistent homology rather than Gaussian noise. Time tracks destruction of first-homology holes, eliminating them by persistence. The reverse network inverts that structured damage to predict the clean state in a single step. MNIST trials on digits 0, 1 and 8 show it beats a baseline at making requested Betti numbers and handling shifted-distribution tasks. It is the first such architecture, though limited to low-resolution pixel proxies.
arxiv-2605-17655: Trujillo, Tessa and Cresci grade how well platforms report under the Digital Services Act, covering the eight largest platforms in the European Union. Their review of key reporting areas finds mixed compliance and data quality, with every platform flawed on format, timing, consistency and completeness. Some platforms use different steps across mechanisms, giving conflicting data, and cross-system sharing still fails despite harmonization. Many old flaws remain unfixed. The authors urge audits and targeted fixes to make DSA reporting more reliable and joined up.
arxiv-2605-17755: Jinghui Liu and Anthony Nguyen ask whether mixing medical-code training data across versions helps. Hospitals adopt ICD-9 and ICD-10 at different times and places, so version gaps are a real problem. Adding ICD-9 records to a label-wise attention model for ICD-10 prediction lifts micro F1 by 27% on 18,000 rare codes, despite the version mismatch. Frequent codes improve too, and the mixed-version model uses far fewer parameters, suggesting version-independent coding is workable even for the long tail of rare diagnoses.
arxiv-2605-17955: Harish Balaji and eight colleagues tackle post-quantum TLS deployment in finance. Standards exist for key exchange and signatures, but the bottleneck is operational, not algorithmic. Banks terminate TLS at endpoints, each a quantum-vulnerable target, yet teams lack visibility into configurations and methods. The paper presents a parsing method that extracts and normalizes TLS cryptographic posture across web server stacks into an inventory. It demonstrates on 8,443 Nginx configurations and a bank trial, where MLKEM and hybrid MLKEM exchanges run with zero application changes and low overhead.
arxiv-2605-18055: Qi Si and seven colleagues present FLAG, a diffusion-based framework treating spatial gene expression as shaped spread model, not solo pointwise tasks. FLAG keeps gene teamwork and spatial layout in view, joining a spatial graph reader with gene foundation model alignment. The team also names a Gene Dimension Curse, where joint model of output and spatial links fails in big spaces. New scores, Gene Structural Correlation and Spatial Structural Correlation, score this fidelity. Tests show FLAG matches usual accuracy while greatly improving structural fidelity.
arxiv-2605-18455: Prasoon Patidar and eleven co-authors present OrganicHAR, a 2026 activity discovery system that centers sensor capabilities instead of forcing privacy-preserving sensors to mimic camera labels. It finds natural signal patterns from radar, lidar, and thermal sensors, calling vision-language models only at key moments for scene understanding. With twelve participants it reaches 79 percent accuracy on coarse activities and 73 percent on fine-grained ones, while cutting vision-model queries by 90 percent.
arxiv-2605-18555: Alexey Dolotov gives, in a 2026 paper, fully checked prime proofs for three Wagstaff numbers, W2617, W10501, and W12391, with 788, 3161, and 3730 digits. The proofs use the Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge N-1 test on cyclotomic splits, free of ECPP. Factored content comes from Cunningham project tables, with every factor re-checked, and each cofactor proven outright by APR-CL. A Chua N+1 check also confirms the math at each number.
arxiv-2605-18655: Henry Aldridge and three co-authors introduce a 2026 method for gauging uncertainty in rebuilt images without ground-truth data for calibration. Inverse problems recover a signal from noisy, transformed observations, and many plausible images can fit the same data. Their approach builds rough coverages by using data symmetries through equivariant bootstrapping, then refines them with conformal calibration. Tested on weak-lensing mass mapping, it rebuilds the convergence field from galaxy shear measurements. The self-taught route avoids costly simulations tied to specific cosmological models.
arxiv-2605-18855: Cheng Luo, Zefan Cai and Junjie Hu rework how transformer layers share information across depth. Standard attention residuals route cumulative hidden states that grow redundant, so attention flattens in deep layers and stops picking useful states. Their Delta Attention Residuals instead route the change each sublayer introduces, which stays varied and sharpens attention markedly. Across models from 220 million to 7.6 billion parameters the approach improves validation perplexity by 1.7 to 8.2 percent and can be fitted to pretrained models by ordinary fine-tuning.
arxiv-2605-18955: Anastasia Glykopoulou, Ioannis Liodakis and Dmitry Blinov automate finding polarization-angle rotations in blazars, replacing manual work. Their pipeline corrects the 180-degree ambiguity, segments light curves with Bayesian Blocks and checks each event. On RoboPol data it finds 48 rotations across 25 sources, including 27 new ones, with sizes from about 91 to 360 degrees and lengths from 7 to 111 days. Longer rotations tend to track stronger gamma-ray output, while size alone does not predict gamma-ray brightness.
arxiv-2605-19455: Wu and team lay the theory for fluid antennas, where one element slides across a region rather than sitting on a fixed grid. For direction finding they derive a dual degrees-of-freedom bound that fluid positions can approach, growing linearly with aperture over wavelength rather than saturating. Error bounds fall faster with aperture than grid designs allow, and two-stage FAS-MUSIC tracks those bounds while resolving grating-lobe ambiguity. Simulations show error 17.5 times lower than uniform linear array MUSIC, with four fluid antennas beating eight classical ones.
arxiv-2605-19855: Astolfi and colleagues test zero shot text to image models as a source of made concept sets for XAI. Concept methods link internal codes to class guesses through traits people can grasp, but need large tagged image sets per concept. The team makes concepts from preset prompts and checks fit with real concepts through four tests: code match, inner match at growing sizes, downstream account quality, and concept removal effects. Current makers promise a shortcut, but the study raises open gaps.
arxiv-2605-20055: Dominique Briechle and seven co-workers recover software architecture for real ROS 2 robotic systems with help from large language models. In such systems the hierarchy of parts and their integration rules hide implicitly across code and launch files, beyond simple node lists and wiring. Their staged, blueprint-guided pipeline refines prompts for consistency and rebuilds structure level by level from atomic nodes and launch dependencies. Tested on a real automated product-disassembly system with cooperative arms, recovery gains structural consistency, scalability and robustness, though dynamic integration semantics remain a challenge.
arxiv-2605-20255: Prakash Aryan and three co-workers test multi-agent learning for self-driving under pedestrian uncertainty. They co-train a car and 12 pedestrians: walking is scripted, a policy picks go or wait, and jaywalking chance rests on a hidden trait. In 500 tests, the co-trained car reached seventy-eight percent of goals with a fourteen percent crash rate. Jaywalking was thirteen percent of crossings but sixty-two percent of crashes, and co-training cut crashes by thirty percent versus single-agent learning.
arxiv-2605-20355: Srivastava and eight co-workers tackle skill loss when people share control with AI helpers. Their Proximal State Nudging method steers users toward states judged most learnable, balancing skill growth against task success. Tests with simulated learners in LunarLander beat older shared-control baselines on that balance. In driving trials with 60 people in CARLA, the method gave up to 7 times larger solo-skill gains and 50 percent fewer crashes than solo practice.
arxiv-2605-20555: Xingwei Gan and Ying Zhu improve post-training of language models by averaging output scores from two models. One is a frozen supervised model, and the other is being trained by reinforcement learning. Unlike standard methods, theirs needs no penalty term pulling the learner back and no separate critic network. The averaging keeps the learner's reasoning skill while borrowing the reference model's formatting strength.
arxiv-2605-20655: Guanjian Hu and three colleagues trace coupled spin-light signals in hexagonal boron nitride to pairs of defects that interact. These defects promise room-temperature quantum tools, but their true identities were largely unknown. First-principles calculations show pair spacing controls charge transfer, electron structure, and spin coupling. That in turn shifts light emission lines, lifetimes, and magnetic contrast, and the authors find two charge-dependent coupling regimes.
arxiv-2605-20755: Haoyang Zhang and fifteen colleagues present DuplexSLA, a full-duplex spoken language model that syncs speech, language, and action. Recent spoken dialogue models listen while responding, but most miss a native path for in-conversation planning and tool calls. DuplexSLA reads assistant audio together with a structured action flow on a shared 160-millisecond chunk timeline. A dual-stream, three-channel design lets listening, speaking, planning, and tool calling run on one shared clock.
arxiv-2605-21255: Helmut Prodinger finds the generating function of OEIS sequence A348410 using the diagonal method. The sequence terms are coefficients of a product of powers of one minus x and one minus x squared. Applying a 1971 method of Hautus and Klarner with the Gfun software, he derives an algebraic equation for the generating function. A second identity uses the generalized binomial series popularized in Concrete Mathematics.
arxiv-2605-21455: Calvin Isley, Johann D. Gaebler, and Sharad Goel propose cutting label bias with clear rubric codes. Decision algorithms deployed where true labels are scarce, such as hiring and school entry, may inherit biases if past human judgments unjustly favor certain groups. Their method replaces black-box codes with features derived from expert-defined criteria matching the core construct of interest. By tying predictions to clear axes, it guards against biased proxy signals.
arxiv-2605-21555: Kritika Babbar, Mo Javed, and Amit Maji characterize partially isometric truncated and dual truncated Toeplitz operators. Let theta be a non-constant inner function and phi equal conjugate-u times v, where u and v are inner functions such that v divides theta. They characterize partially isometric truncated operators A-phi and dual truncated operators D-phi with symbols of that form, plus the space of extremal vectors for non-zero cases.
arxiv-2605-21855: Joseph Pollard and Richard Morris study the particlelike kinematics of charge-carrying topological defects in nematic media through a field theory. Unlike electromagnetism, it lacks gauge invariance, so its free-energy rules face constraints a gauge-invariant theory would ignore. Hodge theory captures these as harmonic excitations, joining defect orientations and topological solitons. Energy shifts that add non-linear terms to the Euler-Lagrange equations produce defect effects beyond pairs despite abelian U-one symmetry, seen in non-zero extrinsic curvature and elastic anisotropy.
arxiv-2605-22155: David Mendez and co-authors test Algebraic Machine Learning against strong standard baselines on small-to-medium datasets. AML learns via subdirect decomposition of algebraic structure rather than numerical optimization. On image datasets with 50 to 2000 training examples, AML without validation beats cross-validated baselines including CNNs. On tabular data in the same range, XGBoost leads overall, yet AML matches methods with task-specific biases like LightGBM and random forests. AML needs no cross-validation, since no task-dependent hyperparameters need tuning.
arxiv-2605-22355: Guo and colleagues present TransitLM, a large dataset for map-free transit route generation. It holds over 13 million route planning records from four Chinese cities, covering 120,845 stations and 13,666 lines. A language model trained on the data produces structurally valid routes at high accuracy. It also grounds arbitrary GPS coordinates to suitable stations with no explicit mapping. The work shows route planning can be learned from data alone, directly from origin to destination.
arxiv-2605-22455: Pais and colleagues use synthetic RAW image augmentation to probe pedestrian detection in low light. Real datasets are sparse and uneven, with long tails that hinder generalisation, and few samples in low-density regions. Synthetic samples fill gaps and sample the input space more continuously, improving benchmark coverage. For the safety-critical case of pedestrian detection in the dark, they generate low-light samples matching the camera sensor's noise model. Performance on real and synthetic low-light data is similar, suggesting the model struggles to tell them apart.
arxiv-2605-22555: Delmonte and Schirò track how watching one site for lost particles reshapes quantum entanglement across a narrow junction. Without watching, the shared link grows slowly, but watched losses first drive a fast linear rise to a size scaled peak, then a slow fall to zero as the setup empties. A particle picture ties the early rise to a loss made voltage gap that fades as matter drains away.
arxiv-2605-22655: Mehrotra and others test radius inflation in brown dwarfs and low mass stellar companions using 50 transiting objects with solid ages and model limits, drawn from a wider set of 85. Measured radii exceed model radii by 8.7 plus or minus 1.9 percent, a 4.6 sigma gap confirming inflation at population level. Close companions within 0.05 astronomical units inflate far more, with a median of 16 plus or minus 6 percent, and inflation fades at wider separations. The authors read the pattern as fading stellar heating with distance and share their compilation for community use.
arxiv-2605-23055: Li and six coauthors split evaluation awareness into environment and model components. Frontier models sometimes spot testing and shift conduct, which can weaken benchmark trust. That side uses eight trigger factors, such as placeholder names and grading-style formats, studied via chain-of-thought tracking. Across nine models and four benchmarks, spotting rarely changed conduct. Its way varied with the seen test type. Safety tests proved more sensitive than skill ones. Their EvalAwareBench offers 100 paired safety and skill tasks with factors toggled one by one.
arxiv-2605-23255: Blue, Im, and Lindermayr provide the first study of learning-boosted planning that curbs pauses while tuning latency. Old work tunes job latency while relying on many, blind pauses, missing the trade-off between scores and pause cost. Their results include O(1)-competitive methods for single and mixed side-by-side units with only O(1) pauses per job under good guesses. By giving the first bounded-pause proofs for mixed and soft units, they extend the learning-boosted setup to tighter, real settings.
arxiv-2605-23355: Wang and three colleagues tackle fine-grained action spotting in professional badminton video, where fast, subtle strokes are hard to tell apart. They release Fine-Badminton, a benchmark of 31 matches with 29 stroke types across 2104 rallies and 27597 marked actions. Their adapter splits motion into three parallel branches for time and for vertical and horizontal space, letting a model separate near-identical strokes. Tests on their set and on ShuttleSet reach top scores at little extra cost.
arxiv-2605-23455: Yamauchi, Stearn, and Tovey propose a quantum-Hamiltonian-learning framework that rebuilds changing magnetic-field maps step by step, using a local likelihood model drawn from a nitrogen-vacancy spin-1 Hamiltonian. Local readings come from nitrogen-vacancy spin dynamics set by local field values and a shared coupling parameter, rather than direct observation. Tests on synthetic maze-like field sequences show the method recovers the dominant spatial structure of the tested class. The shared coupling parameter proves only partly identifiable: its posterior narrows but stays frame-dependent and biased.
arxiv-2605-23655: Li and colleagues present CVSearch, a training-free framework that schedules search for high-resolution image perception by multimodal language models. Expert search is efficient but blind when proposals fail. Scan search covers everything at high redundancy and fragmentation cost. CVSearch first tries expert search when global information falls short, then triggers semantic scanning on failure. Semantic-guided patching splits images into consistent regions. A bottom-up search driven by a visual complexity prior then explores local detail, reaching top accuracy with far better efficiency.
arxiv-2605-24055: Liu, Yang, and Yang restore time series with Cascade-KDE, a training-free method for factory, health, and energy data. It first gauges a temporal-amplitude density, then applies a robust average step capping distant odd points, and polishes the sequence via an exponential cascade with tuned stopping. The design targets impulse damage outside the training data while keeping fixed curves close to the local shape, with derivative peaks and key cues intact. Across benchmarks it beats filters and learning-based rivals on curve fidelity, slope peaks, sorting, and runtime.
arxiv-2605-24355: Jong Yoon Hyun and three colleagues explore deep links among three mathematical objects: combinatorial designs, linear codes, and Boolean functions. Designs arrange points into blocks, codes are strings that guard data against errors, and Boolean functions map bit strings to one bit. The paper also treats plateaued functions, a special class named in its title, as part of the same web of connections. Its contribution is that map itself, linking results across the three areas, published in 2026.
arxiv-2605-24555: Syo Kamata builds Floquet algebraic tomography for non-Hermitian monodromy arrays, piecing them from trace strings. Those strings obey the matrix's own formula, so the inverse problem is algebra, not curve fitting. The rebuild uses the resolvent, determinant, and Dirichlet spectral data, splitting a spectral frame from dressing that depends on what is seen. Cayley-Hamilton and Hankel methods recover spectral data that survive same-shape transforms; knowability limits leave hidden sectors. Two cases, a transmon qutrit and a non-Hermitian Floquet SSH chain, show leakage-induced sight growth.
arxiv-2605-24755: Feng Chen and others automate delusion-related content detection in audio diaries with a multi-agent pipeline. Spoken diaries offer a window on mental illness and flare-ups, and language models need labeled data mainly for testing. It extracts delusional themes plus behavioral and affective signs from transcripts of people with moderate ideation. Careful diagnostic prompts cut false positives for themes but constrain affective and behavioral readings. Complex agent debate hurts scores on ambiguous text through premature consensus, while majority voting proves robust, with micro F1 of 0.872 for delusion detection.
arxiv-2605-24955: Chengmei Niu, Sachin Garg, Michał Dereziński, and Zhenyu Liao expose a hidden bias in random sampling methods for large matrix problems. Because inverting a sketched matrix is nonlinear, even an unbiased sketch can yield systematically biased projections. That skews subsampled least squares and fast low-rank approximations. The authors build a unified theory for these random oblique projections in high dimensions and a principled correction, sharpening bias-variance analysis for least squares and improving accuracy for CUR decomposition.
arxiv-2605-25055: Lucia Gomez Tejeiro and colleagues map cross-boundary collaboration across 464 cybersecurity projects and 11,372 contributors, October 2001 to May 2022, finding 163 communities. Cross-community work concentrates in a carrier layer: nine people span seven or more communities, authoring 14 percent of 4,015 merged pull requests, while the top 50 produce 54 percent. Boundary friction is a recognition cost. Acceptance rises from 42 percent at breadth one to 87 percent at breadth five to nine, and median latency falls from 147 hours to 49 hours. Survival is cohort-structured: residualisation hazard grows tenfold from pre-2010 to 2018 cohorts.
arxiv-2605-25155: Jochen Nießer and colleagues automate isotope-based metabolic flux analysis at microliter scale, running many tiny experiments in parallel instead of a few costly bioreactor runs. Using an evolved Corynebacterium glutamicum strain grown on ethanol, robotic handling and rapid quenching feed mass spectrometry data into joint models of fluxes and metabolite pools. Net fluxes prove stable across data sets, while pool sizes do not converge. The resulting flux map highlights the glyoxylate shunt during ethanol growth.
arxiv-2605-25255: Navil Nandhan, Abbas Khademi, and Antonio Silveti-Falls extend boosted Frank-Wolfe to stochastic, constrained, nonconvex problems. Boosting aligns updates with the gradient, but prior analysis covered only convex cases. The team devises a step-size strategy independent of the gradient's Lipschitz constant, compatible with estimators from SAGA to heavy-ball momentum and zeroth-order methods. Their analysis keeps stochastic Frank-Wolfe rates and gives first boosted rates for nonconvex and quasar-convex objectives. Experiments on logistic regression and quantum tomography show faster convergence per call and in wall-clock.
arxiv-2605-25655: Lu and colleagues present THInfer, a framework for running language models on many-core processors on the Tianhe supercomputer's MT-3000. Limited bandwidth and a distributed memory hierarchy block direct migration of GPU inference frameworks. THInfer combines a hand-optimized operator library, density-driven graph fusion with unified kernel scheduling, and a Prefill-Buffer-Decode pipeline with bounded buffers. On Llama models it beats DeepSpeed on two V100S cards by 62 to 73 percent on the 7B model. It also runs the 70B model where typical GPU frameworks fail.
arxiv-2605-26355: Athanasios Zeris's 2026 paper adds two biases that standard transformer attention lacks: energy salience, which tokens gather information energy, and scale-wise reach, how far influence extends at each frequency. Energy-Gated Attention gates value pooling by a learned energy estimate from a single linear mapping, choosing what to attend to. Morlet Positional Encoding swaps fixed sine codes for learned Gaussian-window wavelets, deciding where focus works at each scale. Alone, each part helps a little, but combined they beat the sum of their parts, the paper's central finding.
arxiv-2605-26455: Shuhong Jiang and nine colleagues show a mid-infrared single-photon ranger using upconversion. Sensitive ranging stayed in visible or near-infrared bands, so the team probes the mid-infrared, reading it in a crystal with pump pulses at a different repeat rate. That mismatch scans time in picosecond steps at kilohertz refresh over 50 nanoseconds. The upconverted trace stretches twenty thousandfold for a silicon detector. Time-correlated photon counting brings precision to 4 micrometers at a flux near eight hundred-thousandths of a photon per pulse, far finer than detector jitter.
arxiv-2605-26655: Shuzhi Gong and Hechuan Wen probe why tuned prompts often shine on one test and flop on another. They study optimized prompts across frameworks, model families, and benchmarks with a causal-style observational design. Complexity-raising and meta-instruction edits drag down math and multi-hop reasoning, while step-by-step and meta-cognitive edits lift logical and sequential tasks. The patterns hold across annotation schemes and transfer across optimizers, pointing to task-edit interplay rather than random luck.
arxiv-2605-26955: Jin and seven colleagues present JuICE, a benchmark for testing whether language-model judges can spot cultural errors in long-form responses. The dataset holds 7,470 span-level annotations across 1,050 query-response pairs from four countries, in English and local languages. Even the strongest judge model scores only 0.52 F1 on erroneous span detection and routinely misses thick cultural errors that locals catch at once. Cultural evaluation, they argue, must go beyond surface detection toward depth and situated meaning.
arxiv-2605-27155: Steckhan and three co-authors present SemProbe, a tool for probing object finders in safety domains, beyond pixel damage. Users upload images, create masks by hand or by machine, pick design factors or custom prompts, and run diffusion-based controlled refill. The tool supports batch jobs, varied runs, and tunable settings. After each output, model scoring runs and shows labeled before-and-after views with score deltas, with each probe logged for traceable evidence. The team shows SemProbe on hand spotting for table saws, aimed at insurance test rules.
arxiv-2605-27255: Tan and co-authors speed up decoding by pairing input compression with multi-token prediction. Their design treats a latent compressor and a prediction head as mirror images. The compressor packs two input tokens into one latent form, while the head unfolds one hidden state into an extra output token. A confidence head accepts or rejects draft tokens, removing the verifier pass, and it trains alongside on-policy distillation at negligible cost. Tests show gains of up to about 7 points on pass-at-4 scores and more than twice faster latency.
arxiv-2605-27655: Xiaoxiao Zhou and colleagues tutor trial staff in the principal stratum strategy for intercurrent events with survival outcomes. The tutorial defines causal effects for a binary treatment with a single binary stop-treatment event, reviewing mixture-model and weighting methods with assumptions, models, sensitivity checks, and example code. Simulated studies mimicking a real cancer trial test how the methods operate.
arxiv-2605-27755: Sravan Reddy Chintareddy and colleagues present an open-source platform testing cell and Starlink links for low-flying drones in rural flights. The satellite link wins on delay, with 95 percent of round-trip times below 50 milliseconds against 80 percent below 150 milliseconds for cell links. Satellite downloads also win, with 95 percent above 25 megabits per second against 5 for cell links, though higher flight raises handover rates.
arxiv-2605-27855: Wei and colleagues design a mid-infrared camera that can switch between an ordinary bright-field view and an edge-enhanced view, which outlines boundaries in a scene. Their nonlinear filter shapes the system's optical response, and tuning the crystal's temperature flips between modes without changing the setup. The same device can even capture both views at once using two-color illumination.
arxiv-2605-27955: Li and colleagues stop language-model agents from stumbling over free-form skill prose by rewriting skill libraries as typed pseudocode. Each procedure gains a clear contract for inputs plus a concrete template for calling it, checked by a four-part verifier. On a text-adventure suite the rewrite won far more paired games while using fewer tokens and calls.
arxiv-2605-28155: Yi-Ling Kuo, Hao-Yu Tien, and Shih-Yu Tsai predict internet round-trip delays with geometry matched to the network's shape. Their HERMIT framework pairs a hyperbolic temporal graph network, which suits hierarchical scale-free routing, with a random forest regressor. On a decade of real internet data it beat a strong statistics-only baseline and prior hyperbolic models.
arxiv-2605-28255: Gor and colleagues study when humans should hand question-answering to AI and when they should overrule it. In a game pairing expert humans with AI agents, teams beat either side alone, yet humans both under-trusted correct suggestions and over-trusted misleading ones. Confirmation bias drove much under-trust, pointing to calibrated confidence and evidence-grounded explanations as fixes.
arxiv-2605-28355: Soi and colleagues detect diffusion-generated time series under generator shift, where the maker is unknown. White-box reconstruction detectors collapse under shift, lacking the universal prior that images enjoy, while a simple off-the-shelf black-box classifier scores an average F1 near seventy-nine. Time-series detection, they conclude, is not a straight transfer of the image problem.
arxiv-2605-28455: Balázs Gerencsér and Levente Szemerédi bound the convergence speed of ratio consensus algorithms under a broader protocol family. Their analysis recasts the protocol as linear updates of vector values on an enlarged, augmented network. The advance allows zero values on auxiliary nodes infinitely often, widening the technique's reach. That relaxation makes the technique apply to a much larger family of consensus algorithms, with almost-sure rate bounds.
arxiv-2605-28555: Logan Knudsen and three colleagues examine parametric subharmonic instability in ocean bottom boundary layers over sloping ground. Strongly baroclinic submesoscale flows lower the minimum frequency of internal waves, letting near-inertial waves go unstable and feed small-scale turbulence and mixing. Linear analysis and nonlinear runs tie growth to bottom-layer stratification and the slope Burger number, with wave shear as the main energy source. A partly offset loss to geostrophic shear grows near marginal stability, pointing to instability as a source of near-bottom mixing.
arxiv-2605-28655: Shanghua Gao, Ada Fang, and Marinka Zitnik present AutoScientists, a decentralized crew of AI agents for long-running computational experiments. Single-path or centrally planned agents struggle to sustain parallel exploration, adapt to new evidence, or preserve knowledge of failed directions. AutoScientists agents read a shared test state, self-form around strong hypotheses, critique proposals before spending compute, and share wins and losses. Under matched budgets it beats prior agents on biomedical learning, language-model training tuning, and protein fitness scores, reaching the 74th percentile on BioML-Bench.
arxiv-2605-29055: Diego Gosmar and Deborah Dahl test hallucination mitigation with nested learning and semantic caching on 310 prompts. A pipeline scores responses on four dimensions, improving by about 6 percent of its attainable range. About 84 percent of the gain comes from Explicit Contextualization alone, while Factual Claim Density stays flat. In stress tests, about 11 percent of final answers still present invented items as real. Semantic caching serves about 48 percent of model calls, and cross-family judges confirm the gain.
arxiv-2605-29255: Hwiyoung Lee and Shuo Chen study a hidden bias in least-squares prediction. While least squares is unbiased given covariates, its error is generally not unbiased given the outcome. Large outcomes tend to be underpredicted and small ones overpredicted, the classic regression-to-the-mean pattern. This bias corrupts studies built on predicted outcomes, as in brain-age work. They propose outcome-calibrated regression, a closed-form fix that forces predictions to line up with outcomes. Their method removes the bias and enables valid inference from predicted outcomes.
arxiv-2605-29855: V. M. Litvyak and three colleagues measure how well light can cool nuclear spins in a cadmium telluride quantum well under an external magnetic field. Their results confirm a best field for optical cooling, tied to a kinetic local field set by heating of the spin-spin reservoir through hyperfine fluctuations. They also propose a technique to measure that kinetic local field. The measured value proves independent of electron polarization and pump power and matches a theoretical calculation that accounts for indirect spin-spin interactions and differing hyperfine constants.
arxiv-2605-30055: Simon Coste and Michael Goldman study the Wasserstein cost of importance sampling, which reweights samples to mimic another distribution. In three or more dimensions, the expected cost shrinks with sample size at a rate set by dimension and exponent, between two constants depending only on those parameters. The constants coincide for exponent two and are conjectured to coincide always. When they do, the best sampling distribution is a tempered version of the target, not the target itself, echoing Zador's theorem.
arxiv-2605-30255: Abbas M Sherif and Peter K S Dunsby map the Newman-Penrose and 1+1+2 formalisms onto each other. They express all spin coefficients, Ricci scalars and Weyl scalars in 1+1+2 scalar, vector and tensor variables. They also compare the gauge structures of the two formalisms. The mapping gives a dictionary linking two widely used approaches to general relativity, explaining Newman-Penrose quantities in 1+1+2 variables. They use the mapping to derive inequalities on Newman-Penrose scalars and the cosmological constant, limiting future outer trapping horizons in symmetric spacetimes.
arxiv-2605-30555: Struck and colleagues study how neurodivergent developers fare in agile software teams, a topic past work has largely ignored. They pair a review of online talk with eleven expert interviews from a German firm's staff network, and find team habits split and shaped by solo coping rather than shared norms. Agile routines and helpful tools can aid taking part, but rigid rules, stereotypes, and same-for-all habits often block it. The authors urge bendable setups and custom support over same-for-all rules.
arxiv-2605-30655: Gutierrez and Neira study distance-k domination in triangular matchstick graphs, where a dominating set must put every vertex within k steps of a vertex. They show two upper bounds claimed by Harris and colleagues for k equal to one and two are incorrect. They replace them with a corrected general bound obtained by refining the earlier tiling method. For k equal to one, they sharpen the construction with an explicit quadratic bound. They determine the graph's radius, which implies a single vertex dominates whenever k reaches that radius.
arxiv-2605-31155: Lunardi, Shrestha and Andreoni frame time-series out-of-distribution detection as learning embeddings on a sphere. A von Mises-Fisher objective shapes class structure, while separate encoders merge time- and frequency-domain views into one joint space. Detection then scores new series by distance, using nearest neighbours or Mahalanobis scores. Tested across the full UCR and UEA archives, the method consistently beats strong contrastive and post-hoc baselines.
arxiv-2605-31255: Andrade-Sánchez and Camacho-Guardian study a charged impurity moving through a quantum fluid, a Bose polaron at finite momentum. Past work stressed ground states and static properties, while momentum behaviour governs transport, dissipation and quasiparticle stability. Using second-order perturbation theory with finite-range ion-atom interaction, they find dressing and dissipation peak at a characteristic momentum scale, then fall unevenly. At high momentum, a scaling law signals fading many-body dressing and a return to near-free impurity motion.

arxiv-2606-04355:
Yuanchu Liang and a team including Lydia Kavraki and Hanna Kurniawati present an online planner in 2026 for robots that must act under uncertainty. The setting is formalized as partially observable decision processes. Long horizons defeat most solvers, which must enumerate actions or beliefs in full.

Their solver samples the state space with very fast motion-planning techniques. That mints a diverse set of macro actions on the fly. The macro actions then steer belief-space search toward good policies. Its convergence rate depends on how many actions were sampled, not on the full action space size. On problems with lookahead up to three thousand steps, it beat leading methods by up to several fold in success rate. The team also demonstrated it on a physical robot.
arxiv-2606-04555:
Liu and colleagues argue that AI agents with long conversation histories should organize memory by time as well as topic, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Then the context shifts. Histories thus form temporally ordered segments. These compose into larger episodes. Existing tree-based memory systems mostly build topical hierarchies. They ignore sequencing. Two questions stay open: how to update such a tree online, and how to retrieve through it.

Their system, SegTreeMem, represents history as a segment tree over utterances. The tree preserves temporal order. It inserts new utterances incrementally while keeping segments temporally contiguous. At retrieval, it propagates relevance signals through the tree. It integrates information across related parts of the conversation. Across three datasets and two language model backbones, SegTreeMem improved LLM-judged accuracy by nearly 20 percent. It beat non-temporal tree baselines and other strong memory systems.
arxiv-2606-04855:
The ATLAS Collaboration measures how strongly the Higgs boson couples to the top quark, and whether that coupling mixes CP parities, in a 2026 arXiv particle physics paper. A CP-odd component in any Higgs interaction would be evidence of physics beyond the Standard Model. Using 164 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions at 13.6 tera-electronvolts, the collaboration studies Higgs production alongside top quarks.

The production cross section times branching ratio is measured at 1.13 times the Standard Model prediction. For production with a single top quark, the observed upper limit is 6.2 times the Standard Model prediction, the most stringent from a single measurement to date. Combining with earlier data at 13 tera-electronvolts, the collaboration excludes a CP-mixing angle beyond 38 degrees at 95 percent confidence, and excludes a purely CP-odd Higgs-top coupling at 5.8 standard deviations.
arxiv-2606-04955:
Annis, Kassem, and Coleman test whether a popular guide for choosing quantum circuits survives contact with real noise and error fixes, in a 2026 arXiv quantum computing paper. The variational quantum eigensolver is a leading near-term quantum chemistry algorithm, but picking its ansatz circuit is guesswork. Expressibility was proposed as a selection guide.

Error mitigation does not reliably restore expressibility's predictive power. Zero-noise extrapolation reduces error for only a third of the circuits, while error cancellation increases error in nearly all of them. Circuit rankings scramble under noise, extrapolation largely preserves the noisy rankings, and cancellation actively reorders them. Noisy expressibility predicts performance strongly for one system but is computationally intractable at scale, while free topology metrics like two-qubit gate count predict mitigation degradation.
arxiv-2606-05255:
Naoyuki Uchida proposes Oklch+ in this 2026 arXiv paper, an extension of the Oklab color space that predicts perceived color differences almost as well as the standard formula. Oklab and its cylindrical form Oklch are popular in design workflows, but their difference predictions fall well short of CIEDE2000, which needs 17 parameters. Oklch+ aims to close that gap while staying a coordinate system.

The extension applies a power transformation on the lightness axis and a Naka-Rushton compression, a saturating response curve, on the chroma axis, then computes Euclidean distance in the transformed coordinates. On the COMBVD collection of 3,813 suprathreshold color difference pairs from six experimental datasets, Oklch+ scored a STRESS value of 29.09 against 29.13 for CIEDE2000, essentially matching it with three parameters. On a held-out dataset it scored 26.14 against 51.45 for Oklab, and the improvement over Oklab held across all six sub-datasets.
arxiv-2606-05555:
Obando-Ceron and colleagues ask what really lets one learning agent master many tasks in a 2026 arXiv paper. The field is reinforcement learning, where an agent learns by trial and reward. Recent leaders use world models and planning, which are costly to train. The authors argue the true driver is representation learning, meaning how the agent codes what it sees. They test a plain agent with no planning at all.

Their agent, MR.Q, pairs prediction-based coding with a large value function that scores actions. Across a wide suite of control tasks it beat a recent world-model method and several standard rivals. It also cut computing cost and training time by a wide margin. Tests that removed parts of the design showed the predictive coding did the heavy lifting. Bigger models kept improving, which points to a path that scales.
arxiv-2606-05955:
Cyril Belardinelli asks again why electric charge comes only in fixed portions, using a solenoid and a school-level setup in a 2026 arXiv paper. Dirac explained charge steps with magnetic monopoles, never yet observed. This route needs no monopoles. A charged particle moves in the field-free zone around a current-carrying solenoid, where only the quantum phase feels the hidden flux.

Solving the Schrödinger equation for that motion yields a joint rule. Magnetic flux and electric charge turn out to quantize together, each fixing the other's steps. The rule must also survive relativity to count as physics. Belardinelli shows magnetic flux transforms as a Lorentz pseudoscalar, flipping sign under reflections but not under boosts.
