Gokhale, Khodak, and Silwal develop a general method for estimating properties of a sequence that changes only slightly from step to step, in a 2026 paper on algorithms. Many tasks track a slowly evolving system through limited queries: a drifting data stream, a changing network, or matrices met during optimization. Earlier work showed that reusing past queries saves cost when consecutive elements are close. It covered few targets, though, and charged every step for the worst change seen.

The new framework handles many linear and nonlinear targets on varied spaces. Applications include Monte Carlo integration, matrix powers, and spectral densities, plus a boundary value problem from differential equations. A fresh algorithm scales each step's budget with that step's actual change, so total cost grows with the sum of changes rather than the maximum. In some cases the changes themselves can be estimated on the fly at almost no extra cost.
arxiv-2606-23755:
Toth documents the recovery and release of engineering telemetry from the Pioneer 10 and 11 spacecraft, in a 2026 explanatory almanac written to accompany the data release. The twin Pioneers, launched in the early nineteen seventies, were the first craft to cross the asteroid belt and visit Jupiter and Saturn. Their engineering telemetry, once used to monitor onboard systems, was nearly discarded under retention schedules. Preserved copies on durable media saved it, and the release aims to let researchers test how onboard forces affected the probes' orbits.

The document recounts the history of the raw telemetry and the documentation needed to interpret it. It describes the extraction tools, the scripts used to generate release files, and the manual editing process. All released files use standard formats, plain text tables or spreadsheets, readable with ordinary data tools.
arxiv-2606-24055:
Magsarjav and colleagues examine a humble but decisive step in sentiment analysis, the automatic tidying of social media text before a learning algorithm reads it. Cleaning steps such as splitting text into tokens, fixing spelling, stemming words to their roots, and dropping common stop words are usually applied in whatever order comes to hand. Their 2026 study tests whether that order changes results on Twitter data.

Order matters, the team finds, but unevenly across steps. Spelling correction shifts outcomes least, while tokenisation, the initial splitting step, shifts them most. Stemming and stop-word removal can swap places safely, and keeping negation words while removing other stop words works better. The best sequence runs tokenisation first, then text cleaning, then stemming, and stop-word removal last. Magsarjav's group offers the ranking as a shortcut so practitioners can skip costly trial-and-error searches.
arxiv-2606-24255:
Wang and colleagues generate two-person motion from text by modelling the social script before the movement. Text-to-motion systems handle solo movers well, but two interacting people must follow an unfolding social structure: phases progress, roles are assigned, and each actor's motion answers the partner's. Their 2026 study first probes what large language models can and cannot do for this task.

Language models, the analysis shows, can recover phase decompositions and partner-aware roles, thinking through an interaction's structure convincingly. They cannot, however, emit dynamic, physically plausible, partner-aware motion directly. The resulting design splits labour: a language-model planner converts hidden interaction semantics into motion-aligned supervision, decomposing phases and assigning roles, while a dedicated motion executor renders continuous three-dimensional movement. Wang's planner-executor paradigm, thinking with the language model and moving with motion skills, grounds social structure into bodily coordination between the two actors.
arxiv-2606-25055:
Noga Alon and Varun Sivashankar study a problem about vector pairs, motivated by a generalisation of the Sauer Shelah Perles lemma. Take length k vectors over an alphabet of size b. Join symbol i to symbol j in a bipartite graph whenever a coordinate realises the pair. How large can a family be if every pair produces a cycle in that graph? The authors give a construction for such families and conjecture it is optimal when k is large relative to b.

Their upper bound is of LYM type, asymptotically matches the construction, and is exact for large k divisible by b. An ordering argument gives the sharp full support bound when k falls one short of a multiple of b. For alphabet size three, the result is proved for large k. The problem connects to the Daniely Shalev Shwartz dimension, a learning theory measure.
arxiv-2606-25355:
Many learning problems are nonconvex and nonsmooth yet still structured, and adding real world constraints stated as averages makes them harder again. Lixin Tang, Xingyu Wang, and Liwei Zhang propose a solver in 2026 that handles mixed equality and inequality constraints in one loop. Older approaches nest penalty loops inside the main algorithm and demand delicate tuning. Their primal dual method, built on Halpern iteration and a variance reduced gradient estimator, needs only one simple subproblem and one projection per step.

Despite that simplicity, the authors prove the method reaches the best possible sample complexity known for this problem class, matching theoretical lower bounds. For polyhedral domains they also prove the dual variables stay stable under a standard constraint qualification. That closes a gap where earlier guarantees held only under artificial caps on the error measure used to judge solutions.
arxiv-2606-25655:
Particle detectors for future colliders need silicon sensors that are thin, fast, and precise, and monolithic designs print the electronics into the sensor itself. Michele Rignanese leads the ARCADIA collaboration's first beam test report in 2026 on its Main Demonstrator chip, a fully depleted monolithic pixel sensor two hundred micrometres thick. A beam of high energy protons at one hundred twenty gigaelectronvolts probed the device, sweeping settings for threshold, front end current, and backside bias.

Detection efficiency exceeded ninety nine percent across the working settings. Position resolution reached down to a few micrometres, well inside what tracking detectors require. Cluster size and efficiency responded to the swept knobs in the expected directions, giving the collaboration a calibrated picture of the design's behaviour. The sensor is built in a commercial imaging process adapted for full depletion of its high resistivity substrate.
arxiv-2606-25755:
Can a black hole's interior be extended past its singularity in some rough, merely continuous geometry? For the classic Schwarzschild case, Sbierski proved it cannot. Karim Mosani generalises that verdict in 2026 to a broad family of warped product black holes. These spacetimes have a static outside region, a two dimensional fibre warped by a radial coordinate, and a singularity where a curvature scalar blows up as the radius shrinks to zero. The class covers non vacuum models and shapes well beyond spherical symmetry.

Under stated conditions, the fibre closed, connected, homogeneous, and orientable, Mosani establishes future inextendibility at the continuous level. The spacetime simply has no continuous continuation through the singularity. The argument adapts Sbierski's proof rather than starting over. The result extends further, to spacetimes with more than one regular black hole horizon. Each case trims the room left for cosmic censorship to fail.
arxiv-2606-26055:
Elliot Anshelevich, Jianan Lin, and Noah Prisament add synergy to the classic Hotelling-Downs location game. In the classic model, customers visit the nearest facility. Real shoppers often prefer a mall, where many facilities cluster, even at extra distance. Their variant lets clients weigh cluster size against travel distance together. Facility placement becomes a richer strategic puzzle.

Existence results come first. Nash equilibria always exist in the synergy model, unlike the classic one. One equilibrium even matches the cost of the optimal placement exactly. The headline bound caps the price of anarchy, the worst-case cost of selfish play versus the optimum. That ratio stays below roughly three and a half. Client behaviour is more complex and often more realistic here. Selfish choices still cannot drift far from the social optimum. The mall effect, it turns out, does not wreck efficiency.
arxiv-2606-26155:
Maty Bohacek and colleagues build better tools for finding and steering sycophancy in language models. Sycophancy is the habit of flattering a user's views instead of answering straight. Activation steering can detect and dial such behaviour, but it needs many contrastive examples. Binary pairs, sycophantic versus not, blur the feature they aim to isolate. Their pipeline instead generates cascading samples. Examples show the behaviour in graded degrees that scale linearly.

Graded samples separate the features more cleanly. The features form cleanly separable groups in activation space. Signals tied to the behaviour can then be picked with more confidence. Detection, scoring, and steering all get tested. The cascading approach matches or beats judge-model and system-prompt baselines across the evaluations. It does so with lower computing demand and clearer guarantees about what is being steered. Cleaner features mean steering can target the habit without dragging neighbouring traits along.
arxiv-2606-26255:
Jon Wallem Anundsen and Mads Hustad Sandøy extend a shortcut for computing Hochschild and cyclic homology, invariants that describe an algebra's structure but are notoriously hard to calculate. Etingof and Eu had shown the job becomes easy for preprojective algebras of ADE type using a graded Euler characteristic.

The generalization covers higher preprojective algebras, including those built as tensor products of type-A hereditary algebras. For these, knowing just the algebra's center and its zeroth homology determines the graded structure of all the rest, in every degree. The proof again runs through the graded Cartan matrix, turning a hard computation into bookkeeping.
arxiv-2606-26555:
Mohamed Majdoub and Berikbol T. Torebek determine how long solutions live for a class of heat-like equations. Their equation spreads a quantity with a fractional diffusion operator, a version that weights long jumps more heavily. A power-law weight tied to distance from the origin shapes the reaction term. Such equations model anomalous diffusion with a source that strengthens the solution.

The central quantity is the Fujita exponent, a threshold value of the power. Below it, every positive solution blows up in finite time. Above it, small solutions can live forever. At the threshold itself, solutions survive an extremely long but finite time. The authors prove sharp lifespan estimates for small starting data in all three regimes. Fractional heat-kernel estimates support the lower bounds. A test-function method delivers the matching upper bounds.
arxiv-2606-26655:
Parvathy K. Kannan and seven colleagues model how surfactants behave where a droplet's edge meets a solid surface. Surfactants are soap-like molecules that gather at interfaces. The droplet edge, the contact line, moves as surfactant redistributes. Earlier simulations missed one mechanism: surfactant also sticks directly onto the solid wall. That omission flipped predictions away from experimental trends.

The authors build a phase-field model, which tracks the droplet with a smooth indicator field. Their model respects thermodynamics and includes adsorption on both the liquid surface and the solid. With wall adsorption included, surfaces of every starting type shift toward water-loving behaviour. That matches experiments. Earlier models without the mechanism wrongly pushed each surface further its own way. The authors argue solid adsorption is the missing piece for predictive contact-line modelling.
arxiv-2606-26755:
Vasileios Aravantinos-Sotiropoulos, Theofilos Tsantilas, and Christina Vasilakopoulou extend classic results about monoids to the richer world of double categories. A monoid is a set with an associative combining rule and an identity. In category theory, monoids live inside structured settings and enjoy strong properties. Monads, their cousins, are central to both mathematics and computer science.

Double categories carry two kinds of arrows at once. The authors ask when the class of monads inside one behaves well. Under conditions on the base, it is captured by algebra over the self-map class, meaning it can be described by algebraic rules. It also inherits good limit properties. The dual story for comonads is treated as well. Free monoid existence and colimit compatibility drive the results.
arxiv-2606-26855:
Pranav Debbad, Kanish Thiagarajan, Victor Dhédin, Shafeef Omar, and Majid Khadiv present Humanoid-DART, a framework that teaches humanoid robots whole-body skills from few demonstrations. That work means moving while handling objects. Human demonstrations teach it well but are costly to collect. Failures usually demand fresh human correction. Their system expands its own repertoire from a sparse starting set.

A diffusion model, which generates motion trajectories step by step, proposes new goal-directed motions. Relabeling reinterprets practice attempts as successes for the goals they did reach. Reinforcement learning then trains the robot to track the generated trajectories. The loop explores the goal space with little expert supervision. Wide tests on several skills showed the method works, the authors report.
arxiv-2606-27055:
Nasios presents solarsystem, a lightweight Python package that computes planet positions without heavy data files. This package instead uses compact analytic formulas, so it needs no outside datasets and installs easily. It gives Sun-centred and Earth-centred positions for major planets, selected dwarf planets, the Moon, and the Centaur Chiron. Sunrise, sunset, moonrise, moonset, and moonlight share routines come built in for 2026 users.

Checks against the JPL DE440 ephemeris, handled through the Skyfield framework, span many bodies and long time spans. Average planet longitude errors sit near half an arcminute, with latitude errors even smaller. Sun and Moon event times differ from reference values by only a few minutes. Moon illumination estimates differ by roughly two tenths of a percent of full brightness in the checks. An optional precession correction lets users work in a corrected frame or a fixed epoch.
arxiv-2606-27455:
Shafipour leads a team inferring the wiring of a directed network from node measurements alone. Signals diffuse across the hidden graph through a graph filter, a polynomial of the graph's shift operator with unknown coefficients. Unlike classic undirected settings, the operator and the data covariance share no common basis, and input signals may be linked across nodes. The filter is pinned down first, from outputs plus input statistics. In 2026, the resulting equations are shown identifiable under spectral-diversity assumptions.

Optimisation over a Stiefel manifold solves it smoothly. Topology recovery then seeks a sparse shift that commutes with the identified filter. An alternating joint algorithm improves sample use by letting the two stages reinforce each other. Tests on test graphs and real data, including urban mobility and portfolio cases, confirm the recovery. Directed influence networks become readable from behaviour alone. Hidden wiring leaves readable traces.
arxiv-2606-27555:
Selvakumaran and colleagues show, in theory, that a single photon can trigger an avalanche in a bistable optical cavity. The cavity, coherently driven and nonlinear, rests in its low-photon state of an optical bistability loop. One extra photon arrives from a two-level emitter. A full quantum description, keeping the field's quantum fluctuations and the photon's discrete nature, tracks the response. The cavity can jump to its high-photon state, a macroscopic change from a single quantum of excitation, in a quantum optics paper published in 2026.

The giant response grows out of the phase-transition picture of optical bistability: biased near a tipping point, the system amplifies a whisper into a switch. The work clarifies how quantum fluctuations drive the non-equilibrium dynamics of nonlinear cavities. This yields a route to an all-optical single-photon avalanche detector. Detection sensitivity reaches its logical floor.
arxiv-2606-27755:
Robot control models inherit huge language backbones from vision-language pretraining. Robotic instructions are short, so much of that capacity may be wasted. Guoheng Sun and ten colleagues measure the waste in 2026 with a protocol called Drop-Then-Recovery. Blocks are removed from a pretrained vision-language-action model. The cut model is then fine-tuned to see if performance recovers. A metric called GateProbe ranks blocks first.

The recovery pattern is strikingly uneven. Language backbones prove highly redundant for standard manipulation tasks. Vision and action pathways tolerate removal far less well. On the LIBERO benchmark, one model even improved when half its language blocks were cut. OpenVLA-OFT rose from ninety-five to over ninety-eight percent success. Keeping only two language blocks still recovered baseline-level performance. The authors argue current benchmarks press too little on deep language grounding. Future designs should allocate capacity more deliberately.
arxiv-2606-27855:
Muscle-signal decoders work best when tuned to each user. Surface electromyography, or sEMG, reads muscle activity through the skin. Tuning data are scarce by necessity. Long sessions burden users, and small datasets invite overfitting. Stephan Lehmler, Tobias Glasmachers, and Ioannis Iossifidis test early-warning signs in 2026. The signs come from activation statistics inside the network. They need no held-out validation data at all.

A convolutional network was first trained on many subjects. It was then fine-tuned per user with only a few repetitions. The data came from the NinaPro DB2 benchmark. During tuning, the team watched accuracy and behaviour in the last hidden layer together. When test accuracy fell, the activation rates of rectified linear units shifted in characteristic ways. Those shifts mark memorisation in progress. The results give first evidence that such signs can flag failing calibration early, using training data alone.
arxiv-2606-28055:
Truck makers test new drivelines with physical prototypes. A simulator could allow earlier evaluation, but only if drivers feel small acceleration differences. Erik Gustaf Lilljebjörn and three colleagues measure that sensitivity in 2026. The just-noticeable difference in longitudinal acceleration is the target. Two launch-tuned motion-cueing variants are compared with a general variant, in a simulator on a long linear track. A weighted staircase procedure supplies the data.

No significant differences were found between the cueing variants. The mean threshold across participants and variants was five point four percent. Participants were thus sensitive to fairly small acceleration changes. The point of subjective equality sat at minus one point nine percent, so the second stimulus in a pair felt stronger than it was. Subjectively, most participants preferred the launch-tuned variants. Filter cut-off frequency had no observed effect. Limited statistical power is flagged as a caveat.
arxiv-2606-28355:
Yuyan Qian, Claude Montacie, Milan Stankovic, and Victoria Eyharabide ask whether public knowledge can make business-to-business sales recommendations smarter. Sales teams choose which companies to approach using scattered information, and modern platforms learn compact numerical profiles of companies, called embeddings, to recommend and rank likely clients.

Qian and colleagues enrich those profiles with semantic knowledge drawn from DBpedia, the structured companion of Wikipedia, inside a working pipeline that also uses firm attributes and text profiles. They judge the result on a real platform's interaction-prediction task, scored with genuine user feedback. Adding the DBpedia knowledge improved scores on both ranking and discrimination, suggesting that what a company is openly known to be helps predict which prospects will actually engage.
arxiv-2606-28755:
Vardoulaki reviews radio galaxies, the brightest objects in the radio sky, whose jets come from matter falling onto a supermassive black hole. These galaxies, a type of active galactic nucleus, have been studied for over seventy years, yet parts of their physics remain unclear. Her focus is what the next generation Square Kilometre Array telescope will reveal once it starts producing huge, sharp radio images.

Extended radio lobes, the vast clouds a jet inflates, act like a fossil record of past activity around the black hole. Reading them shows the duty cycle, meaning how often the central engine switches on and off over time. Vardoulaki explains how the new telescope should sharpen views of particle acceleration, ageing plasma and magnetic fields. Dying and restarted galaxies, whose jets have faded or fired again, should become far easier to spot.
arxiv-2606-28955:
Opryshko, Jain and Gilitschenski present a defence against reward hacking, where a learning agent games its reward signal instead of doing its intended task. Standard practical defences keep the agent's updates close to a safe reference policy. That creates a tension: tighter leashes suppress hacking but also block legitimate improvement beyond the reference.

Their method, MCVL, wraps an existing off-policy learner and inspects each new experience before admitting it into training. For every candidate transition, it forecasts two training paths, one including the data point and one excluding it. A frozen estimator, built from a value function and a learned reward model, scores both paths. A transition enters training only if including it does not lower the score. The authors state when this filter is both safe and permissive. Across gridworlds and modified continuous-control tasks with varied hacking tricks, MCVL curbed hacking while still improving the intended objective.
arxiv-2606-29255:
Han and eight colleagues build a network that matches laser damage sites between two kinds of inspection images. In high-power laser facilities, online images of final optics contain fake damage sites that look much like real ones. Telling them apart needs accurate matching to offline ground-truth sites, but features are weak, shapes distort locally, and many distractor sites confuse the match.

Their model needs only the centre coordinates of each site. After each matching round it estimates how matchable each site looks, and feeds that confidence back as a weight guiding the next round's feature mixing. That feedback suppresses distractors instead of letting them spread. A geometric consistency check reins in false high confidence, and a hard-example loss sharpens the split between look-alike sites. On their Complex-Scene dataset the method reached a matching F1 score of about ninety-six percent.
arxiv-2606-29455:
Głazek tackles a technical obstacle in describing hadrons, particles such as protons, through the front form of quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the theory of quarks and gluons. Precise calculations hit divergences, infinities that must be tamed, especially small-x divergences tied to gluons carrying tiny momentum fractions. His proposal adds a gluon mass parameter plus an auxiliary colour-octet scalar field that stands in for longitudinal gluons.

As the mass parameter tends to zero, the auxiliary field decouples from the hadron dynamics, as gauge theory requires. The same device helps cancel quadratic ultraviolet divergences in self-interactions. Głazek explains the method first for scattering amplitudes, then for bound-state eigenvalue problems. Second-order results for heavy quarks follow, including confinement, the trapping of quarks inside hadrons. A heuristic scenario extends the Hamiltonian approach toward light quarks.
arxiv-2606-29855:
Seong and three colleagues present RainODE, a system for forecasting rain that treats time as continuous rather than as fixed steps. Fine time detail matters for rain forecasts, but dense step-by-step models are costly.

RainODE models how a rain pattern evolves inside a compressed latent space using a Neural ODE, an equation-based model that can be queried at any time. Pure equation-based motion tends to smooth away local growth and decay of rain cells. The authors add a stochastic module based on a Brownian Bridge, a random path pinned at both ends, to restore fine structure. On the SEVIR storm dataset and a new radar dataset called RAPID, the system improves forecasts across time intervals and rain regimes.
arxiv-2606-29955:
Zhu and thirteen colleagues introduce SpreadsheetBench 2, a benchmark for AI agents doing full business spreadsheet workflows. Older tests check isolated skills such as writing one formula, while real work spans many linked sheets.

The benchmark's 321 tasks cover generation, debugging, and visualisation, built from authentic business data such as financial reports and corporate filings and validated by domain experts. Each task averages 11.8 worksheets and about 594 cell modifications. Testing eight frontier language models under one agent scaffold, plus several spreadsheet products, the best model reaches only 34.89 percent overall accuracy, and debugging accuracy drops to 12.00 percent. Weak inspection of the workbook and wrong target-cell choices are the dominant bottlenecks.
arxiv-2606-30255:
Maximilian Rottensteiner, Dorian Schiffer, Tobias Pausch, Alois Mair, and Anton Zeilinger build a teaching experiment that violates Wigner's inequality with photons. Bell-type inequalities expose how quantum correlations defy classical intuition. Wigner's version needs only minimal set-theoretic assumptions. That simplicity makes it ideal for introductory physics courses. The paper joins derivation, experiment, and data analysis in one package.

The authors first derive the inequality for students to follow. They then describe a quantum-optical setup that tests it directly. Measured data from that setup violate the inequality clearly. Raw data are openly provided for classes to analyze themselves. Students and instructors can repeat the full analysis independently. The resource connects theory, laboratory practice, and statistics authentically. It aims to give educators a ready route into quantum correlations. Deeper understanding of quantum systems is the stated goal.
arxiv-2606-30555:
Dvir Alsheich and five colleagues, writing in 2026, expose a security hole in systems where several AI agents share work. Such multi-agent systems need a router that sends each task to the best-suited agent. Most routers trust agents' self-descriptions or stored profile vectors, neither verified. A dishonest agent can inflate its profile or hide a backdoor and attract tasks it should never receive.

Their system, ANTAP, tests agents directly instead of trusting descriptions. It questions each agent, measures performance, and stores results as behavioural operators, mathematical maps inside a shared meaning space. At routing time, only algebra on those operators decides, never the agent's own words, a linguistic firewall. Attack success against description-based tricks fell to near zero, versus at least sixty-seven percent for a description-based router. Against adaptive embedding attacks, ANTAP cut success by about twenty percent.
arxiv-2606-30655:
Anshumali Shrivastava designs course assessments that stay fair when students can use AI freely. In senior computer science courses, he argues, grading should reward AI-resilient skill: achieving outcomes beyond a strong AI baseline. A good assessment should also stop bigger private AI budgets from buying grades by themselves. His minimal formal framework has four parts: a real task, an executable evaluator, a declared AI baseline frontier, and a grading rule.

The grading rule uses Pareto surplus, the amount by which a submission beats the baseline's best trade-offs. Surplus gives a measurable certificate that the work achieves something the declared AI baseline did not already supply. Supporting protocol elements, such as design reports, ablations and oral checks, help interpret surplus as student skill. Extensions handle self-improving AI loops, budget neutrality and red teaming. A concrete example is a Bloom filter assignment built for Rice University courses.
arxiv-2606-30855:
Yuan-Sen Ting and colleagues present an open textbook, Deep Learning for Astrophysics, grown from a NASA interest group's lecture series. Community assessments name education, not access to tools, as the main barrier to astronomers adopting machine learning. The NASA Cosmic Origins AI/ML Science and Technology Interest Group formed to close that gap with short, field-specific teaching, and this book collects its lectures for free online.

The textbook holds 23 chapters in six parts, drawn from 17 lecturers. It runs from computing foundations and network architectures through generative modelling, simulation-based inference and reinforcement learning to language-model agents, closing with the practice of AI-assisted science. Many chapters carry executable notebooks. The group also sketches its next year, centred on agentic research and NASA's ASTRA mission-concept initiative.
arxiv-2606-30955:
Pokou Nagacy, Bérenger Akon Kpata and Nouffou Diarra prove boundedness results for smoothing operators on a new family of function spaces. The spaces are called generalised Fofana spaces. They blend Lebesgue spaces at two scales under a growth function. They extend both Fofana spaces and Nakai's generalised Morrey spaces. The team study three operators. One is the fractional integral, a Riesz potential that smooths a function by a fractional order. The second is the fractional maximal operator. The third is a generalised fractional integral.

All three operators are bounded on these spaces under the stated conditions. Boundedness means outputs stay in the space with controlled size. As a consequence, the team obtain generalised Olsen-type inequalities. These link the Riesz potential with the generalised fractional integrals.
arxiv-2606-31055:
Hallur and four colleagues work on evaluating speech-to-speech AI agents. These are systems that talk back in a generated voice. Judging them needs speech-native measures of prosody and rhythm: pitch, speaking rate, and pausing. But pooled statistics from many speakers misjudge any single output. These traits shift with the speaker and with the state of the conversation.

The team drew on more than 4,000 hours of two-person English conversation. From it they built matched reference groups for pitch level, pitch expressivity, speech rate, articulation rate, and pause behavior. An output is scored by percentile against its closest matched human group. Outputs outside the central range get flagged. On held-out human speech, matched references flagged about the expected share of cases. Pooled references over-flagged, and the direction of each deviation stayed easy to read.
arxiv-2606-31455:
Kordalis and Trevezas build a renewal theory where events unfold along several time axes at once. Classical renewal theory tracks repeats along one clock. Many real problems carry two attributes at once, such as age and usage in a warranty. Their multi-time renewal chains place the waiting times on a multi-index lattice.

Multi-index convolution and multivariate power series give explicit renewal equations and formulas for their coefficients. Fast Fourier methods plus Newton-type iteration handle large grids. Strong laws and central limit theorems cover the long-run behaviour. Fixed-horizon data bring a multivariate censoring structure with an exact estimator. Uses range from two-attribute warranty costing to availability models for systems that alternate between states.
arxiv-2606-31555:
Romano and Gambassi study a quantum impurity that starts to propel itself when its coupling to its bath oscillates. A polaron, an impurity dressed by the quantum gas around it, normally feels drag. Here the coupling flips sign periodically in time, and the authors integrate out the bath to find the effective drag force on the impurity.

Once the modulation frequency passes a critical value, the drag coefficient turns negative at low speeds, the signature of self-propulsion. In the classical limit they map the transition against modulation frequency and bath chemical potential. Leading quantum corrections keep the transition alive, though very precise position measurements can suppress it. The result adds a driven quantum route to active matter, where motion emerges from a timed coupling rather than a built-in motor.
arxiv-2606-31655:
Shamoto and six colleagues develop a real-space way to study magnons, the collective waves of magnetic spin, using the dynamic magnetic pair-density function. Standard inelastic neutron scattering reports a structure factor in momentum space, which suits perfect crystals but hides local behavior. Fourier transforming that factor instead yields correlations between spin pairs at actual distances and energies.

Deriving low-energy formulas for simple magnet models and testing them against simulations and materials such as FeTiO3 and YBa2Cu3O6, the team shows a characteristic energy dependence for local magnon modes. This includes a switch from acoustic to optical character. Each spin-pair correlation flips sign at a given energy on nanometer scales, even without periodicity, giving a tool for local magnetic dynamics that momentum-space analysis cannot provide.
arxiv-2606-31855:
Balbiani, van Ditmarsch and Lerouvillois present a logic for distributed knowledge when information sharing happens asynchronously. Distributed knowledge is what a group could know if members pooled what they know. Existing resolving logics assume synchrony: everyone notices when a subgroup shares, as if a global clock were common knowledge.

Their semantics is history-based. Truth is judged against a world plus a history of past resolutions, and each agent observes only part of that history. An agent can simply miss a sharing event between others, which breaks axioms that held in the synchronous system. The authors argue the modelling gains for distributed computing are substantial, even though the technical complications around axiomatization are real.
arxiv-2608-00255: Artificial Intelligence for Spatially Reconfigurable Antennas, arXiv 2608-00255. The reconfigurable antennas. The work is kept for study. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
arxiv-2608-00355: CurveShift: Is Agent Progress Scalar? arXiv 2608-00355. The agent progress. Researchers may consult the paper. It waits for future eyes. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The archive guards it with care.
black-experiments-magnesia-alba-1755:
Joseph Black, a Scots doctor and chemist, read these trials to a learned group in Edinburgh in 1755. His test stuff was magnesia alba, a white earth used in drugs of the day. He also worked on quicklime and other such stuffs.

By weight and heat, Black showed that these stuffs hold a gas he named fixed air. That gas is what we now call carbon dioxide, though he had no such name for it. His strict use of the scales set a new bar and shook the old phlogiston scheme.
braid-physiology-fascination-1855:
James Braid defends his life's work in The Physiology of Fascination, from 1855, his late reply to the critics of hypnotism. Fascination, the fixed stare of man or beast, gets his close physiological study. He refines his theory of suggestion while answering skeptics point by sharp point in print.

The founder writes with the vigor of a man still fighting for his science. Cases, trials, and tart rejoinders fill the combative pages here. He insists that trance is real, lawful, and open to study. The book is key for the history of psychology's most argued method, showing its maker in his final, feisty form.
browning-men-and-women-1855:
Robert Browning was an English poet who made his fame with dramatic monologues, poems spoken by a single character. Men and Women, published in 1855, collects fifty-one of them. It was the book that finally won him a wide audience.

Each poem lets a speaker reveal himself while telling a story. Readers meet Renaissance painters, scheming dukes, lovers, and monks. Famous pieces include Fra Lippo Lippi and Andrea del Sarto, both about art and ambition. Because the speakers expose their own motives, the poems feel like short plays. The collection is Browning's breakthrough work, the one that fixed his place among the major Victorian poets.
capron-modern-spiritualism-1855:
E. W. Capron told the first tale of the Fox girls in Modern Spiritualism, his book of 1855. Capron was a news man who knew the kin at first hand. Two girls in a farm house heard raps that seemed to spell words. Crowds came, press took it up, and a faith was born in a span of months.

Capron prints the facts as he saw them, plus the wild zeal they sparked. His sub name grants both: facts and fanatic zeal. The book is the first full past of the faith. All tales since start with his pages.
cia-0000008655:
A wounded American prisoner of war was observed in a Haiphong hospital, according to a report dated August 1972. Haiphong, North Vietnam's main port, was heavily bombed that year during the spring offensive's response. A hospital sighting implies a prisoner hurt badly enough to need open care.

Such glimpses were precious because prisoners were usually kept hidden. A confirmed hospital visit could prove a man alive at a known date. Analysts filed the detail beside names and photographs in case it matched a missing airman. The report shows the POW record built from rare, brief sightings.
cia-0000009855:
A Caucasian prisoner of war was observed in Hanoi, a March 1968 CIA report states. Caucasian was file language for a Western-looking man whose name and nation were unknown. Hanoi sightings of unknown prisoners were maddening: close to the system's center, yet anonymous.

An unnamed man could not be matched to a family or a loss list directly. Analysts compared the description with airmen missing on matching dates. Sometimes a match emerged; often the file stayed open. This report preserves one such observation in the enemy capital at the war's height, during the Tet year's spring.
cia-0000010555:
A pilot's reported death in Thai Nguyen city, in Bac Thai province, is recorded in an October 1972 item. Thai Nguyen, north of Hanoi, was a steel and rail center struck often from the air. A death inside a city pointed to a pilot brought down, or brought in, among civilians.

The word reported carries the file's honesty: the death came by witness account, not recovery. Urban losses could hide in plain sight, recorded by residents rather than units. Officials filed the account against the names of men lost near Thai Nguyen. This entry preserves that city report in the air war's last autumn.
cia-0000012355:
Leadership changed hands at the agency in 1962, and a Helms memo that May went to the Acting Director of Central Intelligence. Acting chiefs hold the chair between directors, and the Penkovsky case did not pause for the transition. The file's summit channel simply bent toward the new name, its traffic on Military Thought matters flowing as before.

Handovers at the top are where great cases can stumble, and this one did not. The memo shows the guard changing with the case intact. For readers, it is a small lesson in how bureaucracies keep faith with a source through their own upheavals.
cia-0000013855: Vietnamese and American soldiers were captured in Binh Dinh Province in 1965, and a CIA note dated June 6, 1967, looks back at the case. Binh Dinh, on the central coast of South Vietnam, saw heavy fighting early in the war. The note shows that capture reports were still being filed on old cases two years later.
cia-0000013955: A detention camp in Kien Phong Province is the subject of a CIA note dated January 1, 1969. Kien Phong lay in South Vietnam's delta, near the Cambodian border. A camp there showed the Viet Cong held prisoners deep in the south. The note keeps the southern system in view beside the better known northern camps.
cia-0000014655: Operational is the tag on a CIA file about an East German engineer, dated October 3, 1955. The man's name is cut down to a code-like entry, Gelbin, with his first name unknown. Engineers from the east drew interest as sources or defectors in the Cold War. The file hints at a live operation the public record barely shows.
cia-0000015255: Antarctic flying saucers over Argentina anchor a CIA file dated June 3, 1965. The file holds just its first page, per the title. Reports from the far south mixed cold war bases, whalers' tales, and bright skies. Even a single page was filed, since no one could say which scrap might matter.
cia-0000015355: The California Committee for Saucer Investigation is named in a CIA file dated January 1, 1953. Citizen groups sprang up to study saucers on their own in those years. A state committee with a formal name drew a file of its own. The record shows the agency watching the watchers as well as the skies.
cia-0000015455: The National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena, called NICAP, appears in a CIA record dated January 4, 1953. The catalog notes that the publication date is unknown, so 1953 is the file's own dating. NICAP grew into the best-known civilian group pressing for open study of saucers. An early agency file on it shows officials watching the watchers from the group's first years.
cia-0000022155: Accounts of a supply plane shot down in Savannakhet fill a CIA record dated in 1963. The catalog spells the Laotian city Savanmarket, a garble kept in the title. Supply flights kept remote posts alive in Laos, and each loss cost a crew. Gathered accounts, plural in the title, suggest more than one witness told the story of the fall.
cia-0000022355: The Attorney General spoke by phone about the prospects of Powers writing a book, a CIA record dated in 1962 notes. The title does not name who held the office, so no name is relied on here. A book by Powers could embarrass the agency that once employed him. The call shows the worry reaching the top of the Justice Department.
cia-0000036855:
Havana's newspaper Granma published an interview with prisoner of war McCain, and a CIA record dated January 5, 1970 kept the item. The file also notes a meeting involving a Spanish party in connection with the interview. Granma was Cuba's official newspaper, and its pages carried weight across Latin America.

Inside, readers find the interview as Havana chose to print it for its own audience. Cuba used such pieces to show sympathy with Hanoi and scorn for the American war. The record shows how a prisoner's words could be picked up and reused far from Vietnam itself, in a third country's press campaign.
cia-0000037155:
Two Caucasians, apparently Americans, and one Japanese man were detained in the Bien Hoa area, a CIA record dated November 6, 1978 reports. The detention came more than three years after the war in Vietnam had ended. Who the men were, and why they were held, is the puzzle at the file's center.

Inside, the report sets down what was known about the three detained men. Unidentified Westerners in postwar Vietnam always drew attention, given the missing men still unaccounted for. The file stayed open because the report could not be confirmed, yet it could not be safely dismissed either, and so it was kept.
cia-0000037955:
A CIA Latin America review dated September 5, 1982 weighs counterterrorist capabilities in the region. The title pairs Peru with the security forces of Chile in its subject line. Both countries faced armed movements, and both drew American study.

Inside, the review grades how well security forces could fight terrorist groups. Judgments of this kind shaped aid, training, and advice from Washington. A low grade could cost a government money it badly wanted from the United States. The file shows the colder side of the era's policy work. Officers in Washington measured other nations' forces the way accountants measure firms, and the grades they gave could move money and weapons.
cia-0000045155:
The PRTC claimed responsibility for killing Marines, in a CIA record dated May 5, 1985. The title ties the claim to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. The PRTC was one faction inside that wider rebel front.

Inside, the faction's own claim to the Zona Rosa attack is preserved. A small faction gains standing by owning a famous strike. The claim also fixed blame at a level below the front's high command. That placement mattered in the arguments that followed over who had ordered the attack. The file holds that act of ownership from May 1985, one of several records in this set that circle the same attack from different sides.
cia-0000045255:
ARENA's Calderon and D'Aubuisson condemned the kidnapping, in a CIA record dated August 4, 1985. Roberto D'Aubuisson was the hard right's best known leader. Condemnation from that quarter was aimed at more than the kidnappers.

Inside, the right's public outrage over the seizure is preserved. ARENA used the crime to attack the government's weakness as well. A president whose daughter could be taken looked, in their telling, unfit to guard the country itself. The charge was cruel, and it was meant to be remembered at election time. The file holds that double-edged denunciation from the case's first week, when even sympathy from the right arrived with a blade inside it.
cia-0000049355: Dated June 2, 1982, declassified CIA document 0000049355 is a summary on El Salvador's performance on certification issues, noted for the Truth Commission. Its subject is how El Salvador measured up on the certification questions named in the heading. The file survives as a summary item, preserving the agency's framing of a review that its title describes only in general terms.
cia-0000096655: Soviet Defense Budget is the plain title of declassified CIA document 0000096655, dated October 4, 1978. The heading names the budget as the whole subject in three words. Readers find a short declassified item on Soviet military spending, its title giving no breakdown. It is preserved as one of the agency's recurring efforts. Each such effort tried to size up that budget.
cia-0000108155: National Intelligence Estimate Probable Economic Effects of a Severance of East is the heading, cut off mid-phrase, on declassified CIA document 0000108155, dated March 3, 1958. The title marks a formal estimate on the economic effects of a severance. What would be severed breaks off at the word East in the heading. The brief record preserves the break exactly as released.
cia-0000112355: Ufo Sighted Over Urumqi Evening of 6 Sep is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112355, dated August 3, 1989. The title dates the sighting to the evening of September 6, a month after the file's own August date. That ordering stands on the face of the record itself. The brief record is a sighting item over Urumqi, in Xinjiang, China.
cia-0000115455: Guatemala: Prospects for the New Government -- National Intelligence Estimate is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000115455, dated January 6, 1986. The title marks a formal estimate on the prospects for Guatemala's new government. New is the heading's own word for that government in the title. The brief record is a government prospects estimate from the first week of 1986.
cia-0000117855: Title Deleted re: Answers to Questions Posed to Colonel Oliver North is the surviving heading on declassified CIA document 0000117855, dated August 3, 1985. The catalog notes the title was deleted, then names its subject: answers given to Colonel Oliver North. Questions and answers are the form named in the heading itself. The brief record preserves the deletion note with the subject as released.
cia-0000126955: A May 1961 CIA report gives the short-term prospects in Haiti. Francois Duvalier, known as Papa Doc, was tightening his grip on the Caribbean nation. The paper forecasts what Washington could expect as Haiti slid toward one of the hemisphere's darkest dictatorships. Prospects papers on Haiti recurred for decades because the country combined poverty, a feared police state, and a shoreline ninety miles from Florida in Washington's thinking.
cia-0000132455:
Communist influence in Cuba fills a CIA document dated February 2, 1960. By early 1960 communists sat inside the revolution's inner circle. The old question of whether they held influence had given way to a harder one: how much they held.

The document measures that influence across the government and its new bodies. For readers, it records the agency's answer at a key turning point. Within another year the revolution would declare its socialist character in public. The entry shows analysts reaching that conclusion in private well before the announcement was made. Their judgment came from watching posts, parties, and unions change hands.
cia-0000132655: Cuban communists telling foreign comrades how they won fills a CIA paper dated January 3, 1961. Victory had made Havana a classroom for the world's revolutionary left. Party men from Cuba were lecturing abroad on the road they had taken to power. The short paper reports what they said and the lessons they claimed others should draw from Cuba's case.
cia-0000132755: Multiple CIA briefings on Cuba share the date January 4, 1961, and this paper is one of that burst. The cluster followed the cutting of diplomatic ties on January 3, when the agency restated the island's situation from several angles at once. Now open to the public, the declassified text is preserved via the CIA Reading Room and the Internet Archive.
cia-0000134255: The man tipped as Cuba's next ambassador to Washington fills item 21 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated April 5, 1960. Within a year there would be no Cuban ambassador in Washington at all. For the moment Havana was still sending envoys in the normal way. The short item reports the name in prospect and the talk around it.
cia-0000135755: Dated 3 February 1961, this Spanish text belongs to the 2506 Brigade document set. The exile brigade was drilling under CIA supervision, its invasion of Cuba about ten weeks away. The catalog gives the item no subject of its own. It is kept in Spanish as released, one of the many dated records the brigade left from that February, and its content is a matter for the text, not the title.
cia-0000136255: From 6 May 1954 comes a CIA cable, since declassified, on special instructions for broadcasts following D-day, the aftermath scripted before the event. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136355: ODAYOKE's interests are in competent hands, LINCOLN assures CADICK in this June 1954 cable about the SKIMMER and SYNCARP basic agreement. That agreement committed support only to attain the objective of freeing the country, the station notes, not to any person for the top position. Placing CALLIGERIS on top is a policy matter above PBSUCCESS's jurisdiction. He must never assume unconditional backing, and limited concessions now may avert a greater tragedy.
cia-0000136755: The 2506 Brigade's Spanish files contain this document under an estimated date of 1 January 1961, flagged as estimated in the catalog. The brigade, Cuban exiles trained by the CIA, was in its final winter before the Bay of Pigs. No subject is recorded for the item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, one of the estimated New Year records that recur throughout this series.
cia-0000136855: Guatemala's white paper charges are a provocation, this January 1954 cable argues. The charges aim to disrupt hemisphere solidarity at Caracas. They also aim to win outside support. Officers worry about a Bogotazo-style disturbance at the conference. Headquarters asks for plans for counter propaganda. It also orders quick action. Articles should be placed in the publication Alerta. The cable is information war, planned ahead of the Tenth Inter-American Conference.
cia-0000137455: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers, dated only to 1960 and marked as estimated in the catalog. The brigade was the CIA-trained exile force that landed at the Bay of Pigs in 1961, so this record belongs to its training period. The catalog gives an estimated year and no subject. The document survives in the original Spanish in the declassified release, as part of the brigade's early archive.
cia-03003755: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1953/12/08, a CIA publication. Another December briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-03017655: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1954/11/19, a CIA publication. The November briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cia-03155155: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1957/10/30, a CIA publication. The next day's briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-03164655: March 13, 1946: the daily summary circulated in Washington. The postwar world's intelligence digest. The Cold War's infancy, on paper. Tomorrow's readers will find it. This file preserves that declassified summary. The archive guards it with care.
cia-03174755: February 25, 1955: the daily bulletin went to readers. The global intelligence summary for senior officials. The Cold War's late-winter brief. The library keeps the document safe. This declassified paper is stored. It is filed. The text is preserved.
cia-03184155: November 11, 1959 brought this intelligence bulletin. The daily briefing kept Washington posted on global developments. Veterans Day's classified reading. The file is now open to the public. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Kept for readers.
cia-03194455: April 24, 1955: the bulletin briefed Washington on global events. The intelligence analysts' daily product for senior officials. The Cold War routine continued. The archive guards it with care. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Kept for readers.
commynes-memoirs-scoble-vol-1-1855:
Philippe de Commynes served Charles the Bold of Burgundy, then crossed to Louis XI of France and became his trusted adviser. His Memoirs, the first great political memoir of the modern kind, tell what he saw at both courts. Andrew Scoble translated the work, and this first volume, from 1855, holds books one through five.

Commynes watches the wars of Burgundy and France, the cunning of Louis, and the pride that ruins Charles at Nancy. He draws lessons on power with a cool, worldly hand: keep faith, buy peace cheap, fear your own anger. Kings read him for centuries as a handbook of rule. His voice, plain and knowing, still sounds modern.
commynes-memoirs-scoble-vol-2-1855:
The second volume of Andrew Scoble's Commynes, from 1855, holds books six through eight of the Memoirs. It adds the Scandalous Chronicle of Jean de Troyes, a Paris record of the same years. Commynes here follows the French court past the death of Louis XI into the reign of Charles VIII.

The young king invades Italy in 1494, and Commynes, sent as envoy, watches the old Italian order crack. He judges popes, dukes, and his own master with the same calm eye. Jean de Troyes adds the street view of Paris under Louis, its feasts, crimes, and court scandals. Together the two texts close the great memoir of the age. Commynes remains the first modern voice in political writing.
doe-osti-2997623-implementation-risks-of: RFID in TA-55 got its risk review, and this DOE report covers implementation hazards. The pages detail the risk analysis. The facility managers get their briefing. The site was TA-55. The analysis was risk. The managers got briefings. The hazards were implementation.
doe-osti-3017519-final-technical-report-: Climate extremes got structure-discovered, and this DOE final finds physical meaning. The pages detail the DE-SC0022255 findings. The climate folks get their closeout. The data were climate extreme. The closeout was climate. The meaning was physical. The structures were meaningful.
douglass-my-bondage-1855:
My Bondage and My Freedom, from 1855, is Frederick Douglass's second and fuller autobiography. By then he was a famed speaker, editor, and leader, legally free after British friends bought his liberty. He retells his early life with ten more years of thought behind it.

The bondage half gives the fullest account of his enslavement, his masters, and his escape. The freedom half traces his rise as an orator and his break with the Garrisonians. Douglass writes with open anger and sharp analysis of slavery as a system. Many readers judge it his greatest book. An introduction by James McCune Smith frames the enlarged edition.
euler-institutiones-calculi-1755:
Leonhard Euler orders the differential calculus in his Institutiones calculi differentialis, in Latin from 1755. No true textbook of the subject had existed before his. Euler takes the wild new math of Newton and Leibniz and sets it in teachable order, rule by rule, for every student to follow with profit.

Generations learned analysis from these patient, lucid Latin pages afterward. Functions, rates, and curves gain clear forms under his hand. Euler produced more math than any man of his century, perhaps of any century. This book shows his most useful gift: not discovery alone, but the power to make hard things plain for those who came after.
europmc-pmc10022855:
Morton and the FOxTROT trial group report mature results of a large randomized trial of chemotherapy before surgery for colon cancer, in a 2023 paper. Giving chemo first is standard in some cancers but needed formal testing in colon cancer. Patients with locally advanced tumors were assigned by chance to early chemo or to the usual surgery-first path.

The trial gave six weeks of chemo before surgery to the early-treatment group. The paper reports the long-term results on cancer return and safety. Surgeons and oncologists can use the findings to weigh a change in the order of care.
europmc-pmc10060155:
Issa and a large trial team report on revumenib, a drug that blocks the menin protein, in leukemia with certain gene changes, in a 2023 study. The target cancers carry either a rearranged KMT2A gene or a mutated NPM1 gene. Both forms depend on menin to keep cancer growth programs switched on.

The paper reports trial results in patients whose disease had returned or resisted other care. It describes responses to the drug and its side effects. The work supports a new class of targeted drugs for hard-to-treat acute leukemia.
europmc-pmc10166855:
Udeochu and a large team report that tau protein switches on an immune alarm in microglia that weakens the brain's resilience, in a 2023 study. Alzheimer's disease develops for years before symptoms appear. During that silent phase, some brains stay sharp despite building damage, a trait called cognitive resilience.

The team found that tau activates a DNA sensor, cGAS, in microglia, the brain's immune cells. That alarm lowers a protective protein, MEF2C, and resilience falls. The pathway may offer targets to keep minds sharp longer. It also helps explain why resilience varies.
europmc-pmc10191855:
Shalon and colleagues profile the human gut environment under normal, healthy conditions in a 2023 study. The gut's mix of microbes, proteins, and small chemicals changes along its length and over time. Those patterns shape digestion and health, yet most data came from stool alone, which gives only a partial view.

The team sampled directly from different gut regions in healthy volunteers. They mapped microbes and chemicals side by side at each site. The resulting atlas shows how much the gut's inner world varies by place, and sets a baseline for disease studies.
europmc-pmc10464255:
Sharkiya ran a rapid review in 2023 on how talk shapes care results for older patients. Clear talk helps doctors bond with patients and guides joint choices. The review hunted past work on patients aged 65 and over. Five data banks were searched for studies from 2000 to 2023.

Seven studies passed the screen. Sharkiya found that both spoken and unspoken signals lifted every patient outcome checked. Those outcomes covered how happy patients felt, how good their care was, and their health of body and mind. Talk styles ranged from word choice to tone and body stance. The studies had weak spots, though, in design and in small, narrow samples. The author calls for true trials with clear effect sizes next.
europmc-pmc11519755:
Goh and a large team run a randomized trial of whether a language model improves doctors' diagnostic reasoning in this 2024 study. Large language models had shown strong scores on medical test questions. Whether they help working physicians reason through cases was untested in a trial. Fifty physicians in family medicine, internal medicine, and emergency medicine took part.

Physicians were assigned to use a large language model or only conventional resources, such as reference texts. Diagnostic reasoning performance did not improve significantly with the model, the authors report. Scores with model access were statistically indistinguishable from scores with standard resources alone. The finding matters because the model itself scores highly when tested solo. The authors conclude that further development is needed to integrate such models into clinical practice effectively. Simply handing doctors the tool is not enough.
europmc-pmc1261155:
Tomfohr, Lu, and Kepler introduced a pathway-level gene analysis method in 2005. Single gene changes can hide broader biological shifts. Grouping genes by pathway can reveal clearer patterns. Their method scores each pathway activity level per sample.

Activity scores come from singular value decomposition of expression data. Tests used diabetes data and airway data from smokers. Smoker comparisons flagged nicotine metabolism and mucus production pathways. Glutathione metabolism, a defense pathway, also stood out. Tomfohr compares results with gene-set enrichment, a rival approach. Pathway scores give a more readable picture of cell state.
europmc-pmc1361355:
Negrete and co-authors tested whether a second cell protein can host Nipah virus in 2006. Nipah is a lethal emerging virus with no cure. Its known entry receptor is ephrinB2, a cell surface protein. Related ephrin proteins share overlapping body patterns.

Every known ephrin was tested for binding the viral attachment protein. Only ephrinB3 joined B2 in binding it. Binding strength was subnanomolar for both, though B3 released faster. EphrinB3 sufficed for entry of both test and live virus. Two key residues in B3 proved critical for that use. Negrete widens the known entry routes for Nipah.
europmc-pmc1621055:
A fading retina slowly steals sight in retinitis pigmentosa. Hamel reviewed the disease in 2006. Light-sensing cells die off, leaving pigment deposits in the eye. Night blindness comes first, then side vision narrows over decades until blindness.

About one in 4,000 people has the plain form. Forty-five genes or loci were known causes by then, making gene testing impractical for most. No therapy stops the disease or restores sight. Care aims to slow decline with sunlight protection and vitamins, treat cataracts and swelling, and support low vision. Hamel stresses genetic counseling for families.
europmc-pmc1797055:
Yip and Horvath extended in 2007 a network measure used to judge how tightly two genes are linked. In gene networks, direct links can be noisy or missing. The older topological overlap measure counted neighbors that two nodes share, since genes sharing partners often share a function or pathway.

Their generalized version, called GTOM, looks beyond immediate neighbors. It counts neighbors shared at two or more steps away and scales the result to fall between zero and one. Theory, plus tests on a yeast co-expression network and a fly protein network, backed the extension. Pairs with high generalized overlap were more likely to fall in the same functional class. The authors argue the broader view gives a sturdier and more sensitive read of interconnectedness.
europmc-pmc1802755:
Smith, Hay and co-authors recalculated in 2007 the basic reproductive number for malaria across Africa. That number, written R0, counts how many new cases one case can generate in a fully susceptible population. It gauges how hard malaria will be to control in a given place.

Their new method produced estimates for 121 African populations, expanding the known set about tenfold. Values ranged from near one to more than 3,000, a huge spread in transmission intensity. They also show that classic formulas overstate spread in small finite populations. Uneven biting, where some people are bitten far more than others, can raise some measures while lowering the true human-to-human count. Where R0 is highest, control will need several combined methods aimed at the most-bitten people.
europmc-pmc1865555:
Chandran and colleagues compared gene activity in 2007 between prostate cancers that had spread and those still confined to the gland. Spread, or metastasis, is the deadliest turn in prostate cancer, yet neither tumor shape nor blood tests reliably predict it. The team wanted the biology that sets spreading tumors apart.

They profiled 24 metastatic samples, resistant to hormone therapy, taken from four patients, and set them against a published set of 64 primary tumors. After stripping out genes from surrounding support tissue, the spread tumors proved highly varied. Still, 415 genes were at least twice as active in every patient's metastases, and 364 were at least half as active. The changed genes spanned multiple molecular pathways rather than one route. Those pathway sets offer candidate markers and drug targets.
europmc-pmc2124855: A medical paper comparing merits of various complements and amboceptors in serum diagnosis. The immune reagents. This article preserves that immunology. It awaits future readers. Its place in history is secure. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2125255: A medical paper with observations on the succus entericus. The intestinal juice. This article preserves that physiology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2125355: A medical paper with an immunological study of Bacillus influenzae. The flu germ's immunity. This article preserves that immunology. Future scholars will discover it. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2128155: A medical paper with experimental studies on heteroplastic bone formation. The foreign bone. This article preserves that histology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. The library keeps the document safe for everyone.
europmc-pmc2128355: A medical paper with studies based on a malignant tumor of the rabbit. The rabbit cancer. This article preserves that oncology. It awaits future readers. It holds its historical place. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2128455: A medical paper with an experimental study of mitochondrial changes in the thyroid gland. The thyroid's engines. This article preserves that cell biology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
europmc-pmc2128555: A medical paper on the epidemiology of a rabbit respiratory infection, susceptibility of rabbits. The rabbit cold. This article preserves that epidemiology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131155: A medical paper on the influence of ovariectomy on spontaneous mammary carcinoma. The spayed cancer. This article preserves that oncology. Future scholars will discover it. It retains its place in time. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2131555: The germ-growing broth may look dead, but its chemistry tells a tale, which this paper captured. The team measured how the broth handled air and rust. The broth's hidden acts, noted. The article keeps that lab study.
europmc-pmc2292755:
Smith and Kruglyak asked in 2008 how genes and the environment interact to shape gene activity in yeast. They grew two yeast strains, called BY and RM, on glucose and on ethanol as food sources. Then they measured which genes were active in each strain and each food.

Most genes changed activity by strain, by food, or by both at once, and 2,037 genes showed a true interaction effect. By breeding the strains and profiling over 100 offspring, they mapped 1,555 genetic linkages tied to these effects. One hotspot traced to a variant in the gene IRA2, which controls a growth signal pathway. Local control variants stayed stable across foods, while distant ones often flipped direction.
europmc-pmc2361355:
Des Guetz and colleagues pooled studies on blood vessel growth in colorectal cancer in 2006. Tumors need new vessels to grow, a process called angiogenesis. Two measures reflect it: microvessel density, a count of tiny vessels in the tumor, and levels of VEGF, a vessel growth signal.

The meta-analysis kept 32 studies on vessel density, covering 3,496 patients, and 18 on VEGF, covering 2,050 patients. High vessel density predicted worse survival and faster relapse, with a risk ratio of 2.32 for relapse, but only when vessels were stained with CD31 or CD34 markers. High VEGF predicted poor relapse-free survival even more strongly, at a risk ratio of 2.84, and poorer overall survival as well. The authors urged standard ways to measure both markers in future trials.
europmc-pmc2522255:
Sheehan, Didelez, Burton, and Tobin explained in 2008 how a method called Mendelian randomisation can test cause and effect in observational health studies. Such studies often mislead. An exposure linked to disease may not cause it. Hidden factors can drive both. Genes offer a way out, since gene variants are assigned at conception roughly at random, like lots in a trial.

The authors use Katan's cholesterol example: people carrying the ApoE2 gene variant have lower cholesterol from birth without differing in lifestyle. If low cholesterol truly caused cancer, those carriers should show more cancer, and checking this tests causality directly. They set out the three assumptions a gene must meet to work as such an instrument, and review limits like pleiotropy, where one gene affects several traits.
europmc-pmc2588455:
McCurley and Callard tested in 2008 which housekeeping genes zebrafish researchers can trust as measuring references. Gene expression studies normalise results against a supposedly steady reference gene, but common choices wobble with conditions. The team measured eight candidate genes. They covered development stages and adult tissues of both sexes. They also covered embryos exposed to hormone-like chemicals and solvents.

Every candidate varied under some condition. Ranking stability picked 18s ribosomal RNA, beta-2-microglobulin, and elongation factor 1 alpha as most stable during development and across tissues. After chemical treatment a different trio won, while some reliable genes turned unstable. Sex differences appeared for certain genes in certain tissues. Choosing a poor reference even flipped the measured size of a hormone response. The authors urge checking references for each new experiment.
europmc-pmc2653555:
Hampson and co-authors studied in 2009 how rabies spreads among dogs in rural Tanzania, to test whether the disease could be wiped out worldwide. Rabies kills tens of thousands of people each year, mostly in Africa and Asia, and nearly all catch it from dog bites. Eradication would need proof that dog vaccination can break the chain of spread.

The team followed single rabid dogs in unusual detail, tracing whom each one bit. From those chains they estimated that each rabid dog infects only about 1.2 others on average. That is a low spread rate, well within reach of vaccination drives. The catch is speed: dog populations turn over fast, as puppies replace adults. Gains fade unless vaccine rounds return often. With steady effort, the authors argue, ending dog rabies is a realistic goal.
europmc-pmc2760755:
Paulmann and co-authors showed in 2009 that serotonin inside pancreatic beta cells modulates insulin secretion by a process called serotonylation. Serotonin is stored with insulin in beta-cell granules and released with it, yet its job there was a thirty-year mystery. Mice lacking peripheral serotonin, outside the brain, develop diabetes, which pointed to an intracellular role.

Serotonylation is the covalent binding of serotonin to small GTPase proteins by calcium-dependent enzymes, which switches those proteins on. In beta cells, that binding promotes the release of insulin granules when glucose rises. Blocking the process impaired secretion, while the brain serotonin system stayed intact in their model. The work reframes serotonin as an internal signal in insulin release, not just a brain messenger.
europmc-pmc2811155:
Narendra and colleagues worked out in 2010 how cells flag worn-out mitochondria, the cell's power units, for disposal. Two proteins in this system, PINK1 and Parkin, are faulty in some inherited forms of Parkinson disease. Parkin was known to gather on failing mitochondria, but the signal that calls it in was a mystery.

The team showed that healthy mitochondria constantly break down PINK1, keeping its levels near zero. When a mitochondrion loses power, PINK1 stops being destroyed and piles up on its surface instead. That buildup is what recruits Parkin, which then tags the unit for breakdown. Without PINK1's signal, Parkin never arrives, and damaged power units linger.
europmc-pmc2814855:
Lavasani and colleagues tested friendly gut bacteria in 2010 as a treatment for a mouse disease that mimics multiple sclerosis. The disease, called EAE, is an immune attack on nerve insulation. The team screened five Lactobacillus strains given daily to mice, looking for ones that calmed the attack.

Three strains cut inflammation in the brain and spinal cord and raised calming regulatory T cells. Given alone to already sick mice, each strain failed, but a mixture of all three halted the disease and reversed its signs. The benefit ran through a calming signal called IL-10, made by those regulatory cells, and transferring the cells to other mice carried the protection with them.
europmc-pmc2815955:
Luby and a large team combined records from every known Nipah virus outbreak in Bangladesh between 2001 and 2007. Nipah causes fever and brain inflammation and first erupted in Malaysia in the late nineteen nineties, spread there by sick pigs. Bangladesh instead saw repeated small outbreaks with varied virus strains, pointing to fresh spillovers from fruit bats.

Across the seven outbreaks and stray cases studied, more than half of the identified patients caught the virus from another person rather than from bats. That spread pattern sets Bangladesh apart from Malaysia, where person-to-person spread was never confirmed. The team traced how chains of cases build once the virus enters a community, which matters for hospital precautions.
europmc-pmc2846855:
Van der Worp and colleagues examined in 2010 why treatments that shine in animal disease models so often flop in human trials. The essay argues the failure splits into two broad sources. Animal studies themselves often carry design flaws that inflate apparent benefit. And animal versions of diseases can differ from the human condition in ways that doom transfer, however clean the experiment.

Systematic reviews of animal work can help pick the likeliest candidates, the authors contend, but hidden bias poisons that tool too. Companion work on stroke studies showed unpublished negative results inflate reported benefit by about a third. The piece closes with reporting recommendations so animal evidence can be judged honestly before patients are enrolled.
europmc-pmc2939055:
Lebouvier and colleagues tested whether routine colon biopsies can reveal Parkinson's disease damage in the gut nerves, in a 2010 study. Clumps called Lewy bodies, the hallmark of the disease in brain, also appear in gut nerve networks.

Biopsies from patients at different disease stages and from controls were stained for a marked form of alpha-synuclein, the clump protein. Lewy-type damage showed in most patient samples and in no controls, while patients also had fewer gut neurons per cluster. Damage levels tracked neuron loss and certain symptoms that respond poorly to the standard drug levodopa.
europmc-pmc3000155:
Peiris and colleagues reported on children hospitalised with breathing infections in Hong Kong in a 2003 study of the newly found human metapneumovirus. Over thirteen months they tested nose samples from nearly six hundred children.

The virus turned up in about one child in twenty, most often alongside pneumonia, asthma flare-ups, or bronchiolitis in infants. Compared with the better known RSV, these children were older and their wheezing more often reflected asthma than infant bronchiolitis. Activity peaked in spring and summer, all strains fell into known family lines, and admission rates for the virus were substantial.
europmc-pmc3004955:
Feinberg and co-authors unveiled a multiplexed scanning method that images the whole brain in under a second in a 2010 article. Standard echo planar imaging builds one slice at a time, taking seconds per brain volume and far longer for fibre mapping.

Their sequence stacks two tricks: firing several slice bands at once and refocusing echoes simultaneously, multiplying how many images land in one sweep. Whole brain functional scans at a common magnet strength ran several times faster, and fibre imaging sped up two to four times. At the stronger magnet the design also cut energy deposition and removed the need for fat suppression pulses.
europmc-pmc3018455:
Harr and French reviewed Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, two ends of one spectrum of severe drug reactions that strip the skin, in a 2010 article. Both are rare, striking roughly one or two people per million yearly, and both can kill.

Sore, blistering skin and mouth erosions deepen as the surface layer detaches, more extensively in the necrolysis form. Drugs cause most cases, with a known high-risk list spanning gout, seizure, and sulfa antibiotic medicines, though certain infections can trigger it too. Genetic susceptibility is real: one immune marker strongly predicts the reaction to a seizure drug in Han Chinese patients.
europmc-pmc3024255:
