The toxic products gathered inside cortical mitochondria as the disease model progressed, tracking with amyloid and oxidative damage. Deliberately stressing mitochondria with a toxin raised the products further, in whole cells and in mitochondria. A mitochondria-targeted antioxidant did the reverse, lowering the products and improving mitochondrial function. The loop matters because it names a druggable step: calm the power plant's stress, and one class of brain toxins may slow its rise.
plos-pone-0352455:
Erick Jacob Okek and seven co-authors review malaria control in two Ugandan districts with heavy spread of the disease. They used five years of national health records. They compared indoor spraying and treated bed nets, alone and combined. They also compared the chemicals used in each campaign. The outcome was the share of malaria tests that came back positive in Yumbe and in Gulu.

After adjusting for weather, Yumbe's positive rate fell several times faster than Gulu's. One net brand spread in 2020 made no clear change to Yumbe's trend. In contrast, one spray formula showed a strong impact. The authors argue that which products are deployed matters a great deal. The mix matters as much as the act of deploying itself.
plos-pone-0352555:
Zheng Liu examines whether vocational students can actually judge the curriculum designs that artificial intelligence produces for them, in this 2026 classroom study from a Chinese vocational college. Thirty-nine second-year students in a study-tour curriculum course completed AI-assisted planning tasks, then sat a closed-book, handwritten diagnostic test with no AI access. Their responses, amounting to nearly two hundred substantive claims, were analyzed for depth of judgment.

Students could recite sound criteria, accuracy, feasibility, fit to learners, safety, and the need for human revision. Applied diagnosis was thinner. Most spotted surface problems like mismatched learners, time pressure, overloaded sites, and safety gaps. Few caught weak curriculum logic, unworkable assessment plans, unchecked facts, or blurred responsibility for the work. Liu calls this a stated-applied judgment gap and argues no-AI diagnostics expose where AI help has not yet become professional skill.
plos-pone-0352755:
Pérez Molina and colleagues reviewed recent evidence on yellow fever prevention in a 2026 paper. Yellow fever still breaks out in Africa and the Americas despite a strong vaccine that has existed for decades. New outbreaks in Brazil and Colombia showed that coverage stays uneven and responses often start only after spread begins.

The review gathered studies and official reports from 2020 to 2025 in three languages, with focus on global, Latin American, and Colombian findings. It maps what is known about vaccine plans, safety, and immune responses, plus newer ideas for calming harmful immune reactions. Gaps in coverage and in early action stand out as the main lessons for health officials.
plos-pone-0352855:
Dongxiao Fu and five colleagues model how cars follow each other around mountain curves, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study aimed at safer roads. Mountain highways in China combine tight bends, harsh weather, and mixed driving styles, and accidents cluster there. Drones filmed traffic on a curved stretch in Yunnan, and the cleaned trajectories were sorted by algorithm into aggressive, conservative, and standard driving styles.

The three styles differed clearly in speed, acceleration, and following distance. Adding curve radius to a standard car-following model, then calibrating it separately for each style, sharply improved how well the model reproduced real trajectories. Traffic simulators that ignore both bend and temperament, the authors show, will misjudge mountain roads.
plos-pone-0353155:
Gandhi and colleagues tested a leading AI chatbot on judging bias in clinical trials in a 2026 study. Fifty trials drawn from fifty reviews were rated by the original reviewers, by a masked human panel, and by the chatbot using structured prompts from the standard bias tool.

The chatbot called far more trials high risk than either human group did. Agreement with humans was modest at best. Overcalling bias can distort evidence summaries just as undercalling can. The authors' verdict is caution: AI bias ratings are not yet a stand-in for trained reviewers, though they might serve as a first pass with human checks.
plos-pone-0353355:
Erdem Maraşlı, Erkan Ozduran, and Volkan Hancı published this 2026 study grading artificial intelligence chatbots on knee osteoarthritis, a worn-joint condition behind most arthritis disability. They posed common search terms as questions to three leading chatbots and scored the answers for readability, reliability against medical benchmarks, and overall quality.

The chatbots wrote at reading levels many patients would struggle with, and their reliability and quality scores raised real concerns about scientific soundness. The authors argue that medical chatbot answers need an effective oversight system before patients can safely trust them.
plos-pone-0353555:
Ochoa Capera and colleagues compared a key DNA control stretch across thousands of vertebrates in a 2026 study. The stretch governs copying and reading of the cell's small power-station genome, yet its evolution was poorly mapped. More than five thousand species across eleven classes were analyzed for length, repeats, and conserved blocks.

Land vertebrates carried longer, more repeat-rich control stretches than fishes. Copying events appeared only on land lineages, especially birds and reptiles, while birds and mammals later trended shorter. Core working motifs stayed conserved throughout. The survey gives the first full framework for how this control region balances sameness and change.
plos-pone-0353655:
Tianning Li interviews thirty young ethnic-minority migrants who moved from China's countryside to the city of Wuhan, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The participants, from Miao, Tujia, and Tibetan backgrounds, described in depth how their ethnic identity helped or hindered settling into urban life. Their accounts were analysed for recurring lived patterns rather than counted.

Five strands ran through the stories: how they labelled themselves, language skill in ethnic and local tongues, keeping cultural practices, facing discrimination, and stitching two identities together. Ethnic identity worked both ways at once — a shield against prejudice and a source of belonging, yet also a boundary with local residents. Policies, Li argues, must support identity while dismantling structural barriers.
plos-pone-0353755:
Javiera Cartagena-Farías and co-authors study in 2026 whether poor housing raises the risk of falls for older people living at home in England. Two decades of ageing survey data fed models designed to handle cause running both ways and uneven follow up. A cost model then priced the health and social care that followed such falls.

Homes with electrical or plumbing faults or too little space raised fall risk, and homes described as too dark raised both falls and later service use. The yearly care cost tied to poor housing was estimated in the billions of pounds range. Housing fixes could serve as fall prevention, the authors argue.
plos-pone-0353955:
Andrea Ciricugno and co-authors present in 2026 a trial plan joining brain stimulation with immersive virtual reality to train social prediction in people with cerebellar damage. The cerebellum helps predict others' intentions, and damage from birth defects or later disease can blunt social life. Two patient groups will train in interactive virtual scenes over eight daily sessions.

During training, each person receives either real or sham stimulation tuned to their own brain rhythm, measured beforehand. Main checks cover reading intentions, emotions, and traits in social scenes, with brain measures and daily functioning as extra checks. The plan is registered and reports no results.
plos-pone-0354255:
Chen, in a 2026 literary study, reads a novel by Tan Twan Eng through the lens of language patterns. The novel follows a judge who, after trauma and war, apprentices herself to a Japanese gardener in Malaya. Chen asks how the book's word choices carry the main character's personality and shifting feelings.

The analysis pairs a standard five-trait model of personality with a method that studies how language builds meaning. Three phases of the story are tracked: remembering trauma, learning in the garden, and reflective closing. Early passages lean on obligation words and tight sentences, a pattern Chen links to anxious, dutiful self-control. Later passages open into balance and warmth, matching growing openness and easing distress. Two softer traits, kindness and sociability, run quieter but follow the same arc. Chen argues that in this novel, feeling is not fixed weather but a slow adaptation that the language itself performs.
plos-pone-0354355:
Javad Yoosefi Lebni and four colleagues published this 2026 interview study on why young couples divorce in western Iran. They spoke with thirty-two people who had lived through divorce plus sixteen key informants, sorting hundreds of coded remarks into themes about the person, the marriage, and the wider family and culture.

Sexual problems, mental strain, and clashing personalities met weak communication skills and marriages entered for shallow reasons. Family interference and stigma around asking for help added pressure. Lebni recommends teaching couples before marriage, normalizing counseling, and helping families resolve conflict rather than inflame it.
plos-pone-0354455:
Wan Wang and co-authors build in 2026 a scenario based method to judge risks faced by power grid maintenance workers in China. Dangers span worker actions, equipment state, surroundings, and management, making full identification hard. Their method breaks a live line job into stages, weights the factors at each stage, and traces how risk passes from one stage to the next using network logic.

Human and environmental factors carried the highest overall weight, matching real accident patterns. Workers' physical and mental health stood out as an overlooked driver. Poor work early in a job directly endangered later steps. Stage specific control, the authors argue, beats a single blanket checklist.
plos-pone-0354755:
Andrea Bernal-Rivera and co-authors measured blood sugar control across many Neotropical bat species to learn what shapes it. Sugar handling underpins the bats' varied diets, from fruit and nectar to insects and blood. Their 2026 field study used portable glucose meters and weighed diet, family relatedness, season, and body traits.

Fasting glucose tracked diet group and evolutionary kinship, but not sex or body mass. Sugar uptake speed depended on sugar type, diet specialisation, and time of day and year. Fruit eaters flexed their sugar handling with the seasons. Closely related species living side by side showed hints of metabolic separation, as if dividing the menu. The authors link physiology to how bat communities share food.
plos-pone-0354855:
Ayben Leblebici and four colleagues test what Turkish medical students know about acute rheumatic fever, in a study published in 2026 using a survey from the 2019-2020 academic year. The disease follows untreated strep throat and can permanently damage children's hearts; Turkey sits in a moderate-to-high risk band. The authors surveyed first-year students, who had only basic science training, and sixth-year students fresh from clinical rotations, scoring both against American Heart Association guidance.

One hundred sixty-five students responded. Sixth-year students knew significantly more than first-years, as expected. But the study's point is the gap structure itself: awareness of a preventable disease that still harms young hearts depends heavily on clinical exposure. The authors argue that teaching about preventable diseases like rheumatic fever should be woven deliberately into medical curricula rather than left to chance encounters on the wards.
plos-pone-0355055:
Adam Harriman and co-authors look back in 2026 at intensive care patients in Britain who needed a breathing tube through the neck for long term support. Letting air out of the tube cuff is a key step toward speaking and coming off the machine. Records were split by how soon that step happened after the tube was placed.

Later cuff release linked to longer time on the machine, slower removal of the tube, and more chest infections. Those patients also stayed longer in intensive care, felt more anxious, and died more often. The authors stress the link may reflect illness rather than cause it, and call for direct trials.
plos-pone-0355155:
Fawzia Irhayyim Al-Assadi, Osamah Abdulmunem Al-Tameemi, and Aya F Alobaidi study what a breakthrough looks like in modern Iraqi architecture, using three major buildings erected since the early two thousands. Iraqi design has wrestled with honoring deep local identity while absorbing global technology. Through site observation, documents, and interviews analyzed with qualitative software, the team compares a government headquarters, a set of Chinese-built schools, and the new central bank building.

Breakthrough, they find, is never just bold shape. The strongest cases fuse new technology with local values so the building restates Iraqi identity rather than importing a foreign one. Al-Assadi and colleagues propose a framework linking breakthrough, innovation, and transformation, offered as a guide for architects rebuilding in culturally loaded settings.
plos-pone-0355655:
Retraction notice. The PLOS One editors formally withdrew a published study of KIOM-C, a herbal medicine tested on human fibrosarcoma cells. The original paper had claimed the mixture drove cancer cell death through stress pathways. This 2026 notice records why the journal lost confidence in that work.

Editors found panels in several figures that appear to overlap while claiming to show different conditions. The authors could not produce the original image files, so the overlaps could not be explained or ruled out as assembly errors. The notice also faults the statistics for ignoring multiple comparisons. It further records an undisclosed patent interest held by the corresponding author. Readers should not rely on the retracted findings.
plos-pone-0355855:
Takayuki Yamaguchi and colleagues measure a natural germ-fighting peptide in the blood of people with sleep apnea, the disorder where breathing repeatedly stalls at night. Apnea stirs body-wide inflammation and may weaken defenses against viruses. The team compared peptide levels in several dozen patients and healthy controls against detailed sleep study records, including how often breathing dipped and how much deep sleep each person got.

Peptide levels ran lower in patients with more severe apnea and tracked sleep quality closely: lower with more light, broken sleep and more breathing dips, higher with more deep and dreaming sleep. Light sleep share stood out as the independent link. Yamaguchi and colleagues propose the peptide as a blood marker worth testing for apnea's immune toll.
plos-pone-0355955:
Zeinab Ghesmati and co-authors compare tiny parcels released by two lab-grown fat cell types, heat-making brown-like cells and storage white-like cells, across four kinds of human cells. Such parcels carry signals between cells, and fat-derived ones might steer other tissues. Targets included ovary cells, a breast cancer line, and two stem cell sources, treated either with the cells' full broth or with the isolated parcels.

Brown-cell parcels raised a key hormone output from ovary cells. Broth, more than parcels, pushed cancer cells toward death. Both treatments nudged fat stem cells toward bone making while cooling their stem identity, and brown parcels reshaped their fat content most. Ghesmati and colleagues map a cell-by-cell pattern that could inform future fat-based therapies.
plos-pone-0356055:
Catrina MacPhee and three colleagues publish the protocol for a trial of a game-based treatment for spatial neglect after stroke, in this 2026 paper. Neglect leaves patients unaware of one side of space and predicts poor recovery; prism glasses can retrain attention, but the therapy is repetitive, equipment-bound, and little used. Their version, a whack-a-mole style computer game played through prism goggles, is designed to be engaging, portable, and usable at home or in rehabilitation units.

Forty-two patients with right-hemisphere stroke will be assigned, under double-blind conditions, to real prism strength or a much weaker active control, playing for fifteen minutes daily over two weeks. Outcomes span standard neglect tests, daily living skills, patients' and caregivers' reports of impact, plus mood and fatigue. The authors hope the gamified format will show whether prism therapy can finally travel beyond specialist labs.
plos-pone-0356255:
Stefanie M Jungmann and fellow psychologists survey women and mothers about mental load, the invisible work of planning, remembering, and organizing family life. Public debate on the topic has grown, but research has lagged behind. In two online studies, women rated how stressful visible chores felt against invisible ones. The first study had several hundred women. A much larger second study covered mothers only. Participants also named what drives the burden.

Mothers found invisible tasks more stressful and less fairly shared than visible chores. The load tied to worse mood and to higher anxiety and low mood, and endless thinking about unfinished tasks was the most named cause. Personality mattered too, especially worry-prone traits. Jungmann and colleagues draw lessons for partners, workplaces, and policy.
plos-pone-0356955:
The PLOS One Editors issued this Expression of Concern in 2026. It concerns a study of constipation in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. That study had linked gut problems to a disrupted chemical signaling pathway and cell stress responses. An Expression of Concern warns readers that a published article's reliability is under question. The warning stands while issues are examined.

Editors list many figure panels that look alike across figures. Some look alike across other papers. They list spliced gel images. They also list raw data originally missing from the article's files. The authors acknowledged several panels were incorrect. They supplied corrected figures and the missing data. Some similarities were explained as shared control samples and combined gels. The journal's notice leaves the article flagged. Its claims should be read with caution until the case closes.
plos-pone-0357355:
Correction notice: the entry here amends an earlier banana study by Swarup Roy Choudhury and colleagues on a gene-switch protein tied to flowering and fruit ripening. After publication, readers spotted that panels in one figure looked the same across two panels meant to show different fruit zones. The authors confirmed the first set of panels was wrong and supplied replacement images taken during the original experiment.

All underlying images for the affected figure panels are attached to the notice. The authors also note that one older dataset behind another figure is no longer available, while the rest can be requested from them. Roy Choudhury's team leaves the study's claims standing, with the figure record now repaired for anyone checking the ripening evidence.
plos-pone-0357755:
Seung-Hwan Kim published a 2026 modeling paper in PLOS ONE on how childhood leukemia changes over time inside individual patients. Tumor growth in these cancers is pushed around by chance, body development, and treatment, yet doctors rarely sample often enough to see the motion. Kim fitted a Bayesian version of a classic random-walk model, the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, to repeated measurements from children whose leukemia carried a specific gene rearrangement.

The fitted parameters hinted that random fluctuation ran higher in hard-to-treat and very early stages, but uncertainty ranges overlapped too much to claim sharply separate regimes. Simulations showed the Bayesian approach stayed stable and gave honest uncertainty estimates even with sparse sampling, though prediction remained limited. The framework is presented as a careful way to read stage patterns in thin clinical data, not as a tool for forecasting one child's course.
plos-pone-0358255:
Precious Makiyi and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on youth mental health. It traces the referral paths followed by depressed young people in places where services are scarce. The study is qualitative and comes from Ghana and Zimbabwe, two countries where specialist mental care is scarce.

A referral trajectory is the real path a young person travels between teachers, clinics, families, and healers while seeking help. Mapping those paths exposes dead ends and delays that official charts hide. Mental health planners in low-income countries can use such maps to build referral routes that young people can actually complete.
plos-pone-0358455:
Ingrid A Wise led a team of eight authors studying a hormone and diabetic eye disease, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Erythropoietin, best known for boosting red blood cells, may also signal damage in diabetic retinopathy, a leading cause of blindness. The team worked within the LANDMark cohort, tracking the hormone over time.

Wise's longitudinal study links levels of the hormone in the body with the course of eye disease, testing its value as a biomarker. A blood test that warns of worsening eye disease could trigger earlier eye checks and treatment. Cohort data gathered over years are precious for this, since eye damage builds slowly. The study adds a candidate signal to a field that needs early warnings.
plos-pone-0358555:
Yankuba Singhateh led a team of six authors tracking measles and rubella control in Lesotho, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Lesotho, a small mountain kingdom in southern Africa, has worked toward eliminating both diseases for years. The team reviewed progress across the period from 2011 to 2025.

Singhateh's record shows how far the campaign has come and what still blocks zero cases. Elimination efforts often stall on the last hard-to-reach children, so knowing the remaining gaps is vital. The fourteen-year view also shows whether gains held through shocks such as the pandemic years. Other small countries can learn from Lesotho's path, both its wins and its stubborn obstacles.
plos-pone-0358755:
Tobias Gummer, Ko-Hsuan Lu, and Karolina von Glasenapp assessed in 2026 how well survey data gathered in Germany during the COVID-19 pandemic meet the FAIR principles. FAIR data are findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable: in short, data that other researchers can actually locate and work with years later. The pandemic produced a rush of surveys about health, work, and behavior, collected under time pressure.

The authors check that body of data against the FAIR standard and report where it falls short, in documentation, formats, or archiving. Their audit matters because crisis data are often reused for decades, and sloppy stewardship quietly wastes the effort of everyone who answered. The lessons apply to any future emergency data collection.
plos-pone-0360055:
Jennifer Grauer and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies bobcats across the northeast of the United States. The authors map where and when these wild cats were exposed to anticoagulant rodenticides, poisons used against rats and mice that also stop blood from clotting.

The pattern is spatiotemporal, charting exposure across both place and time. Bobcats likely pick up these chemicals by eating poisoned prey, so their exposure signals a wider problem in the food web. Wildlife managers and regulators weighing limits on such poisons are the readers who most need maps like these.
plos-pone-0360155:
Thu Hoang Thanh, Nhan Nguyen Thi, and Toan Nguyen Khac wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on teenage weight. It studies factors linked to overweight and obesity among adolescents, using the 2023 Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System survey in the United States. The authors stress broader factors, beyond diet alone.

The analysis is survey-aware, meaning it respects how the national survey sampled students, and it adds calibrated AI-assisted classification. Combining careful statistics with machine learning can sharpen which groups face the highest risk. School health planners reading this get a wider view of what surrounds teen weight, from habits to environment.
plos-pone-0360355:
Thitirut Jongutchariya and three colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a randomized trial comparing two treatment plans for a painful shoulder and neck condition. The condition is myofascial pain syndrome of the upper trapezius, the muscle running from neck to shoulder.

Both plans use magnetic pulses applied again and again to ease pain. Comparing two versions head to head shows which settings deserve wider use. Therapists treating stubborn neck and shoulder pain are the readers who need this kind of direct comparison before adopting a device-based therapy.
pmc-13122055:
Mayowa J Adeniyi and Ayoola Awosika study drink temperature, caffeine, and standing stress in a 2026 article. Prolonged standing, called orthostasis, can cause near-fainting and fatigue. Whether a cold or warm caffeinated drink changes brain arousal during standing was poorly understood. Thirty-six young men took part.

Brain waves were recorded with an EEG cap, a method that reads electrical activity, while pulse rate was tracked sitting and during twenty minutes of standing. Standing raised pulse and shifted brain wave patterns toward alertness. Cold drinks differed from warm ones on some wave measures. The authors, though, caution that neither drink clearly altered the overall EEG response, and advise care when standing, especially for older or faint-prone people.
pmc-13201255:
Fieldwork in Sana'a, Yemen, by Abbas Mohammed Ahmed Al-Azab and colleagues and published in 2026, asks whether nonbiting flies carry intestinal parasites on their bodies. The research article centers on houseflies and flesh flies in a city where poor sanitation may help parasites spread between waste sites and food.

From June to August 2023, the team collected 300 flies at six locations, including markets, garbage sites, and butcher shops. Washing the flies in saline and examining the sediment under a microscope showed that 195 of them carried intestinal parasites. Nine species were found, and rates were highest at Bab Al-Yemen, which supports stronger hygiene measures around food and waste.
pmc-13201355:
Forty years after a landmark Nobel Prize, a 2026 commemorative article headed by Larissa Junkes looks back at the career of Rita Levi-Montalcini. The article recounts how she discovered nerve growth factor, the protein signal that guides growing nerve fibers, and considers what her work means for psychiatry today.

Working in wartime Italy and later in the United States, Levi-Montalcini used tumor tissue and chick embryos to show that target cells release chemical signals nerves need to survive. Biochemist Stanley Cohen, who shared the 1986 prize, purified the factor and confirmed it was a protein. Her discovery founded the neurotrophin field and still shapes research on brain aging and mental illness.
pmc-13207855:
A freshwater polyp with no brain still links pain sensing to immunity, and a 2026 study led by Veronica D'Ezio traces that link to one channel protein. The research article investigates TRPA1 in Hydra vulgaris, exposing the animals to noxious cold and to lysate from Pseudomonas bacteria, then measuring stress and defense genes.

Both threats switched on the channel's downstream markers for pain-like signaling and innate immune effectors in the polyps. Blocking TRPA1 pharmacologically blunted those responses, showing the channel amplifies both kinds of alarm in this simple animal. The authors read the coupling as an ancient survival mechanism, conserved long before nervous systems grew complex.
pmc-13212555:
Thomas L. Poulos, writing alone in 2026, challenges a published crystal structure of an enzyme that helps plants make isoflavonoid compounds. The original structure looked strikingly unlike every related enzyme, with its essential heme cofactor shifted and rotated in an unprecedented way.

Re-examining the deposited data, Poulos argues the enzyme is in fact a conventional member of its family. He contends a sulfate ion near the heme explains the odd appearance, and that a molecule claimed as water is more likely imidazole from the crystallisation liquid. Comparisons with a close relative and a predicted model support his reading, which matters because unusual structures can mislead later work.
pmc-13215055:
Luan D. Ta and colleagues describe in 2026 seven scoliosis operations where patients were briefly woken mid-surgery to prove their spinal cords still worked. High-tech nerve monitoring was unavailable, so the team modified the classic wake-up test using a fast reversal drug.

The drug, sugammadex, undoes muscle paralysis quickly, letting each patient follow commands and move their legs on cue. Tests lasted fifteen to thirty-five minutes and grew shorter as the team practised. One patient needed a second drug for slow recovery, and only one recalled anything afterwards. No dangerous heart or blood pressure swings followed the reversal drug. The series supports the approach where monitoring equipment is lacking.
pmc-13215555:
Judit del Río and co-authors present a 2026 archaeomagnetic study of five metallurgical kilns at Quillay in northwestern Argentina. The kilns were long assigned to the Inka period, an attribution resting on radiocarbon dates and their copper-working role.

All five structures recorded nearly identical magnetic direction and intensity values, which points to a single shared last heating. Comparison with geomagnetic field models dates that heating to between the late nineteenth and mid-twentieth centuries, far later than the Inka occupation. The authors suggest a wildfire or a later reuse, when people worked the upper chambers again to win copper from slag. The result rewrites part of the site's occupational history.
pmc-13216155:
Cristián Modroño and co-authors present a 2026 brain imaging study asking whether virtual rehabilitation tasks need a realistic virtual hand. Simpler moving dots might engage the same brain networks, which would free designers to build more flexible exercises.

Twenty-four healthy volunteers performed a cancellation task inside the scanner under four conditions, acting or watching with either a virtual hand or a plain dot. Brain activation across frontoparietal and sensorimotor regions looked much the same for hand and dot versions, in both acting and watching runs, with no significant corrected differences in direct comparisons. The authors conclude that, under these conditions, a virtual limb adds little measurable brain engagement.
pmc-13217655:
Lucie Sabin and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review of discrete choice experiments in Iran's health system. These experiments learn what patients, clinicians, and the public value by asking them to choose between carefully varied hypothetical options, and Iranian use of the method is booming.

Thirty studies met the criteria, most published from 2021 onward, concentrated in cities, especially Tehran, and focused on health services and the workforce. Money, time, risk, and health outcomes were the usual attributes traded off. Quality was uneven: pilot testing and groundwork with target populations were inconsistent, nearly half used efficient experimental designs, and reporting of software, blocking, and opt-out choices was often missing. Conditional logit was the commonest estimator. The authors call for more diverse samples and tougher methods.
pmc-13218155:
Hongshan Pu and co-authors present a 2026 protocol for a Chinese cohort study that will build a machine learning model to predict six-month death risk in elderly patients with advanced COPD. The disease follows an unpredictable course, which leads to overtreatment and to palliative care arriving too late. Existing models were not built for elderly Chinese patients, a heavily burdened group.

Recruitment began in May 2024 and runs to December 2026 across centres, with twelve months of follow-up per patient. Baseline data span demographics, clinical and laboratory measures, a geriatric assessment, and COPD-specific prognostic factors. Patients are contacted monthly for the first six months, then quarterly, recording deaths, survival time, end-of-life care use, and do-not-resuscitate status. Several machine learning algorithms will compete to build the model, some centres held back for external validation. Its performance will be benchmarked against the BODE and ADO indices.
pmc-13218255:
Ju Wang and a large materials team introduce a porous bismuth-based liquid metal in a 2026 study. Liquid metals promise flexible electronics and soft devices, but gallium alloys are heavy, oxidize easily, and can leak at room temperature. Bismuth alloys behave differently: they hold their shape and soften with heat, suiting them to load-bearing uses.

The researchers made the porous metal with a sugar template later sacrificed, and by sieving the sugar to grain sizes they could tune the pore structure. The result weighs less than half as much as the solid metal while keeping its electrical conductivity and heat-driven phase change. The pores shield electromagnetic waves and leave channels for moving mass through it. Computer simulations showed how the pore network spreads mechanical stress and scatters electromagnetic waves. The metal stayed stable under flexible wrapping and changing temperatures, a design route for structural, shielding materials.
pmc-13222555:
Iris Smet and co-authors model the cost-effectiveness of a multiplexed spinal cord stimulation waveform for persistent spinal pain in Belgium, in a 2026 analysis. The therapy targets chronic back and leg pain that resists other care. A decision tree covered two years, followed by a thirteen-year Markov model, fed by a European trial and Belgian cost data.

Across ten thousand simulations, the therapy proved cost-effective in nearly every run at the assumed threshold. Patients gained well over one extra quality-adjusted life year compared with conventional management, at a modest cost per year gained. Net benefit turned positive by year five. Medication use and pain-relief quality values drove most of the uncertainty.
pmc-13224755:
Lusine Kostanyan and colleagues report a 2026 phase 3 trial update for mRNA-1083, an experimental combined vaccine against seasonal flu and COVID-19 in one shot. Adults aged fifty and older were randomly assigned to the combined product or to standard licensed vaccines for each disease. Earlier results covered the first month; the new report extends follow-up to six months.

Antibody responses against all matched flu strains held up through six months and matched or beat the standard vaccines. Responses against the coronavirus stayed higher in the combined-vaccine group throughout. Side effects were mostly mild to moderate, and no vaccine-related serious events or deaths occurred, supporting the single-shot approach for older adults.
pmc-13226955:
Ruilin Yang, Wyatt D. Morse, and Peng Zhong describe a 2026 open-source hardware build: an automated device that deprives mice of REM sleep for neuroscience experiments. REM sleep supports emotional balance and memory, but studying it requires waking animals precisely when that stage begins, traditionally a labour-heavy job. No commercial equivalent exists, so the team published full build files under an open licence.

Cost of parts came to roughly six thousand three hundred dollars, and the design files sit in a public repository. Brain and muscle signals identify the REM state, characterised by a wake-like brain pattern with paralysed muscles, and the device intervenes automatically. The build aims to make controlled sleep-loss studies cheaper and more consistent across laboratories.
pmc-13230255:
Sally Kheirandish and colleagues measure in 2026 the carbon-rich particles in air over a rural settlement near Budapest, Hungary. A six-week winter campaign in 2025 tracked particle counts, sizes, and black carbon in real time. Filters collected fine particles each day for lab measures of organic and elemental carbon, while cameras helped link spikes to local burning.

Short bursts of severe pollution appeared, with fine particle levels far above a nearby suburban station. Patterns tied some bursts to burning waste in home stoves rather than normal wood heating or traffic. Certain carbon fractions rose during those odd events, giving a fingerprint for illegal waste burning. Better fingerprints can sharpen emission records and guide local action against stove pollution.
pmc-13230955: Aaron Wacholder and colleagues issued this author correction in 2026 for a community study of finding small unannotated proteins with mass spectrometry methods. The notice is a correction only, fixing the x-axis labels in one panel of the first figure, which were wrong in the first published version. Both journal versions, online and PDF, now carry the amended figure. No findings, data, or conclusions change, and the notice adds no new scientific content beyond the label fix.
pmc-13232555:
Myungsun Park and colleagues give in 2026 underwater robots a soft hair sensor modeled on how fish and seals feel water. Sound-based speed gear is bulky and costly for small vehicles, leaving them nearly blind to flow in dark or murky water. Their sensor bends with the water, and the bend reports speed, direction, and pulsing of the flow.

Mounted on swimming robots, the hairs tracked forward speed, sideways drift, and heading during motion. Even while swimming, the robots picked out the wake behind an upstream object by its rhythm. Small vehicles could thus read currents and nearby obstacles without cameras or large sonar rigs. Flow feeling may help compact robots search and adapt in cluttered waters.
pmc-13232855:
Reza Taherian and colleagues chart in 2026 how life expectancy at birth moved across one hundred ninety countries from 1960 to 2023. They pair those records with a development index blending income, schooling, and fertility. Trend-break models measured yearly change, and a forecasting model projected values to 2050.

Global life expectancy rose steadily across the six decades, with development level tracking it closely throughout. Poorer regions gained faster in relative terms but swung more, while richer regions improved slowly and steadily. Projections point to continued gains, reaching the low eighties worldwide by mid-century on average. The forecast spread widens over time, warning that shared progress cannot be assumed.
pmc-13233655:
Tijn de Vos and Aleksander Christiansen published a 2026 theoretical computer science paper on tree-packings, sets of spanning trees inside a network graph. Tree-packings underpin fast algorithms for finding a graph's minimum cut, the cheapest set of edges whose removal splits the network. The authors revisit a classic result by Thorup that maintained many trees to track the minimum cut as a graph changes.

They show far fewer trees need maintaining than previously thought, only on the order of the cut value cubed times a logarithmic factor. Building on that leaner structure, they give a deterministic algorithm for fully dynamic exact minimum cut with much faster worst-case update times. A companion result speeds up dynamic arboricity, a measure of how densely a graph's edges can be covered by forests.
pmc-13235955:
Sitti Shoimatul Azizah and colleagues surveyed in 2026 two hundred people living with HIV at two Indonesian public hospitals during the COVID-19 pandemic. The disruption delayed HIV counselling and testing services at many facilities worldwide. Questionnaires measured knowledge about COVID-19, anxiety using a standard scale, and access to voluntary counselling and testing. Data collection ran from late 2022 into early 2023.

Better COVID-19 knowledge related strongly to better access to services in the statistical analysis. Higher anxiety also showed a positive link to service access in their results, a counterintuitive pattern. Knowledge emerged as the single most influential factor in the combined model reported. The authors recommend stronger education and support for this vulnerable group during health emergencies. Telemedicine and remote care should expand so treatment continues without hospital visits, they argue.
pmc-13238855:
Mahnoush Mehrzad Samarin and a large team pooled eight randomized trials in a 2026 meta-analysis of Moringa oleifera, a plant promoted against high blood pressure and obesity. From nearly 2,300 candidate articles, only the eight trials survived screening. Outcomes covered systolic and diastolic pressure, body weight, and body mass index.

Moringa significantly lowered both pressure measures, by roughly six and seven points on average. Weight and body mass index did not budge significantly. Subgroup patterns suggested stronger pressure effects at moderate daily doses, in lighter participants, and beyond four weeks of use. The authors judge the blood pressure signal real but preliminary. Larger and longer trials, they say, must confirm the size of the benefit.
pmc-13239355:
David A Neequaye, Alexandra Lorson, and Holly K Barnett report a 2026 psychology study on investigative interviews, where police or officials question people to gather facts. The central puzzle is how an interviewee works out which details the interviewer actually wants to hear.

Two experiments, each with roughly three hundred participants, tested whether question wording changes that judgement. When questions were specific, people narrowed their answers to details that fitted the question closely. When questions were broad, people spread attention across more information. Whether someone was cooperative or resistant made no difference, and people stayed confident in their choices throughout. The findings favour the narrowing explanation.
pmc-13240055:
Ninad Ekbote and co-authors test whether large language models can pull structured facts from end-of-life care notes in a 2026 study. Advance care planning conversations are recorded as free text in electronic records, which makes patients' wishes hard to retrieve quickly when decisions loom.

Clinicians hand-labelled one hundred de-identified goals-of-care notes across four categories, and two general models, Mistral and LLaMA, extracted the same fields without special training. One model matched human labels closely for code status, documentation, and patient priorities, but struggled to name the decision maker. The authors see promise for scalable feedback, with refinement needed for nuanced personal content.
pmc-13240755:
Demetrios Kolokythas and colleagues report a 2026 case of a liver abscess caused by brucellosis, a bacterial infection spread from animals. The patient was a 44-year-old farmer from a rural area where the disease is common. He had low fever for over two months, plus fatigue, sweating, and heavy weight loss.

Early blood tests for the infection came back negative, which slowed the diagnosis. Imaging, fluid sampling, cultures, and tumor markers all failed to settle the question. Standard antibiotics brought no improvement. A later repeat test turned positive, and targeted treatment then helped him recover. The case warns doctors in affected regions to repeat testing when suspicion stays high.
pmc-13241055:
Jerome and colleagues in Tamil Nadu pooled the evidence on treating children's broken wrists, the commonest pediatric fracture. Forty-five studies covering five thousand three hundred forty children entered the review. Twelve comparative studies fed the meta-analysis directly. The team split metaphyseal breaks from growth-plate injuries throughout.

Casts alone let twenty to thirty-five percent of metaphyseal breaks slip, versus almost none with added wires. Healing was near universal and long-term function equal either way. Children under eleven remodeled even fully shifted breaks without surgery. Jerome holds wire fixation for genuinely unstable patterns.
pmc-13241355:
Maram Montaser and co-authors report a 2026 translation and testing study of hot flush questionnaires for young breast cancer survivors in Egypt. Hot flushes are a frequent, distressing effect of hormone therapy. Validated Arabic tools for recording daily symptoms and their interference were lacking.

The team translated a hot flush diary and an interference scale using forward and back translation, then adjusted wording for local culture. Thirty-seven women on hormone therapy completed the interference scale once and the diary daily for a week. Both tools showed strong internal consistency, and every participant finished the diary. Interference was greatest for mood, sleep, and concentration. The Arabic versions appear workable for standard symptom assessment.
pmc-13241655:
Yafen Dong and co-authors report a 2026 mouse study linking bleeding after stroke to faster Alzheimer-type brain changes. Bleeding into treated stroke tissue is a known risk of clot-removal therapy. Whether it speeds existing Alzheimer pathology was unclear.

In mice carrying early Alzheimer-related genes, bleeding after a temporary artery blockage worsened memory and raised amyloid buildup. A plant-derived compound, timosaponin B-II, reduced those effects. Cell experiments showed the compound protected energy-producing structures and lowered cell death signals. It worked through a protective gene switch that curbed amyloid production. The authors propose the compound as a candidate for limiting Alzheimer acceleration after complicated stroke recovery.
pmc-13241955:
Zhimei Zeng and co-authors publish a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis comparing two local anesthetics for wisdom tooth surgery. Bupivacaine and articaine are both common choices, with different speed and duration profiles. The authors searched four databases for randomized trials that compared them head to head.

Eleven trials covering several hundred patients entered the pooled analysis. Bupivacaine gave lower pain scores after surgery at several time points, with the largest gap a few hours after the procedure. Articaine started working faster. Pain during surgery, difficulty, operating time, and blood pressure measures were similar between the drugs. The authors suggest bupivacaine for longer pain relief and articaine when a quick start matters most.
pmc-13242455:
Alice Guionnet and Jiaoyang Huang studied two famous families of symmetric polynomials in the limit as their variable count grows without bound. Their paper appeared in Communications in Mathematical Physics in 2026. Macdonald and Jack polynomials sit at the crossroads of algebra, probability, and physics, but their large-scale behavior had resisted a full description. The authors characterize the limits through variational problems, where an energy-like quantity is minimized.

A key step proves a large deviation principle for a deformed version of non-intersecting random walks. At the special value of one, those walks match random lozenge tilings of strip-shaped domains. That connection lets the paper recover a celebrated tiling result of Cohn and co-authors by a new route. It then extends the principle to every positive value. The work ties polynomial limits to the study of random surfaces.
pmc-13242755:
Fahimeh Safarnezhad Tameshkel and co-authors publish a 2026 cross-sectional study of herpesvirus co-infections in Iranian women who tested positive for human papillomavirus. Whether partner viruses help cervical disease progress is unclear. Leftover cervical screening samples supplied the study material.

Over three hundred samples were tested with a multiplex genetic assay for four herpesviruses. Co-infection was uncommon overall. Herpes simplex virus type 2 was the most frequent partner, followed by Epstein-Barr virus, while one virus was absent entirely. No link appeared between herpesvirus presence and the risk level or number of papillomavirus types. Few positive cases limited statistical power. The authors call for tissue-based studies with viral load measurement to settle the question.
pmc-13243155:
Elizabeth Valles-Capetillo and colleagues charted the brain networks behind social communication and what personal traits predict how well they run. Their study appeared in Cognitive Neurodynamics in 2026. Forty-five neurotypical adults completed tests of language, executive function, social cognition, and reasoning, plus an autism traits questionnaire. The team measured these networks for language, mentalizing, and both combined, then repeated the check in a second sample that included autistic adults.

Language skill was the strongest and steadiest predictor of how well the networks ran, above all in regions that blend meaning with context. Executive function predicted frontal control areas, and reasoning skill tied to a hub used in social inference. Autistic traits changed the strength of several brain-behavior links rather than simply weakening the networks. The authors argue social communication rests on an efficient, flexible system shaped by each person's cognitive profile.
pmc-13243355:
An-Fu Lee and Shang-Yin Wu report a 2026 case where a lung cancer changed its weak point after several drug rounds. Their patient was a 59-year-old woman who had never smoked and had stage IV lung cancer with an EGFR change. Standard targeted drugs held the disease for a time, then it grew again.

Gene testing of an older lymph node sample found a new fusion joining the BRAF and AGK genes. Doctors then paired gefitinib with trametinib, and the disease stayed stable for about 19 months. Brain spread needed surgery and radiation along the way. The case shows that repeat gene testing can reveal fresh targets late in care.
pmc-13243755:
Liang Wang, Xia Lei, and Lingfei Li report a stubborn nail disease that finally yielded to a targeted immune drug. Their case report appeared in the Journal of International Medical Research in 2026. The patient, a woman in her late forties, had nail lichen planus, a chronic inflammation that ridges, roughens, and splits the nails. Standard creams and systemic treatments had repeatedly failed her, as they often do in this condition.

She was started on abrocitinib, a drug that selectively blocks the JAK1 signaling switch inside immune cells. Her nails improved markedly on measured scores, and normal nail function returned. The benefit held through a slow taper and even after the drug was stopped, and her safety record stayed clean. The authors argue the drug hits the core immune mechanism driving the disease. One case cannot set policy, but it strengthens a growing set of reports behind this approach.
pmc-13244055:
Jung Yeon Shim updates care for allergic rhinitis in children in a 2026 narrative review based on fresh guidelines. The condition is among the most common long-term allergies of childhood in Korea and beyond. It also links closely with asthma, so the two are best handled as one airway problem.

Nose sprays with steroids stay the first choice for moderate to severe disease. Adding a spray antihistamine helps when the steroid spray alone falls short. Pills suit mild cases or moments when fast relief matters most. Starting spray treatment just before pollen season can blunt seasonal flares. Shim stresses dosing by age, steady use, and teaching caregivers well.
pmc-13244955:
Eric Amelunxen and colleagues test whether community pharmacies can catch heart, kidney, and metabolic risk earlier than clinics do. Their trial protocol appeared in BMC Nephrology in 2026. The APOSCREEN-1 study runs in twenty pharmacies in Germany's Schleswig-Holstein state. One thousand adults aged forty and over who meet risk criteria get point-of-care testing on the spot: glycated hemoglobin, blood lipids, urine albumin, and blood pressure, plus a clinical history.

Results flow to a study center through an online platform. Anyone crossing thresholds is sent for confirmatory laboratory testing at the center or their general practitioner. The trial's main questions are practical: will people accept screening at the pharmacy counter, and how much undetected disease it finds? Primary-care screening uptake is low, and the syndrome often surfaces only after organ damage. If pharmacies prove feasible and high-yield, they offer an accessible front door to prevention.
pmc-13247555:
Jiang and co-authors tracked eight reintroduced giant pandas to watch their movement styles settle, in this 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. Pandas run on an unusually tight energy budget, eating bamboo they digest poorly, making them a model for how animals move under energetic constraint. GPS collars followed the released animals for well over a year, and the team distilled ten movement measures into two behavioral axes, exploration versus exploitation and path straightness versus consistency.

Early on, individuals differed repeatably: explorers roamed widely while exploiters stayed put. Over the first months the explorers shrank their ranges and the whole group converged toward similar, conservative space use. The authors propose a diet-energy constraint hypothesis, that specialized diets and low energy efficiency push released animals toward cautious movement as they acclimate.
pmc-13247655:
Antuña-Zarzuelo and co-authors reflect on how great writers have grieved, in this 2026 editorial essay in Palliative and Supportive Care. Literature gives language to loss, and the authors read four writers as case studies in contrasting responses: Cesare Pavese, Miguel Hernández, Julian Barnes, and Joan Didion. Each wrote from a broken heart along a different path.

Pavese's diaries show grief as resentment: learning in 1936 that the woman he loved had married another, he armored himself in bitterness that slowly loosened over years. Hernández, imprisoned after Spain's civil war, answered loss with tears in elegies for his friends Sijé and Lorca. The essay uses such examples to remind clinicians that grief wears many faces, including ungraceful ones, and that naming them can be a form of endurance worth honoring in care.
pmc-13248255:
Lin and a large expert panel issued the 2025 Chinese consensus on prolactinomas, published in 2026. Prolactinomas are the most common hormone-producing pituitary tumors. The China Pituitary Adenoma Specialist Council updated its 2014 guidance using newer surgical methods and fresh clinical evidence gathered since then.

The statement gives thirty-six recommendations covering screening, testing, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up monitoring. It explains how these tumors present, how doctors separate them from look-alike conditions, and how care should change for pregnant patients, men, and hard-to-treat cases. The panel stresses team review, with surgeons, hormone specialists, imaging experts, and others deciding together.
pmc-13249055:
Zhao and colleagues taught computers to grade hazy lung spots by invasiveness, in a 2026 multicenter study. Ground-glass nodules on CT scans range from harmless precursor growths to invasive adenocarcinoma, and each class calls for different care. The team extracted texture features from scans of more than eleven hundred patients and trained six machine learning models on the three-way task.

A neural network model beat the other five, holding up best on the separate test set. Its discrimination scores stayed solid across both groups of patients. The authors also used explanation tools to show which features drove each call. They present the model as support for planning surgery and follow-up, not a replacement for pathology.
pmc-13249255:
Valigurová and colleagues give the first full account of a frog blood parasite in Slovakia, in a 2026 Parasite study. Screening two hundred thirty-nine frogs, they found sixty-seven water frogs of three Pelophylax species carrying a Dactylosoma parasite, a distant relative of malaria organisms. Specimens came from three sites in western Slovakia, and the team combined microscope measurements with DNA evidence.

All infections belonged to one species, closely matching the classic Dactylosoma ranarum first described from the same host genus. Flies caught at the sites carried none of the parasite, leaving its carrier unknown. The authors frame the work as a reference description tying old morphology to modern genetic data.
pmc-13249555:
Letizia Pontolillo, Lorenzo Gerratana, and Carolina Reduzzi introduce a research collection on liquid biopsy for early cancer in a 2026 editorial. Finding cancer early decides outcomes, yet scans miss disease that hides below sight. Blood tests for tumor traces promise to catch relapse at a molecular stage.

Fragments of tumor DNA lead the field, letting doctors spot return before images can. Cells, RNA, proteins, and vesicles in blood add further layers of signal. Whether acting on molecular relapse truly lengthens life is still unproven. The collection spans detection, residual disease checks, and early intervention across tumor types. The editors weigh fresh tools against the trials still needed.
pmc-13250255:
Joukar and colleagues check how often hepatitis C spreads inside families in Iran's Guilan cohort. Their 2026 Health Science Reports study followed twenty relatives of twelve people known to carry the virus. Blood tests looked for antibodies and active virus, and positive samples were typed by genotype to compare strains.

Two relatives tested positive for antibodies, and one, a thirteen-year-old girl, carried active virus matching her mother's genotype. She was treated with the combined drug Sovodak and cleared the virus, confirmed twelve weeks after therapy. No other family spread was found, so the authors judge household transmission real but extremely rare. They note that even shared household items could, in theory, carry some risk.
pmc-13251855:
Daniel Gilford and colleagues put a human fingerprint on flood days worldwide in this 2026 study. Sea level rise is raising coastal flood risk, but how much of that extra risk comes from human-caused climate change had never been counted site by site.

Using two estimation methods at 519 tide gauges, the team found the human share measurable at 97 percent of sites. Human-caused rise accounted for about 58 percent of the days when extreme water levels were passed between 2000 and 2018. On average, the count of such blame-carrying flood days has nearly tripled since the 1970s. The numbers are meant for local planning and loss claims.
pmc-13252755:
Michael Smith, Nicole Olynk Widmar, and Valerie Kilders track online investor chatter in this 2026 study whose title nods to a popular market slogan. Social media now hosts huge retail investing communities that can amplify, and sometimes coordinate, market moves.

Using a listening platform, the team collected weekly mentions and mood for four topics from 2020 to 2023: the United States dollar, gold, cryptocurrencies, and attention-shocked stocks such as meme stocks. They tested how chatter reacted to events like regional bank failures and famous short squeezes. Commentary volume stayed high throughout, and the authors find online communities increasingly shape how the public talks about markets.
pmc-13253155:
Fırat Tevetoğlu, Nil Çomunoğlu, and Haydar Yener test two immune markers in throat cancer in this 2026 study. Voice-box cancer survival has barely budged for decades, and newer immune brakes called TIM-3 and LAG-3 might explain who fares worse.

The team re-examined tumour samples from 50 patients who had voice-box surgery between 2016 and 2018, staining for both markers and for overall immune cell presence. LAG-3 positivity tracked with earlier cancer return across the whole group. TIM-3 mattered only in tumours with sparse immune infiltration, where it linked to worse survival. The authors call the results exploratory and ask for larger, multi-centre checks.
pmc-13253555:
Sara Lawhon and a large multi-laboratory team standardise a dog stool test in this 2026 study. Campylobacter jejuni sickens over a million Americans a year, and a 2016–2018 outbreak traced the germ to pet dogs, yet dog samples are not routinely tested for it.

Twenty-seven analysts at nineteen laboratories ran a DNA test targeting the gyrA gene on seeded dog stool samples. Every analyst caught the germ at a high dose. Detection fell as doses dropped: 96 percent at a mid dose, 77 percent lower, and 40 percent at the lowest. Reading DNA straight from stool skips a growing step, cutting contamination risk and turnaround time for veterinary labs.
pmc-13253655:
Thalita Faita and a large team test stranded whales and dolphins for parasites along Brazil's coast in this 2026 study. Sea mammals act as sentinels of ocean health, and land parasites washing into the sea are an emerging threat to them.

Samples from 159 stranded animals of 21 species were screened with DNA methods. Fourteen animals carried infections, and the pattern split by habitat. Nine coastal animals held Toxoplasma or a related species, matching spread from land hosts through runoff into the sea. Six open-ocean animals carried a distinct lineage of the same family, whose closest matches point to sea birds as the likely final hosts in its life cycle.
pmc-13254055:
Lu Liu and a large team design a light-emitting molecule with an unusually pure color in a 2026 study. Organic emitters, carbon-based light sources, often blur in color when molecules clump together. The team's molecule, built around an eight-electron ring system, keeps a flat shape in both ground and excited states.

In solution, its emission width was already narrow. When clumped, a cross stacking pattern held the shape still and cut vibration, narrowing the width to a record-small 13 nanometers. In light devices, the width stayed at 13 nanometers even as concentration rose, aiding sharp display design.
pmc-13254855:
Jia Qi Low and colleagues survey how Singapore's dentists prescribe antibiotics in a 2026 study. Dentistry writes roughly a tenth of all antibiotic prescriptions in human health care worldwide, and a large share are judged inappropriate, feeding drug resistance. Two hundred and eighty dentists answered the 2024 survey sent through professional bodies.

Appropriate prescribing swung wildly by scenario, from 6.5 percent to 97.7 percent correct against guidelines. Periodontal and oral surgery scenarios scored lowest, around a third correct, while restorative cases and care of medically complex patients scored higher. Nonclinical pressure was a weak point: when patients requested antibiotics or the diagnosis was uncertain, only about a fifth to a third of dentists prescribed well. Dentists trained locally, working in the public sector, or earlier in their careers prescribed well. The authors recommend training tied to the new local guidelines plus digital decision support.
pmc-13255855:
Ting Huang and colleagues report a 2026 real-world study of 148 Chinese patients with uterine sarcoma, a rare and aggressive group of uterine cancers. The team combined hospital records with public gene data to compare subtypes. Leiomyosarcoma and low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma were the most common forms in the cohort.

Five-year survival varied sharply, reaching about ninety percent for low-grade stromal sarcoma and only half for undifferentiated sarcoma. Tumor subtype, stage, and a pattern of tissue death independently predicted outcomes. Gene analysis showed immune suppression in high-grade stromal tumors and cell-cycle activation in leiomyosarcoma. The authors stress watching the lungs for spread, warn against reflexive chemotherapy in early leiomyosarcoma, and nominate hormone, immune, and PARP-blocking therapies for subtype-tailored testing.
pmc-13256055:
Michelle R. Dawson and Deepraj Ghosh review a 2026 topic linking cell aging to giant cancer cells that resist treatment. Senescence, where damaged cells stop dividing, first looks protective, yet aged cells accumulate in tissues and secrete signals that remodel their surroundings. The review connects that remodeling to polyploid giant cancer cells, rare oversized cells with unstable genomes.

These giant cells can lie dormant through chemotherapy, then bud off aggressive daughter cells that restart the tumor. Senescent neighbors stiffen and disorder the matrix around tumors, conditions the authors argue help giant cells form. Their physical mechanics, including size and stiffness, feed into resistance and spread. The reviewers propose treating giant cells as a senescence-linked state, and targeting them to prevent relapse after therapy.
pmc-13257055:
Daria S. Vinogradova leads a 2026 methods study on how bacteria start to build proteins. The start step brings the ribosome, a message strand, and a starter carrier together in a set order. Old tests use radio tags or fixed surfaces, which limit what can be seen.

A new test tracks glow signals as parts bind, from simple pairs up to full groups. The team also found a safe way to tag whole ribosomes and checked that tagged ones still work. Salt levels and start factors could be probed step by step on one bench setup. Tests with known drugs showed their effects at once. Bench scientists gain a cheap, sharp tool for this work and for drug screens.
pmc-13257555:
Hryhorii Parkhomenko and co-authors compare two electron transport layers in two-sided perovskite solar cells in a 2026 study. The cells include guanidinium in the absorber and a thin transparent gold back contact, letting light enter from both faces. Tin oxide and titanium dioxide layers were tested head to head.

Crystal quality of the absorber stayed the same on both layers, yet tin oxide passed more ultraviolet and blue light. Detailed loss analysis showed tin oxide sharply cutting non-radiative recombination, the energy leak where charges vanish as heat. Both bulk and surface trap losses fell, while healthy charge transport stayed intact. Solar engineers get a firm interface recommendation. For bifacial designs chasing commercial yield, tin oxide looks close to indispensable in this architecture.
pmc-13258155:
Magdalena Circu and co-authors describe a bacterial protein that quietly retunes metabolism inside infected macrophages. The bacterium is Legionella pneumophila, which can cause severe lung infection when inhaled. Their 2026 paper follows its effector Lpg0393, renamed BinA for the role they uncovered.

BinA moves amino acid transporters toward where they can feed the cell, working through Rab21 and Rab22 proteins. That lowers the trigger point for TORC1, a master growth switch, when arginine or leucine appears. Without BinA, the compartment housing the bacteria ruptured early, in step with the switch. The work maps a new lever Legionella pulls to expand its home.
pmc-13258655:
Salgado-Fernández María Fernanda leads a 2026 randomized trial of citrulline supplements after severe COVID-19 illness. Forty three adults who had been hospitalized joined the three month study in Mexico City. Half received daily citrulline, an amino acid tied to blood vessel health, while half served as controls.

Vessel inflammation markers were tracked alongside body makeup and walking distance. One adhesion marker fell more in the supplement group than in controls. Walking distance also rose more with citrulline over three months. Other vessel markers showed no clear difference between groups. Results support a focused follow up trial on vessel recovery after critical COVID-19 illness.
pmc-13260255:
Alexander A Sulfaro wrote a 2026 theoretical article arguing that measures of mental image vividness rest on an undefined concept. Vividness ratings are meant to capture how sensory a mental image feels, on a scale running to aphantasia, the claimed absence of mental imagery. Such ratings are widely used, and studies of aphantasia are growing. Sulfaro argues the field assumes these measures are valid without a logical basis for that assumption.

The core problem, he says, is that the single axis separating a mental image from other experiences has eluded definition for centuries. While it stays undefined, variation along it cannot be validly measured, and checks against other measures are circular. He also argues that confounding criteria can explain common findings, and that even confident imagery self-reports can be doubted. Better reference definitions are proposed.
pmc-13261055:
Montana Kay Lara leads a 2026 genome-wide association study of cocaine self-administration behavior in outbred rats. Cocaine use disorder is a major public health crisis, and its genes remain largely unknown. The study used 836 Heterogeneous Stock rats, 415 female and 421 male, bred to mimic human genetic diversity. Traits included acquiring self-administration, escalating intake, and compulsive-like responding. Heritability estimates and genome scans searched for linked DNA regions.

The traits were correlated with each other and showed modest heritability, from 0.07 to 0.16. Six genome-wide significant associations were found. One locus on chromosome nineteen, tied to time between cocaine infusions, contains carboxylesterase genes related to human CES1; these enzymes metabolize cocaine. Other loci contained genes previously linked to cocaine, alcohol, or tobacco use disorders in humans. The authors call it the largest rat genetic study of cocaine self-administration.
pmc-13262655:
Rob J Dekker and colleagues reported in 2026 a strange new virus from the brown seaweed Saccharina latissima whose genome seems to encode proteins in both directions. The virus, named SalaUV-NL1, carries two genome segments. Its large segment encodes the copying enzyme on one strand and a similar-sized reading frame on the reverse strand.

True two-way viruses limit their codon choices to avoid stop signals on the reverse strand. This virus instead shows an extreme bias in the third codon position, nearly all ending in G or C, far beyond any two-way need. The reverse frame is therefore likely an accident of that bias, earning the label pseudoambigrammatic. Variant comparisons revealed very fast silent change, mostly swaps toward G and C letters. The authors found similar signatures hiding in other virus records within public databases.
pmc-13263355:
Xinxin Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 phase II trial of nano-packaged chemotherapy for adenoid cystic carcinoma, a slow but stubborn cancer of the head and neck. Patients had tumors that could not be removed or had returned or spread. Thirty-one patients received liposomal doxorubicin plus nab-paclitaxel for three cycles; those fit for radiation then received combined chemoradiotherapy.

The response rate was about ninety percent, with fifteen complete and thirteen partial responses, meeting the trial's main goal. Responses lasted a median of about eighteen and a half months. Patients who went on to chemoradiotherapy stayed free of progression longer. Severe side effects affected about a quarter of patients, and there were no treatment-related deaths.
pmc-13263555:
Barry Ting Sheen Kweh and colleagues reported in 2026 a new back-only operation that corrected a severe forward bend at the top of the thoracic spine. Their patient, a seventy-five-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis and fragile bones, developed an extreme T1/2 kyphosis after earlier neck surgery. Her chin sat too close to her chest for any front approach.

Working from behind, the team used a modified path through the pedicle and facet joint to reach the disc space. They released the front ligament and slid in an interbody cage without sacrificing any nerve root. The deformity corrected excellently, the compressed cord was freed, and her mobility improved. The authors claim the first such posterior thoracic fusion without nerve sacrifice. They offer it for cases where the front route is impossible.
pmc-13264055:
Dianjie Zeng and colleagues present a 2026 genetic study of immune drivers in kidney stone disease. Stones form when minerals collect in the kidney, and immune involvement is suspected but poorly mapped. The team used single-cell genetic data from a large immune atlas. Gene activity in specific cell types was linked with four anatomical stone subtypes, and shared genetic signals were then checked.

Eighty gene and cell type pairs showed strong support. Natural killer cells and certain T cells stood out across subtypes, with pathways tied to antigen presentation and T cell activation. Seven genes were ranked as most actionable for future work. The results may guide risk prediction and immune-focused treatment ideas for a common and painful condition.
pmc-13264355:
P. Meißner and colleagues grow patient tumor organoids with their own immune cells to predict immunotherapy benefit in head and neck cancer in a 2026 study. Mini tumors from surgical samples were cultured with blood immune cells from the same patients, then exposed to checkpoint drugs against one or two targets. Immune mixes were rich in helper and killer T cells plus natural killer cells, though many T cells already showed exhaustion markers at baseline before drug exposure.

Tumor killing occurred in under half the cultures, accompanied by helper cell cytokine patterns including an interleukin-17 signature. That signal tracked with a death-ligand pathway and, in untreated patients blood, higher levels linked with better survival. A living test bed of this kind could flag likely responders before treatment.
pmc-13264555:
Huan Wei and colleagues wrote a 2026 lab study comparing blood safety of coated flow diverters, mesh tubes placed in brain arteries to treat aneurysms. Bare metal can trigger clots, so makers add coatings. The team tested a polymer-coated device, a fibrin and heparin-coated device, and one bare device in a blood loop.

The bare device raised clotting and platelet activity most, with platelets sticking to its surface. Both coatings cut those effects well. The fibrin and heparin device also sparked less immune activation and less inflammation than the polymer-coated one, on the markers used. Blood cell counts and red cell damage were also tracked. The authors judge the fibrin and heparin coating the most blood-friendly of the three.
pmc-13264855:
Yu Yan and colleagues published a 2026 study on how tropical cyclones speed dengue spread in Guangzhou, China. Dengue is a mosquito-borne fever, and the city is China's most dengue-prone coastal megacity. Storms were known to raise risk, but the mechanism was unclear, so the team paired field tests on mosquitoes with epidemic modeling of the 2014 outbreak.

In release and recapture tests, storm winds stretched the flight range of the dengue mosquito by 63 percent and raised human-mosquito contact by about 30 percent. Modeling two 2014 typhoons tied one to 217 extra cases and the other to 5,131 extra cases, with matching money losses. Stronger mosquito control during one storm was projected to avert nearly 60,000 cases. The authors urge early control guided by storm warnings.
pmc-13264955:
Alberto Esteban-Medina and colleagues examine high cholesterol diagnoses around menopause in Andalusia, Spain, in a 2026 cohort study. Health records from 2016 to 2022 covered the whole regional public system. The study compared men and women before and after age fifty. Age fifty served as a proxy for the menopausal transition.

More than half a million patients with high cholesterol were included. Women were diagnosed about three years later than men on average. Diagnoses in women rose sharply between ages fifty and fifty-five. Older women also carried more osteoporosis, anxiety, and hypertension than men. The authors support prevention tailored by sex and age.
pmc-13265255:
Xian An and colleagues link sleep disorders with heart and vessel outcomes in lung disease using UK Biobank data, in a 2026 cohort study. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease already strains the heart. Poor sleep may add risk through low oxygen, inflammation, and metabolic strain. More than twenty-one thousand participants with the lung condition were followed.

Sleep disorders linked to much higher risks of heart failure and atrial fibrillation. Risks of angina and heart attack were also raised. Among those with sleep disorders, male sex, older age, smoking, and obesity added further risk. The authors argue sleep assessment belongs in routine care for these patients.
pmc-13266155:
Jung Min Chang, Su Min Ha, and Heera Yoen sum up ultrasound updates in the 2025 breast imaging system (2026). The sound-scan lexicon guides image capture, wording, and reporting. Must-do density notices in the United States have raised sound-scan screening. The new edition reflects those practice shifts.

Tissue make-up scoring now counts gland tissue amount. Wording for masses, calcium spots, and linked features was fine-tuned. A new non-mass lesion category helps characterise subtle findings that match other scans. Lymph node talk grew wider and deeper. The overview helps sonographers and radiologists adopt the revised language.
pmc-13266355:
Wahyudhy Adriansyah and the team compare open versus keyhole groin hernia repair in children, in a 2026 past-case study. Hernia repair is the most common children's surgery, and method contrasts stay unsettled. Reports from developing countries are limited. Ninety-two children were split between the two groups.

Hospital stay was shorter after keyhole repair by roughly a third of a day. Operating time did not differ between groups. No factor, including technique, sex, age, or prematurity, clearly linked to recurrence. Groups differed in age at birth and at surgery at the start. The authors call for larger planned multi-site checks.
pmc-13266655:
Katharina Flöthmann and the team test pressurised aerosol chemotherapy inside the chest for mesothelioma using tissue outside the body (2026). The rare cancer has poor outlook and few options. Aerosol delivery of cisplatin was compared with heated liquid chemotherapy. Temperature, drug strength, and tissue barrier were varied systematically.

Warmer conditions, stronger drug, and removing the pleural lining each deepened penetration. Under clinically relevant settings, aerosol treatment penetrated tissue better than the heated liquid method. The preclinical results suggest the aerosol approach may be a viable alternative. Further medical study is warranted before patient use.
pmc-13266855:
Mircea Gabriel Stoleriu and colleagues search in 2026 for traits that predict cancer left at the cut edge after lung cancer surgery. Positive margins raise the risk of return, so knowing who faces that risk helps planning. The team reviewed 232 patients who had anatomical lung removal at a German military hospital between 2019 and 2024.

Clear margins were achieved in most patients, yet eighteen had tumor at the edge. Those cases clustered in men, in larger tumors, and in squamous cell cancers, with node spread and vessel invasion also common. Statistical modeling kept tumor stage, squamous type, and male sex as independent predictors. The authors suggest using those flags for closer planning and follow-up, pending larger studies.
pmc-13268155:
