Juliana Ju Yun Hoo and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of how sight and sound shape the restfulness of tropical city green spaces. Most research on restorative places comes from cooler climates. The team gathered 120 stimuli from nature, city, and mixed settings in Malaysia. Eighty-seven participants were assigned to hear sounds only, see images only, or get both, and rated a subset of thirty.

Nature and mixed scenes were generally rated more restful than city scenes. In the sight-only group, mixed scenes, like tree-lined streets, beat pure nature scenes. For nature scenes, sound alone scored about the same as sight alone or both together. The authors suggest small pockets of city nature can restore more than wild forest views, and good nature sounds can stand in when green views are lacking. Planners can use both findings.
pmc-13269155:
Ruitong Liao and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on air chemicals and a blood enzyme in adults in the United States. The chemicals, called volatile organic compounds, come from fuels, paints, and industry. Their traces were measured in urine, and the enzyme LDH was measured in blood.

Data covered 4,907 adults in a national health survey from 2011 to 2018, with 17 chemical traces tested. Several traces were linked to lower LDH, while one was linked to higher levels. Mixed exposure tests also pointed both ways, with different chemicals leading each side. Most links held up in repeat checks. The authors read the pattern as a possible early sign of harm from these chemicals.
pmc-13269555:
Imogen Camp and Nick G Jones published a physics paper in 2026 on matrix-product states, compact formulas that describe quantum systems built in a chain. Certain such formulas are exact ground states, the lowest-energy states, for linked families of system rules. Earlier skeletons of these states were known only for simpler, non-interacting models.

Camp and Jones partly expose such a skeleton in interacting spin chains called chiral clock families. Their states stay dense in the calm regions around a sequence of fixed points. Outside those regions the states remain exact but describe excited, higher-energy levels instead. As an application, they derive a closed formula for a disorder measure in one family of interacting models.
pmc-13270055:
Carmen R B da Silva and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on heat tolerance in 95 wild bee species across Australia. Nesting habits differ: some bees nest in the ground, some in wood cavities, and some in plant stems. The team tested whether nest microclimate, the small local climate, predicts how heat tolerance evolved.

Stem nesters had evolved the highest heat tolerance, while ground nesters had the lowest, since soil lets them dodge extreme heat. Shared ancestry explained part of the pattern through shared nesting habits. That indicates repeated adaptation rather than a hard evolutionary cap. Adding nesting behavior also changed which species ranked most at risk from climate change.
pmc-13271355:
Danping Liu and coauthors report in 2026 on a helper T cell group that seems to organize other immune cells inside lung tumors. These CD4 cells make a signal called CXCL13, which attracts B cells that carry its matching receptor. The question was whether that pairing helps killer T cells attack non-small-cell lung cancer.

Combining single-cell gene data with tissue staining, the team found the three cell types sitting together in tumors. Patients whose tumors held this three-cell grouping tended to fare better. The pattern points to a local immune team that strengthens tumor attack, and it may help doctors judge which patients carry a more active defense.
pmc-13272055:
Kristyna Sintakova and coauthors test in 2026 whether tiny parcels released by neural stem cells can protect injured spinal cord tissue in the lab. Spinal cord injury leaves lasting damage, and stem cell benefits seem to travel largely through these parcels, called small extracellular vesicles. Two human stem cell sources supplied the vesicles for testing.

Rat spinal cord slices were injured and treated at once, then examined after three days. Injury raised cell-death markers and broke down structural proteins, while vesicle treatment pulled those measures back toward normal. Both cell sources protected the tissue, shifting survival signaling in a favorable direction.
pmc-13272155:

Patients first received immune therapy combined with chemotherapy, which shrinks tumors before surgery. How thorough the neck dissection must be after such treatment lacked agreed thresholds.

A training group of 256 patients from one cancer hospital and a validation group of 199 from another hospital supplied the data. Statistical searches found survival-linked cutoffs of twenty nodes for one-sided dissection and an average of eighteen per side for two-sided surgery. Patients meeting the benchmarks survived better, giving surgical teams a concrete adequacy target.
pmc-13272455:
Yue Sun and coauthors mine in 2026 Chinese social media discussion of AI virtual companions to map what users talk about and how they feel. Surveys miss the spontaneous language of real use, so the team collected over twenty thousand comments under 168 Xiaohongshu posts. Topic modeling and sentiment analysis were combined, with human review to consolidate the topics.

Twenty-nine topics grouped into seven broader experience categories. Monetization and platform mechanics drew the most discussion, followed by relationship memory and continuity and virtual romance themes. Sentiment was scored with a Chinese language model tuned on hand-labeled comments, revealing the emotional structure behind the companionship market.
pmc-13272855:
Manuel Juarez-Garcia leads a 2026 study seeking early signs of difficult-to-manage axial spondyloarthritis, a form of inflammatory spine arthritis. Of 311 patients starting treatment, 101 were analyzed, with 42 classed as difficult to manage and 59 as very good responders. Difficult cases were more often smokers, lacked a key gene marker, and had more tendon pain and other illness. Disease activity at six months, not at baseline, predicted later difficulty. The tree models sorted patients fairly well and held up in an outside registry.
pmc-13273155:
Bradley Langford leads a 2026 survey on bringing careful antibiotic use into Canadian community pharmacies. Common barriers were lack of support from non-pharmacist providers and from pharmacy leaders. Supports included providers seeing careful use as important, pharmacists acting as teachers, and the chance to save health care costs. The authors say a better grasp of these factors can help design workable, lasting programs in community pharmacies, where formal programs are still uncommon.
pmc-13273355:
Jihye Seo, Kyuhee Cho, and Jimin Lee described a new copepod species from Korea in a 2026 taxonomic paper. Copepods are tiny crustaceans, and this one belongs to Laophontella, a small genus living in sand and sediment along coasts. It was collected from intertidal habitats on the Korean coast.

Females have a seven part first antenna, a wavy edged expansion under the first free abdominal segment, and curved structures on the tail rami. Males carry a hoe shaped spine on one swimming leg. The authors also describe the fifth copepodid stage, the last young stage before adulthood, which lets them track how traits develop and which persist.
pmc-13273555: Correction notice from Stuart Leishman and co-authors. It corrects a 2024 protocol for a lab assay in cultured cells. The assay detects a fat-based protein mark called S-palmitoylation. Step 32 of the method is also corrected to match. The authors apologize for the errors.
pmc-13273655:
Haojian Sun and colleagues fed a plant oil blend to broiler breeder hens in a 2026 poultry study. The industry wants to cut antibiotic growth promoters without losing output. Thymol and eugenol, oils from thyme and clove, are candidate replacements, and the team also asked whether benefits pass to chicks.

Supplemented hens laid more settable eggs with stronger shells and better internal quality scores. Their gut lining grew taller villi, antioxidant defenses rose, and inflammatory signals in reproductive organs fell. Chicks from treated hens ate less yet gained the same weight, and their blood and tissues showed calmer, better defended chemistry in the first week.
pmc-13274155:
Ahmadreza Soroush Fard and co-authors wrote a 2026 review article on using nanomaterials to build better rotavirus vaccines. Such carriers can shield vaccine parts from the harsh gut, aim them at immune tissue, and stir stronger responses. Designs could work as injections that skip the gut barrier or as sturdy oral doses. The authors see them as a path to lasting protection where current vaccines fall short.
pmc-13274855:

Participants carried zero, one, or two copies of the risk variant in near-equal thirds. Overall, the variant showed no significant link to any single fatty acid in either depot, a mainly negative result. One subgroup hint in men rested on very small numbers and needs confirmation. pmc-13275155:

Only twenty-three articles turned up, fourteen of them original case series, and the largest cohort held just forty-six patients. The commonest fixes were inferior pedicle reductions and round-block lifts, with complication rates under ten percent in all series. Reported cosmetic results varied wildly and inconsistently. The authors lay out a ladder from small reshaping to regional flaps matched to breast size and patient hopes.
pmc-13275555:
Fetriyuna Fetriyuna and colleagues present a 2026 journal article on making cricket protein tastier and more useful for food products. The team chopped cricket protein with an enzyme called ProteAX, varying the dose and the chopping time in a full factorial design.

The winning recipe used 1.5 percent enzyme for five hours. It broke down 67.71 percent of the protein while keeping bitterness and aftertaste low and umami, the savory taste, strong. The resulting flour was 69.51 percent protein and dissolved almost completely in water. It also absorbed far more water and oil than before and held emulsions steady across acidity levels, suiting it to processed foods.
pmc-13276355:
Sindy Chavez and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on how a cancer-causing fusion protein organizes itself inside cells. That same segment shapes the droplets' form and drives activation of the MAPK pathway, a central growth signaling route. The work adds to evidence that the physical organization of fusion protein droplets is not decoration. How the droplets are built helps determine how strongly the cancer signal fires, a point the authors develop across the full paper.
pmc-13276455:
Rika Kusumoto-Matsuo and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how sunlight damage turns into genome instability, a hallmark of melanoma. Ultraviolet light creates two main DNA lesions. One type is usually repaired before cells copy their DNA; the other can linger into the copying phase.

Where damage in active regions was partly repaired first, breaks decreased. In inactive regions they persisted. Irradiated cells also gained structural changes and single-letter mutations matching the known ultraviolet signature in human melanoma. The authors map a pathway that may explain how sun exposure writes lasting changes into skin cell genomes.
pmc-13276755:
Paula García-Barja and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on which coping habits predict anxiety and depression in healthcare workers. Reframing problems positively predicted lower levels of both. Openly expressing emotions predicted slightly higher levels. Surprisingly, avoidant coping predicted lower symptoms in this snapshot. Social support related only to fewer depressive symptoms. Having no family responsibilities also predicted lower distress, and nursing assistants were a higher-risk role.
pmc-13277755:

New isolation methods, from spinning to microfluidics, have sharpened how these vesicles are studied. Their cargo patterns may serve as markers for cancer, heart, brain, autoimmune, and infectious diseases. As treatments, they could deliver drugs or genes with less toxicity than synthetic particles. Scaling up production, setting standards, and proving safety remain the main hurdles to clinic use, the authors say.
pmc-13278955:
V V Mun and colleagues trace the origin of rete testis cells in mouse embryos in a 2026 developmental study. The rete testis links the sperm-producing tubules to the ducts that carry sperm out. Where its cells come from during development has stayed unsettled.

Embryonic gonad and neighbouring tissue pieces, one set glowing green, were grown together in culture dishes. New rete cells appeared inside gonad pieces that had started without any, and some sat among Sertoli cells carrying a Sertoli marker. Keeping more of the neighbouring rete tissue boosted the new cell count, implicating local signals. Reanalysis of single-cell data supported transitions from Sertoli-line cells toward the rete lineage.
pmc-13280555:
Emmanuel Eroume A Egom and team give a 2026 review of HIV linked pulmonary arterial hypertension in resource limited settings. The illness raises pressure in lung arteries in people who live with HIV. It persists despite wider antiretroviral therapy coverage. Modern criteria set the diagnosis by right heart catheterization, with pressure and resistance marks. Global certainty on rates stays uneven, the authors stress.

In high income settings, screens with catheter proof put prevalence near half a percent. A multicentre French study found a near same rate. In sub Saharan Africa, home to more than twenty six million people with HIV, catheter proof rates stay undefined. Echocardiography based studies in symptomatic cohorts report much higher rates. The gap marks a forgotten diagnosis that can imitate other lung and heart disease.
pmc-13281855:
Amos Odiit and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a boy who survived tetanus in Uganda. Tetanus comes from a germ toxin after a wound and locks muscles in painful spasms. The boy was nine and had cut a toe three days before. He had never had the tetanus vaccine or boosters. His spasms were severe, with a locked jaw. The hospital had no intensive care unit for him. He was nursed on a general ward in a dark, quiet room.

Care ran for twenty-five days. It joined wound care, antibiotics, tube feeding, and two calming drugs in turns. A bladder tube eased his care. The anti-toxin shot, scarce in stock, came ten days after arrival. Even so, the boy recovered and went home alive. The authors say strong basic care can save such children where intensive care is absent.
pmc-13282455:
Abdullah Serin and co-authors report a 2026 case of kidney cancer that spread to a small wrist bone, an extremely rare site. Renal cell carcinoma is the commonest kidney cancer and can spread to bone, but carpal bone spread is almost unheard of. Their patient was a forty-three-year-old woman with a past kidney cancer who developed pain on the little-finger side of her wrist. Imaging showed the hamate bone completely destroyed by the tumour.

Surgeons removed the hamate and scraped out the tumour cavity. They rebuilt the space with bone cement and fixed it to neighbouring wrist and hand bones to keep the wrist stable. Fifteen months later there was no local return, no instability, and no implant problem. The authors present removal with cement and fixation as a way to control such tumours while preserving hand use in carefully selected patients.
pmc-13282555:
Mulugeta Fentahun Nega wrote a 2026 review on two Ethiopian drinks made by fermentation, tella and areke. Tella is a home-brewed, beer-like drink. Areke is a strong spirit made by distilling a similar brew. Both are made in small amounts by home sellers, using know-how passed down over time. The ferment is wild and not controlled, and is driven by lactic acid bacteria and yeasts.

The review sets out the steps, the microbes, and the chemistry of both drinks. Tella is made in three named stages. Rising interest in such drinks could bring jobs, income, and tourists, the author argues. But quality varies, proof of safety is thin, and there are no set rules for making them. Wider sale will need more study and better checks, while keeping the craft's roots.
pmc-13282855:
Ola Ekström and co-authors present a 2026 targeted protein study of extreme blood vessel outcomes in type 1 diabetes, comparing patients who escape complications with those who progress fast. Heart and vessel disease is the leading killer in type 1 diabetes, yet some people stay free of major vessel and kidney damage despite decades of high blood sugar. The team profiled ninety-two blood proteins in ninety-two such escapers and fifty-seven rapid progressors.

Twenty proteins differed significantly between the groups after adjustments. Rapid progressors carried higher levels of a cell-death protein, caspase-3, and of several proteins tied to platelet activation and white cell sticking. They also showed more tissue-remodelling and metabolic proteins. Escapers, by contrast, had higher levels of two proteins, von Willebrand factor and paraoxonase 3, as part of a distinct resilience signature.
pmc-13282955:
Rosacea looks different when viewed through gut, brain, and hormone signals together, the lens of Lei Shi's 2026 review. Rosacea is a long-term skin condition that affects about five percent of people worldwide. The review argues that nerve, hormone, and immune signals act together in its four subtypes.

Each subtype gets a distinct account in the review. Face flushing is tied to stress hormones and nerve signals. Pimple-like lesions are tied to male hormones, gut imbalance, and innate immune action. Thick skin and eye disease involve growth signals and low-grade body inflammation. Treatment options are matched to each subtype, from beta blockers to hormone-related drugs and eye care.
pmc-13283755:
Phil Thomas, Brian Sindel, and Gal Winter studied in 2026 which microbes live on tomato roots grown without soil. In hydroponic growing, plants sit in sterile rockwool, so growers focus on blocking germs or adding helpful ones. The team grew tomatoes to maturity in such a system, then applied a Trichoderma-based product meant to protect roots.

Bacterial life on the roots proved rich in species, though a few groups dominated, mainly Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, and Bacteroidia. Fungi were less varied and came almost wholly from two groups. The protective product did not shift bacterial diversity, yet the whole community changed over time in both treated and untreated plants. The authors say rockwool can hold a complex, resilient root community worth managing for plant health.
pmc-13284155:
Aiah M Khateb and a large team studied in 2026 how gene variants in a fungal sensor protein relate to fungal colonisation in people with diabetes. Diabetes raises the risk of harmless-looking fungal growth that can turn dangerous. The protein CARD9 relays signals from fungal detectors, and severe CARD9 faults cause rare childhood immune disease. The team screened 107 diabetic adults across body sites and sequenced the CARD9 gene.

Fungal growth was common, with an Aspergillus niger group the top find at about 28 percent. One gene region acted as a variation hotspot, and over half of participants carried two copies of damaging variants. Yet people with the highest fungal scores often carried the normal sequence, and obesity was the main independent predictor of fungal burden in combined models. The authors still argue the pathway is widely weakened in diabetes.
pmc-13284855:
Mian Usman Sattar and co-authors built a lightweight system in 2026 for classifying brain CT scans, aimed at clinics with modest computing power. CT scans guide diagnosis of tumours, cancer, and aneurysms, yet heavy AI models strain small hospitals. Their framework cleans standard medical image files, borrows features from four pre-trained networks, and can blend model votes, while a heat-map method shows which image regions drove each call.

The compact MobileNetV2 model and the blended ensemble each reached about 97 percent accuracy, with near-top ranking scores. A classic deep model, VGG-16, followed at about 92 percent. Two other modern models failed badly on this task, scoring far lower. MobileNetV2 also trained and answered fastest. The authors recommend it where accuracy and speed must coexist.
pmc-13285255:
Minh Bui and a team of chemists report a 2026 method that turns waste PVDF plastic into fluoride compounds used in aluminium making. PVDF is a tough fluorinated plastic found in battery parts and membranes, and its strength makes it persist in the environment. Natural supplies of cryolite, a key aluminium ingredient, are nearly exhausted.

Ball milling the plastic with a Lewis acid released fluorine that converted salt and aluminium chloride into chiolite, a sodium aluminium fluoride. Heating chiolite then produced cryolite at a 62 percent yield. The route uses no solvents and little energy. Tests confirmed the products, and membrane waste plus plastic recovered from old batteries both worked as starting material.
pmc-13285355:
Shaheen Khazali and Ahmed Karim offer a 2026 commentary on how surgery for endometriosis keeps becoming less invasive, sometimes faster than solid proof can follow. Endometriosis surgery must remove disease while protecting pain levels, fertility, and bowel, bladder, and sexual function. That balance makes progress gradual and shaped by shared experience rather than sudden leaps.

Keyhole surgery first changed what surgeons could do, followed by fewer ports, nerve-sparing work, and gentler bowel operations. The commentary then turns to NOSE, a method that removes tissue through a natural opening so no extra belly cut is needed for extraction. The authors ask whether enthusiasm for each new step is matched by evidence that patients truly benefit.
pmc-13285755:
Hui Yang and co-authors report a 2026 study of pollution swings in six mountain watersheds of China's Taihang range. Monsoon rains reshape how farm and city waste reach rivers across the year. The team set out to measure that seasonal flip and to build a tool that can read it from routine monitoring data.

Water quality scores were best in the dry season and worst when rains ran high across all six basins. Farmland drove most dry-season pollution, while paved city surfaces took over as the lead driver in wet months. Basins shaped by heavy human use swung far more between seasons than forested ones. Two watersheds stood out as most at risk of seasonal decline, a warning that can guide care that changes with the calendar.
pmc-13286355:
Kendall E Martin and co-authors examine how two gene regulators keep heart muscle cells in the zebrafish atrium from changing identity. Published in 2026, the study focuses on the vein-side end of the heart, where pacemaker cells form. The regulators Nr2f1a and Isl1 push in opposite directions there, one restraining and one promoting the pacemaker fate.

Fish missing both regulators lost pacemaker formation entirely. Their atrial muscle cells also dropped muscle markers, switched on genes of the heart's outer layer, and left the muscle wall. Single-cell gene readings confirmed this mixed identity. Removing two outer-layer genes blocked the switch. The results show both regulators are needed again and again to keep neighboring heart cell types distinct.
pmc-13286755:
Ya He and colleagues follow nearly six thousand people with high blood pressure to see whether high levels of homocysteine, an amino acid in the blood, predict later diabetes. The 2026 multicenter study addresses a gap: homocysteine's link with blood pressure is settled, yet its link with diabetes has been disputed.

Risk climbed steadily as homocysteine rose, with each standard-sized increase tied to roughly a quarter more risk. Thresholds emerged near the mid-teens of the measurement scale, slightly lower in women than in men, beyond which risk jumped. The pattern held across many subgroups. Lowering homocysteine might therefore protect twice over, the authors suggest, easing blood pressure and diabetes risk together.
pmc-13286855:
Svanishvili Nino and co-authors measure how acid attack and fluoride treatments change the mineral makeup of teeth. The 2026 laboratory study split 45 extracted human teeth into halves, keeping one half intact as a control and acid-treating the other. Treated halves then received fluoride varnish, fluoride toothpaste with rinsing, or toothpaste without rinsing.

A microscope technique that reads element levels found enamel naturally richest in calcium and phosphorus. Acid stripping cut minerals sharply, especially in dentin, and erased detectable fluoride. All fluoride treatments restored some calcium and fluoride. Varnish trended toward the best fluoride retention in enamel, yet no treatment beat the others clearly on calcium or phosphorus. Clinically realistic studies should follow, the authors say.
pmc-13286955:
Alice Wang and colleagues dissect what Ontario plastic surgeons post on Instagram in a 2026 observational study. Of 261 registered surgeons, 86 ran professional profiles, and the team coded up to 30 recent posts per account, 2,032 in all, by content type and clinical territory. Practice setting, academic, community, or mixed, shaped both the feed and the applause it drew.

Before-and-after results made up nearly a third of posts, and facial aesthetics was the biggest single domain. Academic surgeons leaned toward announcements, research, and reconstruction, while community surgeons posted more advertising and facial work. Engagement ran highest for academic accounts, personal posts, and craniofacial content. The authors flag a mismatch: cosmetic content floods the platform while the reconstructive material audiences reward most stays scarce.
pmc-13287055:
Rachel A. Willand-Charnley introduces a 2026 journal collection on sialic acids, sugar molecules that cap the surface molecules of cells, and their role in cancer. Abnormal sugar coating is a hallmark of malignancy, and excess sialic acid on tumor surfaces helps cancers grow, spread, and hide from the immune system by engaging calming receptors on immune cells.

Enzyme changes drive the extra coating, stiffening the cell's outer layer and aiding movement and vessel attachment. Seven contributions in the collection apply new glycomics tools, genetics, and drug approaches to map these changes. The editor frames sialylation as a meeting point between tumor and immune system, and a promising source of biomarkers and drug targets.
pmc-13287555:
Sultan Onur, Mustafa Çeşme, and Ferhan Tümer report new methoxyphenol-triazole compounds in a 2026 chemistry and biology study. The team designed the hybrids to act on several disease pathways at once. Targets included enzymes tied to Alzheimer's disease and growth of prostate cancer cells. Computer models of docking and drug-like traits supported the lab results, and the authors propose the scaffold for further tuning.
pmc-13287655:
Jay C Dunlap surveys in 2026 how study of daily biological clocks in fungi has advanced since the year 2000, building on classic work in the bread mould Neurospora. The review covers how fungi sense light, reset their clocks, and assemble the core parts that keep near twenty-four-hour timing.

Later work filled in the full parts list and showed how the parts hold timing steady across temperatures. The fungal clock plan turns out to mirror animal clocks in broad design. Dunlap notes that the gains now reach fungi of farm importance, where timing affects growth and infection. The piece frames mould clocks as a model for clock biology at large.
pmc-13287855:

That design aims to spare healthy tissue that also carries EpCAM. Patients had advanced adenocarcinomas that no longer answered standard care.

Most tumors were colorectal cancers, with smaller numbers of pancreatic, breast, and other types. Cytokine release symptoms stayed mild to moderate and manageable in the cases noted. Some tumors shrank even at lower dose levels, and two colorectal patients stayed free of progression for many months. Dose escalation continues to find the best dose.
pmc-13288155:
Chiara Casella and co-authors introduce miniMORPH, a tool for measuring infant brains on low-field MRI, in 2026. Rankings of infants by region size mostly carried over between scanner types. Some fluid-rich regions, such as the ventricles, showed steady size offsets that may need calibration. pmc-13288255:
Anaïs Emmie Bouvier and a large team gave a face memory task inside a brain scanner in 2026 to eleven teenage boys living with obesity and fifteen lean peers. Teenagers learned pairs of faces and backgrounds, then later picked out the faces they had seen.

Boys with obesity recognised fewer faces. During learning, a memory hub and its neighbour fired less strongly in that group. During recall, a different region fired more strongly. The authors link the pattern to weaker memory encoding in teens with obesity. They warn the gap could feed school learning trouble and ask that teen years get more weight in obesity and brain research.
pmc-13288455:

pmc-13288955:

Healthy aging and MS may pull in opposed ways. Trial designers should weigh age, the authors say. A set shrinkage goal may mislead across ages.
pmc-13289155:
Mia Sarah Fischer Button and colleagues profile people sent to social medicine units in Denmark. Their 2026 register study spans 2012 to 2022. Such units assess people with long joblessness. The group held 13,092 first-time contacts. Two matched groups gave contrast.

Muscle and joint disorders were also higher. Mind diagnoses rose over time in that group. The authors urge labor reforms that fit these needs.
pmc-13289355:

pmc-13289855: A 2026 retraction notice withdraws an article on a sunflower oil and chitosan film decorated with fly ash, made using white shrimp shell waste, for antibacterial and immune effects. Concerns focus on overlaps across Figures 4, 9, 11, and 12, with many panels matching panels in other papers. The notice lists each suspect panel pairing in detail. No replacement findings are offered, so the record is limited to documenting the overlaps that prompted withdrawal.
pmc-13290455:
Nutrition belongs inside cancer treatment, not beside it, Aurora Mirabile and co-editors argue in a 2026 editorial introducing a research collection on the theme. pmc-13290855:

Attack and defense came bundled, so producers did not destroy themselves. On this view, antibiotics began as signals keeping microbe communities in balance, not as pure weapons. pmc-13290955:

pmc-13291055:

pmc-13291255: Romain Bolzoni and co-authors published a brief author correction in 2026 to a study on magnetic sense in a freshwater microbe. Only the correction note is present here, and it is very short. Two species names were spelled wrong in the discussion. A third name needed a corrected ending. All three now read correctly in the online versions. No findings can be judged from this note alone.
pmc-13291355:

pmc-13291555:

pmc-13291655:

pmc-13291755:

pmc-13292355:

pmc-13292655:

pmc-13292755:

Hatched chicks showed bursa shrinkage, liver bleeding, and leg weakness, with tissue damage seen under the microscope. The work gives farms and labs a clearer picture of local virus types.
pmc-13292855:

The authors suggest a cutoff level to guide closer watch after surgery.
pmc-13292955:

pmc-13293655:

The team rebuilt signatures for 14 hallmark processes across 23 cancer types by blending reference sets with protein networks and cancer gene data. Software and maps for all pairings are shared openly for other researchers to use in their own work.
pmc-13293755:

Extra checks probed whether hidden gene paths skewed the results.
pmc-13294055:

pmc-13294355:

pmc-13294455:

pmc-13294655: A 2026 correction notice by Elisa Aguzzoli, Magdalena Walbaum, and Martin Knapp amends two references in their scoping review on dementia care among ethnic minority groups. The notice fixes how a 2009 NICE medicines adherence guidance and a 2023 World Health Organization feature on traditional medicine are cited, including access years and capitalisation. The published article itself is only this brief correction, with no new findings or analysis added.
pmc-13295155:
Chikashi Yano and co-authors follow treated adults with spinal muscular atrophy over years in a 2026 study. Long-term paths and simple monitoring markers under modern treatment remain poorly charted for adults. One Japanese centre tracked patients given nusinersen or risdiplam between 2018 and 2025.

Twenty-three adults with confirmed genetic disease had repeated arm and whole-body motor scores plus lab and nerve measures. More copies of a backup gene meant later onset and milder illness. Scores often rose or held steady in the first treatment year, then levelled or slipped for some. Breathing capacity, an enzyme level, and a nerve signal each tracked motor state usefully.
pmc-13295555:
Effrosyni Gerovasileiou and colleagues compare two nasal high-flow designs in stable adults in a 2026 study. High-flow nasal therapy eases breathing effort by washing out stale air and adding gentle pressure. A new uneven design, blocking one nostril more than the other, might strengthen that flushing action.

Each interface ran for 15 minutes at a set flow, with a short washout gap between sessions. Throat pressure was tracked by a balloon tube and breath size by chest sensors, focusing the comparison on breathing effort in the final minute of each phase.
pmc-13295655:

pmc-13295755:
Fanny Anabel Sulistio and colleagues test a leaf extract against nerve harm in zebrafish in a 2026 study. Stress from reactive oxygen drives much nerve cell harm, yet few plant guards have been tried in live animals. Physalis angulata leaves hold plant compounds with known protective traits.

Growth, yolk use, heart rate, and swimming all bounced back, while wary edge-hugging eased. Lab checks showed key cell paths near normal again, and the extract beat a standard guard drug on most scores.
pmc-13296055:
Gonul Hazal Koc and colleagues apply, in 2026, new international definitions for hard-to-manage psoriatic arthritis in a Dutch early-disease cohort. pmc-13296155:
Xueyuan Jiang and colleagues compare, in 2026, two feed additives for weaned piglets, copper glycinate and potassium diformate. Copper is widely used in place of antibiotics, but it pollutes and can breed resistant gut germs. The team test whether the acid salt can take its place.

pmc-13296855:
Catalin-Bogdan Satala and colleagues argue that a promising stomach cancer target must be read as a nuanced biomarker, not a yes-or-no label, in a 2026 review. pmc-13297255:
Ernest Lee and co-authors pool, in 2026, twenty-nine studies hunting bedside and lab clues that flag double-hit lymphoma, an aggressive B-cell cancer carrying two gene swaps. The confirming gene test is costly and scarce, so the team ask which features should trigger it.

pmc-13297355:
Zeliha Emrence and colleagues test a tiny RNA that reins in a gene-editing enzyme inside breast cells, in a 2026 laboratory study. pmc-13297455:
Inês S. Almeida and colleagues tune a wobbling flow reactor that grows algae while capturing carbon dioxide, in a 2026 study. pmc-13297955:

pmc-13298355:
An Sen Tan leads a team surveying fracture risk prediction for spinal metastases beyond the widely used SINS score, in a 2026 survey. Patients sharing one score can fare very differently, and manual scoring takes time with variable agreement between observers. The authors propose multi-part stability scoring after proper checking.
pmc-13298455:

pmc-13298555:

Hard times in the land, with shaky rule and thin funds, made each gap worse. The team call for fixes at the root. pmc-13299655:

pmc-13301055:
Hyonjee Yoon and co-authors chart thirteen years of hyperprolactinemia care in Korean women using nationwide insurance claims, in a 2026 population study. pmc-13301655:

pmc-13301755:

The authors pitch process data as a richer lens for testing programs and cognitive research.
pmc-13302255:

In adults, unipolar voltages ran slightly higher than omnipolar ones, while children showed the reverse pattern. The gap between the two measures shrank predictably with age. The authors suggest the fixed electrode spacing suits small hearts poorly and propose child-specific cut-offs.
pmc-13302355:
A balloon that delivers drug and leaves no metal behind tempts cardiologists treating acute coronary syndrome, Sheref Zaghloul and colleagues review in a 2026 narrative survey. pmc-13303855:
Xuefei Chen and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study on whether intense interval exercise can ease liver scarring in fatty liver disease. The condition, tied to metabolic problems, is rising worldwide, and drug-free options with clear mechanisms are still wanted.

pmc-13303955:
Yuchen Peng and co-authors compare Mycoplasma pneumonia in children and adults after the COVID-19 pandemic in a 2026 hospital study. This lung infection once mainly struck children, but adult cases have grown and are less well described.

After matching, children ran higher fevers and showed different blood patterns than adults, while adults recovered faster. pmc-13304755:

pmc-13305955:

pmc-13306455:
Juan Du developed a camera method for measuring round holes in sheet metal with very high precision in a 2026 study. Manual inspection lacks accuracy for factory quality checks, so a full automated system was built on the MATLAB platform.

pmc-13306855:
Elpida Foti linked hip movement to pain change in long-term low back pain in a 2026 motion study. Hip bending measured right at the moment back pain starts was tested as a more telling sign than plain range checks.

pmc-13307855:

Interviews traced outcomes for 541 people bitten between 2010 and 2020, gathered through community snowball sampling. Snakebite hits rural workers hardest and is often counted only roughly.

About a quarter of victims suffered lasting morbidity and roughly an eighth died, giving adjusted rates well above official impressions. Total burden reached about thirty-two healthy life years lost per hundred thousand people each year. pmc-13308555:
Zhe Tang and co-authors show in 2026 that a simple salt, cesium iodide, beats fancy organic add ins for carbon based perovskite solar cells with no hole transport layer. They spun the salt into a two cation film in one step, with no extra layers or surface drugs in the build.

pmc-13308655:

pmc-13308755:

pmc-13309055:
Shaurya Tewari and colleagues present in 2026 a thirty-four-year-old man from a high tuberculosis region of Madhya Pradesh. pmc-13309355:

pmc-13309455:

pmc-13309655:

The pilot drew 400,719 responses between late 2022 and late 2025, and results fed staff dashboards for local action. pmc-13310055:
Yachen Li and co-authors study how implant placement shapes results in a side-approach spine fusion in a 2026 article. Whether the cage sits toward the front or back, and how screws angle, may change pain, alignment, and complications.

pmc-13311155:

Review found a wall lesion that stood out most on contrast images. Muscle and skin spread from liver cancer is uncommon but changes care once found. pmc-13311955:

pmc-13312055:

pmc-13312155:

pmc-13312255:

pmc-13312355:

pmc-13312655:

pmc-13312755:

pmc-13312855:

pmc-13313155:

pmc-13313755:

pmc-13314355:

pmc-13314455:
