The team gathered randomized trials from Chinese and English databases and pooled pain scores, stiffness, function limits, and a blood inflammation marker. Probiotics showed no worse side effects than placebo and no grave safety flags, by the results reported. Gains looked best for two strains named in the report, Saccharomyces boulardii and a sakei strain called LB-P12. Yet the trials were few and small, which weakens the proof. The authors call for bigger trials before probiotics join standard knee care.
pmc-13315855:
Thanh Nguyen, Issei Komuro, and Jianyi Zhang introduce in 2026 a third volume of collected work on bioengineering and biotechnology for cardiovascular science. Heart failure still kills widely, with only about half of patients alive five years after diagnosis, and new care aims to replace lost muscle with engineered working heart tissue.

After more than twenty years, cardiac tissue engineering now underpins ten cell-based trials worldwide. Contributions in the volume tune tissue maturity and contraction through adhesion and gap junction regulators such as laminin and connexin 43, and propose gene profile checks of engineered tissue. Engineered tissue also serves as a test platform beyond therapy.
pmc-13316155:
Lingli Jiang and a large team studied in 2026 how cutting the spinal cord changes the response of a cut leg nerve in rats. Patients with spinal injury often develop stubborn wounds in paralyzed limbs, hinting that nerve health guides repair. Yet how spinal injury reshapes distant nerve breakdown was unclear.

Rats got a sciatic nerve cut alone or plus a full spinal cord cut at the lower back. Nerve stumps were sampled at zero, three, and seven days. Stains, microscopy, and vessel markers tracked degeneration and new vessel growth, while small RNA sequencing spotlighted miR-134-5p in Schwann cells, tested further with mimics and blockers.
pmc-13316455:
Dengke Fu and a team of Chinese researchers compare, in a 2026 study, three fruit shapes of Lanxangia tsaoko, a spice plant grown across southeast Asia. No full comparison of shape, chemistry, and function existed before, so they measured the fruits from outer looks down to tiny compounds.

Redder, longer fruits smelled stronger, and that scent tracked with flavonoids and phenolic acids, whose making paths drove most shape differences. A few sharp-smelling compounds dominated the flavor scores. The team also built a light-based scanning model that sorted fruit shapes with perfect accuracy after tuning. Linking chemistry to light signals points toward fast, cheap, non-destructive sorting for growers and traders.
pmc-13316655:
Rongxia Li and co-authors pooled, in a 2026 meta-analysis, real-world cohort studies on whether GLP-1 drugs, widely used for diabetes and obesity, change the risk of cancers of the female reproductive organs. Metabolic illness itself links with these cancers, so a drug effect would matter widely.

Nine retrospective cohort studies met the rules. Overall, drug use showed no firm link with combined gynecologic cancer risk, with a pooled hazard ratio of 0.80 and a range crossing no effect in the combined estimate. Ovarian cancer alone showed a lower risk signal, while womb, cervical, and other types showed none. Wide differences between studies urge caution: the authors call the findings ideas to test, not proof.
pmc-13316755:
Tao Liu and co-authors examined, in a 2026 Singapore cohort study, whether well-known healthy eating patterns guard against mild memory and thinking decline in older adults. Most proof comes from Western groups, so Asian data were needed.

The Diet and Healthy Aging cohort supplied 620 older adults for a snapshot analysis and 313 healthy starters for follow-up tracking. Closer following of a Mediterranean-style pattern linked with lower odds of impairment in the snapshot, with an odds ratio of 0.35 in the adjusted model, while two other patterns showed no link. Over time, none of the patterns predicted new decline. The authors urge larger studies with repeated diet checks before drawing firm lessons.
pmc-13318155:
Bjarke Sihm Stender and colleagues track, in 2026, how faithfully Danish patients kept taking blood-thinning tablets after a procedure for atrial fibrillation. Lifelong direct oral anticoagulants are advised for high-risk patients after catheter ablation to prevent stroke. Long-term use in real life was the question.

National registries identified 13,438 people who had a first ablation between 2017 and 2024. Among high-risk patients, a large majority still met the adherence threshold three years later, though the share fell under a stricter threshold. Persistence, meaning continued coverage at each time point, dropped more, with over a fifth no longer covered by year three. Rates of stroke-like events and major bleeding were both low. The authors call for efforts to sustain protection.
pmc-13318255:
Shuaixin Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 network analysis of Buyang Huanwu Decoction. They asked which parts of the herbal formula might act on both ischaemic stroke and heart attack. The two conditions share blocked blood flow and artery disease.

The team ranked formula ingredients by network closeness. They ran enrichment checks and tested binding to the protein GSK-3β. Docking and a resonance experiment both pointed the same way. Thirteen shared core targets emerged, led by lipid and atherosclerosis signalling. Ten ingredients were put forward as possibly dual-acting. Myricanone bound most strongly, and the lab test backed that result. The findings support a multi-target case for the formula.
pmc-13318755:
Sumaira Hussain and co-authors present a 2026 study of lightweight deep learning for spotting brain bleeds on CT scans. Intracranial haemorrhage is life-threatening and needs fast reading. Manual review is slow and varies between readers. Small models could help in clinics with limited computing power.

The team compared a custom small network with two mobile designs, MobileNetV2 and EfficientNet-B0. Data came from a public brain CT haemorrhage dataset. MobileNetV2 performed best, reaching 87 percent accuracy and an AUC of 0.94 in their tests. The custom network reached 79 percent accuracy. EfficientNet-B0 competed well but needed more computing resources. The authors back such models as decision support, pending better sensitivity and clinical validation.
pmc-13318855:
Simone Frediani and colleagues present a 2026 national survey of children's polytrauma care in Italy. Multiple injuries at once carry high illness burden, yet no clear guidelines exist for young patients. The survey asked senior doctors in paediatric surgery and intensive care societies. It compared paediatric hospitals with mixed hospitals, and busy centres with quieter ones.

Fifty-two institutions answered the survey. A third were paediatric hospitals and two-thirds treated adults too. Most had a dedicated children's emergency department, at 89 percent of institutions in the responses. Multidisciplinary trauma teams existed in 72 percent, and internal protocols in 94 percent of sites. A senior paediatric surgeon was on call in only 44 percent. The authors urge standardisation, training, and a national trauma registry.
pmc-13319055:
Ryma Toumi, Simonne J. Guenette, and Shannon K. Oda review, in 2026, fusion proteins that add costimulation inside engineered T cells for cancer therapy. Cell therapies excel in blood cancers but struggle in solid tumours. Hostile surroundings sap the cells' strength and staying power. New designs sense those surroundings and answer with tailored activation.

Fusion modules can be built into receptor-based and standard engineered T cells. They steer cell development and function at the tumour site. Anchored or secreted versions can wake dendritic cells and reprogramme suppressive myeloid cells. Cold, quiet tumours may thus become treatment-responsive. The authors set out a design framework linking sensing, activation control, and surroundings repair. Their goal is wider, more durable benefit in solid tumours.
pmc-13319255:
Wendy Yi-Ying Wu and co-authors report a 2026 study of mood drugs and tumor chemistry in people with glioblastoma, a fast growing brain tumor. Use of these drugs is common in this group, but how they link to tumor traits and length of life has stayed unclear.

Two groups were studied side by side, one drawn from national records with 801 people and one hospital group with 153 people whose tumors were tested. Drug use as a whole tracked with shorter life, while two named drugs tracked with longer life than other drugs of the same class. Higher tumor levels of one brain chemical also tracked with better felt health before surgery.
pmc-13320255:
Juan-juan Ji and co-authors test a stiffness score as a flag for fatty liver in a 2026 study across two large health cohorts. Fatty liver tied to body metabolism is the most common long term liver illness in the world, yet scan based checks cost too much for wide screening. A stiffness score figured from age and blood pressure was tried as a cheap stand in.

One cohort in Japan held 14251 people and one in the United States held 12767 people, and higher stiffness tracked with fatty liver in both after full checks. Those in the top quarter of stiffness faced clearly higher odds of fatty liver in each cohort. The link bent rather than running straight, with risk rising fast at low stiffness then leveling off. The score may help sort who needs a scan first.
pmc-13320355:
Wenqi Yin and co-authors pair a smart gel with special nerve cells to mend spinal cord cuts in a 2026 rat study. A cut cord loses its circuits and gains a hostile scar zone where grafted cells die fast and link poorly. Their soft gel mimics cord tissue, heals its own cracks, and flexes with the body, and it carries young V3 nerve cells that help set movement rhythm.

In rats with fully cut cords, the gel plus cell mix lifted movement scores, grip, and walking form far past controls. Scar growth shrank, guard cells shifted to a healing mode, and new fibers and vessels grew in. Switch tests proved the grafted cells wired into host circuits and did real work. Joint design of gel and cells is the key lesson.
pmc-13320455:
Xiaochun Xiao and co-authors brew a prized plant scent compound in yeast in a 2026 study of a new enzyme from a mugwort kin plant. The compound guards crops against disease and pests and holds drug promise too, yet pulling it from plants or making it by chemistry gives low yields that block wide sale. Gene hunts found a fresh maker enzyme in the plant, and its shape was tuned for speed.

One tuned change in the enzyme lifted output sharply by steadying its fold, as motion models showed. A yeast strain was then rewired step by step to pour its carbon toward the compound. Cold batch feeding reached the highest brew level yet reported for this compound in the work, which may open green supply at scale.
pmc-13320955:
Ema Ozaki and co-authors build a cell atlas of scarring in the back of the eye in a 2026 study. In age-related macular degeneration, excess matrix tissue under the retina causes lasting sight loss, but which cells supply that matrix was unknown. The team compared an injury model that heals with one that scars.

Single cell gene reading and cross organ matching showed choroid fibroblasts as the main matrix source in scarring disease. Some fibroblast types appeared in both healing and scarring, with shared repair or immune roles. One retina specific group, marked by high Fap plus Fgl2 and Postn, grew only in scarring and was confirmed in human donor eyes. That group is a focused drug target.
pmc-13322855:
Rebecca Reichel and colleagues study how German medical students handle conflict and how that links to stress, in a 2026 cross-sectional survey. Their group held 219 ninth-semester students at the Medical Faculty of Tübingen, who completed German versions of conflict and stress questionnaires.

Students favoured working together and compromise most, and competing least, when facing conflict. Conflicts within teams linked to higher perceived stress in the analysis, while a stronger pull toward compromise linked to lower stress. The authors propose adding reflective training on conflict handling into medical teaching, to support teamwork skills and reduce stress, and they note that more research should test whether such training works.
pmc-13324655:
Bozidarka L. Zaric and colleagues review precision delivery tools for type 2 diabetes drugs and genes in a 2026 article. Hitting the right tissue hard while sparing the rest could raise benefit and cut side effects.

Three delivery families anchor the review. Cell-penetrating peptides ferry cargo across cell membranes, while peptide nucleic acids bind gene targets tightly and resist breakdown by enzymes. Antibodies and receptor ligands steer loads toward pancreas beta cells and other metabolic tissues. The authors set out the strengths of each route, from the neutral charge of peptide nucleic acids to fragment-based antibody designs. Together the methods point toward gene control tuned to insulin signaling and beta cell health.
pmc-13325155:
Marianna Barbalinardo and colleagues test whether a pre-made albumin coat changes how silver nanoparticles behave in cells in a 2026 study. Protein coronas form on particles in body fluids and blur their designed traits.

Negative citrate particles and positive polymer-coated particles were pre-coated with bovine serum albumin and tried on three cell lines. The coat kept particles stable in complex media, above all the positive ones, yet it did not change which proteins gathered later or how toxic the particles were. Without serum, the coat became vital for stability and cell contact. Surface charge, not the coat, governed the biological outcome.
pmc-13325355:
Chokri Saidi, Mourad Debbichi, and Noureddine Chaaben model lead-free strontium perovskite solar cells from first principles in a 2026 study. Lead perovskites perform well but raise toxicity worries, so stand-ins are in demand.

Quantum calculations found Sr3SbCl3 and Sr3PCl3 stable, with direct band gaps of 1.704 and 1.677 eV for the two materials. Both drank in visible light strongly and moved charges at useful speeds. Device simulation then tuned layer thickness, doping, and contact choices. The best builds reached power conversion near 25.80 percent for the antimony version and 26.22 percent for the phosphorus version. A graded mix of the two gave no extra gain.
pmc-13325455:
Daniel A. Taylor and colleagues automate a signal-boosting trick for benchtop NMR mixture analysis in a 2026 study. Small NMR machines are cheap and handy but suffer weak signals and crowded peaks.

Parahydrogen-driven SABRE boosting was put under machine control, giving steady gains with a spread of just 2.5 percent across 100 runs. Each refresh took about 13 seconds, fast enough to slot into advanced pulse sequences. A three-part pyridine mixture at natural isotope levels gave a clean carbon spectrum in 18 minutes of averaging. Two-dimensional runs untangled peaks that overlapped in plain proton spectra. Even a dilute mix at 750 micromolar per part yielded a usable map in one scan.
pmc-13325855:
Sebastian Fernández and co-authors review metal halide perovskites built to emit violet and ultraviolet light in a 2026 article. Perovskite LEDs shine with pure colors and cheap processing, shining in red, green, and blue devices.

The short-wave end lags because of shaky stability, poor charge flow, and trouble reaching ultraviolet tones. The review covers bulk films, flat sheets, nanoplatelets, and colloidal crystals as material forms. Lead-free options, including rare-earth halide perovskites, get their own survey. Uses stretch from public health lighting to 3D printing and chip making. The authors lay out routes to fix stability and scaling while cutting toxicity.
pmc-13325955:
Josef Finsterer writes a 2026 letter questioning a study of sleep problems in children with fatty liver disease. The study by Ozkan and co-authors found more disturbed sleep in children with metabolic steatosis and gut symptoms.

Finsterer raises four gaps. Many outside factors shape child sleep and were not weighed in the analysis. The Child Sleep Habits Questionnaire rests on parent reports and lacks solid checks against measured sleep. No brain imaging ruled out nervous system causes of poor sleep. The letter also asks how many children had raised ammonia or scan signs of liver-related brain effects. Objective sleep measurement is his main demand.
pmc-13326655:
Yang Xu and colleagues test insect skin compounds on the infection structures of a pest-killing fungus in a 2026 study. Metarhizium anisopliae must form appressoria to breach insect cuticle, and that step tracks its killing power.

Several added compounds, including L-aspartic acid and glycyl-L-phenylalanine, sped spore germination and appressorium building. Aspartic acid helped at every dose for germination and peaked at 1 mg per mL for both measures. Two compounds helped at low doses yet blocked growth when strong. Others, like mitifos at high dose, simply inhibited. Metabolite profiling found 367 changed compounds after appressorium formation under aspartic acid.
pmc-13326955:
Marie K Fialkowski and colleagues relate total breastfeeding time to later diabetes in mothers in a 2026 multiethnic cohort study. Feeding history may guard mothers against type 2 diabetes, but proof across ethnic groups was patchy.

Women who answered the 2003 to 2008 follow-up in the Multiethnic Cohort were tracked for new diabetes, yielding 5,122 fresh cases. Mothers whose combined feeding across children reached 24 months or more had an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.87 for diabetes. Any breastfeeding lowered risk in White women, also at 0.87 on the ratio scale. The long-duration gain stood out in Native Hawaiian women, at 0.65 in the adjusted model.
pmc-13327655:
Yue Zhao and co-authors test a herbal sugar extract on inflammation in loach fish in a 2026 study. Polysaccharides from Polygonatum sibiricum, a Chinese medicinal plant, are known to calm inflammation, but how they act in fish was unclear. Loaches with bacteria-triggered inflammation were fed the extract, and liver gene activity was read by RNA sequencing.

Treatment changed 10,250 genes, with 5,652 turned up, and the shifts centered on sugar metabolism and the immune system. Follow-up checks confirmed the sequencing, and one route stood out: Fc receptor driven engulfing of particles by immune cells. That pathway may carry much of the extract's calming effect, giving fish farming a molecular lead for natural anti-inflammatory feeds.
pmc-13327855:
Jennifer Schlie, Timo Schinköthe, and Annette Schmidt survey contraceptive use among German servicewomen in a 2026 nationwide study. No systematic figures existed for this group, though hormone use bears on health and readiness. An anonymous online survey with 40 questions drew 2,818 completed replies, a response rate of 11.2 percent.

Current hormonal contraceptive use stood at 38.1 percent, led by combined pills at 18.5 percent, then hormonal coils at 8.9 percent and progestin-only pills at 8.4 percent across the sample, and use fell with age. Preventing pregnancy drove choices for 82 percent of users, ahead of easing period pain and bleeding, while only 13 percent cited cycle control for performance. Long-acting implants and injections were almost absent.
pmc-13327955:
Sooah Cho and colleagues validate a quality-of-life pain question after keyhole bowel cancer surgery in a 2026 study. The EQ-5D-5L survey includes one pain and discomfort item, and the team asked whether it can stand in for numeric pain scores. Data came from a Korean recovery registry covering 333 patients at one center.

Across the first three days after surgery, the item tracked numeric scores at rest and while coughing with moderate strength, correlations running 0.44 to 0.57 on their measures, and it changed over time about as well as the numeric scale. It also separated recovery-program patients from standard-care patients. One simple item may thus serve pain tracking when fuller scoring is impractical.
pmc-13328255:
Loreto Sanhueza and co-authors test grape waste compounds as antibiotic helpers against Staphylococcus aureus in a 2026 study. The bacterium resists drugs partly by pumping them out, and blocking the NorA pump could restore ciprofloxacin. Extracts of grape pomace were split to find active flavonoids, then paired with the antibiotic in checkerboard tests.

Quercetin, catechin, and epicatechin were identified, and all extracts and compounds acted in synergy with ciprofloxacin, with index values from 0.076 to 0.281 across the strains tested, including one that overproduces the pump. Epicatechin stood out for direct pump blocking, shown by dye buildup inside cells. Winemaking waste may thus supply adjuvants that rescue fading antibiotics.
pmc-13329355:
Yaping Gao and team built a pathway-free, three-part self-starting control system and used it to make 3-hydroxypropionic acid. Their 2026 paper sets out a multi-part control design that works apart from metabolic pathways, timing many gene readouts by self-starting rather than outside triggers or pathway-tied controls. The system is built from three parts that line up gene readout timing inside the production host.

The use case was making 3-hydroxypropionic acid, a flexible base chemical, showing the control system can steer a build pathway toward a target product. The team frames the pathway-free design as a broad tool. Since control does not hinge on the exact metabolic pathway, the same part logic could fit other products needing timed, lined-up gene readouts. The paper places the system as a step toward bendier, self-controlling microbe cell factories.
pmc-13329555:
Zhenyang Li and a large team report in 2026 that ondansetron, a drug used against nausea, also fights enterovirus A71. That virus causes hand, foot, and mouth disease and can harm the brain and heart in severe child cases. No approved virus-specific drug exists for it, so the team screened for new options.

Tests in cells and in living models showed strong action against the virus, the authors report. The drug acted early, at the steps where the virus attaches to and enters cells. Genes tied to cholesterol handling, including ABCA1, ABCG1, and HMGCS1, changed with treatment. The authors propose targeting host fat balance as a fresh antiviral strategy worth further study.
pmc-13329855:
Handrean Soran and a large team compare two targeted drugs for a rare fat disorder in a 2026 indirect analysis. Familial chylomicronemia syndrome causes very high triglycerides and repeat pancreas attacks, and standard fat-lowering drugs fail since a key enzyme is missing. Both olezarsen and volanesorsen block apolipoprotein C-III.

Patient data for olezarsen came from the Balance trial with 45 people, weighted to match the APPROACH trial group of 66 people on volanesorsen. At 52 weeks, gaps in fat and target protein change favoured olezarsen in point values, yet none reached statistical clarity in the reported ranges. Pancreas attack and harm risks also showed no clear gaps. The work gives context where direct trials are absent.
pmc-13330255:
Chen-ying Ma and team assessed a specialty assessment curriculum for radiation oncology trainees. Their 2026 single-center prospective intervention, using past controls at a major cancer center, enrolled 21 trainees in the new course against 19 controls. Skill here is still usually thought to grow through apprenticeship, yet tasks such as target marking, plan review, and multidisciplinary reasoning are not well sampled by end-of-rotation exams alone.

The curriculum mixed exam-style clinical tests with workplace-based assessment across three disease modules. The modules covered locally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma without induction chemotherapy, middle and lower thoracic esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, and FIGO 2018 stage IB3 to IIIC1 cervical cancer. The team argues that repeated practice on clear cases, comparison with accepted standards, and feedback pointed enough to change the next attempt lift performance. A single end-of-rotation score is an unlikely measure of skill in this high-stakes specialty.
pmc-13330355:
Nfwama Kawatu and colleagues revise headache estimates for school pupils in Zambia in a 2026 study. An earlier count used a narrow rule for mild short headache, which may have inflated migraine rates. Pupils in nine schools filled standard questionnaires in class sessions, with 2,089 of 2,759 invited pupils completing them.

Under the wider rule, migraine prevalence fell from 51.6 percent to 42.9 percent in the recalculated figures, still flagged as doubtful by the authors. Burden still split types clearly: migraine was strongest, most frequent, and longest. Headache cost an estimated 3.5 percent of school time among those affected in the reported burden work. Frequent daily headache drove the largest losses.
pmc-13331455:
Arindam Pande and colleagues describe a 2026 case report of a 57-year-old woman whose fainting spells were treated as epilepsy for years. She later developed repeated runs of torsades de pointes, a dangerous heart rhythm that needed electric shocks to stop.

Testing showed a long corrected QT interval with no acquired cause, and gene analysis found two previously unreported variants together in the AKAP9 gene. Doctors stopped her seizure drugs, fitted a dual-chamber defibrillator, and treated her with a beta blocker and mexiletine. At six months she had no further rhythm events and her QT interval had improved. The authors use her story to stress genotype-guided care after a late and missed diagnosis.
pmc-13331955:
R. Max Petty and colleagues measured the glow of two red dyes, Eosin Y and Phloxine B, set inside polyvinyl alcohol films at room temperature for a 2026 spectroscopy study. Such long-lived glow in the red to near-infrared range is rare in plain organic materials, yet useful for sensing, security printing, and light devices.

The films showed three kinds of emission: instant fluorescence, delayed fluorescence, and phosphorescence lasting milliseconds. The first two sat in the orange-red range, while the phosphorescence stretched past 800 nm into the near infrared. Both dyes were fairly bright, and their phosphorescence was strongly polarized, a trait the authors link to direction-sensitive optical uses. They present the pair as promising ready-made materials for red and near-infrared room-temperature phosphorescence work.
pmc-13332455:
Virinca Jaipuriyar and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for developing and pilot testing RISE, a telehealth program for sexual and gender minority adults who drink hazardously and carry trauma symptoms. Stigma, high trauma exposure, and scarce affirming care drive both problems in this group, and combined alcohol and trauma programs are rarely adapted for them.

Guided by the ADAPT-ITT framework, the first phase adapts RISE with input from 20 community members and 10 providers. The second phase randomizes 60 participants to start at once or wait six weeks. Treatment pairs four adapted Unified Protocol sessions with five days of expressive writing about trauma or stigma, backed by clinician check-ins. The pilot will measure feasibility, acceptability, and early clinical signals through self-report and clinician ratings, shaping a later full trial.
pmc-13332955:
Noelle M Cocoros and colleagues build a 2026 Danish resource for population studies of infectious disease. Infections cause major illness and death, yet many aspects of their population patterns stay unknown because key data are missing. The team created the Danish Infection Cohort by linking national health survey data, including self-reported behavior and health, to diagnosis and medication records in Danish national registries. Adults aged eighteen or older in surveys from 2010, 2013, 2017, and 2021 were included.

Infection in the year after each survey was flagged two ways: hospital-diagnosed infection from discharge diagnoses in the national patient registry, and community-treated infection from systemic anti-infective prescriptions filled at pharmacies. Among 609,224 people, about one third had at least one infection by those definitions. The cohort gives epidemiologists a large, linked base for studying who gets infections, how they are treated, and what follows.
pmc-13333455:
Chi Wang and colleagues built a prediction model in 2026 for spotting sepsis patients headed toward acute kidney injury using only the first blood tests drawn at admission. The complication sharply raises intensive care deaths, and the earliest possible warning is what clinicians lack.

The retrospective study covered 1,573 sepsis patients at West China Hospital between January 2024 and December 2025, split into training and validation groups of 1,102 and 471. Screening the admission labs with LASSO selection, then confirming with logistic modeling, left eight independent signals: myoglobin, the liver enzyme ALT, phosphorus, sodium, potassium, carbon dioxide combining power, platelets, and neutrophils. The model discriminated well, with AUC values of 0.839 in training and 0.832 in validation, stayed steady across age and sex groups, and is presented as a nomogram for bedside risk estimates. The authors ask for outside testing in other hospitals before wider use.
pmc-13333655:
Yangfei Che and co-authors analyzed daytime sleepiness during digital cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia in a 2026 retrospective study. Some patients feel sleepier early in this online treatment, and the team asked what drives that change and whether it predicts success.

The records came from 2,271 insomnia patients seen at the Hangzhou Seventh People's Hospital sleep clinic between November 2016 and January 2024. Sleepiness scores rose by weeks 2, 4, and 6, peaking at the second week, with sex, medication use, snoring, and starting sleepiness among the influencing factors. Patients whose sleepiness rose early later showed larger gains in sleep quality through week 16. Early sleepiness may therefore signal that the therapy is taking effect rather than failing.
pmc-13334955:
Xiaoqin Zheng and co-authors trialed a staged cardiac rehabilitation program built on the Health Belief Model in a 2026 randomized study of older heart patients. Fear of movement, or kinesiophobia, is common in elderly coronary patients and keeps them out of rehab.

The single-blind trial enrolled 139 elderly patients with coronary heart disease, giving 69 the staged belief-based program plus usual care and 70 usual care alone. Fear of movement, daily living ability, and exercise self-efficacy were measured at admission, discharge, and one and three months after discharge. The program group improved more on every outcome, with lower fear scores by the later checks and higher function and confidence from discharge onward. No exercise-related adverse events occurred.
pmc-13336355:
Xiang Pei and co-authors devised a making strategy for strained two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks in a 2026 chemistry study. Frameworks with deliberately unreacted groups offer extra tunability but resist crystallization, above all strained designs like the [4+3] type.

Their approach splits the process into a kinetic polymerization step and a thermodynamic repair step. Tuning reaction time or solvent polarity sets how far the kinetic intermediates polymerize. Only intermediates at an optimal degree convert cleanly into highly crystalline frameworks during thermal repair, as shown with models COF-221 and COF-222. A high-polarity solvent such as nitrobenzene offers another control knob. The recipe gives chemists a general handle on crystal quality in a class of photocatalyst materials that has been hard to make well.
pmc-13336855:
Jian Wang and co-authors copy ligament and bone to build a record energy-storing film in a 2026 study. Polymer films for capacitors must juggle strength, stored energy, efficiency, and toughness, and gains in one usually cost another. Their design pairs a flexible constraining polymer with hard coated ceramic cores wrapped in a responsive shell.

The film stored an energy density of 26.1 J per cubic centimeter with 90.2% efficiency at 600 MV per meter in lab tests, alongside a stiffness of 2.13 GPa in the reported measures. Live checks and simulations showed chains and interfaces reshaping under strain to spread fields and charges evenly. Body-inspired layouts could serve electronics that face extreme demands.
pmc-13337755:
Dennis P. Orgill and fellow editors mark ten years of the journal Frontiers in Surgery in a 2026 editorial. By April 2026 the journal had published 6,659 papers, as stated in the editorial. The piece looks back at broad shifts in surgery and ahead to what may come next.

Progress is grouped under three pillars: precise surgery, decisions guided by data, and joining biology with technology. Robotics, imaging, printing, and navigation illustrate the first pillar. Data tools and AI support illustrate the second. Subspecialty advances are highlighted alongside shared gains in safety, patient selection, recovery, and long-term outcomes, with predictions for multidisciplinary surgery.
pmc-13338755:
Joseph A White and colleagues described a bedside ultrasound case in 2026 involving a 26 year old man with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt. Blocked brain fluid flow can kill if missed, and shunt failure is common yet hard to diagnose from vague symptoms and slow imaging. Point of care ultrasound offers a fast bedside adjunct.

The patient arrived with fever and altered mental state amid concern for shunt failure. Pulse wave Doppler ultrasound was used to assess shunt flow at the bedside. The case shows how a quick, noninvasive check can support urgent shunt decisions while definitive imaging is arranged, above all where scanners or specialists are scarce.
pmc-13339155:
Rowan M. Bailey and co-authors dissect a cobalt light-driven reaction that builds amides in a 2026 study. Carbonylation with cobalt photocatalysis is efficient, yet its step-by-step kinetics were unmapped. Rates, substituent effects, and light dependence were measured in depth.

Rare cobalt NMR pointed to a cobalt carbonyl anion as the working intermediate. Data showed its attack on the aryl bromide limits the whole cycle, most likely as light-promoted nucleophilic attack in the reported analysis. That insight extended the method to aryl chlorides and weaker amines. Turnover gains above tenfold followed, strengthening the case for industrial use.
pmc-13339855:
Joshua Plener, Gaelan P. Connell, Carol Cancelliere, and Scott Howitt design and test an online concussion course for clinicians in a 2026 study. The self-paced course used short chunks, quizzes, game elements, and case videos built on current sport concussion guidance. Clinicians tried it and rated usability.

Eight clinicians from three Canadian regions, spanning physio, chiropractic, and occupational therapy, completed testing as reported. All felt confident navigating the course, and 87.5 percent praised its integration in the reported shares. Confidence in adult concussion care rose for everyone, though persistent symptom assessment lagged at 37.5 percent. Feedback refined the course before wider release.
pmc-13340655:
Surgery for a rare female urethral stricture is reported by Hung L. Do and coauthors in their 2026 case report from Vietnam. The 60-year-old patient had years of urinary trouble and many prior dilations before imaging and cystoscopy confirmed the narrowing.

Surgeons rebuilt the urethra with a graft of cheek lining placed on the dorsal side. Four months later she urinated normally, with a top flow rate above 15 mL/s and no leakage. The authors note this graft approach is widely viewed as the best option yet is seldom used because of recurrence fears and technical difficulty, especially where resources are limited.
pmc-13341355:
Natalie Segev and colleagues tracked blood sugar in 2026 in teens with type 2 diabetes right after sleeve surgery. Youth onset type 2 and obesity are rising burdens. Newer type 2 drugs lower HbA1c with mixed weight effects, while surgery improves sugar and weight. Yet sugar patterns after vertical sleeve surgery in youth type 2 were unstudied.

In the ST2OMP study, 73 teens wore glucose monitors for fourteen days. A total of 33 began one to two days after surgery. Early post surgery glucose patterns show how fast sugar control shifts after the op. The data help teams advise teens and families on early recovery after bariatric surgery.
pmc-13341455:
A plant saponin protecting the injured spinal cord is tested by Guoqing Zhu's team in a 2026 rat study. Esculentoside A, drawn from Phytolacca esculenta, was given daily at 10 mg/kg after a contusion injury made with a standardized impactor.

Treated rats scored better on walking scales, grid walking, and footprint tests, and their cord tissue showed less damage under several stains. Oxidative markers fell while protective enzymes rose. Blotting, imaging, and docking work pointed to the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway as the mechanism damping both oxidative stress and neuron death. The findings nominate the compound for further development.
pmc-13341855:
A waist measure adjusted for weight tracks death risk closely, in a 2026 systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis by Pengyu Yang and colleagues. Cohort studies through April 2026 were pooled, with care taken to avoid double-counting overlapping public datasets such as NHANES.

Across 47 studies, each 1 cm/√kg rise in the weight-adjusted waist index carried a hazard ratio of 1.21 for all-cause death and 1.27 for cardiovascular death. Top versus bottom categories reached 1.40 and 1.54 respectively, and the dose-response looked linear. Evidence certainty was graded formally, and most studies rated moderate to high quality.
pmc-13342055:
A hunter's prion disease prompts a zoonotic investigation, in a 2026 case report by Eithan Kotkowski and colleagues. The 72-year-old lifelong hunter in Louisiana, a chronic wasting disease region for deer, developed fast-progressing dementia with startle jerks and classic scan patterns.

Spinal fluid markers and autopsy confirmed sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, subtype MM1, not the variant form tied to animal transmission. Similar illness among hunting lodge peers triggered a public health inquiry. An episode of reversible brain swelling during admission complicated the imaging picture. The authors frame the case as surveillance practice for a feared but unproven deer-to-human prion jump.
pmc-13343355:
Xiaojing Guo and co-authors scope the evidence on perfluorocarbon oxygen carriers in surgery in a 2026 review. These lab-made liquids dissolve large amounts of oxygen and could ease reliance on donor blood, which stays scarce. The team mapped basic and translational studies from 2000 to 2025 under PRISMA-ScR rules.

Fifty-five publications, including 13 randomized trials, met the bar. Carriers improved tissue oxygenation and organ protection across bleeding shock, brain injury, and lung injury, with the steadiest gains in organ preservation, and they cut donor blood needs in major surgery. Inflammatory reactions and platelet drops appeared repeatedly, though, and old formulations failed historically. Better designs and large trials must come first.
pmc-13344255:
Navin Mathiyalagan and colleagues reported in 2026 on a 65-year-old woman whose bladder and ureters became inflamed during breast cancer treatment. She had HER2-positive disease and had just finished a first round of four-drug therapy given before surgery, when she developed visible blood in her urine and sudden kidney injury.

Scans showed swelling and fluid build-up in both urinary tracts, pointing to drug-related inflammation rather than infection or blockage. Washing out the bladder, fluids, and antibiotics did not settle the bleeding, so the team gave a daily steroid, and her urine cleared and kidney function returned within three days. The report warns clinicians to weigh this rare reaction early when similar symptoms appear during this drug combination.
pmc-13344855:
Jonathan J H Bray and co-authors pool every study of heart energy status in a 2026 meta-analysis. The phosphocreatine-to-ATP ratio gauges how well heart muscle fuels itself. It is read by phosphorus magnetic resonance scans. Single-center studies stayed small, so the team gathered 176 studies covering 7,843 scans from 1987 to 2025.

Healthy hearts averaged a ratio of 1.96, while failure with weak pumping fell 21 percent to 1.54 and failure with preserved pumping fell 18 percent to 1.60, with valve disease and diabetes also reduced. Scanner settings swayed readings but could not explain the gaps. Higher body mass and natriuretic peptides tracked lower ratios, tying energy failure to heart disease of many causes.
pmc-13346055:
Kobi Faierstein and co-authors compare surgery against catheter valve replacement in two-leaflet aortic valves in 2026. Bicuspid anatomy warps the usual playbook. The team reviewed 480 patients, 405 treated surgically and 75 by catheter. They adjusted for the catheter group's older age, then repeated the check with age-matched pairs.

Across nine years of average follow-up, catheter patients died more often, needed pacemakers more, leaked around the valve more, and returned to hospital for heart failure far more, while stroke rates matched. Age matching softened but never erased the mortality gap. Surgery wins this round, the authors conclude, while demanding randomized trials for a fair final word.
pmc-13347155:
Jianxia Ma and co-authors compare two laxatives in older patients who have both constipation and weak kidneys, in a trial from 2026. Thirty patients took lactulose daily for four weeks while 26 took polyethylene glycol. Stool scores, blood tests, and gut microbe checks ran before and after treatment in both arms.

Both drugs eased constipation to a like degree, with no clear gap between groups on symptom scores in the reported test. Only the lactulose arm showed falls in creatinine, uric acid. The inflammatory marker IL-6 after treatment, plus shifts toward gut types tied to helpful acids and away from types tied to toxins. The team links the kidney gain to gut and inflammation changes.
pmc-13347355:
Laura Beatriz Souza e Souza and co-authors develop a greener lab method to check ibuprofen in soft gelatin capsules from Brazil, in a study from 2026. No official quality method exists for this capsule form. So the team built a five-minute liquid method using mostly ethanol and tracked how fast capsules release the drug in a standard bath.

Greenness scores came out at 2 of 4 on one index and 0.72 on another scale in the reported scoring. Checks showed low detection limits, tight repeat results, and no matrix interference. Release across samples ranged from 81.96 to 105.1 percent within the test window, with all samples following first-order release patterns.
pmc-13347655:
Le Thi Cam Tuyen and co-authors watch ultrafast relaxation in a magnetic bilayer film with two-colour light pulses, in a study from 2026. Layers of a ferromagnetic manganite over bismuth ferrite were grown on a crystal base. Thickening the lower layer from 40 to 120 nm was tracked for strain, magnetism, and pulse response against single-layer films.

Thicker lower layers cut the coercive field from 8.34 to 3.52 mT and the Curie point from 343 to 295 K in the reported measures. While carrier-lattice handoff sped from 10.07 to 0.65 picoseconds across the same range. Single layers relaxed far more slowly, so layer thickness gives a clear knob for tuning spintronic response.
pmc-13349755:
Gen Gang and co-authors feed a desert plant extract to broiler chickens and track defence and immunity gains, in a trial from 2026. A total of 160 fifteen-day-old birds were split into five diets with extract at zero to 2,000 mg per kilogram for 28 days. Blood and gut samples came at two ages. They fed enzyme, damage, and immune signal checks.

By day 42 the extract raised blood and gut defence enzymes while cutting a damage marker in blood and gut. Immune signals plus vaccine antibody levels rose at day 28 in the reported results. Gene activity for defence enzymes also climbed in gut sections, and the authors name 1,000 mg per kilogram as the best dose for a green feed add-on.
pmc-13350255:
Jun-Phil Uhm and Seungmin Lee tested how crowded sponsor logos on sports jerseys affect shoppers in augmented reality in a 2026 experiment. Seventy-eight participants viewed professional baseball jerseys with low or high logo density inside an AR shopping setting.

Denser logos made the jersey feel significantly more cluttered and changed how much attention and arousal viewers reported. Attitudes toward the jersey, however, did not differ clearly between the two versions. As AR shops invite close inspection of complex products, the findings suggest visual overload works on perception and focus first, before it ever changes whether people like the product.
pmc-13350355:
Yan Shao and co-authors compared radiation planning styles for central lung tumours in a 2026 dosimetry study of 20 patients receiving focused high-dose treatment. Simple conformal plans depend heavily on planner skill, while finely modulated plans spare healthy tissue better but are harder to deliver accurately.

For each patient they built four plans: a hybrid mixing both styles and a fully modulated plan, each checked on two treatment machines. Dose to tumour and nearby organs and delivery accuracy were compared. Central tumours sit close to airways and vessels, so a plan style that keeps precision without excess complexity could widen safe access to this treatment.
pmc-13350455:
Mohamed H Eldesouki and co-authors found in 2026 that colorectal cancer is being diagnosed younger in people with hereditary gut cancer predisposition syndromes, plus Lynch syndrome. This mirrors a shift already seen in average-risk groups. Hereditary syndromes raise colorectal risk markedly. Yet time trends in diagnosis age in these groups were little studied.

Using the TriNetX national base from 2010 to 2024, the team found 136,394 patients with hereditary syndromes, of whom 6,561, about 4.8 percent, grew colorectal cancer, against 0.34 percent in an average-risk group. Peak diagnosis age shifted ten years sooner over the study span. The trend backs sooner screening and gene testing in families with hereditary risk.
pmc-13351655:
Antonio Di Lorenzo and Taito Kitano argue in 2026 for wider flu vaccine uptake in children and more spending on new paediatric flu vaccines. Flu shots are advised most strongly for high-risk groups, since drug treatment after infection offers limited help. Their comment discusses a study by Hayek and co-authors on vaccine effect in children.

That study found protection against emergency visits and hospital stays for children with and without other conditions. Protection was 53 percent in healthy children and 43 percent in children with one or more conditions. The authors note that judging vaccine effect in children with other illnesses is hard. They call for stronger uptake so health systems face less strain each flu season.
pmc-13352155: Frontiers Editorial Office issued a 2026 retraction notice for an article first published on 22 August 2025 about triglyceride-glucose indexes and heart disease risk in cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome. A check found an unacceptable level of similarity in figures and tables to a Springer Nature article by Hong and co-authors. The journal editors approved the retraction, the authors agreed, and thanks went to Jame Yu and PubPeer users for raising the concern. The item itself is only a retraction notice, so its scope is the withdrawal and its stated grounds.
pmc-13352955:
Marcin Grochowski led a 2026 study that helps cancer organoid testing by adding tumour surroundings and smarter study. Patient-derived organoids are lab-grown tumour models used to predict drug response, but their truth suffers when the tumour microenvironment is missing and only static viability is checked. The team built on a living biobank of thirty marked organoids from pancreatic, colon, and gastric cancers.

Cancer-linked fibroblasts were included with the organoids, and a convolution approach to organoid assembly was applied to model care results. The joined method forecast patient care results better than organoids alone. The work moves organoid testing closer to the clinic, where a reliable pre-care forecast could spare people ineffective care.
pmc-13353355:
Haas and colleagues pooled the evidence in 2026 on whether low fat-free mass, body tissue other than fat, predicts higher death risk in adults living in the community. Single studies disagreed, so the team ran a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies that measured body composition by scan, electrical impedance, or simple measures such as calf size.

From nearly eight thousand records, 49 studies qualified, covering more than a million people and close to 84,000 deaths. People with low fat-free mass had about 42 percent higher death risk than those with high fat-free mass, and the link held across ages, regions, and causes of death. The tie was stronger in men than women, and strongest when calf size was the measure. Checks for bias softened but did not erase the link. The authors urge routine body composition checks to flag high-risk adults.
pmc-13354555:
Shan Zhang and colleagues solved how the protein WTAP assembles the m6A writer complex, in a 2026 structural study. The writer tags messenger RNA with methyl groups that tune stability and translation, but how its parts lock together was unclear. WTAP, a conserved regulatory subunit, is essential for tagging and for cell growth.

Crystal structures showed WTAP first pairs up, then forms a stable four-part tetramer through its middle coiled-coil region. Breaking that interface cut its ties to METTL3, METTL14, and ZC3H13, weakened m6A tagging, and left growth defects unrescued. Live imaging tied WTAP to faithful chromosome splitting, marking its tetramer as a scaffold for both RNA tagging and mitosis.
pmc-13354955:
Maike Krause and co-authors mapped the proteins in growing nerve tips in young mice in a 2026 study. These tips, called growth cones, sit at the end of growing nerve fibers and steer them toward their targets in the hippocampus, a brain area key for memory. The team sampled two sub-areas on days one, three, and five after birth.

At day one, both areas shared a protein mix tied to energy and protein making. After that, one area shifted fast toward proteins for synapse building, while the other kept an exploring mix for longer. The dataset gives other labs a base map for how brain wiring unfolds on distinct timetables.
pmc-13355255:
Arthur L Burnett and Jeffrey H Owen describe a 2026 surgical technique to trigger erection during prostate removal surgery, as a way to test nerve health. Sparing the nerves near the prostate matters for erection and bladder control after surgery. Their method places thin needle electrodes through the skin of the low back to send current toward the sacral cord.

In a pilot of seven men, the stimulus raised blood flow signals in the penis of five men with mild or no erection problems, and caused visible swelling. Two men with worse problems showed no response, and no harms occurred. The authors propose the method for nerve monitoring during surgery, pending more study.
pmc-13355955:
Arijita Banerjee and Pradosh Kumar Sarangi review in 2026 the role of faulty blood vessel control in normal-tension glaucoma, an eye disease that harms the optic nerve despite normal eye pressure. Because pressure alone cannot explain the damage, vessel factors are key. The team searched major databases for work from 1985 to early 2026 on vessel control, blood flow, and treatment.

Patients with this vessel pattern show poor self-tuning of optic nerve blood flow, chemical imbalances, and steep night-time blood pressure dips. Certain drugs, magnesium, and a plant extract helped in selected groups, alongside sleep pressure care and lifestyle steps. The authors urge trials in clearly defined vessel-type patients.
pmc-13356655:
Takuya Nagai and co-authors surveyed parents in Miyazaki City, Japan, in 2026 on follow-up after school scoliosis screening. Early checks matter because bracing can stop curve worsening, yet not all flagged children attend the second screening. An online survey went to parents of more than thirty-one thousand screened children, and about three thousand replied.

Of children advised to attend, about two-thirds had gone and a quarter planned to go. Parents who sought scoliosis facts online were more likely to intend follow-up, while general awareness alone showed no link. Many parents welcomed QR-linked facts. The authors note the low reply rate and say digital tools need prospective testing.
pmc-13356955:
Katalina M Lopez and co-authors studied in 2026 how alcohol exposure in newborn mice affects the subiculum, a brain area that passes memory signals from the hippocampus to the cortex. People with fetal alcohol spectrum disorders often have memory trouble and a smaller subiculum. Seven-day-old mice got alcohol shots, and their brains were checked in adolescence.

Male mice lost neurons in the area, while females gained cells of a special bursting type that helps process memory. Burst firing weakened in both sexes, and females showed lower overall excitability. The authors suggest broken burst signals weaken memory circuits, which may help explain thinking deficits in fetal alcohol disorders.
pmc-13358755:
Maximilian Vorstandlechner and co-authors study the microbes that live in the airways around lung transplant in a 2026 paper. A donated lung meets the outside air directly, so germs present before, during, and after surgery may shape how the organ fares. The team tracked airway germ findings in 345 transplant patients treated from 2014 to 2019.

Yeasts called Candida and a bacterium called Pseudomonas were among the most common finds. The team linked these patterns to later rejection, long-term lung decline, and survival through 2024. Knowing which germs warn of trouble could help transplant teams adjust antibiotics and watch high-risk patients more closely.
pmc-13358855:
Takayuki Takahama wrote a 2026 commentary on targeted drugs for uncommon lung cancer mutations. Most gene-driven lung cancers carry one of two classic changes in the EGFR gene, and modern drugs handle them well. About ten to twenty percent carry rarer changes, where proof is thin. A study by Park and colleagues tested the drug lazertinib in exactly that group.

Takahama sets the new results against the older standard drug and explains why this niche matters despite its size. Rare mutations differ from one another, so lumping them together can mislead. His piece helps doctors judge where lazertinib fits while stronger proof builds.
pmc-13362355:
Irene Creus-Martí and co-authors present CoDaLoMic, a software package for microbiome time-series data, in a 2026 paper. Microbe data are compositional, meaning each sample reports shares of a whole, and studies often track the same hosts over time. Both traits break standard statistics. The package, written for the R language, implements three models built for exactly this kind of data.

Unlike methods that only weigh pairs of microbes, CoDaLoMic also captures how groups of bacteria interact as communities. It can link microbe variability to the host's health status and find taxa that rise and fall together over time. Watching dynamics, not just snapshots, reveals succession patterns and early signs of change. The tool gives microbiome researchers a sturdier frame for longitudinal work.
pmc-13362955:
Keith Attenborough wrote a 2026 acoustics study that asks whether simpler sound-absorbing panels can match three fancy published designs. The fancy designs mix porous layers with tuned cavities, stacked plates, or perforated shells to soak up sound across a wide pitch range in a thin sheet. Attenborough compared their measured and predicted curves with plainer options of the same thickness, such as porous layers cut by a few solid walls or made from natural fibers.

The plainer panels reached about the same wide-range absorption in his comparisons. That matters for planes, cars, and buildings, where thin, light treatments are wanted and low pitches are hardest to tame. Simpler builds could also be cheaper to make and easier to recycle, which strengthens the case for testing them in products.
pmc-13363755:
Natalia Fuentes Molina, Ana Fragozo Molina, and Kennys Cujia Jiménez report a 2026 study on seed-cover membranes spun from farm waste cellulose, meant to replace plastic mulch in dry regions. They made membranes from rice husk, banana pseudostem, and sugarcane bagasse, then measured pore structure, strength, moisture flow, and how well cauliflower seeds sprouted under water stress on each cover.

The three wastes gave three personalities: rice husk dense and strong, banana open and stretchy with the fastest moisture flow, and bagasse the best water holder. Bagasse won where it counted, with the highest sprouting rate under stress, which shows that holding moisture beats moving it fast. All covers rotted in soil on schedule, backing their use as green mulch.
pmc-13364355:
Weida Wang and co-workers give a 2026 no touch way to judge thin water films that fall over rows of tubes in heat gear. Bright glare makes such films hard to read from film shots alone. Their plan turns fast film into maps and scores that a user can grasp at a glance.

Water tests ran on a five row tube bank across a wide flow range, with two thousand frames per run. The scores caught the shift from sparse drip lines to full sheets, and row by row gaps in film change. Checks for noise back the scores for side by side watch use.
pmc-13364755:
Cheal Huh and co-workers weigh in 2026 if long use of strong acid cut pills lifts gut cancer risk, in a huge UK health bank study. They match more than forty thousand new pill users to the same count of non users, plus a group on a mild acid drug. Watch time ran a mid span near seven years.

Pill users faced more than twice the gut cancer rate of non users, and a yet higher rate than mild drug users. Risk rose with more time and dose on the pills. Raw risk stays low, the team notes, but long pill use calls for care and a clear need.
pmc-13365355:
Jiang and colleagues test whether a food supplement can guard muscle while adults with obesity lose weight. Their powder adds calcium HMB, a body-made compound tied to muscle upkeep, plus extra protein. Adults ate fewer calories for twelve weeks and took the powder or a matched control drink.

In the trial with just over one hundred adults, the supplement group held its muscle mass. The control group lost muscle over the same twelve weeks. The supplement group also lost more belly fat and more total body fat. Its daily energy use held up better, and blood sugar fell a bit more. No side effects were reported in either group.
pmc-13367555:
Sabyasachi Bal lays out in 2026 the surgeon's part in lung TB care, a team role that shrank once strong drugs came, yet still saves set cases. Drugs lead care, he grants. But knife work can find the ill when tests fail, and can clear drug proof germs, pus sacs, and thin air ways.

Knife work also eases harm left by past TB, like wide air tubes and mold balls. New keyhole ways cut harm and death from such work. Joint teams should weigh each case in time, he urges, so the right folk get knife aid.
pmc-13369255:
Helerin Raikkerus and co-workers hunt in 2026 for proof that mind trip drugs help attention ill, the jump and focus fault of youth. Trip drugs now draw hype for mood care, and some ask if they aid this ill too. Their scan of two banks finds near a thousand works, of which six fit.

Proof is thin and mixed, they find: too thin to back any use call. Half the kept works rest on self told data. No work splits folks by ill cause type. Mood trials of one such drug skip the ill whole, so joint gains stay in doubt.
pmc-13375155:
José M. Alegre and co-authors compare the cell toxicity of resins used for temporary fixed dental prostheses, made either by 3D printing or by milling. Their 2026 laboratory study fabricates 216 standardised discs, half from printed resins and half from milled polymethyl methacrylate resins, and exposes mouse fibroblast cells to them.

Cells met the materials two ways: through liquid extracts of the resins, and by direct contact with the discs, with survival measured after seventy-two hours. In the extract test, milled resins left 87 percent of cells alive against 65 percent for printed resins; in direct contact the figures were 89 percent against 48 percent. Under international thresholds, printed resins rated slightly toxic indirectly and moderately toxic on contact, while milled resins stayed in the non-toxic to slightly toxic range. The authors caution against stretching short laboratory results into clinical claims and call for longer studies.
pmc-13375255:
Manal Derkaoui and co-authors report bone-first lymphoma in a young man in a 2026 case report. The man, aged 23, had a sore, swollen right knee. Scans showed a hole in the thigh bone's end, with rot through the hard shell and spread to soft parts near by.

Chest and belly scans showed no more ill spots, so the case was a one-site stage. Tissue tests showed sheets of large odd immune cells of one set type. pmc-13376355:
Suzuki Uemura and colleagues investigate why an emollient oil, ditrimethylolpropane tetracaprylate, keeps skin hydrated after washing, in 2026 cosmetic science research. Permeability analysis confirmed it penetrates and stays inside the stratum corneum, unlike agents that sit on top or wash away. Calorimetry showed it blends into the model lipid matrix with compatibility and minimal structural disruption. Suzuki Uemura concludes the mechanism, penetration plus compatible integration, explains why the effect lasts and offers a rule for better moisturizers.
pmc-13377155:

Heat tests and crystal shots showed how the grip works, face to face. The reshaper's kin grips a touch more hard than the reshaper itself. The tagged virus part sits in the grip in a flipped way next to host parts. That flip is a fresh clue to how the virus fools the cell's own shape code.
pmc-13378155:
Amelia Fernández-Avendaño and others describe surgery for rare front chest single fibrous tumours in a 2026 case series. Definitive treatment is complete removal with clear margins plus tissue finding.

The series discusses criteria for choosing between open and robotic approaches, balancing tumour size, site, invasion risk, and surgeon experience. The cases show that both routes can achieve complete resection when selection is careful.
pmc-13379155:
Arnold and colleagues describe a youth-driven approach to sharing research findings about child farmworkers' health in North Carolina, in 2026 community research. The youth collaborators shaped the content and the language of the infographics, choosing which findings mattered most to families like theirs and how to phrase risks without jargon. Distribution targeted community settings rather than journals. Arnold argues the process built literacy and leadership in the youth, beyond the products created. The model, they suggest, transfers to topics where affected communities are young, rural, or Spanish-speaking and poorly served by academic publishing.
pmc-13380755:
Javad Jalili, Sarah Vaseghi, and Mahdiyeh Baastani Khajeh present a 2026 case series on sealing holes in large central veins caused by catheters, using a balloon pressed against the injury from inside. Balloon pressure stopped the bleeding fully in six patients, and one case settled without balloon inflation. No patient bled again during follow-up of six to twelve months. Access through the vein was preserved.
pmc-13382255:
Caroline Owens and co-authors wrote a 2026 scoping review of Food is Medicine programs and how they adapt to individual people and communities. Searching three databases in January 2025, the team screened more than six thousand abstracts and included 89 papers. Produce prescriptions were the most common program type. Adaptations were sorted by age and household size, by disease, and by culture and community. The map shows where tailoring is routine and where programs still deliver a standard package to everyone.
pmc-13383355:
Giancarlo Gonzalez-Areizaga and co-authors show that stiffening a leukemia-linked kinase changes both drug response and cell spread in 2026 work. The tightened kinase bound its fuel less readily, so ATP-site drugs hit it harder in lab tests. Human myeloid cells carrying the altered kinase also stopped growing sooner under drug treatment. In animals, those cells settled into bone marrow poorly, which hints that drugs that lock the kinase shape could offer a new treatment route.
pmc-13383555:
Yage Wang's team pooled trials of vibration therapy after stroke, in a 2026 review that pools prior trials. The team searched six databases for randomized trials, assessed bias with the Cochrane tool, and graded evidence with GRADEpro.

Thirty-seven trials with 1492 stroke survivors showed vibration significantly improved motor function, muscle stiffness, balance, and gait, plus overall daily task performance. Social role participation did not improve. Stiffness gains ran stronger in chronic stroke. The synthesis supports vibration as an adjunct for physical recovery, while social participation needs broader rehab beyond the device.
pmc-13384955:
Kexin Zhang and colleagues compare fatty liver disease burden and care quality across world regions in 2026 work. Metabolic liver disease is rising fast, yet care quality gaps remain poorly mapped. The team used 2023 global burden data, a composite care index, and machine learning to rank drivers and forecast new cases.

South and East Asia held the most new cases, while North Africa and the Middle East showed the highest adjusted rates. Care quality scored lowest in South Asia, western sub-Saharan Africa, and Eastern Europe. High body mass and blood sugar stood out as key contributors, with new cases projected to keep rising through 2050.
pmc-13386455:
Hubert Daisley, Nathan Williams, and Arlene Rampersad report a lethal diffuse stomach cancer in a young migrant in a 2026 case report. A 22-year-old Venezuelan woman arrived with vomiting and weight loss, then developed bleeding, fluid build-up, and widespread swollen glands. She declined fast despite supportive care and died soon after readmission.

Autopsy found a thickened stomach wall with spread across the belly lining, nodes, and both lungs. Microscopy showed an infiltrative cancer with heavy scarring and vessel invasion, in a linitis plastica-like pattern. Lung spread crept along air sac walls in a pattern that mimicked another cancer type, which deepened the diagnostic trap.
pmc-13386555:
Sophie Pajoux and Valerie Loizeau studied how joint scheduling affects nurse morale and loyalty in France, in a 2026 mixed-methods study. Nurses' active role in schedule preparation raised morale, and empowerment plus team discipline reinforced morale and involvement. Joint management thus acts as a lever for hospital appeal and loyalty building. The authors stress gradual adoption of team governance and a central role for front-line managers in enabling adaptable, flexible workplaces.
pmc-13387755:
Hung-Chin Tsai replies to commenters about a fever reaction that can follow syphilis treatment in a 2026 letter. His reply urges care before concluding that the reaction is widely undercounted in early syphilis.
pmc-13388455:
Couto and colleagues compare three materials as the sensing layer in a glucose biosensor for point-of-care diabetes testing, in 2026 biosensor research. pmc-13390355:

pmc-13391655:

pmc-13392255:

pmc-13392955:

pmc-13394655:

pmc-13394855:

pmc-13395855:

pmc-13395955:

pmc-13396055:

Bond strength was measured by push-out and pull tests, and the joint was checked after soaking.
pmc-13396455:

pmc-13396655:

pmc-13396855:

pmc-13398355:

pmc-13400455:

pmc-13400655:

pmc-13400755:

pmc-13401155:

Their patient was a 74-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and several other conditions. His scan showed pneumatosis intestinalis, meaning gas in the bowel wall, along with free air in the abdomen.

Because he had no abdominal symptoms, stayed stable. Showed no scan signs of bowel ischemia, the team chose observation and temporary fasting rather than an emergency operation. pmc-13401555:

pmc-13402355:

pmc-13402655:

pmc-13402855:

pmc-13403155:

pmc-13403555:

pmc-13403755:

pmc-13403855:

pmc-13404155:

pmc-13406455:

pmc-13406755:

pmc-13407455:

pmc-13407855:

pmc-13407955:

pmc-13408055:

pmc-13408355:

pmc-13408455:

pmc-13408655:

pmc-13410855:
Kassahun Ayele and colleagues reviewed in 2026 whether farming programs designed with nutrition in mind improve diets in Ethiopia. Evidence on body measures like growth stayed thinner, so the review backs diet gains while calling for stronger proof that farm programs also shift nutrition outcomes.
pmc-13411055:

Their handheld reader uses light clouding from antibody reactions to count albumin in urine within moments.

Sensitivity and specificity both sat near 99 percent, figures the team says beat common dipstick tools. Protein leakage clustered in older patients with diabetes, high blood pressure, or known kidney disease.
pmc-13411255:
Gillianne Crystina dos Anjos Cardoso and co-authors sort in 2026 Brazilian teenagers into mental health profiles and probe links with activity and television time. Active travel to school, by contrast, tied to the severe profile, a link that may reflect hardship rather than exercise itself. Moderate TV time landed in mixed profiles, while very heavy viewing oddly avoided the severe groups. Setting and amount both matter, the authors conclude.
pmc-13411355:
Ja Seng Ing Manam and Davud Shahidi explored in 2026 how decades of civil war in Myanmar's Kachin State shaped trauma and group identity among the Jinghpaw people. Working with 18 people across six families, both displaced and not, the authors treat trauma as something passed through families and communities. They do not treat it only as a private clinical wound.

The paper shows suffering woven into a story of cultural survival and shared strength, which matters for any healing work with this community.
pmc-13411755:
Fatma Sule Bilgic and colleagues tested in 2026 how often babies with diaper rash should spend time without a diaper. In a trial of 130 infants aged up to three months with mild rash, one group got five minutes of air six times daily. The other group got the same five minutes twelve times daily. Rash scores and mothers' confidence were tracked until healing.

The twelve-times group healed in about two days against about three days for the six-times group, and their mothers' confidence rose further. The paper offers parents a free, simple routine that speeds healing and steadies new mothers at the same time.
pmc-13411955:
Bolat Sadykov and colleagues analyze, in a 2026 national survey study, which women in Kazakhstan have lower blood levels of the hormone estradiol. The authors therefore read hormone levels as part of a personal age-and-metabolism profile, not a map pattern. They also caution that future surveys should record cycle timing and menopause status.
pmc-13412655:

pmc-13412955:

Their retrospective cohort followed 274 patients operated on for non-spread colorectal adenocarcinoma at an Ankara hospital, grouping them by lymph node ratio at zero, up to a fifth, and above a fifth.

The top group kept a nearly five-fold adjusted risk of recurrence or death events. Overall survival differences faded after adjustment, so the authors pitch the ratio as a recurrence-risk refiner.
pmc-13414555:
Omkulthom Al kamaly and co-authors set up three green analytical methods in 2026 to measure salicylamide and vitamin C together in medicines, even as the first drug degrades into salicylic acid. Environmental scoring favoured the water-based spectra approach, at 0.72 on the AGREE scale, over the plate method's 0.62 in their assessment. Practicality scores of eighty for both routes support routine quality control use.
pmc-13414855:
Phichsinee Rerkshanandana and co-authors test plant extracts against stress-linked behavior changes in rats, in a 2026 experiment. pmc-13415655:
Orit Bain and co-authors scan injured thumbs with high resolution ultrasound to map the full pattern of damage, in 2026. Ligaments on both sides and the extensor system on top were graded systematically.

The ulnar ligament, famous from skier's thumb, was hurt in about 83 percent of patients. The radial ligament on the other side was hurt in about 55 percent. Top side extensor problems appeared in about 41 percent. Nearly half of ulnar cases also involved the radial side, so checking neighbors matters.
pmc-13416155:
Shu Li and colleagues delete two detox enzymes in zebrafish to expose how reactive carbonyls wreck sugar and kidney health, in 2026. Feeding arginine brought back a key insulin signal step and eased kidney harm. A carbonyl to arginine axis emerges as a driver of diabetic injury in this model.
pmc-13416655:
Clay Garrison, Joel Bird, and Srinath Kamineni report fifteen year results for one patient with a Sorbie elbow hemiarthroplasty, in a 2026 case report. Badly shattered lower arm bone fractures near the elbow can defy fixation, and full elbow replacement restricts lifting for life. A hemiarthroplasty replaces only the arm bone side, keeping the patient's own forearm joint surfaces.

pmc-13416755:

Over five years, 592 people developed cardiovascular disease. Every adverse path carried higher risk than the low path after adjustment, with hazard ratios above one third higher. pmc-13418855:
Hamparsumian and colleagues report a 2026 study of frailty in myelodysplastic syndrome, a bone marrow disease that lowers blood counts. They followed 2,285 patients who began a common drug treatment between 2004 and 2023. Standard scoring for this disease ignores how well a patient functions day to day. The findings argue for a frailty check beside disease scores when doctors plan care for older patients.
pmc-13420155:
Indracanti and colleagues surveyed in 2026 how research skills grow among allied health students in Hyderabad, India. Skills fell steeply along the steps, from about three in four students showing basic awareness to only about one in four with real research experience. Scores were nearly the same across all ten programmes, suggesting a shared curriculum gap rather than a weak field. Students who had formal research training took part in research at much higher rates than untrained peers. The authors say courses build awareness well but fail to carry students into practice. They recommend active learning, mentoring, and built-in research placements to close the gap.
pmc-13420355:
Peng Chen and colleagues describe a new entry route for hip scope surgery that reaches cysts at the back of the joint without pulling the leg or using live X-ray guidance. Hip arthroscopy is a settled, gentle route for many joint problems, yet back-side lesions sit in a blind spot of standard entries. Nerve injury from traction is a known cost of the usual setup.

Working with the patient lying on one side, the team entered behind the joint through a gap between two muscles. That corridor let them feel the back capsule of the joint directly and reach the cysts. Dropping traction and radiation removes two burdens at once for patient and staff. The technical note gives other hip surgeons the landmarks and steps to try the route.
pmc-13420855:
Writing to the editor, Ignazio De Trizio and colleagues test whether delirium bends the accuracy of a standard intensive care death prediction score. The score, SAPS-II, guides mortality forecasting and unit benchmarking worldwide. Their cohort study covers 10,378 adult ICU patients treated from February 1, 2019 to December 31, 2024 at one center.

Mortality was scored against both the original formula and the value recorded in the first day of care. One high-risk group without delirium was small, and the authors warn against reading its numbers as proof that delirium protects. Calibration gaps by mental state argue for reporting scores split by delirium group.
pmc-13421455:
Lei Chen leads a nine-author team building, in a 2026 paper, a converter that moves quantum information both ways between light waves and qubits. Their photonic converter transfers information deterministically and reversibly, and its error falls exponentially as qubits are added, so a few qubits already give high fidelity. With it, the team reconstructed continuous light modes using discrete measurement techniques and generated non-Gaussian light states directly from qubits. The authors present the device as a missing component for hybrid quantum processors.
pmc-13421555:
Hurst and colleagues introduced in 2026 ImPaqT, a modular toolkit for making transgenic zebrafish quickly. Transgenic fish, carrying added genes, are workhorses of developmental and immune research. Although built for immune studies, the framework accepts complex designs such as multi-part promoters.
pmc-13421655:
Stewen and co-authors refine a mouse model of viral myocarditis in this 2026 study, aiming for better science with less animal suffering. pmc-13422355: Zhang and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their 2024 article on a pig interferon that blocks a swine coronavirus. Readers had spotted errors in the description and display of Figure 1A. One panel of Figure 2G also overlapped with another image. The correction revises the protein purity account. Gel scanning and mass spectrometry showed both bands were the target protein, with high measured purity. A replacement ileum image from retained raw data is supplied, with raw files provided.
pmc-13423055:
Nemati Saray and co-authors present a numerical method for fractional diffusion-wave equations, in this 2026 mathematics paper. Such equations serve when matter keeps its past. Creeping polymers and anomalous spread through porous media are two cases. Standard solvers err more on these problems. They can also be costly to run. So the team built a pseudospectral scheme. Legendre cardinal functions are its building blocks.

They rewrote the equations in integral form. They built direct matrix versions of the fractional derivative and integral operators. That turned the problem into algebra. A quirk of cardinal functions helps here. Each equals one at its own grid point and zero at others. This lets the team compute coefficients without numerical integration. Cost falls sharply. Convergence analysis and test problems showed spectral convergence. Error falls faster than any fixed power as resolution rises. The scheme beat finite difference and collocation rivals in their tests.
pmc-13423355:

pmc-13423955:

pmc-13424055:

pmc-13424155:

pmc-13424355:

pmc-13424455:

pmc-13424555:

pmc-13425655:

pmc-13425955:

pmc-13426355:

pmc-13426455:

pmc-13427555:

pmc-13427755:

pmc-13429255:

pmc-13429655:

Expert interviews then explained the numbers. Training programs get a pinpointed curriculum fix, since running a game well is not the same as coaching thinking within it.
pmc-13432955:
