Four themes shaped the polish: parts of the list, words and images, patient feel, and blocks to use. Cash, room, and old builds stood as chief blocks. The team closed with steps to put the list to work on real wards.
pmc-13433255:

Biocoin unifies them in a reconfigurable, general-purpose framework, with a 530-square-millimetre wireless device offering over ten multiplexed sensor inputs and broad physicochemical sensing. pmc-13433355:

Top air use on the course matched the treadmill read near exactly, with a tight bond between the two. Burst marks from run times, set beside a repeat sprint test, showed no real bond at all. pmc-13433555:

pmc-13434055:
Eleni Triantafyllou and co-authors heard midwives in 2026 who staff walk-in clinics in refugee camps under a care frame built for migrant mothers, asking what helps and what still blocks good care. Still, the midwives bent with team play, craft fixes, and soft cross-faith care. Camp training lifted their nerve and eye, yet they asked for more stock, tongue help, and mind care for staff.
pmc-13434555:
Sophia Lin and coauthors scan world research in 2026 for food literacy programs that push greener diets in minority communities. Nine databases were searched for work with adults in rich countries. Of 3,128 records screened, just two studies fit the brief.

The near empty shelf counts as the key finding here. Future programs should blend culture fit, health gains, and green aims from the start, then track results over years.
pmc-13434755:

pmc-13435455:

pmc-13436455:

pmc-13436955:
Yeqiu Huang and colleagues searched gene activity data for shared markers that could flag both sepsis and acute kidney injury, two dangerous conditions that often strike together. Their 2026 study combined several patient data sets, used two machine learning tools to narrow candidate genes, and checked the results in separate cohorts. Single-cell data then showed where the chosen genes act.

Four genes stood out as a shared signature: FBXO21, FLOT1, TMC6, and KLRB1. A scoring chart built on them separated sick patients from others with strong accuracy across the check cohorts. The genes clustered in certain immune cells and in injured kidney cells, and they tied closely to T-cell activity and immune signals. Messages passed between cells also differed in the two conditions. The authors propose the four-gene set as a lead for earlier diagnosis and for future treatment work in kidney injury tied to sepsis.
pmc-13437355:
Xiaochi Ma and colleagues review the shifting role of macrophages in lung injury caused by chest radiation. The treatment cures many chest cancers but also harms healthy lung, first as inflammation and later as stiff scarring. Their 2026 review shows macrophages, the immune system's cleanup and repair cells, standing at the center of both stages.

Later, the same cell family switches toward a repair form that instead drives scarring. It wakes fibroblasts, lays down excess tissue matrix, and pushes lung lining cells to change character. Radiation also rewires how macrophages burn sugar, fat, and amino acids, and it strains their power plants, locking in each harmful mode. The authors sort treatment ideas that follow: retune the cells, fix their fuel use, deliver drugs straight to them, or engineer them. They warn that modern immune cancer drugs make prevention harder, so safe ways to shield the lung remain an urgent need.
pmc-13437955:
Jennifer Michaelson and colleagues review T cell engagers, antibody constructs grabbing a T cell with one arm and a target cell with the other, forcing a kill. Twelve such products have won approval in the United States and Europe for blood cancers and a few solid tumors, often working alone in patients out of options. Their 2026 review maps how the next generation is being built to widen the safety margin.

The first wave proved the idea in stubborn leukemias, lymphomas, myeloma, and small cell lung cancer. Where rough comparisons exist, response rates rival engineered cell therapy, without the wait of growing a personal product. New designs aim at three problems: a narrow window between benefit and harm, targets varying across a tumor, and immune side effects that can turn dangerous. Variants in labs and trials tune grip strength, add safety switches, and chase target pairs.
pmc-13439255:
Alexandra C Pike and co-authors put the maths tools of computational psychiatry to a basic quality test, reporting in 2026. The field fits models of learning and choice to behaviour, hoping the fitted values will track mental health symptoms. That hope rests on hidden premises: values should be recoverable, stable over time, alike across tasks, and tied to symptoms. The team recruited 548 online volunteers who finished five tasks and seven symptom questionnaires.

A subset of 115 people repeated the tasks two weeks later. Winning models recovered their values well and held steady across sessions. Values meant to capture the same process in different tasks mostly failed to match, though. Only two tasks yielded values linked to symptoms, and those links were weak. The authors urge early quality checks before such tools guide care.
pmc-13439455:
Ji-Hwan Park's team built a postmortem CT triage tool in 2026 for fatty liver, aiming to prioritize autopsy cases before dissection. Fatty liver grading normally needs histology, yet CT density could flag likely cases early. One hundred sixty-six deceased people had whole-body postmortem CT then autopsy with liver histology, and volumetric versus four-point liver density measures were compared against steatosis grades.

Four-point density fell as steatosis worsened. A cutoff near forty-three Hounsfield units separated suspected cases with high specificity, and three bands, normal, borderline, and suspected, validated at about eighty-seven percent accuracy in a second group. Forensic pathologists get a practical rule-in aid for autopsy workflow. Mild versus moderate grades still overlap, so the tool triages rather than diagnoses.
pmc-13439655:
Anna Wolf and co-authors watch a catalyst precursor crystallise, step by step, to understand how it forms. The material is a nickel-magnesium hydroxycarbonate used to make catalysts for green methanation, turning carbon dioxide and hydrogen into methane. Their 2026 study focuses on the hydrothermal aging step, previously unexplored.

The team combined measurements taken during the reaction, including infrared spectra and pressure, with after-the-fact X-ray diffraction, microscopy, and chemical analysis. Within thirty minutes of reaching hydrothermal conditions, the amorphous starting precipitate began converting into a crystalline mixed compound in which magnesium replaces part of the nickel. They established the starting material's formula and tracked how the metal ratio evolved and carbonate was taken up as two phases interconverted. Dissolved species in the surrounding liquid proved important to the transformation.
pmc-13439855:
Anastasia Shpichka's team tested stem cell spheroids in 2026 to repair scarred vocal folds in rabbits, where cell suspensions wash away too fast to heal well. Forty-eight male rabbits with vocal fold scars were split into untreated, gel-only, gel plus cell suspension, and gel plus spheroid groups, with tissue examined after three months. Both cell treatments restored folds, but spheroid results came closer to healthy tissue.

Spheroid-treated folds showed thin, loose lamina propria with aligned collagen and spindle fibroblasts, matching intact folds, while suspension-treated folds ran thicker with denser tissue beneath the surface. Voice surgeons get evidence that spheroid form improves retention and regeneration. Human trials must confirm safety, voice outcomes, and durability.
pmc-13439955:
Alcala and colleagues examine how two cell stress systems talk to each other in the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans. Their 2026 paper focuses on the heat shock response, which protects proteins in the main cell body, and the endoplasmic reticulum's unfolded protein response, which guards a folding compartment. Both systems switch on protective chaperone proteins when proteins misfold.

Using glowing reporter genes in living worms, the authors showed that heat switches on the reticulum response in an unusual way. Two master regulators, XBP-1 and HSF-1, acted together to drive that activation. Turning on the reticulum response in nerve or glial cells also strengthened the heat shock response in distant tissues. Worms with this cross-tissue signalling survived heat better, showing the two responses reinforce each other.
pmc-13440055:
Semën Gorfman and colleagues set out a recipe for measuring total X-ray scattering from single crystals on an absolute scale, reporting in 2026. Total scattering blends sharp Bragg peaks, which encode the average crystal structure, with a smooth diffuse glow that betrays local deviations. Powder versions of the method flatten direction, hiding how those deviations align. Their protocol captures both signals from one crystal in one dataset, with a full reduction workflow to place intensities on a shared scale.

Scale factors drawn from Bragg refinement matched those from comparing the whole signal against a computed baseline. That agreement is the key test, since joint refinement of average and local structure needs both parts on the same footing. The authors present the workflow as a step toward fitting Bragg and diffuse data together in a single structural model.
pmc-13440255:
Min Zhao's team traced hair loss biology in 2026 in male-pattern balding, where dermal papilla cell aging drives thinning but its gene-level trigger was unclear. Human scalp tissue, primary and lab-grown papilla cells, and a hormone-induced mouse model were paired with aging, energy, gene, and protein checks. ACOD1 and its partner DDX1 emerged as a control pair.

Balding papilla cells showed aging markers, weak growth and movement, more death, and energy failure, with ACOD1 shortage driving DDX1 methyl-linked trouble. A lab-made treatment, 4-octyl itaconate, improved hair measures in mice. Hair teams get an energy aging mechanism with a trial treatment, still early-stage for human use.
pmc-13441155:
Bancos and colleagues report real-world experience in 2026 with givosiran, an RNA interference drug, for acute hepatic porphyria at Romania's largest porphyria center in Cluj-Napoca. The inherited disease causes buildup of heme-building compounds that trigger disabling attacks. Givosiran silences the first enzyme in that pathway, cutting the buildup at its source.

The center's cohort held fifteen diagnosed patients, ten of them treated with givosiran. Attack frequency fell significantly after treatment began, and patients felt improvement as early as one month in. Among treated patients who had started with frequent attacks and repeated admissions, seventy percent stopped having attacks entirely. The rest dropped from over three attacks to between one and three. The authors also describe two families with clustered gene mutations.
pmc-13441255:
Feng Tian and Weijian Yang spotlight a 2025 advance in miniature brain microscopes, describing a mask-based system called DeepInMiniscope in a 2026 breakthrough summary. Lens-free miniscopes encode a scene through a thin optical mask onto a nearby sensor, trading bulk for computation. Keeping image quality high across large volumes while cutting computing load has been the field's choke point. The highlighted system was built jointly as hardware and reconstruction software.

Its scalable algorithm rebuilds sharp three-dimensional volumes from weak, noisy signals far more cheaply than earlier pipelines allowed. Demonstrations recorded neural activity in mouse brain at near-cellular sharpness across a wide field. For freely moving animals, that mix of small footprint and volume coverage matters, since behaviour unfolds while brains work. The authors present the system as a step toward routine large-scale three-dimensional recording in behaving animals.
pmc-13441755:
Yu Qi, Huihui Sun, and Chunhong Hou test whether adding simple immune counts back into a severity score sharpens death prediction in suspected infection, reporting in 2026. The updated SOFA-2 score grades organ failure but leaves the immune system out over specificity worries, even though sepsis means a dysregulated host response to infection. The team analysed 75,203 adults across three large critical care databases. The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, white cell counts, and lymphocyte counts were folded into the score under agreed, data-driven cutoffs.

The immune-augmented score beat standard SOFA-2 in every cohort, with a significant pooled gain in discrimination. Risk reclassification also improved meaningfully, moving patients into truer risk bands. Gains were modest in size, yet the added markers are cheap and available on routine blood counts. The authors argue that excluding immunity blinds the score to the very process that defines severe infection.
pmc-13442655:
Li-Dan Xu and colleagues review a classic Chinese herb, Euonymus alatus, as a diabetes aid in a 2026 paper. Old herb books list the plant, and labs have found more than 230 compounds in it so far. Groups span flavonoids, triterpenoids, and lignans, three broad plant chemical classes.

Body-handling data stay thin, since no compound from the herb has firm lab-measured travel marks yet. Test work shows five routes to lower blood sugar, from slow gut uptake to calmer swelling paths. Gut microbe shifts and more short-chain fatty acids form one route. Cell and animal work also shows less harm in kidney and eye tissue tied to diabetes. The authors weigh the herb as a multi-route lead, while they flag the lack of human trials as the chief gap.
pmc-13442855:
Moriah Mitchell and colleagues chart how virus antibody records change across life in a 2026 study. A scan called VirScan reads which virus bits a person's antibodies grip, a log of past meets. Babies start with mother-passed antibodies that fade fast, replaced by their own replies to about 22 fresh virus meets within three years.

Child records kept shifting until about age seven, with broad grips that often faded. Adult records stayed remarkably steady and personal, so steady that a tool named Immunoprint could match donors with accuracy past 99.99 percent in their tests. Some virus families left longer marks than others, with cold and gut virus kin outlasting flu and corona kin. First grip strength and star bits forecast which replies would last. The atlas may guide shot design and outbreak watch.
pmc-13443555:
Yvette Z. Szabo and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of how depression links to blood inflammation markers differently in women and men. The team pooled 124 papers covering 423,421 adults, tracking C-reactive protein, interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor alpha, interleukin-1 beta, and fibrinogen across cross-sectional and longitudinal designs.

Depression linked modestly to higher combined markers in both sexes, slightly more in males. Interleukin-6 stood out in females, while C-reactive protein and interleukin-6 stood out in males, and only the longitudinal links ran from markers to later depression, not the reverse. The pattern supports inflammation as a shared thread in depression with subtle sex-specific details worth carrying into treatment research.
pmc-13445555:
Carolina Jiménez-González and colleagues argue that statins, best known as heart drugs, may also act straight on the fatty liver in metabolic liver disease, in a 2026 review. Heart disease is the top killer in this liver condition, so statins already anchor care. The question is whether part of their liver benefit goes past cholesterol lowering.

The review gathers cell work, cohort data, and indirect trial proof around one hub: a pathway whose blocking alters fat harm, inflammation, scarring, and cancer risk in the liver. A further strand links statins to better blood flow inside the liver, with trial support in early cirrhosis. One trial in late cirrhosis found no gain, which helps mark where benefit may stop.
pmc-13445655:
Abbas Al Mutair and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of benralizumab, an antibody that blocks an interleukin-5 receptor to cut eosinophils, for severe eosinophilic asthma. The team pooled 15 randomized trials covering 5,502 patients, with 3,061 on the drug and 2,441 on placebo, tracking lung function, symptom control, and safety.

The drug improved lung capacity by about 0.11 liters on average and significantly improved symptom control scores, while adverse event odds did not differ from placebo. Gains fell under the bar for a minimal clinically important difference on control scores, and heterogeneity ran high. The treatment offers a small but real gain for heavily obstructed patients, with individual response varying.
pmc-13446355:
Yaru Ji and colleagues turn sour orange leaves, a citrus farm by-product, into a rich phenolic extract with possible blood sugar benefits, in a 2026 study. Leaves pile up as waste in citrus processing, though they hold prized plant compounds. The team sought a green way to pull those compounds out and prove what they do.

Sixteen candidate liquid salts were screened, and one won on fit for the target compounds. Paired with ultrasound, it beat plain ultrasound and hot soaking for yield, and microscope views showed deeper cell wall tearing. A resin step polished the extract to a pure, well-mapped fraction with forty-seven named parts. In insulin-resistant liver cells it raised sugar uptake and storage, a hint of diabetes promise.
pmc-13447055:
Sergio Castaño Castaño and colleagues run a pilot brain study on how emotional distraction plays out in cannabis users after three days without the drug, in a 2026 paper. Non-users, occasional users, and chronic users took a word-color test with emotional words before and after the pause, the users only. A cap that reads blood oxygen in the forehead tracked brain effort through the tasks.

Behavior shifts clustered in the emotional test alone. Occasional users answered faster to negative words after the pause, while chronic users showed no clear change and non-users showed a drift the team reads as practice. Brain signals for spent blood shifted by group over time in right and shared forehead zones. The authors call the early pattern a lead, not a verdict.
pmc-13447155:
Yiheng Liu, Bin Liu and Weiran Dai pool evidence in 2026 on swapping aspirin for indobufen after a heart stent procedure. Patients need two anti-clotting drugs after the procedure, yet aspirin can cause bleeding and stomach harm. Indobufen blocks a similar pathway in a reversible way and might be gentler.

Six databases were searched to early 2026, yielding twelve studies with close to eight thousand patients. Heart events such as heart attack and death occurred at similar rates with either drug pair. Bleeding was notably less common when indobufen replaced aspirin, and the pattern held in heart attack subgroups and with different partner drugs. The reviewers still urge caution, since the underlying studies carry limits that a larger trial could settle.
pmc-13447255:
Yanyan Dong and colleagues survey self-compassion and burnout among young and mid-life nurses in Zhejiang, China, in 2026. Heavy workloads and tense patient relations leave nurses prone to exhaustion and detachment. Being kind to oneself in hard moments, rather than harshly self-critical, might buffer that strain, and the survey tests the link.

Five hundred sixty-four nurses aged eighteen to forty-five completed standard scales in late 2024. Self-compassion sat at a moderate level overall, while burnout fell in the mild to moderate range, led by emotional exhaustion. Higher self-compassion scores tracked with lower burnout in a clear pattern, and self-compassion alone explained a sizable share of burnout differences. Because the design captures one moment, the authors recommend manager-led training in self-compassion as a plausible next step to test.
pmc-13447355:
Alex Ascunce-París and colleagues build a quality grading system for computer models of immune receptor complexes in 2026 work. T cell receptors grip small protein fragments shown on cell surfaces, and knowing those shapes guides immunotherapy design. Lab-made structures are scarce, while computer models vary in accuracy and lack a trusted score that needs no lab reference.

Seven modelling tools rebuilt every known lab structure of the class studied, and one leading tool performed best overall. A learning classifier then combined several confidence scores from more than a thousand models to sort new models into four quality tiers. Tier calls beat any single score and held up on two held-out collections of thousands of complexes. High tiers enriched for real interactions and exposed false entries in a public database.
pmc-13447755:
Fulco and the Microcephaly Epidemic Research Group tracked 278 children in Brazil born during the 2015-2017 outbreak. Their mothers had caught Zika virus in pregnancy, alone or with both Zika and chikungunya. The team tested whether dual infection made newborn results worse. Mothers had come in with rash in Pernambuco and got lab testing for both mosquito-borne viruses during pregnancy.

Of the children, 198 were exposed to Zika alone and 80 to both viruses before birth in the cohort. Specialist checks found no clear differences between the groups for microcephaly or low birth weight. Prematurity and small size for gestational age at birth also matched. Swallowing problems and brain, eye, hearing, and imaging problems showed up at similar rates across the groups. The authors note each virus alone has been linked to newborn harm in other work. In this cohort, adding chikungunya did not compound Zika's effects.
pmc-13448255:
Betof and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract TPRG-01, the design of TRIO-MBM, a multicenter phase two trial testing a three-drug immunotherapy combination for melanoma brain metastases. The trial includes the symptomatic patients whom standard dual therapy serves worst.

The trial adds relatlimab, a LAG-3 blocking antibody, to nivolumab plus ipilimumab. It enrolls sixty patients: forty without symptoms, and twenty whose brain lesions cause symptoms or require substantial steroids. In that second group the standard pair historically benefited only about a fifth of patients. Everyone receives the triplet on a four- or eight-weekly schedule. The main endpoint is the share whose brain disease is controlled for at least six months. Blood, tumor, and spinal fluid studies are built in to hunt for response markers. The trial was enrolling at Stanford, with expansion underway, so no results are reported.
pmc-13448455:
Tavakkoli and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract PACM-06, a pig model built to develop laser interstitial thermal therapy as a gentler alternative to separation surgery. The therapy cooks tumor tissue with a laser fiber. Separation surgery is currently needed when spinal metastases crush the spinal cord, to move tumor away before radiation.

The team implanted human breast cancer or bone cancer cells into the vertebrae of five immunosuppressed mini pigs, tracking growth by CT and MRI. Commercial laser fibers were placed through the skin using image guidance and standard spine tools, achieving excellent targeting accuracy. Breathing badly corrupted the live MRI temperature maps the technique depends on, but their motion-compensation algorithms substantially cleaned the estimates up. Comparing MRI damage estimates with tissue examination afterward still showed discrepancies, which the authors say must be resolved before clinical adoption.
pmc-13448655:
Jong Woong Park and co-authors present a light-emitting display that visualises two kinds of particle-moving forces in a 2026 device study. Electric-field forces and acoustic forces can herd microparticles for sorting and sensing, yet watching those forces directly usually needs separate sensors and processors. A display that lights up in response to the forces themselves would simplify such systems greatly.

Conductive microparticles assemble under the electric force and brighten the display's emission, while an acoustic wave scatters that assembly and switches the glow off. Frequency and intensity of either force tune the response, giving a rewritable dual-mode sensing surface sensitive across a wide force range. Demonstrations covered visualising temperature change, checking microfluidic channels without contact and tracking motion as it happened. Biomedical and physical sensing systems are the intended beneficiaries.
pmc-13448855:
Ninoschka D'Souza and colleagues report in 2026 on rat experiments with a drug that blocks the somatostatin receptor 2. They tested whether it keeps the body's defense against low blood sugar working over a week of doses. The blocker, ZT-01, is meant to free glucagon, the hormone that raises blood sugar, during insulin overdoses. Male rats with induced type 2 diabetes and healthy controls received daily doses before insulin challenges.

The blocker strengthened glucagon responses to both insulin challenges, in diabetic and healthy rats alike. Given without a challenge, it briefly raised glucagon and glucose, yet food intake and body weight stayed unchanged. Diabetic rats on the drug across days 8 to 22 needed less daily insulin while their overall glucose levels did not worsen. The authors conclude that repeated dosing preserves the counterregulatory benefit without costing glycemic control.
pmc-13448955:
Janet McGill and a large team revisit in 2026 the CONFIDENCE trial to check whether starting two kidney-protective diabetes drugs together works equally well at every starting blood sugar level. Adults with type 2 diabetes and albumin in the urine were randomized to finerenone, empagliflozin, or both, with urine albumin change at day 180 as the main outcome. Baseline blood sugar was available for 781 of the 800 participants, averaging 7.3 percent.

Patients were split into four bands of starting HbA1c, from 6.4 percent or below up to above 7.9 percent. In every band, the combination cut urine albumin more than either drug alone, with reductions between 47 and 63 percent. Blood sugar itself eased slightly on empagliflozin-containing arms and stayed flat on finerenone alone. The authors conclude the pairing's kidney benefit does not depend on how controlled a patient's sugar already is.
pmc-13449355:
Melinda Rushing and colleagues dig in 2026 into why emergency departments so often miss national targets for treating sickle cell pain crises. Guidelines say a first pain dose should land within thirty minutes of triage and a second within thirty minutes of the first. The team worked from records of a large New Jersey health system between January 2022 and September 2025. They covered 7,160 visits by 1,401 patients and tested how volumes, shift, and triage severity shaped care.

Only 14.2 percent of visits met the first-dose target, though 52.6 percent met the second. Sickle cell volume, overall department volume, shift, and severity score all related to whether a visit followed the guidelines, yet none sped up average times. Shift did: evening arrivals waited about sixteen minutes longer for a first dose than night arrivals. The authors draw a line between hitting guideline checkboxes and genuine timeliness.
pmc-13449455:
Takaaki Nakano and colleagues reported a 2026 case of a rare lymphoma that first appeared as stomach pain in an emergency room. Extranodal natural killer and T-cell lymphoma is an aggressive, Epstein-Barr virus-linked cancer that usually strikes outside the lymph nodes. Involvement of the gut is extremely uncommon and often mimics ordinary abdominal illness.

A previously healthy twenty-year-old man arrived with sudden abdominal pain and bloody stool, but early scans showed nothing abnormal. Pain persisted, and a repeat scan on the second hospital day revealed free air in the abdomen, leading to emergency surgery. Surgeons found a perforated lesion that proved to be lymphoma. The case warns emergency doctors that a normal first scan does not rule out a dangerous gut lymphoma.
pmc-13450255:
Stephanie Khoury and colleagues listen in 2026 to mothers, fathers, and officials in low-income São Paulo neighborhoods about why breastfeeding fades before the recommended six months. Brazil averages fifty percent exclusive breastfeeding, but poor communities fall behind wealthy ones. The study ran three focus groups, two with mothers and one with fathers. It added five interviews with insiders from nursing, neonatology, social work, and the health and social ministries, nineteen voices.

Goodwill toward breastfeeding was nearly universal, yet three barrier families emerged. The first was money, since work and food costs squeeze feeding choices. The second was the health system, whose support thins after discharge. The third was social norms that undermine mothers' confidence. A cash transfer, the Auxílio Nutriz program, was seen as a realistic lever against the barriers. The authors argue strengthening that program inside a cross-sector effort offers a credible path to lasting breastfeeding.
pmc-13452155:
Peine and colleagues report a urine germ that fooled a routine lab test into calling it a far more feared germ. Their 2026 case report is about a woman aged thirty-eight with germs in her urine but no signs of illness. She had a past of repeat urine infections. Two top lab tools named the germ as E. coli ST1193. One reads germ proteins; the other reads the full gene code.

The germ grew slowly, made pale small spots on test plates, and did not use milk sugar as most E. coli do. Tests showed it resisted a key class of antibiotics, the fluoroquinolones, plus some older drugs. It stayed open to several other drugs. The team warns that a wrong name can spark the wrong public health steps. Staff should check by gene or protein tests when panel results clash with the rest of the case.
pmc-13452355:
Deng and a large team uncover a molecular chain reaction in this 2026 study that makes Klebsiella pneumoniae sepsis, a severe bloodstream infection, so destructive. Working from human sepsis data, single-cell sequencing, and mouse models, they focused on ZBP1, a sensor protein inside macrophages, the immune cells that engulf bacteria.

Damage to mitochondria switched ZBP1 on. Activated ZBP1 then grabbed a signaling protein called STAT3. This blocked STAT3 from turning on the gene for legumain. Legumain is an enzyme that normally calms macrophages and supports tissue repair. Mice engineered to lack ZBP1 produced fewer inflammatory cytokines and survived sepsis at higher rates, while mice lacking legumain in macrophages fared worse. Delivering extra legumain by gene therapy or as a recombinant protein quieted inflammation, restored gut barrier function, and improved survival, marking the pathway as a drug target.
pmc-13453955:
Amber John and thirteen co-authors chart recorded ADHD in England across a quarter century of primary care records. Their 2026 study uses a national database covering millions of patients, with pooled sets reaching over 42 million people for some counts. Recorded cases at mid 2025 sat at 1.19 percent of the population, higher in males and lower with rising age.

That recorded rate sits far below research estimates of how many people truly have ADHD. The coverage gap ran from about 28.71 percent in young men to 93.51 percent in people over 65. New recordings per year climbed steeply across the period and sped up from 2020. The rise was sharpest in males under 18, while rates in the oldest group stayed low and flat. The authors offer the map as a guide for service planning.
pmc-13454255:
Reyhane Fooladi Vayqan and others tested fat-bubble carriers in 2026 to kill pancreatic cancer cells by silencing a survival gene. Protein tyrosine kinase 6, known as PTK6, helps tumour cells stay alive and is a drug target in pancreatic cancer. The team built cationic nanoliposomes loaded with an asymmetric PCR product that targets PTK6 messenger RNA.

An antisense single-stranded DNA matching the PTK6 code was made by asymmetric PCR, cleaned, and packed into positively charged nanoliposomes. The carriers were near-spherical, roughly thirty to one hundred twenty nanometres across, with a positive surface charge. In dish tests, they cut viability in PANC-1 cancer cells, spurred cell death, and lowered PTK6 protein levels, with less harm to non-cancer pancreatic cells. The work offers a targeted delivery route for pancreatic cancer therapy.
pmc-13454355:
Andreea Molnar and Patty Kostkova report, in 2026, an evaluation of a phone game that teaches young children about hygiene and careful antibiotic use. The game, part of the Edugames4all project, is named MicrobeQuest in the study. Health games for children often skip proper checks of whether children actually enjoy them. The study measured fun, engagement, and willingness to play again among 19 children.

Children rated the game well on all three measures. Scores also moved together: children who had more fun tended to stay engaged and wanted to keep playing. The authors stress that appeal cannot be taken for granted just because a product is a game. With a small group, the results serve as an early check rather than proof for all classrooms.
pmc-13454455:
Xiaoyun Yang and others tried gas-curing tricks for salty soil set with geopolymer in 2026, to make a weak build soil firm. Salty soils are weak and shaky, and geopolymer set with gas-curing might firm them up, but gas tricks had not been set side by side. The team scored break shapes and crush strength.

Gas-cured set soil topped four point one crush units at geopolymer shares past twenty-five percent with mixed gas-curing. Plain gas-curing topped three point eight units, and stacked gas-curing topped six point two units, at shares past twenty percent. For shares of twenty to thirty-five percent, strength ran from two-hour stacked gas-curing down to mixed gas-curing. Breaks shifted from cracks to crumbling as shares rose. Builders gain a ranked gas-curing guide.
pmc-13455055:
Bolin Tang, Yuhuai Wu, Jianping Liu, and Rui Pan review, in 2026, why immune therapy keeps failing against osteosarcoma, a bone cancer of the young. Standard treatment still leaves relapsed and spread disease with poor odds, and lung relapse dominates deaths. The authors argue the bone niche itself organizes the immune failure.

Their framework layers several effects. The bone setting steers immune cell traffic and fattens suppressive myeloid cells. Repair programs switched on by treatment further shield the tumor. Signals also travel to the lungs, preparing the ground where relapse appears. Each claim is graded by how direct the osteosarcoma evidence is, with testable checks proposed for the shakier ones. The authors suggest a timed sequence for care: reprogram the niche first, fire up immunity second, and guard the lungs throughout.
pmc-13455455:
Parinaz Alizadeh and colleagues price three ways to screen premature babies for blinding eye disease in Iran in a 2026 model study. Retinopathy of prematurity affects over 20 percent of premature infants in Iran, yet few subspecialists can reach every nursery in time. A lifetime Markov model compared three options, using national data and a 5.8 percent discount rate. The options were universal referral to tertiary centres, nurse-led RetCam imaging with remote specialist review, and local screening by general eye doctors with selective referral.

Local screening cost least at 33.52 dollars with 16.83 quality-adjusted life years, while RetCam telemedicine cost 122.69 dollars for 17.14 life years, an extra cost of 288.81 dollars per life year gained, far below Iran's willingness-to-pay threshold. Universal referral cost more and gained less, so it was dominated. RetCam won in 95.2 percent of simulations, backing scale-up with training and quality checks to cut preventable childhood blindness.
pmc-13456855:
Caterina M. Nava, Antoine Nobile, François Pugin, and Raffaella Sguinzi present, in a 2026 case report, gut bleeding from a Meckel diverticulum in a young adult. The pouch is the gut's commonest birth defect, a leftover stub on the small intestine, yet adult bleeding from it is rare and hard to pin down.

Their patient was a 20-year-old man passing blood for two days, growing unstable and fainting as his blood counts slid. Scopes from above and below found nothing. A contrast scan then spotted the blind-ending pouch. Keyhole surgery confirmed it, and the team removed a ten-centimeter bowel stretch with the pouch and rejoined the ends by hand. Tissue study showed stomach-type lining inside the pouch. A brief gut stall followed, managed without surgery, and he went home on day six. The authors urge early scans and surgery for unexplained bleeding in the young.
pmc-13457055:
Kun Hong and six colleagues compare, in a 2026 records study, two routes for delivering chemotherapy into the spinal fluid of patients whose cancer has lined the brain's membranes. The disease, leptomeningeal carcinomatosis, was joined here by fluid buildup in the brain, a grim pairing. Thirty-six patients received methotrexate either through an implanted Ommaya reservoir or by repeated lumbar punctures.

Reservoir patients responded far more often, about 87 percent against 48 percent, and every reservoir patient gained clinical relief against about half by puncture. Pressure inside the skull eased better too. Side effects matched between routes. Survival did not separate clearly, at a median of about 55 weeks against 44. Independent guards of longer life were targeted therapy alongside, while cancer spread outside the nervous system spelled higher risk. The authors favor the reservoir for comfort and control, not longevity.
pmc-13457555:

pmc-13471355:
Xia and colleagues built a prediction tool to flag, at hospital admission, which children with pertussis (whooping cough) will need intensive care. Their 2026 model rests on records from 662 children with lab-confirmed infection treated at one provincial children's center in China.

Sixty-one children, 9.2% of the group, entered intensive care, and they were far younger than the rest, with a median age of 2 months versus 60 months. The model combines seven admission details, including age, white blood cell count, and episodes of turning blue during coughing fits. In internal testing it separated future ICU patients almost perfectly, scoring an AUC of 0.953 on a scale where 1.0 means flawless ranking, though outside validation is still pending.
pmc-13471455:
Hunjan and colleagues reviewed emergency records of teenagers treated for binge drinking in Milan to learn how often the episode damages their muscles. Their 2026 retrospective study covered 150 adolescents aged 13.2 to 18.0 years seen between 2013 and 2023, defining muscle damage by a creatine kinase blood level above 1.5 times the normal ceiling.

Muscle damage appeared in 61 cases, or 41% of the adolescents, and it fell overwhelmingly on boys: 66% of males were affected versus 16% of females in the cohort. Average blood alcohol sat near 2.0 grams per liter, yet damage showed no correlation with alcohol level, potassium, or blood osmolality. The authors suggest an inherited susceptibility to alcohol-driven muscle injury may explain who gets hurt.
pmc-13471555:
Peng and co-authors standardized a same-day cell therapy for women whose womb lining stays too thin for embryo transfer. Their 2026 prospective single-arm study at Peking University Third Hospital treated patients whose endometrium measured under 7 mm. The protocol harvested their own fat, extracted stromal vascular fraction, a mix of repair cells, and infusing it into the uterus in one visit.

Thirty-five patients aged 20 to 45 were treated, with a mean age of 35.6 years, and the cell product kept viability above 90% at infusion. By three months, 18 of the 35 patients, or 51% of the group, had reached the target thickness of 7 mm or more. Because the cells are the patient's own, rejection risk disappears, the authors note, and no long laboratory culture is needed.
pmc-13471655:
Vico-Rodríguez and co-authors pooled randomized trials of exercise therapy for shoulder pain from rotator cuff trouble in middle-aged and older adults. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis covered 21 trials with 1,152 participants, comparing strengthening, stretching, and stabilization programs against usual care or add-on treatments over the past decade.

Exercise significantly improved pain, daily function, and range of motion across the pooled analyses, though the overall effect size was small. Strength gains were the exception: they came in smaller and missed statistical significance, with an effect of g 0.229 at p 0.085 in the pooled estimate. Studies disagreed heavily with each other, with heterogeneity of I² 95.96% across outcomes, which the authors attribute to differing programs and measures. Rotator cuff problems drive up to 70% of shoulder pain diagnoses.
pmc-13472255:
Binbin Ji leads a fourteen author review in 2026 on marrying biomaterials with electroporation, the pulse based method that opens cell membranes for delivery or ablation. Gentle pulses briefly permeabilize cells so genes, proteins, and drugs can enter. That enables gene editing and engineered cell production. Harsh pulses kill tissue outright without heat, a tool for tumor ablation and electrochemotherapy.

Nanocarriers, hydrogels, soft conductors, and engineered interfaces each reshape the pulses reach. They shield cargo, confine fields, hold material in place, and match soft tissue shapes. The review compares the design logic of the major platform families across gene editing, cell manufacturing, cancer treatment, immune modulation, and skin delivery. Translation hurdles close the account, from pulse and material compatibility to manufacturing scale, dose measurement in the body, and regulation.
pmc-13473055:
Ângela Leite and João Marôco test a short phone attachment scale with young adults in Portugal in 2026. The scale has six items that ask whether the phone feels like a comfort or a burden. A group of 648 people aged 18 to 35 filled it in for this check. The authors used factor methods suited to ranked answers.

The two-part shape of the scale held up well, with strong fit scores for both parts. Scores were steady across men and women, while links to schooling level differed in part. People with more schooling scored apart on the comfort-versus-burden balance. Clinicians and researchers gain a checked tool for studying how young adults relate to their phones.
pmc-13473455:
Luis Alberto Rodriguez Linares and six colleagues ran a 2026 randomised, double-blind trial of a steroid added to a nerve block after heart bypass surgery. Pain control after cardiac surgery remains imperfect, and the erector spinae plane block, which numbs the chest wall, wears off too soon. Forty-three patients having elective bypass received blocks on both sides with ropivacaine alone or ropivacaine plus 8 milligrams of dexamethasone placed beside the nerve.

Pain at rest on the first day after surgery, the main outcome, did not differ between groups, and opioid use over 48 hours was likewise similar. Time on a ventilator ran shorter with dexamethasone, at a median of 11.6 hours against 14.7 hours, and pain intensity was lower at 60 days but not at 30 or 90 days. The authors treat the steroid as no help for acute pain, with later hints needing larger, better-blinded trials.
pmc-13473555:
Qiuping Xu and five colleagues tested in 2026 whether two cheap blood markers can predict survival in non-small cell lung cancer. Inflammation shapes cancer outcomes, yet simple, low-cost prognostic tools remain valuable. The cohort included 748 consecutive Chinese patients. Relationships between markers, tumour features, and survival were examined through chi-squared tests, Cox regression, and spline models, with survival estimated by Kaplan-Meier curves.

Two markers stood out independently: the systemic inflammation response index, with a hazard ratio of 1.506, and the albumin-to-globulin ratio, with a hazard ratio of 0.749, meaning higher values of the first and lower values of the second went with worse survival. Combining them into a three-tier score separated risk sharply, with the highest-risk group facing a hazard ratio of 1.974. Predictive accuracy held steady near an area under the curve of 0.70. The authors offer the score as a convenient aid for risk stratification.
pmc-13473955:
Kai Zhang and a broad team trace how brown fat shields the heart from deep cold in 2026 mouse work. Brown fat burns fuel to make heat, and animals trained by mild cold survive harsh cold better. Mice exposed to minus twenty-five degrees kept heart function when they had first adapted to cold. Removing brown fat erased that protection, which showed the tissue was required.

Tiny parcels released from brown fat carried the protective effect to heart cells. A long RNA strand inside those parcels rose after cold training, and silencing it removed the benefit. The strand lifted a guard protein in heart cells that curbs cell death. The brown-fat-to-heart path could inspire ways to guard hearts during cold stress or surgery.
pmc-13474655:
Seung Won Lee and co-authors follow sleep disorder risk after epilepsy in 2026 using Korean national health data. More than twenty-four hundred people with new epilepsy were matched to ten times as many peers. All were tracked for up to ten years for a first sleep disorder diagnosis. Risk was split by time since diagnosis, age, sex, and smoking history.

Fifteen percent of patients developed a sleep disorder, against about eight percent of peers. Risk ran highest in the first two years after diagnosis, at roughly two and a half times the peer rate. Younger patients, men, and former smokers carried higher risk. Early sleep screening after epilepsy diagnosis is the clear takeaway.
pmc-13474755:
Binmi Tang and colleagues link nurse artificial intelligence literacy to evidence-based practice skill in 2026 in one Sichuan district. Nurses answered three surveys covering background, tool literacy, and skill at finding and using research proof. Group-finding math sorted literacy scores into hidden levels. Links between level and practice skill were tested with care.

Nearly half of nurses fell in the low literacy group, while only about one in seven reached the high group. Prior tool training and practice skill both shaped which group a nurse joined. Higher literacy groups scored higher on all four parts of practice skill. Managers gain a map for lifting both tool skill and research use together.
pmc-13474855:
Jiong Wang and colleagues trace a small RNA that calms spine tuberculosis in 2026. Spine tuberculosis is a common form of the disease outside the lungs, causing lasting back damage. Tissue from twenty patients and twenty matched controls fed a genome-wide small RNA scan. Lab models used immune cells infected with a vaccine strain of the microbe.

The RNA, called miR-29a-3p, ran low in patient tissue and in infected cells. Raising it cut inflammatory signals and a matrix-chewing enzyme, while lowering it did the reverse. It binds directly to a growth pathway gene, and blocking that pathway copied its effects. The RNA-pathway pair offers fresh targets for diagnosis and care.
pmc-13474955:
Xu and Liu turned hospital network analysis on bedside ultrasound services in 2026, using one year of data from Yixing People's Hospital in Jiangsu, China. Point-of-care ultrasound, or POCUS, brings scanning to the patient's bedside, yet fixed staffing often mismatches surging demand. The team mapped 2,281 examinations from 2024 as a network linking patients, departments, and the sonographers who scanned them, inside a 1,700-bed teaching hospital.

The network proved efficient but fragile, depending heavily on hub units such as intensive care and one heavily loaded sonographer. Demand surged in repeating extreme waves, and workload sat unevenly across staff groups, with one community of staff handling 57.8 percent of all examinations in the year studied. The authors propose forecast-based staffing alerts, fast-track channels for critical scans, and workload-based assignment to balance speed with resilience in the service.
pmc-13477055:
Benjamin A.Y. Cher and five colleagues tested in 2026 whether a post-hoc finding on lung cancer surgery is sturdy enough to guide practice. The CALGB 140503 trial supported smaller sublobar resection over lobe removal, but its post-hoc comparison of wedge resection against anatomic segmentectomy found no survival difference. Surgeons doubted it for hidden bias and small numbers.

The team applied robustness of inferences to replacement, which counts how many patients would need different outcomes to overturn a finding. The wedge-versus-segmentectomy result proved robust under that test. The authors present the method as a plainer guide than p-values for deciding whether post-hoc results should change practice.
pmc-13477555:
Velez-delValle and colleagues report a 2026 cell study of how biotin, a B vitamin, affects fat storage in developing fat cells. Biotin shortage is known to impair fat buildup even though cells still mature into fat cells. The team focused on transglutaminase, a protein-stiffening enzyme tied to lipid droplets, in a mouse fat cell line grown with and without biotin.

Without biotin, cells formed fewer lipid droplets, showed empty bubble-like spaces, and made less transglutaminase with lower activity. Blocking the enzyme with a drug also cut fat accumulation and lowered a partner enzyme in fat building, suggesting a link through the cell's reducing power supply. The work names transglutaminase as a biotin-sensitive part of fat storage. It helps explain how a vitamin gap rewires fat tissue.
pmc-13478155:
Chiang-Wen Lee and colleagues present a 2026 study of interleukin-11, a signaling protein, as a driver of lung cancer spread. Public datasets showed the protein raised in non-small cell lung cancer and tied to lymph node spread and poor survival. Laboratory assays then traced how it changes cancer cell behavior.

Interleukin-11 switched on MMP12, an enzyme that breaks down tissue scaffolding, through a receptor pair and a chain of signals ending at NF-κB. An approved drug, bazedoxifene, blocked this chain in cells and reduced migration. In mice with lung tumors grown in place, silencing the interleukin gene shrank tumor growth and spread within the lung, with lower levels of the whole pathway in tissue. The authors nominate this pathway as a treatment target.
pmc-13478455:
Jiayun Wang and colleagues report a 2026 study of FOXP4, a gene-switching protein, in colorectal cancer spread. Spread to distant organs causes most deaths from this cancer, and the shape-shifting program that lets cells migrate is only partly mapped. Data from patient cohorts and single-cell profiling showed the protein concentrated in malignant lining cells and linked to poor survival.

Removing the protein weakened cancer cell behaviors in the lab and reduced tumor growth, blood vessel formation, and liver spread in animals. The protein switched on BAG3, a helper protein, by binding its control region directly. Restoring or silencing BAG3 partly reversed the effects of changing FOXP4, confirming the partnership. The authors present this two-gene axis as a window into how colorectal tumors gain invasive flexibility.
pmc-13479555:
He and colleagues mapped in 2026 how single symptoms of fear of missing out link to parts of mobile phone addiction among Chinese college students. Earlier work compared total scores, which hides which feelings drive which habits. A network approach treats each symptom as a node and shows which ones bridge the two problems.

The team surveyed 1,616 students aged 18 to 25 with two standard scales. Links inside each symptom group were stronger than links between groups, yet some cross links stood out. Feeling anxious and lost when cut off from news ranked as both a central node and a bridge. Time wasted tracking updates played the same double role on the phone side. The authors suggest easing those two nodes might loosen both problems at once, a claim they say needs testing.
pmc-13480055:
Gabrielle dos Santos Feijó and colleagues present a 2026 study of moral resilience among hospital nurses. Thirty nurses from adult and child medical and surgical wards at a teaching hospital gave in-depth interviews in mid-2025. Transcripts were sorted with text software into five groups of wording, which the team then shaped into three broad themes.

Nurses described frequent clashes between their own values, work rules, and ward limits. Staying morally steady grew through experience, reflection, faith, and honest talk with peers, rather than through grit alone. Bonds at work, the ethical tone set by the hospital, and real staffing limits all shaped how well nurses coped. The authors urge training and ward policies that protect time for dialogue and peer support, since these steps guard both staff well-being and safe care.
pmc-13480255:
Qianqian Wang and co-authors report a 2026 study of gentle ultrasound aimed at a deep brain hub in a Parkinson mouse model. The mice carry a faulty gene copy tied to family forms of the disease, which drives faulty rhythm patterns between the subthalamic nucleus and the movement cortex. The team sent low-strength ultrasound through the skull to that hub and tracked brain signals plus movement before and after.

Treatment calmed faulty activity inside the hub itself. The faulty lockstep between hub and cortex loosened. Walking and movement skill in the mice improved in step with those signal changes. Since the method needs no surgery or implants, the team frames it as a hopeful path toward human testing, while noting that long-term effects still need study.
pmc-13480955:
Roberto Oleari and colleagues show that two sugar-coating enzymes must work together for the brain's fertility neurons to form and migrate in mice. These neurons make GnRH, the hormone signal that starts puberty and drives reproduction.

Both enzymes are switched on in the mouse nose tissue where GnRH neurons and their guiding nerve are born. Knocking out either enzyme alone caused little harm, but losing both together warped the smell organ that spawns the neurons. With both gone, fewer neurons reached the brain, matching what happens when key guide signals fail. Binding tests showed a guidance cue stuck poorly to nasal tissue without the pair, Oleari reports.
pmc-13483055:
Yanxiao Yin and Xuanguo Xu present a 2026 study of whether a new style of farm productivity lifts green performance across China. The team built scores for both ideas from panel data on thirty provinces, where the new score rewards better inputs and cleaner methods, and the green score counts pollution against output.

New-style productivity clustered high in the east and south and low in the west and north, while green scores clumped in high and low pockets. Raising the new score clearly lifted green performance, with the strongest push in the west. The lift ran through better green efficiency rather than new green technology, whose effect showed threshold behaviour instead. Stronger state farm support and greener state concern each magnified the gain. Province-tuned policy may spread the benefit more evenly.
pmc-13483155:
Xiaojin Luo and co-authors describe a 2026 review of 92 pregnancies where the fetus carried a mosaic form of Turner syndrome, a mix of cells with one X chromosome beside normal cells. Records spanned twelve years at one Shenzhen centre, drawn from near thirteen thousand amniocentesis cases in high-risk pregnancies. The team charted chromosome mixes, scan findings, choices, and child follow-up.

Most mixes paired the single-X line with a normal line, and scans spotted problems in only ten fetuses, chiefly heart flaws and growth lag. Two cases carried heavy multi-system flaws. Sixty-nine pregnancies ended by choice, while twenty babies were born live and followed. A few showed slow speech or movement, hearing loss, or short stature, all with abnormal cell shares in a middling band. The authors counsel against ending pregnancies for low mosaic shares and urge close growth checks after birth.
pmc-13483655:
Wiśniewska-Ślewicz and co-authors compared activity habits and body measures in young women with and without insulin resistance, a condition where cells respond poorly to the hormone that manages blood sugar. Their 2026 study enrolled 443 women aged 18 to 35, including 301 with confirmed insulin resistance and 142 healthy controls. Participants measured their own waists and hips by a standard method and reported activity on a global questionnaire.

Women with insulin resistance scored higher on every body measure, including body mass index and waist-to-hip ratio. They also moved far less, logging about 2,615 activity units against about 3,679 in the healthy group. Sitting time ran higher in the insulin-resistant group as well. The activity gap held even after body size was accounted for. Wiśniewska-Ślewicz argues movement itself, not just weight, deserves attention in prevention programs for young women.
pmc-13487255:
Obafunsho John Abiola and others test whether a tightly constrained language model pipeline can fix incomplete abstracts of surgery randomized trials. In 2026, the three-phase computer study covers 651 trials indexed in PubMed from 2005 to 2025 with open-access full texts. A fourteen-item rubric based on CONSORT reporting guidance scores each abstract out of twenty-five points.

Original abstracts averaged only about nine points, omitting key details on randomization, harms, and registration. Rewritten abstracts gained roughly seven to eight points at two length limits, improving across all domains while readability rose slightly. The authors propose the pipeline for authoring, peer review, and editorial use, provided humans oversee the output.
pmc-13489555:
Jung and colleagues report a 2026 fly study of how a steroid hormone steers egg production in the Drosophila ovary. The hormone ecdysone acts through a receptor called EcR. Past work showed the receptor working in the ovary's support cells, not in germ cells themselves. The team tested whether the receptor also acts inside germline stem cells and their daughters.

Removing the receptor from stem cells slightly weakened their upkeep. Forcing extra receptor activity in stem cells and young germ cells blocked differentiation, copying the effect of losing a key differentiation gene. The authors propose the receptor works as a brake on gene activity in young cells; as hormone levels rise and a partner repressor falls, the brake lifts and differentiation proceeds. Direct control inside germ cells adds a layer to how hormones time reproduction.
pmc-13491755:
Charles Boudreau and eight colleagues check in 2026 whether stopping GLP-1 weight and diabetes medicines a week before surgery actually leaves the stomach empty. The drugs slow gastric emptying, which raises the danger of inhaling stomach contents under anesthesia. At two Montreal hospitals, ninety-three fasting adults had stomach ultrasound before elective operations.

Patients who had paused their weekly injection for at least seven days showed leftover stomach contents in about forty-two percent of scans, against twenty-four percent in patients not taking the drugs. Most positive scans showed solid food rather than liquid. After statistical adjustment the gap was not significant, and the authors admit the study was too small to settle the question. Still, the numbers suggest a seven-day pause may not guarantee an empty stomach.
pmc-13492555:
Brooke N Bender and four colleagues ask in 2026 whether the way a rat copes during a frightening experience forecasts its later choices about rewards. Trauma and alcohol problems intertwine in people, and predator odor exposure gives rats lasting stress symptoms. Some rats freeze when they smell the fox-derived odor, while others dig frantically, and those styles were already known to predict later drinking.

Rats that dug during exposure later chose small immediate rewards over larger delayed ones more often, a marker of impulsivity. Digging also tracked with weaker pursuit of sugar rewards before and after the stressor. Exposed females in a second experiment worked harder for both alcohol and sugar when the two competed side by side. Behavior during stress, the authors argue, can flag which animals, and perhaps which people, need watching afterward.
pmc-13492855:
Dsouza reports a 2026 school study in India on iron deficiency anemia, a common cause of tiredness and poor growth. The study tested whether one nurse-led lesson could improve what adolescent girls know about the condition. The session covered 136 girls aged 12 to 15 and used video and lecture over one hour, with knowledge tests before and after.

Scores roughly doubled after the lesson. Seventh standard students gained the most, rising from about six points to over thirteen on the test, and eighth and ninth standard students also improved clearly. Regression analysis showed younger students and girls from lower-income homes gained the most ground. Dsouza argues that short, tailored, nurse-led sessions can close knowledge gaps early, before anemia harms health and schooling.
pmc-13493355:
Matthias Augustin and six colleagues reply in 2026 to critics of their indirect comparison of two eczema biologics, tralokinumab and lebrikizumab, in moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. Rand and colleagues had questioned whether patients counted as responders at week sixteen were truly comparable across the rival trial programs. The authors defend their matching-adjusted comparison point by point.

Both trial families judged week fifty-two success among week sixteen responders using the same thresholds, they note, so the two groups start out alike. Design quirks such as a longer pre-trial washout for topical medicines and different loading doses may have worked against tralokinumab early on. They also attack the rival durability claim, arguing the study behind it used a lab-made copy of their drug rather than the marketed product, which undermines its binding comparisons.
pmc-13493955:
Tilahun and co-authors describe a cleaner way to make a light-driven catalyst that splits water into hydrogen fuel and converts carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide. Their 2026 route starts from a porous crystal containing zinc and cobalt, made in water and ethanol, then bakes it into a mixed oxide threaded with carbon. Instruments confirmed the two oxides touch closely, and electrical tests pointed to an S-scheme, a charge-routing pattern that keeps the strongest electrons available for chemistry.

Under optimised light, the material produced hydrogen at a rate above two thousand micromoles per gram each hour, while turning carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide at a smaller but steady rate. After five reuse cycles it kept nearly all of its activity, losing only a few percent. The waste score of the synthesis was low for this kind of chemistry.
pmc-13494555:
Pavinato and Hey built in 2026 a way to weigh the Darwin worth of each quiet codon swap in the fruit fly. Codons are the three letter words that spell proteins. Some swaps change the word but not the protein, yet flies still seem to pick sides. Past counts of that pick clashed, from none to strong. The new way reads spread marks in wild fly genes alone. No far kin counts, no stock word lists feed it.

All swaps weighed in weak, the team found. Half scored near nil in worth. Yet the scores still called the fly's true word use with sharp aim. Genes read loud used high worth words more, though the lift was mild. Swaps that firm the gene's own fold won a plus too. Weak picks, well weighed, can still shape a genome.
pmc-13494655:
Sudeep Jayaram, Neethu S, and Romesh Bagde report a 2026 mixed-methods study of the mental toll of chronic psoriasis, a long-term skin disease that leaves red, scaly patches. Scores alone cannot show how the disease feels from inside, so the team paired a new questionnaire with deep interviews. Sixty adults at a specialist skin clinic took part, with disease severity graded by a standard index.

Four in five showed moderate to severe loss of quality of life, and near three in four reported mental distress. Embarrassment was the most common feeling, followed by anxiety and low self-worth. Social contact suffered for two thirds, and work for over half. Interviews with twenty patients yielded four themes: felt stigma, emotional burden, pulling away from others, and ways of coping. The authors say care must treat the mind and social life, not the skin alone.
pmc-13495155:
Dènoumi B E Capo-Chichi and colleagues map, in a 2026 study, the genes behind growth and yield in the sweet fig banana, a dessert banana grown in Benin. Yield gains matter for smallholder income and nutrition, yet the base of the trait in this crop was unmapped. The team grew 238 accessions at two sites over several years and scanned their DNA for linked spots.

Using five statistical models across about fifteen hundred DNA markers, they found trait variation and dozens of linked markers, 29 for growth and 16 for yield traits. Most hits came from multi-marker models, and sixteen genes stand as candidates. Height and yield traits each rest on many genetic effects rather than a few big ones. Because linked DNA stretches run long in this banana, some hits may flag blocks of genes. The authors offer the map as a start for marker-guided breeding.
pmc-13498555:
Melkamu W/amlak Tafesse, Yosef Haile Gebremariam, and Samuel Alemu Bamboro survey in 2026 work-related muscle and joint pain among ultrasound staff in two zones of southern Ethiopia. Sonographers hold awkward postures for long scans, yet little local data existed on how often such disorders occur or what drives them. The cross-sectional study ran from September to November 2024 in public and private hospitals.

A total of 313 providers took part, and nearly four in five reported a work-related disorder, most often in the shoulder, then the neck. Pain was more likely where screens could not adjust in height and where staff had no break times. Alternating posture with periodic breaks and reporting no work fatigue each linked to lower odds, pointing to practical changes in equipment and scheduling.
pmc-13499155:
Abigail Balsan and colleagues check in 2026 how often patients who report an allergy to beta-lactam antibiotics truly react to cefazolin, the preferred preventive antibiotic for bone and joint surgery. Reported allergies are common and often push surgeons toward weaker alternatives. Records covered one surgeon's elective orthopaedic patients treated between January 2023 and December 2024, with allergy histories sorted by type and severity.

Of 1,603 patients, about one in five reported such an allergy, most often to penicillin, and nearly all of that group received cefazolin during surgery. No patient in the allergy group had a confirmed true allergic reaction during surgery or the immediate recovery period. The authors conclude that reported labels deserve careful review, since holding back cefazolin on label alone may cost patients the best protection without improving safety.
pmc-13499655:
Mozhgan Alipour and others review magnet-sensing protein teams and their possible links to Alzheimer and Parkinson disease. In 2026, the review joins brain science, life physics, and day-night biology around CRY/MagR teams, which may sense magnet fields through cryptochrome radical pairs and iron-sulphur clusters. Both ills share protein clumping, power unit failure, cell damage, and day-night upset.

Cell and animal evidence suggests these pathways can tune cell damage, energy making, clumping, cell cleanup, and day-night control of nerve fuel use. Direct testing in mammals and humans remains limited and disputed. The authors present magnet-sensing biology as an idea-level platform worth strict testing, not yet a proven disease cause.
pmc-13499755:
Monique Verkerk and Thomas P. Shehata analyze five years of animal forensic postmortems in the Netherlands. In 2026, the look-back study covers 346 necropsies from 390 submissions between 2020 and 2024 to the Forensic Animal Research Foundation, examining suspected non-natural deaths by species, cause, manner, region, and time. Most animals were dogs and cats.

Non-natural deaths accounted for about two thirds of cases, against natural deaths near ten percent, accidents near eight percent, and undetermined cases near fifteen percent. Blunt force trauma and neglect or deprivation led non-natural causes. Legal results, retrieved for eighty cases, mostly brought fines or community service, with only one prison term over six months. The authors call for same-form protocols and stronger institutional support.
pmc-13499855:
Valentina Bugelli leads a 2026 systematic review, the second in a series, on artificial intelligence for estimating how long ago a person died, a central forensic question called the postmortem interval. Decomposition depends on many interacting factors, which makes timing hard and motivates data-driven models. Searches of two major databases up to March 2026 followed current reporting guidance, keeping only studies that applied learning methods to real postmortem data.

Sixty-four studies qualified. Models built on body microbes were most common, followed by chemical and protein approaches and imaging-based systems, with one algorithm family, random forests, used most often in microbe work. Reported accuracy varied widely by data type and interval range. Small datasets, mixed methods, and scarce outside validation limit current proof, so the authors call for large shared datasets and models that fuse several data sources.
pmc-13500055:
Anthony L Frank and co-authors present in 2026 a puzzling case after weight-loss bypass surgery, where severe dumping symptoms and stubborn obesity coexisted. Dumping syndrome strikes when food rushes too fast into the small bowel after stomach surgery, causing flushing, cramps, and later low blood sugar. The classic bypass design limits this with a small stomach pouch. Their patient was a 65-year-old woman with prior bypass and revisions who suffered debilitating after-meal symptoms alongside class III obesity.

Camera examination found no pouch or stomach lining at all, with small-bowel tissue starting right below the gullet, an anatomy matching her poor food tolerance, absent fullness signals, and weight regain. Starting tirzepatide, a gut-hormone drug, brought real symptom relief and a notable drop in body mass index. Missing operative records and no objective dumping tests limit firm conclusions, which the authors state plainly.
pmc-13500855:
Razoan Al Rimon leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 mouse study of heart repair after myocardial infarction, the tissue death caused by a blocked coronary artery. The team focused on ADAM17, a cell-surface protease that rises in ischemic heart disease, and switched it off only in endothelial cells. Unexpectedly, male mice lacking endothelial ADAM17 fared worse after infarction: 42 percent died of left ventricle rupture, compared with 13 percent of controls, and heart function kept declining.

Single-nuclei RNA sequencing showed suppressed vessel-growth and tissue-transition markers. It also found a new endothelial population rich in necroptosis markers, a programmed form of cell rupture. Blood vessel density inside the infarct fell, and removing the extra immune cells that accumulated did not rescue survival. Blocking necroptosis with necrostatin-1 markedly improved survival and vessel growth, identifying that death pathway as a key driver of the poor repair.
pmc-13501555:
Mansour Arad leads a five-author team presenting a 2026 umbrella review of moral distress among nurses, a synthesis that gathers earlier systematic reviews rather than primary studies. Moral distress arises when a nurse judges an action ethically right yet cannot take it because of outside constraints. The team searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar up to 10 March 2025, following JBI umbrella review methodology and PRISMA 2020 reporting. Quality was checked with the JBI critical appraisal checklist.

Of 435 records found, 19 systematic reviews published between 2009 and 2025 qualified. Reported distress levels varied by setting and measuring instrument, but intensive care, coronary care, and oncology units consistently scored highest. Contributing factors included younger age, female gender, poor teamwork, scarce resources, and care perceived as futile. Consequences ranged from burnout and depression to medication errors and plans to leave nursing.
pmc-13502555:
Malthe Kjær Bendtsen leads an eighteen-author team reporting a 2026 hunt for enzymes that can digest polyurethane and nylon, two plastics with no industrial recycling route. Enzyme discovery usually mines sequences related to a handful of known examples. This team instead bioprospected legacy plastic waste, feeding bacteria fluorescent plastic mimics and using fluorescence-assisted cell sorting to pull out the eaters. Twenty-nine degrading bacteria surfaced, and mass spectrometry with homology searching pinned down twelve enzymes.

The newcomers outperformed the wild-type enzymes on two axes at once: they tolerated more heat and hydrolysed polyurethane polymers and nylon textiles faster. To the authors' knowledge, these are the first enzymes shown to attack longer chains of polyurethane and nylon, including crosslinked polyurethane, the form that defeats most recycling. The enzymes are offered as starting points for protein engineering campaigns and for guiding computer-based searches for more candidates.
pmc-13503655:
Xiaogang Zhou and three co-authors examine how digital change at work helps staff thrive, in a 2026 survey study. They draw on a theory that treats energy, tools, and support as resources staff try to keep and grow. The study asks whether reshaping one's own job is the path that links the two.

The team surveyed 326 staff in three waves over time and tested the links with a path model. Digital change raised thriving both on its own and through job crafting, where staff adjust tasks and ties at work. Good mood made the effect stronger. The authors urge firms to allow flexible work design and tasks matched to each person.
pmc-13503855:
Simone Balin and others analyze how around surgery steroids affect tumor-infiltrating natural killer cells in brain cancer. In 2026, the single-cell RNA reading study studies immune cells from five IDH-wildtype glioblastomas, two patients treated with dexamethasone and three untreated, with two non-tumor brain samples. Dexamethasone controls around tumors swelling but suppresses immunity.

Steroid contact reshaped inside tumors natural killer cells toward CD56bright subsets and weakened effector programs, with lower cytotoxicity and swelling scores, reduced granzymes, perforin, cytokines, and activating docks, and higher inhibitory molecules. Pathway analysis showed strong fall of natural-killer killing. If larger cohorts confirm this, minimizing steroid contact could improve immune care.
pmc-13503955:
Fan Yu leads a team tuning the recipe for porous concrete that quiets road noise, in a 2026 paper. The material must soak up sound, bear load, and let water drain, three goals that pull against each other. The team aimed to balance all three by design rather than trial and error.

They trained a stacked ensemble model on lab and published data to predict sound uptake, reaching a fit score of 0.97. A genetic search then weighed that model against strength and drainage models to find blends on the best trade-off curve. Stone grading mattered most for sound. The chosen blend met strength and drainage standards while beating all single-size stone mixes on sound uptake. Lab checks landed within about nine percent of the forecast.
pmc-13505055:
Rong Zhou leads a team building explainable AI tools that classify atopic dermatitis in children and adults, in a 2026 study. The itchy skin condition is common, yet adult risk profiling lags and survey data are heavily lopsided toward healthy cases. Plain models trained on such data score little better than chance.

The team drew more than twenty-two thousand people from a U.S. national health survey, split into child and adult groups. After rebalancing the classes and tuning several model types, accuracy rose into the mid-to-high eighties, with strong curve scores. Explanation tools showed which facts drove each call. Diet antioxidants pointed opposite ways in children and adults, a clue that the condition's drivers shift with age.
pmc-13505155:
Jie Liu and colleagues built a vacuum-stabilised window that lets researchers watch living mouse lungs under a microscope while the animal keeps breathing. Earlier methods blurred or could not follow vessel movement and cell signals together. Their setup combines two-photon imaging, glowing tracers in the blood, and a calcium sensor placed only in vessel-wall muscle cells.

When oxygen dropped for thirty minutes, small lung arteries narrowed over time, shrinking about eight percent in mid-sized vessels. Calcium signals inside the muscle cells rose before each narrowing, with the earliest responses in the smallest arteries watched. A drug called dasatinib delayed the calcium response and changed its rhythm, mainly in mid-sized vessels. The platform gives physiologists a direct view of how lung vessels sense low oxygen, a reaction that can turn harmful in lung hypertension.
pmc-13506155:
Immad Attique and co-authors describe a 67-year-old woman who developed Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, often called broken heart syndrome, two weeks after influenza A. Flu is known to trigger heart attacks and heart muscle inflammation, but this stress-type weakening of the heart has rarely been reported after it. Most earlier cases began during the infection or within a few days.

She first came to the emergency department with cough, body aches, and chest pain, tested positive for influenza A, and went home with antiviral medicine. Two weeks later she returned with repeated squeezing chest pain brought on by walking, plus shortness of breath. The delay makes her case stand out from the handful published before. The authors walk through her presentation, tests, and care so that clinicians keep this rare delayed complication in mind when chest pain follows a flu illness.
pmc-13506555:
Jacob W McPherson, Christopher K Williams, Alicia M Berlin, and John M Coluccy report 2026 measurements of energy use in two duck species with falling numbers. Working with captive American black ducks and lesser scaup in Maryland, they measured resting metabolic rate, the energy a bird uses at rest. They also measured how much each behavior raises that rate.

Resting rates fell inside ranges reported before, while behavior costs differed by species and from older values. Cold water raised energy demand for active black ducks, and heavier birds spent more energy in both species. Refined numbers should improve models that estimate how much winter habitat a landscape can support.
pmc-13507155:
Jing-hao Chen, Yi-de Chen, Feng Jia, Lian Gu, and Xiao-yu Qiu study, in 2026 work, what drives public willingness to use government digital humans, virtual avatars that answer questions and handle services.
