China has launched such avatars for tax help and self-service tasks. Their survey model blends expectation confirmation theory with a classic technology acceptance model.

When the avatar met prior hopes, satisfaction rose, and satisfaction raised intent to keep using the service. Six felt qualities carried that effect, including information quality, smarts, ease, appeal, usefulness, and trust in the AI. The authors advise agencies to lift usefulness, smarts, information quality, and appeal first. Better felt quality should raise use rates for digital public services.
pmc-13507355:
Hassan Ali, Samar Fatima, Tanvir Hussain, and Khawar Ismail compare, in 2026 work, two oxide nanopowders, spinel nickel ferrite and perovskite calcium manganite, for energy-related uses. Both families promise magnetic and electrical traits useful in storage and shielding devices. Powders made by the same gel route were baked across wide temperature ranges.

X-ray patterns confirmed both crystal structures, with best grain sizes near 25 nanometers for the ferrite and near 15 for the manganite. Computer calculations echoed the measured structures. Magnet testing showed the ferrite strongly magnetic, reaching 29.61 emu per gram at saturation. The manganite managed only 1.71 emu per gram by the same measure. The ferrite suits magnetic roles; the manganite leans dielectric.
pmc-13507755:
Jacob H. Brady and four colleagues published this 2026 study on reviving axon growth in the visual pathway using two micro-RNAs, gene regulators named miR-135a-1-3p and miR-135b-3p. Both are active during development and switched down as neurons mature and lose regrowth ability. The team profiled the miR-135 family in mouse retinal ganglion cells and cortical neurons, then tested whether restoring these two in adults could restart growth after optic nerve injury.

Injury pushed the two micro-RNAs lower still. Delivering mimics of them into retinal ganglion cells protected the neurons and promoted axon regeneration after optic nerve crush. Combined with a fibronectin-based helper protein the team developed, a subset of axons regrew the full length of the optic nerve. Gene profiling showed growth programmes switched back on in treated cells. The authors propose the pair for treating central nervous system injuries, which heal poorly.
pmc-13508455:
Yan Jiang and Wei Qin study how a no-insulin-needed score for insulin resistance relates to high blood pressure, in 2026 work. The score, METS-IR, is built from blood and body measures. The cross-sectional study covered 1,592 participants, of whom nearly three fifths had hypertension. Models adjusted for age, sex, lifestyle, diabetes, and fatty liver. Curved fitting methods checked whether risk rises evenly with the score or bends at some point.

Each step up in the score raised hypertension odds overall. The curve bent at a threshold in the middle of the range. Below that point, each unit added a hefty rise in odds. Above it, the rise flattened yet stayed real. The pattern differed by sex, body weight, diabetes, and fatty liver status. The authors offer the score as a research marker for pressure risk, while stressing that a one-time study cannot prove it causes hypertension.
pmc-13508555:
Lisa Schmelkin and six co-authors revisit a claim that interaction effects between gene sites lock proteins into their history during neutral evolution, in 2026 work. Entrenchment means a once-tolerated building block later becomes unacceptable as other sites change. Recent computer studies using energy models suggested this arises even when evolution is neutral, with no advantage driving change. The authors suspected the models cheat: they were trained on mixed relatives, letting swaps through that neutral theory would forbid. They reran the simulations with a guard that blocks any swap leaving the neutral zone.

With non-neutral swaps removed, entrenchment mostly vanished. The protein clock's ticking stayed modest and traced to how many lineages showed interaction-driven rate differences, not to lock-in. The authors conclude entrenchment is not a built-in feature of neutral change with interactions. Their baseline helps others spot when entrenchment claims need adaptive explanations instead.
pmc-13511855:
Ebtihal Alharbi and Yousef Almehmadi report a data analysis study, published in 2026. It asks whether activity of a gene called SPAG1 predicts spread of prostate tumours. The spread target is the pelvic lymph nodes. Knowing nodal status before surgery matters. Removing those nodes is a high-risk procedure. The team analysed 497 patients in The Cancer Genome Atlas. Matched clinical and RNA data were used.

Higher SPAG1 expression was associated with confirmed nodal metastasis. This held independently. It added a modest but robust improvement in prediction. Standard clinical staging was the baseline. The authors suggest its value lies in preoperative prediction of nodal involvement. Validation in biopsy samples from independent groups is pending.
pmc-13511955:
Likuan Liu and colleagues sequenced the full chloroplast genome of Myricaria squamosa, a medicinal shrub of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau. Chloroplasts are the green cell parts that run photosynthesis, and their genome helps place species on the family tree.

The genome runs 154,689 letters long with a GC content of 36.3 percent, and carries 129 working genes in total. Those genes split into 84 protein-coding genes, 37 transfer RNA genes, and eight ribosomal RNA genes. The team also mapped 214 short repeat markers useful for telling populations and relatives apart. Family-tree analysis placed the shrub closest to Myricaria laxiflora, Liu reports, giving the genus a firmer genomic footing.
pmc-13514555:
İbrahim Doğan leads a seven-author team examining, in a 2026 retrospective cohort study, whether losing weight quickly early in treatment predicts keeping it off. Regain after lifestyle-based obesity care is common, and clinicians debate whether a fast start helps or sets patients up to rebound. The team followed adults at a tertiary obesity clinic, measuring early loss at three months and checking at one year who had regained at least half of their maximum loss.

Among 79 participants with complete records, only nine crossed that regain threshold within the year. Larger early losses came with clearly lower odds of significant regain, even after accounting for age and starting weight, and the pattern held in women-only and alternative statistical checks. Doğan's group takes the result as reassurance that a strong early response is a good sign, not a warning.
pmc-13516055: Zhongnan Hu and eight colleagues issue a correction notice for their 2026 Pharmaceuticals study of Artemisia extracts against H1N1 influenza A virus. During a review after publication, the team found an accidental duplicate panel in Figure 9B. The correction explains that the figure has been fully remade from raw data of independent repeated experiments. Only the image layout changed, and the authors state the study's conclusions are unaffected. The journal's academic editor approved the change, and the original article has been updated.
pmc-13517155:
Shuaishuai Wu and five colleagues review the hidden regulatory layers that shape mastitis risk in dairy cows in a 2026 article. Udder infection costs the industry billions yearly, and DNA sequence alone explains only part of why some cows resist it. Four further layers matter: chemical tags on DNA, small regulatory RNAs, marks placed on messenger RNA, and the protein spools that package the genome.

The review ties all four to one immune switchboard, the TLR to NF-κB axis, which fires the mammary gland's response to invaders such as Staph aureus and E coli. Marks in milk or blood could flag at-risk cows without invasive sampling. Wu's team looks ahead to breeding that selects on these marks, drugs that tune them, and gene-editing tools that rewrite them. The prize is durable udder health with less antibiotic use across herds.
pmc-13517655:
Ádám Kerek and five colleagues run a safety-first pilot of a bacteria-killing virus product in broiler chickens in a 2026 study. Bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria, promise antibiotic-sparing disease control, yet farm products need tolerance proof before efficacy trials. One hundred twenty Ross 308 birds drank water with Fagovet, a commercial multi-phage mix, for twenty-seven days at the label rate or at threefold and fivefold overdoses, against untreated controls.

Weight gain and feed intake held steady at every dose. No consistent dose-linked pattern of illness, death, or post-mortem damage appeared. The authors are frank about limits: doses were set by product volume, not by counted viruses in the water, and the mix's parts were never separately profiled. They present the results as short-term tolerance of this formulation in unchallenged birds, a green light for stricter studies with measured exposure and real pathogen challenge.
pmc-13518855:
Misa Ito and colleagues uncover in 2026 a backup system for clearing toxic free heme, the iron-bearing fragment released when red blood cells burst. Severe hemolysis overwhelms the usual scavenger proteins, letting heme poison organs. Their work names scavenger receptor BI, a liver protein better known for handling cholesterol particles, as the missing route.

Mice lacking the receptor in the liver cleared heme poorly and died more easily under heme stress. Raising receptor levels with the drug imatinib or gene delivery protected animals. In a humanized sickle cell model, diseased livers carried less of the receptor, and restoring it rescued the mice. The pathway offers a fresh treatment target for hemolytic disorders.
pmc-13518955:
Sergei Tarasov and Josef Uyeda deliver a 2026 mathematical verdict on popular evolution models that test whether a trait speeds up or slows down species diversification. These state-dependent speciation and extinction models are used in over a thousand studies, yet they notoriously cry wolf with false positives. A prior bombshell showed related models can be fundamentally unidentifiable.

Tarasov and Uyeda prove unidentifiability is universal in this model family once hidden states are included: any trait-free scenario matches infinitely many trait-driven ones. They offer an analytical fix that works within each equivalence class and prove no other congruence type exists. False positives, they argue, actually stem from model misspecification and model proliferation across classes, pointing to cleaner testing strategies.
pmc-13519255:
Alfonso M. Cueto-Manzano and four colleagues review in 2026 whether Mexico has enough kidney specialists for its growing chronic kidney disease burden. The disease has climbed the global cause-of-death rankings, and Mexico sits among the top ten countries for end-stage kidney disease incidence, driven by diabetes, obesity, and hypertension.

Registry data come only from Jalisco and Aguascalientes states, since no national registry exists. The Mexican Board of Nephrology counted 1,668 certified active nephrologists in December 2025, split between adult and pediatric practice. Latin America averages 19 nephrologists per million people, below the regional target of 20. Early referral improves outcomes, so the authors frame workforce growth as a direct clinical lever.
pmc-13519855:
Fidaa Mohammed Eltigani leads a seven-author systematic review and meta-analysis in 2026 on whether eye scans reveal vascular damage in adults with ischemic stroke or carotid artery narrowing. The retina's tiny vessels mirror the brain's circulation and can be pictured without contact with OCT and OCT angiography, raising hopes for a window into brain vessel health.

Pooled results showed lower deep retinal vessel density in patient groups, with modest differences in nerve fiber and ganglion cell layers. Several other measures ran lower too, though study gaps were large. Most evidence was observational with mid-level bias concerns and few pooled comparisons. Eltigani's team concludes the measures describe group gaps but are not proven for diagnosis or prognosis.
pmc-13520255:
Yoriko Nomura leads a six-author case report in 2026 on autoimmune encephalitis, brain inflammation triggered by the immune system, striking a liver cancer patient on modern immunotherapy. A 66-year-old Japanese man with tumors in both liver lobes began atezolizumab plus bevacizumab, a standard combination for advanced disease.

Fever, diarrhea, and appetite loss appeared on day 8, and confusion brought him to hospital on day 10, restless and incoherent. Spinal fluid showed raised monocyte counts, pointing to immune-driven brain inflammation rather than infection. Three days of high-dose steroid pulses turned him around dramatically by the second day, and he went home on day 13. Nomura and colleagues stress fast recognition as these drugs spread.
pmc-13520355:
Hande Gurbuz and colleagues compare in 2026 two ways of numbing children for placement of a brain fluid drain, a procedure usually done under general anaesthesia. One group received scalp nerve blocks with sedation, while the other had general anaesthesia plus numbing at the cut site.

Data covered 63 procedures in children under eight years. Heart-rate jumps at incision were far rarer with nerve blocks, and pain relief needs in the first day were also lower. No detail on conversions is given in the opening summary beyond the comparison itself. For anaesthesia teams, the results support blocks as a way to avoid full general anaesthesia in selected children.
pmc-13520455:
Tingfen Wang, Tingyu Wang and Runfeng Zhang test in 2026 a simple blood ratio as a guide to heart artery narrowing. The ratio divides uric acid by creatinine. Angiography judges narrowing well but is invasive and costly. A cheap blood clue could help sort patients first.

The study held 528 patients with heart disease. The ratio rose step by step as lesions grew worse. The ratio stayed a strong marker after other factors were counted. Curve tests beat either part of the ratio alone. A stated cut-off balanced missed cases and false alarms. The authors propose the ratio as an add-on tool, not a swap for scans when scans are due.
pmc-13520755:
Raeghan H O'Leary and colleagues describe in 2026 patients who left a tertiary emergency department without being seen during the year 2025, grouped by neighbourhood income. Leaving unseen can signal system strain and may lead to worse outcomes for those who walk away.

Records held 7,221 such visits at Saint John Regional Hospital, with income linkage succeeding for most visits. Median age was 36 years, with women making up just over half. Visits clustered most heavily in the lowest income neighbourhoods and least in the highest. Recorded primary care status also differed by income group, adding context beyond simple wait-time counts.
pmc-13521455:
Shih-Wei Chiang, Chuan-Yi Yang and Guan-Yu Chen present in 2026 a practical gut-on-chip routine for filming how the intestinal barrier reacts while living E. coli bacteria share the channel. Flat static cultures lack flow forces, while animal work resists detailed live imaging.

A commercial two-channel chip held human gut cells under gentle flow, forming a sealed, polarised layer with continuous junctions and a mucus coat. Labelled bacteria were then added at varied flow rates. Slow flow allowed bacterial overgrowth that thinned and detached the layer within four days, while faster tolerated flow protected structure. Settings guidance should help labs run reproducible co-cultures.
pmc-13521955:
Le-le Ma and colleagues built a catalyst that splits seawater into hydrogen without the usual trade-off between speed and durability. The catalyst swaps in single atoms of samarium, a rare earth metal, into a nickel-molybdenum oxide base.

The swap turns on two reaction routes at once, one using surface-bound atoms and one using oxygen inside the material. At 70 degrees in seawater-like fluid, the catalyst needed only 214 millivolts of extra voltage at strong industrial current. It then ran steadily for 1,500 hours, and early cost checks put its hydrogen near 2.56 US dollars per kilogram. Ma frames the design as a step toward large-scale green hydrogen made straight from seawater.
pmc-13522355:
Alexis Bunster and colleagues compare in 2026 gene activity in young giant kelp from three Chilean zones. Kelp faced cool, mild and warm water in tanks. The hunt seeks signs of local heat fit in a key seaweed. Zones were Atacama, southern Chile and Magallanes.

Stats tests pitched home water against foreign water. That split flags true local edge patterns. Gene sets split by zone, a sign of split pressures. Atacama kelp raised shield genes and protein turnover genes in warmth. Magallanes kelp met cold with a detox path and light-shield pigments. Named genes now await lab proof for kelp rescue in warming seas.
pmc-13522455:
Kim and colleagues reported in 2026 bead catalysts that recycle PET plastic by breaking it back into a single building block. The process, glycolysis, turns waste PET into the monomer BHET, but metal catalysts leave harmful residues and other options cost too much to recover. Their beads are large, porous, and built from polyanions, chains carrying many negative charges, so they can be fished out by simple filtering.

Kim showed the beads kept working over more than 30 reuse cycles, holding monomer yield near nine in ten each time. In a stirred tank run continuously, they converted about eight in ten of the PET fed in over four hours. Cost and life-cycle checks put the product's minimum selling price near that of virgin BHET, with a far lower warming footprint than new PET. The design makes closed-loop plastic recycling easier to scale.
pmc-13522555:
Alice Guerra and colleagues revisit how much teenagers think their parents know about their lives and whether that belief protects against gambling in a 2026 Italian study. Data came from two waves of a nationally representative school survey covering nearly twenty-five thousand adolescents. The analysis traced direct links and indirect paths through risk perception, peer norms, and awareness of legal age limits.

Teenagers who believed their parents knew more gambled less often, both directly and through stronger risk perception and weaker peer gambling norms. Results held across groups, including for online gambling frequency. The authors conclude that perceived parental knowledge still buffers adolescent gambling despite recent digital and social change, a finding relevant to family-based prevention work.
pmc-13523255:
Amer Alzahrani leads a team pooling prospective studies of inhaled nitric oxide after lung transplantation in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. The gas widens blood vessels and counters oxidative damage, and it has been proposed to limit graft injury after transplant. Six eligible studies covering four hundred twenty patients were found across four databases through September 2024.

Patients receiving the gas showed a trend toward less severe early graft dysfunction, yet the difference did not reach statistical significance. No significant differences appeared for intensive care stay, time on a ventilator, or death within thirty days. Treatment was well tolerated in the included studies. The authors conclude that larger, high-quality trials are needed before routine preventive use can be recommended.
pmc-13526055:
Jacopo D'Argenzio and colleagues examine, in a 2026 retrospective cohort study, whether spleen signals on imaging predict early progression in diffuse large B cell lymphoma, an aggressive blood cancer. Spleen uptake of a glucose tracer on PET scans and spleen volume on CT were tested together, including how the two interact.

The cohort held 124 newly diagnosed adults, of whom about thirty-six percent showed spleen uptake above liver background. A standard prognostic index predicted both early progression and progression-free survival. Spleen uptake positivity predicted progression within thirty-six months but not overall progression-free survival. An interaction emerged, where larger spleen volume raised risk only in patients without spleen uptake, while volume was neutral when uptake was present. A sensitivity analysis softened the interaction, and the authors ask for external validation.
pmc-13526755:
Hussain and colleagues present a 2026 review of how drought stress, simulated in the lab with the chemical PEG, affects stevia, the plant behind a zero-calorie sweetener.  The review gathers studies on growth, chemistry, antioxidant defenses, and the sweet compounds called steviol glycosides.

Drought shrank plant height, leaf area, and total mass, the traits growers are paid for. In some studies roots grew longer instead, a foraging response that helps the plant hunt for water. Cells raised their antioxidant enzymes, the proteins that neutralize the harmful oxygen forms drought creates. Sweet compound production also shifted under stress. The double edge matters for farming in dry regions: mild stress may concentrate sweetness, but the yield loss usually outweighs it, so watering strategy must balance both.
pmc-13528155:
Jean Carlos de Goveia and four colleagues survey activity habits among students of physical education at a public university in Brazil in a 2026 study. One hundred ninety students took part. Their mean age was about twenty-one. Just over half were men. Forms covered background, a short activity survey, and a lifestyle score. Activity counted as enough at one hundred fifty minutes a week.

About ninety-four percent met the activity bar. About eighty-three percent showed an adequate lifestyle overall. Yet about thirty-eight percent were overweight or obese. Almost nothing predicted who fell short on activity. Background, diet, smoking, drinking, sleep, and leisure all missed. Only negative view of one's own health linked with inactivity, and strongly. The authors say future health promoters mostly practice what they will preach. Self-perception may be the lever that matters.
pmc-13528355:
Máté Hartyányi and Roland Nagy sketch a working frame for sustainable chemical technology in a 2026 short paper. Green chemistry guides safer reactions at the molecule scale. Real-world impact, though, often hinges on bigger choices. Separations, solvents, energy use, and supply chains dominate at scale. Their frame sorts choices into four levels: material, process, system, and life cycle.

Four core fields follow from the frame. They span feedstocks and raw resources, how reactions and plants are designed, solvent choice with separations, and closing loops on waste. Each field lists typical levers and trade-offs. A light assessment bundle is proposed for judging options. Quick screening scores pair with life-cycle thinking. The aim is to stop gains in one corner shifting harm elsewhere. The authors target readers from first lab work to plant adoption.
pmc-13529155:
Kara and Kara interviewed Turkish nurses who care for Syrian refugees in Hatay, a border province hosting many of the millions of Syrians in Türkiye. Their 2026 qualitative study used in-depth interviews with sixteen nurses, each lasting about half an hour, analyzed with a standard phenomenological method for lived experience. The nurses all provided direct care to refugee patients in daily practice.

Kara organized the accounts into four themes covering work challenges, trouble understanding health needs, blocked access to care, and successful coping strategies. Language barriers and differing health beliefs made accurate histories hard to obtain, while trauma signs and gender-sensitive needs were lost in translation. Long registration steps plus a shortage of trained interpreters delayed care. Nurses improvised with phone translation apps, coworker help, and emotional self-management, but the authors stress that lasting institutional support, revised training, and reliable interpreter resources remain limited.
pmc-13530155:
Yingke Zhang studies wind safety in 2026 for tall buildings joined by an elevated corridor. Such linked towers bend easily and damp motion poorly, leaving them sensitive to gusts. Computer airflow modeling joined with structural simulation measured sway and twisting under steady wind loads.

Two defenses received testing: a streamlined airfoil-shaped section and the connecting corridor itself. Square and oval towers served as comparison cases. Floor-to-floor drift and twist angle judged each design. The analysis showed how shape and linkage change peak movement, giving designers numbers for support choices and wind limits in future linked towers.
pmc-13531755:
Hanbo Lu and colleagues pit two leading chatbots against each other in 2026 on urology exam questions from China. A total of 809 single-choice questions from the national attending physician exam were put to ChatGPT-4o and DeepSeek R1. Each model answered in basic mode, deep-thinking mode, and web-search mode.

DeepSeek R1 beat its rival in every mode, with accuracy in the low-to-mid eighties against the high seventies. Its edge grew on complex case-based questions, and its scores varied less across modes. The authors see promise for exam preparation in Chinese settings, not yet for live clinical advice.
pmc-13531855:
Igor Lurin and co-authors report a 2026 war injury case where a drone shrapnel fragment traveled through a soldier heart into a gut artery. The 41-year-old serviceman took a chest wound from an FPV drone munition in the Russia-Ukraine war. Layered scans traced a channel from chest to abdomen and found metal lodged inside the superior mesenteric artery.

No critical gut starvation appeared, so surgery waited for consent and planning. On day 14 surgeons opened the abdomen, cut the artery, removed the fragment, and repaired the wall. The patient recovered and left care after 21 days.
pmc-13532955:
Mike van Kessel and colleagues test in 2026 a long-held claim about electroconvulsive therapy for major depression. Some have argued that loss of personal memories after treatment helps lift depression by fading painful recollections. The team studied 71 patients and checked memory steadiness and mood scores before and within one week after therapy.

Patients who reached remission had less memory loss, not more, with the clearest gap for recent memories. Older age and a shorter episode also raised the odds of remission. Readers see direct proof against the idea that forgetting personal events drives the benefit of this therapy.
pmc-13537455:
Nadia A Rojas and colleagues link sleep habits to thinking scores in middle-aged Latina women in a rural California farm community in a 2026 study. Data came from five hundred women with an average age near forty-nine years, surveyed between 2022 and 2024. Night sleep length, sleep quality, and weekly nap counts came from self-report. A standard battery supplied global and domain scores for memory, control, and word fluency.

Memory followed a curved pattern with sleep length, favoring a middle range over short or long sleep. One or two naps weekly tracked with better memory yet lower word fluency, while three or more naps tracked with worse memory. Sleep quality showed no clear link to any score. The authors frame sleep as a changeable factor for lowering dementia risk and urge longer follow-up.
pmc-13538655:
Jonathan Munro and colleagues hunted early Parkinson's signs in the eyes of monkeys given a Parkinson's-causing toxin. Published in 2026, the study measured four monkeys before and after MPTP, a toxin that kills dopamine neurons. Parkinson's is now spotted from movement signs, by which time about half the key midbrain signal cells are already gone.

Eye-current tests showed slower daylight-wave timing and smaller wave ripples in both daylight and dim settings after the toxin. Pupils also stayed wider after light, and post-mortem checks found a thinner outer retina layer with fewer signal-making and light-sensing cells. All told, the results point to eye changes that current tests can pick up before movement signs appear. Readers get new early clues for spotting Parkinson's.
pmc-13538755:
Abby Yu and colleagues weigh the costs of team diabetes care before surgery in Australia in a 2026 trial-based study. Adults with poorly controlled diabetes awaiting planned non-heart surgery got a team pre-surgery service. A model compared their costs and outcomes against usual care, drawing on the trial, national surgery data, and past studies.

The service arm had fewer patients back in hospital for infections within thirty days. Total cost per patient also ran lower, saving several thousand dollars each. Seven returns per hundred treated were avoided. Chance-based testing gave the service a very high chance of staying both cheaper and better. The authors call the service good value from the hospital view.
pmc-13538955:
Karin Wallin and colleagues gather expert agreement on health care that supports sexual and reproductive health for young women with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Living with the condition can complicate sexual health without tailored support. An expert panel rated candidate care parts across two survey rounds. The panel mixed young women aged 19 to 29 years with the condition and staff from sexual health and mental health clinics.

Agreement formed on about two thirds of the statements. Top picks included training staff on the condition and sexual health in both clinic types, including hormone effects. Routine questions about sex, partner ties, and sexual violence ranked high. Easy-to-reach care, info for all, group talks, and weaving sexual health into current teaching also scored well. The authors outline a cross-clinic package for safer, more positive care.
pmc-13540855:
Clara Heinze and three colleagues follow, in a 2026 longitudinal study, a health promotion program rolled out across eight Danish vocational schools using a whole-systems approach. Such schools serve many young people from poorer backgrounds, where unhealthy habits cluster and programs often fade away.

Quarterly interviews with coordinators and managers, fifty-nine in all, were mapped for ripple effects over two years. Forty-two actions had been put in place, and six schools reported real structural, relational, or deeper change. Two pathways explained most success: change driven from inside by committed staff, and change backed by outside community partners. Turnover, time pressure, and workplace training spells were the main brakes.
pmc-13540955:
Janani Pinidiyapathirage and five colleagues evaluate, in a 2026 study, an Australian rural medical training programme called Longlook, designed to pull graduates toward country practice where shortages bite hardest. Students spend long clerkship stretches in rural communities instead of rotating through city hospitals.

Records covered Griffith University graduates from 2010 to 2023, of whom 384 spent at least a year in the programme. Longlook graduates outperformed metropolitan peers academically and stated stronger rural intentions. Two thirds of those completing the full two years were practising rurally in 2024, against about a third after a single year. Specialty and location data came from the national practitioner register.
pmc-13542155:
Jiahui Yang and colleagues surveyed mitophagy, the cell's cleanup of damaged energy hubs, as a shield for neurons. Published in 2026, the review explains how neurons, with huge energy needs and weak regrowth, suffer when energy hubs fail. Failure drains energy, spills harmful oxygen, and upsets calcium, driving stress and cell death.

Mitophagy clears broken mitochondria through the cell's reuse route, guarding energy output and network health. Control routes include PINK1-Parkin and docking paths with BNIP3 and FUNDC1. Weak mitophagy marks Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, ALS, and Huntington's disease, adding to damage and nerve stress. Drug, gene, and diet plans that boost mitophagy show early hope but face a hard clinic leap. Readers get a map of a strong target for saving neurons.
pmc-13543355:
Yan and colleagues built a sharper scalpel for plant genetics: an improved laser capture method that cuts defined cell groups from rice flower tissue and extracts messenger RNA clean enough to sequence. The prize is the branch meristem, the growing tip whose decisions set how many branches, and thus grains, a rice panicle carries. Their 2026 protocol adds an integrity check for the minute RNA amounts involved. It then profiles three meristem types: the initial inflorescence tip and the primary and secondary branch tips it produces.

Differentiation rewired the transcriptome extensively, with hormone-making, hormone-moving, and hormone-responding genes shifting significantly at each step. Follow-up tests with targeted amplification and tissue staining confirmed the sequencing: three selected genes lit up strongly in both branch meristem types, marking them as candidate regulators of the branching decision.
pmc-13543455:
Ekaterina Nadbitova and colleagues published a 2026 replication study testing a reported genetic modifier of spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 in Japan. This inherited movement disorder is caused by a repeated DNA segment in the ATXN3 gene; repeat length predicts onset age only partly. A study in European and American cohorts had linked a PRKN gene variant, especially in two-copy carriers, to earlier onset. The team genotyped 228 Japanese patients with the ataxia and 260 patients with a related type as comparison.

Variant frequencies in patients matched both the comparison group and East Asian reference data. Only two patients carried the double copy of interest, leaving the study little power for that exact claim. Comparing single-copy carriers instead, onset age and repeat length were essentially identical, and adjusted analysis found no link between the variant and onset. Repeat length remained a strong predictor. The reported modifier effect did not replicate here.
pmc-13543555:
In 2026, Baiye Chen and colleagues published a study tracing how low oxygen drives hypertrophic scars, the thick raised scars that follow abnormal wound healing. Scar tissue and cultured scar fibroblasts were compared with normal counterparts, and two proteins were manipulated: HIF-1alpha, the cell's oxygen sensor, and NREP, a protein tied to regeneration. Reporter and binding assays tested whether the sensor directly switches the second gene on.

Scar tissue carried much more of both proteins, plus more of the activated form of a collagen-promoting signal. Low oxygen raised both proteins in fibroblasts and spurred growth and collagen output; silencing either one cancelled those effects. The sensor bound the NREP gene's switch region directly, and extra NREP restored growth even when the sensor was silenced, acting through the TGF-beta and Smad pathway. Blocking this axis is offered as a strategy against stubborn scars.
pmc-13547755:
Yuna Jo, Ju Hyeon Kim, and Hyung Chul Lee studied in 2026 how the edge of a chick embryo's early cell sheet grips the membrane around the yolk. It needs that hold to spread evenly. Classical work showed the edge is naturally sticky, yet where that stickiness lives and how it changes over time were murky. The team cut tissue pieces from defined regions at several stages and laid them on the membrane to test their grip.

Pieces from edge regions stuck at every freshly cut side early on, while later the grip narrowed to the far edge only. In cultured pieces the sticky zone widened beyond its size in the intact embryo, and the molecular marks of edge identity spread unevenly through it. The authors conclude that physical grip and molecular identity are coordinated but partly independent.
pmc-13548655:
Weiqiang Liang and colleagues divide brain tumors into imaging neighborhoods to predict dangerous glioma types before surgery, in a 2026 radiomics study. Diffuse gliomas vary hugely in genetics and outlook, and a scan that reads that risk early could shape treatment. Using perfusion MRI from 197 adults, the team clustered tumor and surrounding swelling into habitats with similar blood flow, then mined hundreds of measurements from each habitat to train a classifier.

Habitat models beat whole-tumor models at spotting high-risk molecular types. Blood flow features alone outperformed standard anatomical images, and the best model used only flow data from the combined habitats. Adding ordinary sequences on top brought no gain. The authors conclude that how a glioma is plumbed, mapped region by region, carries the strongest signal of its aggression.
pmc-13550455:
Li Kong and colleagues work out how matrine, a plant alkaloid, kills retinoblastoma cells, in a 2026 laboratory study of the childhood eye cancer. Combining network pharmacology with protein profiling, the team intersected the compound's predicted targets with the disease's and landed on a nuclear receptor, NR1D2, as the key responder. Experiments then followed two standard retinoblastoma cell lines.

Matrine slowed growth in proportion to dose and time, curbed migration, and pushed cells into programmed death. It sharply lowered NR1D2 at both message and protein level. Silencing the receptor copied the death effect, while restoring it blunted matrine's action, proving the receptor sits on the causal path. Downstream, the survival pathway PI3K and AKT kept their totals but lost their activating phosphates, and the cell-death protein balance tipped toward death.
pmc-13550655:
Paulo Ricardo Martins-Filho and three colleagues published this 2026 commentary on an outbreak of Andes hantavirus aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, sailing between Argentina, Antarctica and remote South Atlantic islands. They describe it as the first hantavirus cluster on a cruise vessel. By June 2026 the outbreak had been linked to 13 confirmed cases and three deaths, triggering international contact tracing and repatriation.

Andes virus is unusual among hantaviruses, which normally spread through rodent droppings, because person-to-person spread is documented, though uncommon and confined to parts of Argentina and Chile. Shipboard life, with close contact, can make even limited spread serious in practice, the authors argue. Cruise health protocols grew up around stomach bugs and respiratory viruses, not local animal-borne diseases. They call for ship health surveillance that includes exposure history and rodent-risk screening before boarding, especially on expedition routes through remote regions where the virus circulates.
pmc-13551855:
Heli Soni, Greg T. Sutherland, and Markus J. Hofer published a 2026 review of an immune system in Alzheimer's disease. The system is called complement. It is a set of blood proteins that fight germs. Complement touches the plaques and tangles that mark Alzheimer's. It also switches on in sick brain areas. The authors ask whether its levels can serve as a test marker.

Complement shifts fast and spans many states, they note. Blood levels also reflect age, body-wide inflammation, and vessel disease. A leaky brain barrier muddies the signal further. Present proof does not back complement as a stand-alone test. The authors place it inside multi-marker panels instead. There it can add context on inflammation, pending large long-term checks.
pmc-13551955:
Navneet Upadhyay, with ten colleagues, published a 2026 study of second-line drugs for ulcerative colitis. The bowel disease often needs advanced drugs. Many patients start with a TNF blocker. When the first such drug fails, doctors can switch within the class or change class. The team used a large US database of claims. Adults whose first advanced drug was a TNF blocker from 2015 to 2022 were tracked.

Failure was a bundle of signs, from new drug switches to surgery. Within-class switchers failed more often than class changers. About three fifths of them met a failure sign within a year, versus about half of changers. Their time to failure was a bit shorter too. Total care costs ran slightly higher for switchers. The team concludes that changing drug class beats cycling within it.
pmc-13552255:
Guido Gainotti reviews how familiar-people recognition breaks down in the right and left variants of semantic dementia. Such disorders rank among the most common marks of frontotemporal degeneration. The review first sums up cognitive models of recognition and the brain correlates of each stage. It treats familiarity feelings apart from semantic aspects of recognition.

Gainotti then weighs patient results on familiarity feelings and on general and social knowledge. He concludes right-variant disorders stem more from broken familiarity routes than from semantic defects. The right anterior temporal lobe, he argues, favors concrete parts of social knowledge over abstract ones. It stores only facts that fit a concrete picture form, while the left lobe stores facts held only as abstract word claims.
pmc-13552455:
Heran Cao and five colleagues set the first scrotal ultrasound reference values for men in Guangdong, China. Male infertility affects over 12 million men in East Asia, mainly from azoospermia in its blocked and unblocked forms. Current diagnostic norms come from European men and lack validation for Chinese men. Their 2026 study enrolls 424 men aged 20 to 45, including 245 fertile controls.

Fertile Guangdong men showed much smaller testicular volumes than European reference values. Testicular volume fell as FSH and LH rose, and rose with sperm count and concentration. Men with non-obstructive azoospermia had smaller volumes, while obstructive cases showed dilation of the epididymal caput. A two-measure approach using volume and caput diameter may aid non-invasive typing and cut biopsies.
pmc-13554255:
Gloria Ho, Chun Wei Yap, and Lixia Ge track how changing social ties shape later health costs in Singapore in a 2026 study. Survey data from 1,182 public healthcare users were linked to hospital records. Two yearly waves sorted people into four patterns, from staying connected to staying cut off. Care use and costs were then followed for one and three years.

People cut off at both waves used hospitals and emergency rooms more, and cost more, than those who stayed connected. They also visited clinics more often at both follow-ups. People who gained ties still showed higher emergency use and costs than the always-connected group. The authors suggest that fostering connection could ease pressure on costly hospital services.
pmc-13556055:
Ting-Ting Huang and three colleagues compared in 2026 two ways to treat advanced lung cancer after a first round of immunotherapy stops working. Their retrospective study covered patients treated between 2019 and 2025 whose disease had progressed on PD-1 or PD-L1 blocking drugs. One group received further PD-1 based combinations, with chemotherapy or a blood-vessel targeting drug, while the other received the standard chemotherapy drug docetaxel alone.

Response rates were modest in both groups, yet disease control was markedly better with the combination approach. Patients on PD-1 based regimens went longer before their cancer grew and lived longer overall, with median survival near seventeen months against about nine and a half on docetaxel. Side effects were compared as well. The authors frame the work as exploratory, since treatment was not assigned at random.
pmc-13556255:
Bélanger and colleagues showed in 2026 that two HIV proteins shield infected cells from being eaten by immune cells. Antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis, or ADCP, is a process where antibodies flag infected cells for swallowing by scavenger cells. HIV's envelope protein is the only viral target on an infected cell's surface, but it usually stays in a closed shape that antibodies miss.

Deleting Nef and Vpu from HIV copies made infected cells vulnerable to swallowing when HIV-positive plasma was present. Small compounds that mimic CD4 forced the envelope open and likewise sensitised infected cells to ADCP. Boosting surface envelope through an interferon-driven protein raised the effect further. The authors argue ADCP can be harnessed alongside other antibody attacks to shrink the HIV reservoir.
pmc-13557855:
Collazo-Lorduy and co-authors report a trial that recruitment defeat turned into a descriptive paper in this 2026 article: Neo-DIANA, a phase two study of pre-surgical combination therapy for EGFR-mutated lung cancer. The rationale was strong. Tumors carrying EGFR mutations relapse at distant sites after surgery, often in the brain. Yet the landmark chemoimmunotherapy trials excluded these patients. They were seen as poor immunotherapy candidates.

The Spanish multicentre trial planned combination treatment before surgery. Patients would get atezolizumab plus chemotherapy and the vessel-blocking drug bevacizumab. Atezolizumab would then continue afterward. The stages covered were IIIA and IIIB. Slow accrual, reflecting how uncommon resectable EGFR-mutated cases are in Spain, forced premature termination with only a very limited number of patients enrolled, as the authors state plainly. No efficacy conclusions can be drawn, and the paper's real message is about structure. Answering such questions demands international collaboration.
pmc-13558055:
Sajad Hamid Ahanger and eight colleagues showed in 2026 that where a gene sits inside the nucleus helps decide whether it stays poised or switches on during brain development. They mapped which parts of the genome touch the nuclear edge, called the lamina, and which gather near internal structures called speckles, in cells from the mid-gestation human cortex. Hundreds of neuronal genes moved from edge to speckles as development proceeded.

Genes carrying two opposing chemical marks at once, a poised state called bivalency, sat nearly silent at the lamina. After relocation to speckles, the repressive mark was shed and gene activity rose more than eightfold. Experiments showed that closeness to the nuclear edge, rather than the repressive mark itself, kept such genes quiet, partly because the machinery that extends gene messages stays away from the edge. Location, the authors argue, is part of the gene's regulation.
pmc-13558555:
Qing-qing Liu and nine colleagues tested in 2026 whether breathing hydrogen gas can slow lung tumours that grow under the stop-start oxygen shortage of sleep apnoea. That pattern, called chronic intermittent hypoxia, is known to help cancers invade and spread. The team combined cell co-cultures, where cancer cells and immune macrophages shared dishes under intermittent low oxygen, with a mouse model exposed to the same cycling while tumours grew.

Hydrogen shrank tumour growth in the animals. Immune macrophages shifted toward their inflammatory, tumour-attacking state, and a chemical signalling axis that recruits tumour-friendly cells was suppressed. In dishes, hydrogen directly reduced cancer cell survival and movement, echoing the effect of a drug that blocks the same axis. Treated tissue also showed less new blood vessel support for tumours. The authors propose hydrogen as a candidate add-on therapy worth clinical exploration.
pmc-13558655:
Xin Xu and three colleagues coupled in 2026 a digital twin of a railway bridge with a reinforcement learning controller that decides when to sound alarms and when to spend on sensing. Bridge signals drift with weather and traffic, so fixed thresholds cry wolf, while twin models alone react slowly. Their system fuses the twin's surprise signal, a safety margin measure, and an inconsistency score from a sequence encoder into one belief state for a duelling Q-learning policy.

Rewards punish delay, false alarms, missed damage, and sensing cost together, so the policy learns an explicit trade-off among speed, accuracy, and budget. On two public bridge datasets the method reached F1 scores in the low to mid nineties with high precision on one of them. Operating point analysis showed how an operator can slide between caution and economy. The authors pitch the design for retrofit periods, when risk is highest.
pmc-13560255:
Merve Nur Gucluer Kocaoglu and four colleagues analyze Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infection in a Turkish tertiary hospital, asking what drives death within twenty-eight days. Their 2026 retrospective cohort includes 372 adults treated between January 2019 and May 2023. Most episodes, 78.8 percent of the total, involved methicillin-susceptible bacteria rather than the resistant form.

Appropriate first antibiotics reached susceptible cases far more often and faster than resistant ones. Yet death rates at seven, fourteen, and twenty-eight days did not differ clearly between the resistance groups. Overall, thirty percent of patients died within twenty-eight days. Adjusted analysis blamed older age, a higher Pitt bacteremia severity score, and intensive care admission, not resistance or treatment timing. The authors argue that early risk sorting at diagnosis should guide how closely patients are watched.
pmc-13562555:
Mattia Prosperi and colleagues tested whether large language models reason consistently about cause in HIV treatment scenarios, publishing the evaluation in 2026. Causal reasoning underpins diagnosis and drug choices, yet most benchmarks test pattern matching rather than the three rungs of Pearl's ladder: association, intervention, and counterfactuals. The team prompted several open and closed models, including GPT-4o and LLaMA-3, with rich HIV antiretroviral vignettes about interactions and side effects.

Models agreed with themselves moderately well, but agreement faded from association to counterfactual questions, and agreement between models was notably lower. Some models cited inaccessible online sources, and clinical experts only modestly aligned with model outputs, rating counterfactual scenarios weakest in realism and depth. The authors conclude the models are not yet reliable enough for causal reasoning in HIV pharmacoepidemiology.
pmc-13562755:
Thomas Olumide Adeleke and nine colleagues mine ten years of screening records to track haemoglobin types among Nigerian university students. Inherited haemoglobin disorders, sickle cell disease above all, weigh heavily on health systems in the region. The 2026 study extracted 8,890 records from annual undergraduate screening at Bowen University Hospital in Iwo, covering 2015 to 2024. Machine learning helped clean and analyse the archive across regions and demographic groups.

The normal genotype, HbAA, dominated at 75.11 percent of students. Sickle cell genotypes together held near 1.2 percent all decade, with a slight downward drift that statistics could not confirm. Carrier types stayed stable too. The authors are careful about reach: admitted students are healthier and better educated than the general public, so the figures describe that slice of Nigeria only. Even so, a decade of steady institutional screening shows how a university can anchor surveillance and health education.
pmc-13563855:
Linghui Tan and five colleagues build an atlas of how cancers learn to resist a drug that blocks the FGFR receptor. The drug AZD4547 works until tumours rewire around it, by routes that vary by cancer. Their 2026 study merged two drug-response databases with single-cell gene data, covering 312 cell lines from eight cancer types. Machine learning models predicted sensitivity, and a synthetic-lethality screen looked for second targets whose loss would kill resistant cells.

Resistance wore many faces: a gene amplification in glioblastoma, marker shifts toward fat-burning metabolism and a mobile cell state elsewhere, and subpopulations present before treatment began. One bypass converged everywhere, though: resistant cells leaned on the related EGFR pathway and its downstream cascades. A prediction model scored 0.73 on held-out lines. In two FGFR-dependent cell models, hitting both receptors together killed more cells than either drug alone, confirming the screen's lead.
pmc-13563955:
Aiping Deng and co-authors ask, in a 2026 retrospective study, whether early eye scans predict later vision gains in diabetic macular edema treated with aflibercept injections. They followed 112 eyes from 112 patients and measured retinal thickness, layer damage, and small bright spots on scans taken one and four months after treatment began.

Vision and scan measures both improved by twelve months. Scan features at one month predicted a gain of at least five letters fairly well, features at four months did slightly better, and combining both time points predicted best. Eye clinics could use the early scans to counsel patients about likely progress and to flag those needing closer attention.
pmc-13567255:
Christina A. Kapala and colleagues examined whether rural living and neighbourhood deprivation shape colorectal cancer treatment in Maine, publishing the registry study in 2026. Rural and low-income patients already face poorer cancer outcomes, and earlier Maine work linked later-stage diagnosis to rural residence and Medicaid coverage, hinting at access gaps. The team drew on the Maine Cancer Registry for adult colorectal cases diagnosed from 2017 to 2021.

After exclusions, 3,085 cases remained, with colon, rectal, and anal cancers analysed separately. The authors mapped each case to rurality tiers and a state deprivation index, then modelled receipt of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation against age, sex, race, insurance, stage, and year. The study aims to pinpoint where access falters so policy and health-system changes can target the right barriers.
pmc-13568755:
Abdulsamad and colleagues identify a resistance circuit in this 2026 study of castration-resistant prostate cancer, the advanced form that keeps growing despite hormone suppression and eventually defeats the drug enzalutamide. Mining tumor genome data and testing a resistant cell line, they connected a fat-handling protein, FABP5, to the transcription factor Sp1 and onward to the androgen receptor and its drug-proof variant, AR-V7.

FABP5 ran high in tumors and rose with Gleason grade, the pathology score for aggressiveness. Deleting FABP5 in the resistant cells slashed AR-V7 levels and restored enzalutamide sensitivity, while extra FABP5 boosted Sp1. A Sp1-blocking drug, mithramycin A, dragged the whole axis down together and cut both anchorage-free growth and invasion in the cell experiments. The authors propose FABP5 as both a biomarker of resistance and a target for resensitizing tumors.
pmc-13569155:
Dineshi Sewvandi Thalakiriyawa and co-authors study, in a 2026 laboratory project, how inflamed immune cells and dental pulp stem cells together grow new blood vessels. Such growth is a step needed to repair an inflamed tooth pulp. Cells were combined in a vessel-on-a-chip device and in shared cultures, with gene and protein checks tracing the signals involved.

A modest number of inflammatory macrophages boosted vessel segments and sprouts as strongly as the repair-type macrophages. The effect ran through a signal called IL-8, which pushed pulp stem cells to release a vessel growth factor. Too many inflammatory cells, in contrast, risk harm. The work clarifies how early inflammation can aid, rather than only block, pulp healing.
pmc-13569355:
Leonardo L. Miraldo and a large team evaluate, in a 2026 study, a genetically modified soybean carrying two bacterial Bt proteins against the main caterpillar pests of the crop in Brazil. Leaf feeding tests and multi-site field trials covered both the two-protein soybean and a stacked version carrying five Bt proteins.

Leaves from both versions killed all newborn caterpillars of three major pest species across growth stages, and they worked even against colonies resistant to an older Bt protein. Field plots showed far less leaf damage and fewer pests than ordinary soybean. The results support stacking several Bt proteins in one plant as a strategy to slow pest resistance while keeping strong protection.
pmc-13572355:
Xuezhong Zhang and colleagues scan, in a 2026 pan-cancer analysis, a little-studied RNA-binding protein called MEX3D across human tumors using large public atlases of gene, protein, and clinical data. Expression, stage links, survival, genetic changes, RNA modification partners, and immune patterns were all mapped together.

The protein ran abnormally high or low across many cancers and tracked with tumor stage in five of them. High levels matched worse survival in several malignancies, including adrenal, brain, lung, and lining cancers. Alterations clustered as extra gene copies in sarcoma and ovarian tumors, and levels tied to mutation load and immune cell patterns. The broad map marks MEX3D as a candidate marker whose role differs by cancer type.
pmc-13572455:
Domenica Lovecchio, with 16 colleagues, reports a 2026 study of a protein-building error that shows up when cancer cells lack histidine. That amino acid is a building block the body must get from food. When it runs short, cells can swap it for a close cousin, glutamine, at the wrong spots in new proteins.

In lab cancer cells starved of histidine, that swap was the strongest such event seen. Scans of cancer protein data found the swap rich in pancreatic, uterine, and kidney cancers. The team links the error to a misaligned transfer RNA, the molecule that carries building blocks to the protein factory. A tweak to that carrier raised the swap rate and changed how well cells survived the shortage. Host proteins kept being made despite the swap, which hints at a managed response, not random damage.
pmc-13573355:
Min Du, with eight colleagues, reports a 2026 survey of what pregnant women and their partners in China know and feel about pain relief in labour. Neuraxial analgesia, a shot near the spine, is the top standard for labour pain worldwide, yet use in China stays low. The team probed both members of each couple, since partners shape birth choices.

The survey ran across thirteen hospitals between April and December 2022, drawing 1,164 pairs. A knowledge-attitude-practice form gauged what couples knew, how they felt, and what they did or planned. The design lets the team sort barriers, such as fears or gaps in knowledge, from aids, such as trust or past good care. Those patterns can guide talks and leaflets in antenatal clinics. The authors aim to lift informed uptake of a proven pain option.
pmc-13575155:
Kamal Narayana and five colleagues report a surprising result on blood flow after stroke in a 2026 mouse study. After a stroke, a gene called Serpine1 rises sharply in brain vessel cells. Its protein, PAI-1, blocks clot breakdown, so the team expected that lowering it would raise blood flow and aid recovery.

Imaging showed flow near the stroke first fell, then overshot in normal mice. Knocking the gene down in vessel cells kept tiny vessels narrower and flow lower than expected. Despite that, treated mice had less damage to the blood-brain barrier, calmer inflammatory gene activity, and better recovery of cortical responses, movement, and cognition. The authors suggest finely tuned flow, not maximum flow, may serve recovery best.
pmc-13575255:
Shaochao Zhan and seven colleagues build a gene-based risk score for clear cell kidney cancer in a 2026 study. Outcomes in this cancer vary widely between patients. The team focused on long non-coding RNAs, RNA strands that do not build proteins, linked to three stress-related cell death programmes: ferroptosis, cuproptosis, and disulfidptosis.

Working from 533 tumours in a public atlas, they split cases into training and test halves. Screening across all three death programmes left 176 candidate RNAs, narrowed to a six-RNA signature. High scores marked patients with clearly worse survival in both halves of the data. The score also tracked with immune patterns in tumours and higher rates of changes in two key genes. The authors offer the signature for risk sorting, pending outside validation.
pmc-13576655:
Verena Chung leads a 2026 paper presenting OpenChallenges, a central registry for crowdsourced research competitions in biomedicine. Such challenges benchmark computing methods on shared data, yet more than 2,000 of them sit scattered across many platforms with no shared index. Finding and comparing them is needlessly hard.

OpenChallenges gathers and standardises challenge records into one searchable hub, aligned with the FAIR principles for data: findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. Each entry earns a completeness tier, from baseline to gold standard, so users can see how rich its record is and curators can see what to fix first. The platform runs on open-source, API-driven code and supports community editing. The authors aim to turn a fragmented scene into a connected knowledge base for computational biology.
pmc-13578755:
Dennis Bardoe and colleagues trace three decades of child deaths in Ghana and look ahead to 2035, in a 2026 study. Deaths before age five fell from about 120 per thousand births in 1992 to about 42 in 2022. The team split the trend by sex and by family wealth, using a World Health Organization equity toolkit, then forecast the path forward with a time series model.

Boys died at higher rates than girls in every year, though the gap shrank by close to half. Poor children still died far more often than rich ones, even as that gap also narrowed. The steepest yearly drops came between 2008 and 2016. Forecasts show a slower decline ahead, so the authors press for better mother care, food, and action on social drivers.
pmc-13579055:
Joseph L Izzo and colleagues compare day long blood flow patterns in people at risk of heart failure with those who already have it, in a study using a wearable pulse monitor. High blood pressure is the most common road into heart failure, yet how flow shifts along that road was little mapped. Just over one hundred at risk patients were set against fifty two with established disease, split further by how well the heart squeezes.

The sick group pumped less blood per beat and ran a faster pulse across the full day. Stiffer artery behavior rose as well, while total flow and vessel resistance stayed alike. The two key measures moved in lockstep in both groups: a faster pulse came with a smaller stroke. Low stroke values alone flagged established disease fairly well, and pairing them with a fast pulse sharpened the call.
pmc-13579955:
John S Luque and a large team of co-authors explore how Black patients at Florida community health centers view colon cancer screening, in a 2026 interview study. Six staff from two centers described how screening runs, and six focus groups heard from patients who had finished screening recently. Stool blood tests are cheap and offered widely at such centers, which serve many uninsured patients, yet uptake lags.

Three themes ran through the patient talks: trust in providers and comfort seeking care, what people know about the cancer and its warning signs, and family history plus test options. Staff valued their university partnership and named gaps in outreach and teaching. Centers leaned on stool tests with colonoscopy referrals for follow up. The authors use the findings to shape screening drives built for these clinics.
pmc-13580255:
Eva Billat, Léane Legrand, Tony Avril, and Elodie Lafont propose a name for genes caught between two opposing orders from one stress sensor, in a 2026 review. The sensor, IRE1, guards protein folding in the cell's workshop. Under strain it does two things at once: it builds a factor that switches genes on, and it shreds select messages, cutting their proteins down. A few genes take both orders at once.

The authors call such genes dual IRE1 targets and list the known cases, led by a death receptor gene and a tagging enzyme gene. Two older examples from split studies join the set. Their wager is that these tug of war genes help decide whether a stressed cell adapts or dies, a balance that matters in cancer and other diseases. The review maps the control wires and the open tests.
pmc-13580755:
Chavarría-Rojas and colleagues audit the software that predicts how drugs move through the body, asking whether its virtual women are built from female physiology. Sex changes stomach acidity, gut speed, and body makeup, so absorption can differ by sex. Their 2026 study reviews three platforms for sex specific gut settings. It builds models of the painkiller ketoprofen in men and stretches them to women, first with default settings and then with gut values refined for women.

All three platforms included sex differences in anatomy but skipped sex specific gut details. With default female settings, the models overshot drug levels, understated the time to peak, and produced curves identical to men's, erasing differences. Feeding in corrected gut transit values brought the predictions in line with observed data. The fix, the authors conclude, is in users' hands: default virtual populations need tuning before sex claims from a model can be trusted.
pmc-13586155:
Weihong Liang and colleagues found the genetic switch behind extra-sticky biofilms in the dangerous fungus Candida auris. The yeast persists on skin and hospital surfaces, driving outbreaks, and biofilms strengthen that persistence. Their 2026 study compared clinical strains with strong biofilm formation against others, sequenced their genomes, and tested the prime suspect gene, WOR2, by deleting and restoring it.

Strong-biofilm strains carried a broken WOR2, a regulator of white-opaque switching, and a survey of 13,314 published genomes found WOR2-breaking mutations in 23.3 percent of strains. Deleting WOR2 boosted biofilm, restoring it tamed biofilm, and inactivation switched on biofilm genes including GFC1 and ALS4. The authors present WOR2 loss as a key driver of persistence and transmission.
pmc-13593555:
Yuta Sakaguchi and colleagues report a patient whose surgical ablation lines for atrial fibrillation partly reconnected long after the operation. Testing during surgery had confirmed that signals could not cross those lines in either direction. The 2026 case centers on the inferior line across the back wall of the heart after a biatrial Cox-Maze IV procedure.

Only that one line regained conduction, while the rest of the lesion set stayed intact, which suggests that separate lines within the same operation can age at different rates. The authors stress that patients whose rhythm problems return late after surgical ablation deserve a careful, high-density remapping study. Such mapping can show exactly which line failed instead of assuming the whole procedure has worn out.
pmc-13595455:
Martina Gambron and colleagues asked whether gene-guided dosing for two chemotherapies should vary by exact gene variant. Gene variants in DPYD and UGT1A1 strongly affect safety of fluoropyrimidines and irinotecan, and gene-guided dosing cuts severe toxicity, yet variant-level effects were little studied. Their look-back study covered 178 cancer patients with actionable variants, split between standard care and gene-guided dosing.

Gene-guided dosing cut clinically relevant toxicity from about 43 percent to 16 percent overall. Variant detail mattered: one DPYD variant saw toxicity only under standard care, while another, HapB3, saw markedly lower drug exposure under gene-guided dosing with no toxicity gain. The authors argue uniform gene-based dosing misses variant-specific effects and call for more flexible dosing.
pmc-13595755:
Yanhui Yang and colleagues describe a pause-ventilation technique for removing hard-to-reach lymph nodes during single-port lung surgery. Complete node removal guides staging and prognosis in lung cancer, yet nodes below the left chest prominence resist single-port dissection. Their 2026 report details a 72-year-old woman with a left upper lung mass and non-small cell lung cancer, operated through one 3-centimetre incision.

Through nasal high-flow oxygen, the team paused ventilation in bursts to expose nodes near the left bronchus, windpipe prominence, and right bronchus. The pauses gave clear views of surrounding tissues and organs, and the authors judge the approach safe and workable for this tricky dissection. An operative video accompanies the report.
pmc-13596055:
Shen Han leads a nineteen-author team announcing a previously unrecognized crystal defect in half-Heusler compounds. These are a versatile family of materials. Their ideal structure leaves one of four atomic sublattices empty. Their 2026 study shows that atoms can fill that empty layer in flat sheets, a filling fault, and swap places between neighboring sublattices in the process.

The fault forms completely in nickel-based members, partly in a cobalt-based one, and barely in iron-based relatives, a tidy rule that resolves long-standing puzzles about these compounds' real structures. The authors present filling faults as a new design lever, letting materials scientists tune properties by cultivating a defect once mistaken for disorder.
pmc-13600355:

Contrast sensitivity, picking out faint differences in shading, measures how well someone sees. The team compared the filtering lens against a similar clear lens in a randomized study where neither wearers nor testers knew which was in use.

The filtering lens improved the overall contrast sensitivity score in every setting. Gains appeared both under bright and dim light, and held up when glare was added. The authors conclude that filtering this band of light can give a measurable visual edge, including in the glaring conditions drivers and outdoor workers face.
pmc-13616955:

They analyzed more than seven hundred forty thousand adults from biobank studies in Finland and the United Kingdom, including people with non-European roots. Genetic risk was summed into polygenic scores, while social position came from education and occupation.

Both genetic scores and social position were linked to disease risk for most conditions, largely independent of each other. For seven diseases, genetic effects ran stronger among highly educated people, while occupation mattered less. Combining education with genetic scores improved risk prediction modestly for most diseases in both biobanks. The authors argue that doctors should weigh social context alongside inherited variation, not treat genes as the whole story.
pmc-13618255:
Clare Stawski and three colleagues use heart rate logging to measure the energy budgets of Krefft's gliders, small tree-dwelling marsupials of about one hundred twenty-five grams. Metabolic rate is usually measured in a laboratory, which misses real life. Because heart rate predicts metabolic rate well, implanted loggers can estimate daily energy spending in free-ranging animals over long periods, a boon for conservation planning.

Gliders lived in a large outdoor aviary under natural weather while implants recorded heart rate and body temperature continuously, with laboratory respirometry sessions calibrating the relationship. Heart rate tracked metabolic rate along a rising curve. Daily energy expenditure fell from winter to spring, a strong seasonal effect, so females nursing young in spring actually spent less energy than pregnant females had in winter. The authors say such life-stage budgets are vital for understanding ecology and managing species under environmental change.
pmc-13619355:

Fish were identified by appearance and by two tree-based methods that group DNA into species-like units.

The combined data yielded seventy molecular units matching sixty-two named species, plus three lineages nobody could name. That total is only a little over half the species recorded historically in the region. Several widespread fish split into multiple distinct genetic groups, hinting at hidden species. The authors offer the dataset as a first regional reference while warning that a single gene cannot settle very recent splits.
pmc-13619755:
