The PreserFlo MicroShunt lowers eye pressure by giving fluid a new escape route. Eighty-eight eyes with open-angle or exfoliation glaucoma were followed, and scans one month after surgery showed which way the fluid filtered.

Median eye pressure fell from nineteen to ten units over the year, with success rates depending on how strict the target pressure was. Eyes whose fluid filtered toward the edge of the cornea failed far less often from high pressure. Longer eyes also did better under the looser targets. Older age and exfoliation glaucoma raised the risk of pressure dropping too low instead. The authors suggest pairing a pre-surgery measure of eye length with early scan patterns to judge each patient's likely course.
pmc-13621355:
Iftikhar Ahmad and Muhammad Tahir synthesized a three-part nanoparticle that cleans polluted water under light and fights microbes at the same time. The composite marries silver with nickel oxide and titanium dioxide, two workhorse light-activated materials, using a hot water method. They aimed it at two industrial dyes and one widely used antibiotic, ciprofloxacin, which lingers in waterways.

Within an hour of light exposure, the composite removed most of both dyes from solution, about nine tenths of each. The antibiotic proved tougher, with a little over half removed after three hours at the tested dose. Separate tests showed strong killing of the bacterial and fungal strains tried. The authors argue the pairing of cleanup and disinfection in one material fits wastewater treatment, where dyes, drug residues, and germs arrive together.
pmc-13623155:
Yaregal Admasu Alelign leads a review and meta-analysis of person-centred maternity care in East Africa, asking how respectfully women are treated while giving birth in health facilities. Care of this kind covers dignity, communication, and support, and poor treatment drives women away from facility care. No regional summary existed, so the team pooled the available studies.

Twenty-three studies covering 15,325 women, published between 2017 and 2025, were combined with statistical methods that allow for wide variation. The average care score reached roughly sixty-three percent of the best possible mark. Dignity and respect scored highest, while communication and patient autonomy scored lowest, which points to weak shared decision-making. Scores fell for night deliveries, late starts to pregnancy care, and rural residence, and rose with the mother's education. The authors recommend communication training, better night staffing, and routine tracking of these scores in quality systems.
pmc-13624555:
Jinjin Zhao and colleagues report a light-based treatment for oral leukoplakia, white mouth patches that can turn cancerous. Thirty-one patients received three sessions of therapy in which a drug, 5-aminolevulinic acid, is painted on the patch and then lit with red light. The team scored each patch one month after treatment and kept watching patients for a median of fifteen months.

Nine in ten patients responded, with nineteen patches clearing fully and nine shrinking in part. Three patches later returned, and two turned malignant during follow-up. Patches under the tongue responded best, and soreness or ulcers after a session oddly marked a better result, while uneven patches with mid-grade cell change returned most often.
pmc-13625455:
Özlem Çelebi and colleagues compare two designs of metal stent used to reopen a food pipe blocked by cancer. Expandable stents restore swallowing, yet they can slip, clog with food, or be overgrown by tumor. The team reviewed cases from several centers between 2014 and 2023. They studied 188 patients who received either a fully covered or a partly covered stent. Then they tracked which problems followed each type.

Problems struck about three in ten patients overall, and fully covered stents failed more often, mostly by migrating from their spot. Partly covered stents, whose bare ends grip the wall, migrated far less. Within the fully covered group, wide strictures and tumors of rarer types carried the highest risk. The map of predictors can guide which design a doctor picks for a given blockage.
pmc-13625755:
Alexander Muacevic and colleagues present a 65-year-old man whose heart tracing gave away a fast-growing danger. Ten days after a hospital stay for pericarditis, inflammation around the heart, he returned with three days of worsening breathlessness. His earlier scan had shown no fluid. Yet now his neck veins bulged and his pulse raced. His tracing showed electrical alternans, a beat-to-beat swing in signal size. That swing hints at a heart sloshing in fluid.

A bedside ultrasound at once showed a large fluid sac pressing on the heart. Minutes after transfer his breathing crashed while his vital signs still looked fair, and urgent drainage drew off about 1,200 milliliters of bloody fluid, with swift relief. The case warns that fluid can gather within days, even after a clean scan.
pmc-13626855:
Xi Chen and colleagues put a traditional Chinese herbal formula under a modern lens for polycystic ovary syndrome paired with insulin resistance. The modified Huanglian Wendan decoction is used clinically, yet its working parts were murky. The team combined network pharmacology, molecule docking, and motion simulations with chemical fingerprinting of the brew. Then they fed the brew to rats made to mimic the condition. A hormone drug and a fatty diet did the mimicking.

Treated rats recovered regular cycles and healthier ovaries, while fasting insulin, hormone levels, and inflammation markers all fell. Fingerprinting found hundreds of candidate compounds, and network math pointed at a sugar-damage pathway, AGE-RAGE, with two relay proteins moving as predicted. The authors stress the pathway link is an association, not proof of cause, in a multi-ingredient medicine.
pmc-13627455:
Omar El Sewify and colleagues systematically review sentinel lymph node biopsy for skin squamous cell carcinoma. The biopsy samples the first node a tumor would drain to, and its use in this cancer is growing despite unsettled accuracy. Following standard review rules, the team searched four databases to January 2025 and kept forty-four studies covering 3,043 patients with confirmed, non-mucosal tumors.

Surgeons found the sentinel node in nearly ninety-seven percent of attempts, and about eleven percent of patients proved positive. Missed spread was uncommon in absolute terms. Yet positive patients carried bigger, deeper, more aggressive tumors and far worse fates. Recurrence and death ran several times the negative group's rates, while complications stayed low. The authors advise selective use in high-risk cases, with close watching after a negative result.
pmc-13628155:
Nasser S. Alqahtani and four colleagues compared two forms of quinoa as protection against stomach damage caused by indomethacin, a common pain drug known to ulcerate the gut lining. Thirty-six male rats ate white quinoa or tri-color quinoa diets for twenty-one days before the injury was induced, and the team then measured tissue damage and inflammation markers.

Tri-color quinoa, a blend of red, black, and white grain, outperformed the white form. It cut tissue death sharply, eased oxidative stress, and left the stomach lining close to normal under the microscope. Computer docking work suggested that quinoa compounds grip several injury-related proteins tightly, which the authors credit for the stronger protection.
pmc-13628555:
Colm Bradley and three colleagues argue, in an editorial, that Gaucher disease needs a firm place in training for blood doctors. Gaucher disease is the most common storage disorder of its kind. A faulty enzyme lets fatty waste build up inside immune cells that should clear it.

Its first signs sit squarely in blood clinics. They include a swollen spleen, anaemia, low platelets, and bleeding. Bone trouble and marrow changes can mimic cancer. Late diagnosis stays common because awareness is patchy. The authors set out the core knowledge trainees need. It runs from the basic chemistry and the hundreds of known gene variants to first-line tests. It also covers modern treatment rules. Their aim is that general blood doctors spot the disease early. They should then work well with specialist centres.
pmc-13629455:
Nguyen Thanh Vu and eleven colleagues mined leftover DNA reads from a breeding programme to profile disease in farmed barramundi during scale drop disease outbreaks. Published in 2026, the study reused genotyping data from 4,593 fish across four commercial sea cages, classifying the unmapped reads that genotyping normally discards.

Fish sampled mid-outbreak carried strong signals of the scale drop virus, frequent traces of a second virus, and bacterial communities dominated by Vibrio. Healthy fish after outbreaks showed faint viral signals and more diverse, stable microbial mixes. Genetic analysis suggested susceptibility is mostly environmental rather than inherited. The authors present recycled sequencing reads as a cheap companion to targeted diagnostics, with honest caveats about bias.
pmc-13631455:
Kim and colleagues compare the lived recovery from two keyhole routes to the same brain operation in this 2026 prospective study of unruptured aneurysm clipping. One approach slips through an incision in the eyebrow, the other through the scalp above the ear. One hundred eleven patients rated six symptoms daily for five days after surgery on a ten-point scale.

Surgical success and complications were indistinguishable between approaches, but the patient experience was not. By day five the eyebrow group reported wound pain of 3.34 against 4.70 for the scalp group on the scale, with parallel advantages in headache, depressed mood, fatigue, and appetite, all statistically significant. Significant low mood struck 16.4 percent of the eyebrow group versus 34.0 percent of the scalp group on day five. Statistical modeling named the scalp approach a dominant predictor of the worse symptoms.
pmc-13632055:
Anthony Mufarreh and five colleagues published this 2026 study asking whether firearm use relates to heart health in the United States. Around thirty percent of American adults own a gun, and violence exposure brings chronic stress, which is tied to cardiovascular risk. The team used national health survey cycles from the twenty tens. Participants answered whether they had ever used firearms for shooting sports, hunting, work, or military service.

The researchers combined survey answers with exam and lab results, plus national death records, to compare firearm users with non-users. They weighed the data so results represent the wider civilian population. Their models tested links between firearm use and risk factors such as blood pressure and cholesterol, along with later deaths. They also checked whether money and social position changed those links, an angle rarely studied for firearms and heart disease.
pmc-13632255:
Rebecca Tarpey and five colleagues published this 2026 review of do-it-yourself strategies for menstrual cycle symptoms. Discomfort, fatigue, and mood swings around periods lower quality of life for many women. Plenty of women manage symptoms without clinical care, yet trial evidence for those habits is mixed. The team searched four databases for blinded randomized trials published since 2000 that tested self-management options in adult women.

Thirty-nine trials with more than thirty-eight hundred participants qualified. Physical activity, especially yoga, reliably eased discomfort, exhaustion, and mood problems. Nutrition trials, mostly on vitamins and minerals, were the most common and leaned positive. Heat, low light, music, and drawing also helped in some trials. Combining strategies reduced symptoms and pain intensity in several studies. Weak methods were common, though, so the authors urge stronger trials and longer follow-up.
pmc-13632955:
Gerelt-Od Khenmedekh and four colleagues report a case where a gallbladder problem posed as a stomach tumor. A seventy-one-year-old woman arrived with severe belly pain and signs of a blocked small bowel. Scans showed a large mass on her stomach wall that seemed to invade the liver, and doctors suspected a stromal tumor, a growth arising from the stomach's deeper layers. Her gallbladder, an early clue, could not be seen at all.

The supposed tumor proved to be her gallbladder stuck to the stomach, with an abnormal channel, called a fistula, joining them. Tissue study confirmed a benign, inflamed gallbladder wall condition, not cancer. She recovered and went home about a month later. The authors list warning signs that can spare future patients a cancer misdiagnosis.
pmc-13636655:
Luyue Zhang and three colleagues, writing with a large Alzheimer's imaging initiative, tested whether anatomy helps decide where tau strikes first. The entorhinal cortex, a memory gateway, collects tau tangles earliest in Alzheimer's disease, for reasons nobody knows. The authors propose that its closeness to a stiff membrane edge inside the skull exposes it to chronic mechanical stress. They built a contact score measuring that closeness from images of forty-seven participants.

After accounting for standard risk factors, tau signal in that cortex predicted who would slide from mild impairment into Alzheimer's dementia only in the high-contact group. In low-contact participants the same signal carried no such warning. The authors present the closeness score as a possible new anatomical risk marker. They argue the results support a biomechanical contribution to tau vulnerability. That idea could open prevention routes aimed at tissue stress rather than chemistry alone.
pmc-13639355:

Patient comfort is a recognized quality measure, yet no performance benchmark existed to judge it. The team first ran focus groups with patients, nurses, and physicians to agree on an acceptable comfort threshold, then applied it to procedures at St. Paul's Hospital from 2021 through 2023.

Focus groups settled on a SPECS score of three or lower as acceptable. Applying that line to 17,405 colonoscopies by eighteen physicians and 6,180 upper endoscopies by thirteen physicians, three benchmark methods converged near the same answer. The 75th percentile method gave 96.3 percent for colonoscopy and 95.9 percent for upper endoscopy, while top-performer and volume-adjusted methods landed near 97 percent. pmc-13641955:

The study covered 899 valve replacement patients treated from 1996 to 2023, seventy-five of whom had enlargement. Survival, early complications, and valve-related events did not differ between groups after matching. Heart mass shrank faster with enlargement only when the outflow tract was wider than the ring. The authors advise measuring both structures before planning surgery.
pmc-13642455:

The researchers housed resident bats with wild-caught newcomers and tracked the key call frequency in 101 individuals over a month. The two groups began apart, then gradually converged as overall scatter shrank. The shift was one-sided: bats with lower pitches raised them, while higher-pitched bats barely moved. The authors suggest convergence leaves a shared quiet band above the call for hearing faint echoes.
pmc-13642555:

Designers usually trade shape freedom against ease of making and optical quality. The group combined smooth curve based building blocks with deep learning to escape that trade.

Liu used a Transformer model, a type of neural network, to predict optical behaviour without slow repeated simulation. A corrected electron beam writing step then kept the made shapes close to the design intent. The finished lens focused colours across the visible range from violet to red with little shift between them. Its 200 micrometre lens resolved details near two micrometres wide and could sense tiny changes in how cells bend light.
pmc-13642955:

pmc-13643455:

About fifteen percent met criteria for at least one disorder, boys more than girls, and nearly half of those had two or more diagnoses. Each added diagnosis nearly tripled the odds of a substance use disorder. Grade repetition, maternal drinking, and witnessing domestic violence raised risk most.
pmc-13643755:

No drug yet slows the disease, and the authors stress the need for clear test markers.
pmc-13645555:

The authors present the work as early evidence for planning transplant care budgets in middle-income settings.
pmc-13646055:

Answers backed by higher path scores were more often correct, above all for questions needing several steps of reasoning. Checks on outside question sets suggested the gain came from the structure itself. The authors offer the framework for professionals who give lifestyle guidance.
pmc-13646155:

Tests showed the image features added real information, encoding style period, subject, color strength, and composition. Stress checks mapped where the model weakens in economic shocks. The authors offer the tool to banks and wealth managers who price art-backed risk with data rather than taste.
pmc-13647555:

pmc-13648855:

pmc-13649455:

Doctors judged most of its outlines fine as drawn or in need of only small fixes. A small post-surgery group gave weaker but workable results. The authors back doctor-checked use next, with tests at more centres to come.
pmc-13649755:

Fifteen trials with 457 children were included. Against routine care, family-centred care raised asthma control scores, life quality, and lung function in clear ways. Children also hit symptom control far more often, and carers mastered care knowledge at more than twice the rate. Trips back to hospital fell sharply. The authors back wider use of the model in clinic care for young children with asthma.
pmc-13650355:

Each printing method trades cost against precision, and some need lengthy finishing work. The authors warn that most evidence is observational, with few proper trials, and that waste, material strength, and price still limit adoption. Progress, they argue, depends on stronger trials, better materials, and safety rules fit for personalized devices.
pmc-13650555:

pmc-13651655:

pmc-13652055:

pmc-13652755:

pmc-13655055:

For developmental biologists, the study maps a control layer that sits alongside genes and chemical signals in shaping the embryo.
pmc-4010955:

pmc-5316555:

pmc-6227755:

High blood pressure, smoking, and high blood sugar sit near the top of the list. Results differ sharply by region and income. Prevention budgets lean on these rankings to pick fights with the largest payoff.
pmc-6582955:
Malte Luecken and Fabian Theis wrote this tutorial on single-cell RNA analysis in 2019. The method measures gene activity cell by cell at striking resolution. Its promise draws a fast-growing crowd of new users.

Tool choice has become bewildering, with new packages appearing monthly. The tutorial walks through each stage, from quality checks to clustering and trajectory building. It names a current best choice for each step and explains why. New analysts use it as a map, and experienced ones cite it to justify pipeline choices in papers. Each stage closes with a short list of common mistakes and how to spot them in plots.
pmc-7164555:
Luca Ferretti, Chris Wymant, Michelle Kendall, and coauthors quantified SARS-CoV-2 transmission for digital contact tracing in 2020. The new virus spreads faster and is harder to trace by hand than the earlier SARS virus. Many infections pass on before symptoms start.

From detailed case data, the team estimates how much spread happens at each stage. Manual tracing alone is too slow, they argue, but a phone app that warns contacts instantly could cut spread enough to control the epidemic. Their analysis set the speed targets that national tracing apps were later judged against.
pmc-7619455:
Spyros Lytras and two colleagues review how artificial intelligence tools that predict protein shapes are opening up the deep history of viruses. Viruses mutate so fast that their gene sequences stop resembling one another, erasing the record of ancient relationships. Protein structure survives far longer than sequence, yet shapes used to be measured one at a time in the lab, which starved evolutionary work of data.

Prediction software now produces millions of viral protein structures, and the review weighs what that flood can and cannot do. Uses include lighting up unknown viral proteins found in environmental samples, placing orphan virus lineages on the family tree, and guessing the jobs of proteins too strange for sequence comparison. The authors also mark the limits of predicted shapes, keeping the review a guide to a powerful method rather than an advertisement for it.
pmc-8084355:
The RECOVERY Collaborative Group reported in 2021 the results of a large randomized trial of tocilizumab for patients in hospital with COVID-19. The trial enrolled adults who had low oxygen levels and signs of strong inflammation throughout the body. Tocilizumab blocks a receptor for interleukin-6, an immune signal suspected of driving the harmful inflammation of severe disease.

Patients were assigned by chance to receive the drug or usual care alone, within a platform trial testing several treatments at once. The group reports how the drug affected survival and other outcomes in this severely ill population. Because the trial was large and randomized, its verdict carried weight with doctors deciding how to treat the sickest patients.
pmc-8262755:
Kai Blin and colleagues released antiSMASH 6.0 in 2021, the newest version of a widely used tool for mining microbial genomes. Many microbes make natural products, the source of numerous antibiotics, antivirals, and other drugs. Genome mining, searching a genome for the gene clusters that build such products, now complements older screening methods.

Since its first release in 2011, the antiSMASH platform has become a standard way to find and compare those clusters. The authors describe improvements in how clusters are detected and in how results can be compared across genomes. Each version widens the net for discovering new chemistry hidden in microbial DNA.
pmc-8273155:
Huakan Zhao and colleagues reviewed in 2021 how inflammation and tumor growth drive each other, and where treatment might break the cycle. Cancer development and the response to therapy are both shaped by inflammation, which can restrain tumors in some settings and feed them in others. Long lasting, chronic inflammation is the dangerous partner, easing tumor growth and helping cancers resist treatment.

The authors trace the main signaling pathways through which inflamed tissue and tumors exchange their corrupting messages. For each pathway they discuss targeted interventions, drugs designed to cut a specific line of communication. The review maps a central dilemma of cancer medicine: the same immune activity that can destroy a tumor can also be turned into its ally.
pmc-8942855:
Raquel Viana and colleagues reported in 2022 how the Omicron variant of SARS-CoV-2 expanded rapidly through southern Africa. The region's epidemic had already passed through three distinct waves, driven first by mixed early lineages, then by the Beta variant, and then by Delta. In November 2021 a new variant appeared and began spreading at unusual speed.

The authors describe how they detected and tracked Omicron, and how quickly it displaced the variants before it. Their account draws on genomic surveillance and case data from the region where the variant was first characterized. The report documents the opening chapter of the pandemic's Omicron era, and shows the value of the monitoring networks that caught it early.
pontoppidan-natural-history-norway-1755:
Erik Pontoppidan, a Norwegian bishop, published The Natural History of Norway, and English readers got it in 1755. He described his country's coasts, fish, birds, and weather with a pastor's care. Mixed into the sober survey sit the most famous sea monster accounts of the age.

Pontoppidan reports the Kraken, an island-sized beast that could drag down ships. He also gives classic accounts of the sea serpent and the merman, drawn from sailors he trusted. Half natural history and half sailor's yarn, the book is never dull. It fixed the Kraken in the world's imagination. The north's monsters stand here in a bishop's careful catalogue.
romanus-pontifex-1455:
Pope Nicholas V issued Romanus Pontifex in 1455, addressed to King Afonso V of Portugal. Portuguese ships were then pushing down the coast of Africa, seeking trade and a sea route east. The bull backed Portugal's claims against rival Christian powers.

The text grants Portugal rights over lands its sailors reached along and beyond the African coast. It also permits war against non-Christian peoples there and supports their capture and enslavement, language that reads brutally today. Portugal used the bull to defend its growing sea empire. The document is a key paper source for Europe's early age of expansion.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave: Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States from talks with former slaves, rests on typed records made by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936-1938. The Library of Congress project put the set together, with photos, at Washington in 1941. One part is Volume IX, the Mississippi Narratives. Its list of those who spoke begins with Jim Allen, Anna Baker, John Cameron, Gus Clark, and James Cornelius.
snow-cholera-1855:
John Snow argued in On the Mode of Communication of Cholera that the disease travels through fouled water. The second edition of 1855 is the famous one. Snow mapped deaths around the Broad Street pump in London's Soho. The cluster of cases pointed at the pump's water like a finger.

He traces outbreaks to sewage leaking into wells and rivers. His evidence joins maps, case counts, and door to door inquiry. The book founded epidemiology, the science of tracking disease in populations. Germ theory later confirmed what his method had shown. The Gutenberg text keeps his tables and reasoning clear. Public health still teaches his pump story.
tales-and-novels-volume-03-belinda-pg945:
Belinda, Volume III of Maria Edgeworth's Tales and Novels in ten volumes with engravings on steel, appears here in the 1857 printing. Its contents run further than a bare chapter list usually reaches, through fifteen heads in the pages at hand.

Characters and Masks open the novel, and Lady Delacour's history, told across two chapters, gives Belinda the inside story of a fashionable marriage. Birthday dresses, ways and means, the Serpentine river, a family party, advice, the mysterious boudoir, difficulties, and the macaw follow, then the sortes Virgilianae, the exhibition, and jealousy. Edgeworth sets her heroine's clear judgment against a circle where show, scandal, and mercenary matches pass for life, and lets a reformed rake's sister-in-law-to-be learn from another woman's wreck.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-:
The issue of November 25, 1897 is No. 55 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It, a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Its lead item says this has been an exciting week for Cuban matters. Mr. Taylor wrote an article on Cuba in The North American Review. He said Spain did not seem able to settle the Cuban question. It was clearly the duty of the United States to interfere. The Madrid papers took the matter up with indignation.

A Spanish senator, Senor Salvani, wrote an angry letter to the Madrid papers. Taylor, when minister to Spain, had declared there was no fear of American interference. Taylor answered that the Spanish authorities were unreliable. The United States should insist that the war end by a fixed date, or end it for Spain. Cuba, he held, would fight till her last drop of blood.
the-marrow-of-alchemy-1655-1655: The Marrow of Alchemy was printed in London in 1655 by R. I. for Edward Brewster, at the sign of the Crane in Paul's Church-yard. Its title page credits Eireneus Philalethes, though the name is partly garbled in the printing. It promises the second part of the work: three books explaining the practice of the art and the philosophers' elixir for young practitioners. Only the title page and the heading of an experimental treatise are present here, so the three books themselves do not appear.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Milan and Mantua, part of the Venetian Years in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, comes from the 1894 London edition translated by Arthur Machen, with chapters discovered by Arthur Symons. Chapter Twenty opens on Low Sunday with a visit from Charles and his wife Christine. Casanova notes her powdered hair pleases him less than her former raven locks and country dress. Husband and wife bear the stamp of happiness.

Charles reproaches Casanova for never calling, and a visit follows with M. Dandolo. Christine, now idolized by her husband's aunt and sister, shows her copy-book to display her progress in writing. She tells Casanova she discovers virtues in Charles daily, and that Charles laughed at the informer who reported their two days together at Treviso. Casanova adds that Charles proved a friend twenty-six years later, when money was needed. Readers see an old affair settled into gratitude and trust.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, August 15, 1829, No. 385, illustrates Hampton Court from one of Kip's bird's-eye views of Queen Anne's time. The palace stands on the Thames's north bank, two miles west of Kingston. Cardinal Wolsey built it magnificently after taking the manor's lease. Stow is quoted: Wolsey bestowed great cost converting the mansion into so stately a palace that it excited much envy.

To avoid that envy, in 1526 Wolsey gave the palace to Henry VIII, who licensed him to lodge at Richmond in recompense. Wolsey still occasionally inhabited Hampton Court, perhaps as keeper. In 1527 he entertained French ambassadors there at the king's command. Cavendish's Life of Wolsey, quoted from a British Museum manuscript, details ushers travelling from chamber to chamber to garnish rooms nobly. Readers see a cardinal's gift that was really a surrender, furnished room by room.
the-moonstone-pg155:
Contents alone are present here for Wilkie Collins's romance The Moonstone, so no part of the narrative appears. The list is fuller than a sibling record's: after a prologue and the heading The Story, the First Period runs to twenty-three numbered chapters, again without titles.

A Second Period then begins, announced as a set of separate narratives, and its First Narrative lists at least seven chapters before the pages end. That structure, one story retold by several voices in turn, is the only clue these leaves give about how Collins built his mystery. Titles, dates, and the author's name stand at the head of the list, with Wilkie Collins styled simply as the book's author.
the-parent-s-assistant-or-stories-for-ch:
Maria Edgeworth wrote The Parent's Assistant, or Stories for Children, shown here in the 1891 Routledge edition from London, with illustrations by F. A. Fraser. The same edition and preface open a second record of this book in the library; the two records share their front matter. Her preface, addressed to parents, begins with Dr. Johnson's praise of Dr. Watts.

Johnson praised Watts for laying aside the scholar and wit to write poems and lessons for children from their fourth year. Edgeworth builds on that praise to explain her own aim. The title page carries Pope's lines on education bending the twig, and with it the growing tree.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-03:
Motley's third volume opens on October 25, 1555, with the estates of the Netherlands assembled in the great hall at Brussels to witness Charles the Fifth's long-resolved abdication. A chapter summary promises portraits of those present, the ceremony's formalities, universal emotion, and remarks on Charles retiring to Juste.

Motley notes that the emperor loved great political spectacles and knew their influence on the masses, though plain to shabbiness in his own black dress. Ceremony and character meet at the transfer of power to Philip. The abdication scene gives the revolt its starting tableau.
tob-10455:
Kabir was a fifteenth-century weaver and poet in India whose songs, presented here in English translation, have been sung for five centuries. He wrote in the common tongue rather than learned Sanskrit. His target, again and again, is empty ritual, whether Hindu or Muslim, performed without love or honesty.

Against temple and mosque formality, Kabir points to the one God found within. Short, fierce songs mix longing for God with a workman's bluntness about priests, pride, and death. Villagers and saints alike kept his verses alive by singing them. Readers meet mysticism with calloused hands, spoken by a man who earned his bread at a loom.
tob-11055:
Rudolf Steiner first issued his manual How to Attain Knowledge of the Higher Worlds in 1904, promising readers no shortcuts. Perception of higher, spiritual worlds, he argues, can be developed like a sense organ, through meditation, concentration exercises, and moral self-training. The student must change habits of thought and feeling, not just read.

Exercises proceed in stages, with warnings about self-deception and the need for reverence, patience, and healthy judgment. Steiner presents the path as systematic and demanding, closer to a discipline than a revelation. The book became the practical companion to his theoretical works, used by Anthroposophists as a training text ever since.
tob-13155:
Sayings of Confucius, gathered by his students, fill the Analects, the most quoted book in Chinese history. James Legge translated them from his Chinese Classics series into a standalone English volume. Confucius lived in troubled times and taught rulers and pupils how to live rightly.

The short dialogues cover learning, kindness, ritual, family duty, and honest government. Confucius praises the person who studies gladly, admits fault, and puts others first. Legge's Victorian English is formal, but the Master's voice comes through: dry, warm, and practical. For over two thousand years, students in China learned these lines by heart.
tob-13455:
The Liezi is one of the classic books of Taoism, named for the sage Lieh Tzu, said to have lived in the fourth century BC. Its chapters mix fable, dialogue, and wonder tales. Chinese tradition ranks it beside the works of Laozi and Zhuangzi.

Stories tell of the Yellow Emperor's dream journey, a man who feared the sky might fall, and dreamers unsure which world is real. The tone is witty and skeptical, quick to mock pomp and fear. Beneath the humor sits a steady teaching: let things take their course, hold life lightly, and distrust the busy mind's alarms.
tob-4055:
Anthropogenesis, volume two of the four-volume Secret Doctrine, turns from cosmos to humanity. Blavatsky traces the descent of spirit into matter through a sequence of root races, naming vanished peoples and continents: Hyperborean, Lemurian, and Atlantean among them. Human evolution, in her telling, is spiritual first and physical second.

Lost lands and giant early races fill the narrative, drawn from her reading of myth, geology, and Eastern scripture. By today's anthropology the scheme is untenable as science, a point even sympathetic readers concede. Yet the volume holds the core of Theosophical lore, the source from which a century of occult lost-continent tales flowed.
tob-4155:
Anna Bonus Kingsford and Edward Maitland published The Perfect Way in 1882, presenting teaching they said was received in dreams and visions. Esoteric Christianity is the subject: the soul's nature, reincarnation, and the finding of the Christ within each person. Kingsford, a doctor and campaigner against cruelty to animals, led the pair.

Lectures move from the soul's fall into matter to its return through purity and compassion. Vegetarian ethics and attacks on vivisection belong to the same gospel, in their view. Verified from the 1919 edition, the book made its authors famous in London's occult circles and still marks a high point of Victorian visionary religion.
tob-4255:
Newbell Niles Puckett, a sociologist, gathered Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro from fieldwork across the South, and his 1926 book became a classic of American folklore. Hoodoo, haints, conjure, and rootwork fill its chapters, reported from the people who practiced and feared them.

Puckett sorts cures, charms, omens, and ghost lore with a scholar's care and a collector's ear. The beliefs he records blend African inheritances with Southern life. Later students of Black religion and folklore build on his record at every step. Verified from the 1919 edition record, the volume remains an invaluable witness to a living tradition.
trollope-warden-1855:
Anthony Trollope published The Warden in 1855, the gentle opening of his Barchester novels of cathedral life. The tale turns on Mr. Harding's conscience over his cathedral sinecure at Hiram's Hospital in Barchester town. Trollope, a post office surveyor, found his true subject in the clergy and county society of Barsetshire here.

Harding, a kind old clergyman, holds a rich wardenship over twelve bedesmen with a tiny true workload. A young reformer, John Bold, charges in the press that the charity's funds are being misused by the church. Archdeacon Grantly urges fight, but Harding's conscience will not let him keep a post under public doubt. He resigns, the suit collapses, and the hospital stands empty in one of Trollope's saddest quiet closes in fiction. The small scale hides the moral care that made Barchester a world readers revisit.
un-ga-res-1755:
Crisis in Southern Rhodesia drove Resolution 1755, adopted by the General Assembly on 12 October 1962. Four months before, the Assembly had affirmed that the British colony was a land not yet self-governing. Since then, the white regime had declared a state of emergency, banned the Zimbabwe African Peoples Union, and jailed the party's leaders. The text calls the state of affairs deplorable, critical, and explosive.

Britain is urged to act at once and with force. The party's president, Joshua Nkomo, and all other jailed or held nationalist leaders must be freed without terms. The ban on the party must be lifted. Britain must also report back to the Assembly on what it has done.
un-ga-res-a-69-55:
Care for the earth belongs in arms deals too, says Resolution A/69/55, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The link had been on the Assembly's books since 1995, in a chain of yearly votes. Green rules, the text holds, must be kept in mind both when arms pacts are drafted and when they are put into force. Deals struck at the 1992 world earth summit in Rio count among the guides.

The Assembly takes note of the report of the Secretary-General on the point. Arms cuts, it argues, should not be won at the cost of the soil, air, and water that people live from. Even the grim work of disarmament, in this view, owes a duty to the world it claims to make safer.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 1755 (XVII) was adopted on 12 October 1962. It returned to Southern Rhodesia, weeks after the Assembly had declared it a Non-Self-Governing Territory. The mood had turned grave. A state of emergency was in force. The Zimbabwe African Peoples Union had been banned. Nationalist leaders had been arrested or held.

The Assembly pressed Britain, as a matter of urgency, to free the union's detained president at once. It pressed Britain to free all other nationalist leaders at once and without conditions. It also demanded that the ban on the union be lifted. It asked Britain to report back within the same session on what it had done.

Resolution 69/55 of the General Assembly asks that environmental norms be followed when disarmament and arms control agreements are written and carried out. The Assembly reaffirms that disarmament forums should take relevant environmental standards fully into account in talks. It is mindful of the environmental damage nuclear weapons use would cause. States are called on to apply science and technical progress in security fields without harming the environment or sustainable development. They are called on to report their measures to the Secretary-General.
un-sc-res-1355: Security Council Resolution 1355 survives in the official record, and the catalog dates it to 2001. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1455:
The Al-Qaida and Taliban sanctions were tightened on 17 January 2003. The Council restated the web of texts from 1267 (1999) to 1452 (2002). Every state had to freeze the funds of listed persons and bar their travel and arms. Full account was to be taken of the humanitarian exemptions set out in resolution 1452.

The Council improved the way the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo were to be applied. The changes would be reviewed and improved again within twelve months. The sanctions committee would send the consolidated list to all states at least every three months. Every state had to report to the committee within ninety days on the steps it had taken. Fresh monitoring help was arranged for the committee, with a team of experts to track how states carried the measures out. States had to strengthen their laws to enforce the sanctions.
un-sc-res-1555:
Fighting in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo forced a short renewal in 2004. On 29 July 2004 the Security Council extended MONUC, its Congo mission, until 1 October. North and South Kivu and the Ituri district were the hot spots. The Council backed the Congo's transitional government of national unity. It also welcomed a joint check planned with Rwanda.

The Secretary-General owed a report before 16 August on the mission's work. The Council treated the situation as a threat to peace in the region. The mission kept the powers it held under Chapter VII of the Charter. A longer decision on its future would follow the report.
un-sc-res-1655:
UNIFIL was extended as Blue Line violence simmered on 31 January 2006. Hezbollah had attacked on 21 November 2005, and rockets had been fired into Israel on 27 December. Israel kept violating Lebanese airspace. The Secretary-General's report of 18 January pressed Lebanon to extend its rule over the whole south. The Blue Line had to be respected in full, the Council restated.

The Council endorsed the Secretary-General's report. It extended UNIFIL's mandate until 31 July 2006, while flagging that the force's shape would be reviewed. All acts of violence along the Blue Line were condemned. The parties had to keep the pledges they had made to respect the line and the force's safety. Lebanon's government was called again to extend its authority through the south and hold the sole right to force there. The steps Beirut had begun toward that end were welcomed.
un-sc-res-1755:
Sudan drew a formal Council decision in Resolution 1755, adopted on 30 April 2007. The 2005 peace deal had ended the long north-south civil war, but progress was slow. A separate war in Darfur still raged, and a United Nations mission, UNMIS, watched over the main peace deal.

The text extends the mandate of UNMIS until 31 October 2007. It asks the Secretary-General to name a new envoy for Sudan at once. It urges both sides to build joint army units and finish moving their forces by 9 July 2007. It also presses them to settle the Abyei dispute and prepare national elections on time.
un-sc-res-1855: Resolution 1855, adopted in 2009, is preserved here as a Security Council decision in its record wording. English Wikisource is the source of the transcription. The text demonstrates the institution's habits under pressure: recall the past, judge the present, direct the future, all inside a few numbered pages that member states are bound to respect.
un-sc-res-255: Entry number 255 in the Council's official sequence is a resolution the catalog dates to 1968. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-355:
Cyprus was in crisis in the summer of 1974, weeks after fighting split the island. On 1 August 1974 the Security Council acted on the Secretary-General's statement. It recalled resolution 353, which had demanded a ceasefire and talks. All states, the text notes, had voiced respect for Cyprus's sovereignty and unity. The Secretary-General had just outlined his next steps to the Council.

The resolution asks him to take fitting action in line with that statement. He then had to give the Council a full report. The ceasefire, the Council stressed, was only the first step. Full use of resolution 353 was the real goal. That meant talks toward a lasting settlement for the island.
un-sc-res-455: Number 455 marks this Security Council text in the official record, catalogued here at 1979. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-55:
Indonesia's truce was fraying in the summer of 1948. A federal conference had met at Bandung that May. Political talks between the Dutch and the republic had stalled. Trade limits in the islands added to the strain. On 29 July 1948 the Security Council reviewed its good offices committee's reports. Those papers covered the talks, the standstill, and the trade dispute.

The Council calls on both governments to keep the Renville Truce Agreement strictly. That duty covered its military and its economic terms. With the committee's help, both sides had to use the agreed political principles early and in full. Those principles were meant to lead to a settlement. The Dutch offensive that December showed how weak the truce had become.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Foreign armies were still on Congolese soil despite the Lusaka Ceasefire Agreement when this text passed on 15 June 2001. The Council voiced alarm at the war's toll on civilians, including refugees and displaced people, and at rising HIV infection in the east of the country.

The Front de Libération du Congo was told to pull its forces back as agreed in the Harare sub-plans. Ugandan, Rwandan, and all other foreign forces were again told to leave Congo, and Uganda's stated decision to begin withdrawing was welcomed. All parties were told to avoid attacks while disengagement and withdrawal went forward.

Resolution 1455, adopted unanimously on 17 January 2003, tightens the sanctions net around Al-Qaida and the Taliban. The regime, built since 1999, obliged every state to freeze assets, block travel, and stop arms for listed members and associates of the two movements. The Council underlined that the separate, broader counter-terrorism duties of September 2001 also bound all members in full.

States were told to report within ninety days on what they had actually done to enforce the measures, taking account of humanitarian exemptions agreed the previous month. The expert monitoring group watching the regime was kept at work. The resolution's target was a gap the Council kept finding: strong rules on paper, patchy enforcement in practice.

Cyprus won independence from Britain in August 1960 under a delicate power-sharing deal. Greek and Turkish Cypriots were meant to govern together. The new republic promptly sought a UN seat. Resolution 155 was adopted unanimously on 24 August 1960, just days after independence day.

The Council recommended that the General Assembly admit the Republic of Cyprus. The Assembly agreed the next month. Membership placed Cyprus inside the family of states at a hopeful moment. Few foresaw how fast the settlement would fail. Within a few years, UN peacekeepers were patrolling the island. Cyprus's 1960 admission thus marks the calm before decades of division.

Congo's mission gained a two-month bridge in the summer of 2004. On 29 July, the Council adopted Resolution 1555 without dissent. It acted under Chapter VII. Fighting still burned in the eastern provinces of North and South Kivu. Ituri was restless as well. A unity government in Kinshasa held the Council's full backing.

The text extends MONUC's mandate, as set by two earlier texts, to 1 October 2004. The Secretary-General must report by mid-August on the mission's work. The short span came just before a big change. That autumn the Council made the force larger and stronger. The east, it judged, needed a heavier UN presence.

Resolution 1655, adopted on 31 January 2006, extends the UN Interim Force in Lebanon, UNIFIL, for six months. Lebanon's government had asked for the renewal. Tension along the Blue Line stayed high, with attacks started by Hizbullah in November 2005, rockets fired into Israel that December, and ongoing Israeli flights over Lebanese land. Israel had left Lebanon in 2000, and UNIFIL's main remaining task was restoring peace and safety.

The Council extends UNIFIL until 31 July 2006 and stresses its temporary nature. It condemns all violence across the Blue Line and urges both sides to respect the line in full and show the greatest restraint. It presses Lebanon to spread its sole authority through the south, send more of its own forces there, and set up a joint planning cell with UNIFIL. It also welcomes steps to link the Lebanese Armed Forces more closely with the force.

Sudan's Comprehensive Peace Agreement is the frame for Resolution 1755, adopted on 30 April 2007. The ceasefire between north and south was broadly holding, a southern budget had been adopted, and a new currency had come in. The UN Mission in the Sudan, UNMIS, was fully deployed in the south. In Darfur, by contrast, attacks on civilians and aid workers went on, and AMIS peacekeepers had been killed.

The Council extends UNMIS until 31 October 2007 and asks for a new Special Representative to be named urgently, with reports every three months. It calls on the peace deal parties to speed up joint units, fighter disarmament, and full troop pullback by 9 July 2007. It also presses them to mark out the 1956 north-south border, settle the Abyei dispute, and prepare national elections on the agreed timetable.

The bench of the Rwanda war crimes tribunal is adjusted on 19 December 2008 so trials can finish. The tribunal's completion strategy required first-instance trials to end in 2008, but cases remained. Two permanent judges were about to resign, and three more planned to leave when their cases ended, threatening the schedule.

The Secretary-General may appoint extra ad litem judges, within existing resources, to replace departing judges and keep chambers working. The tribunal's Statute is amended to raise the ceiling on ad litem judges serving at one time. The proposals came from the tribunal's president, whose December letter warned that without such flexibility the remaining trials could not be completed as planned.

Resolution 1955, adopted on 14 December 2010, keeps Rwanda tribunal judges in office beyond their scheduled terms. The tribunal's completion report admitted it could not finish all its work in 2010, the deadline set back in 2003 and 2004. Four permanent judges were set to move to the appeals chamber, while another would leave once his cases ended, complicating the roster.

Convinced that continuity was advisable, the Council extended the judges' authorization so trials under way could be completed by the judges who heard the evidence. The pairing with a twin resolution on the Yugoslavia tribunal, adopted at the same meeting, shows the Council managing both courts' endgames together as their work passed toward the residual mechanism.

Resolution 2055, adopted on 29 June 2012, is about staffing the fight against weapons of mass destruction falling into private hands. Resolution 1540 of 2004 obliges every state to keep nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons away from non-state actors, and a committee tracks compliance. In 2011 the Council extended that committee's mandate for ten years, and its workload kept growing.

The resolution's single ask is that the Secretary-General increase the committee's supporting group of experts to as many as nine people. It is pure administrative plumbing, but it mattered: expert reviews are how the 1540 system turns a universal legal duty into country-by-country assessments of export controls, border security, and domestic laws.

Countries that gave up nuclear weapons wanted a promise of help if they were ever threatened with such weapons. Resolution 255, adopted on 19 June 1968, is tied to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. That treaty was opened for signing the same year.

The Council recognized a clear point of law. Nuclear aggression against a state without nuclear weapons would force the Council to act at once under the Charter. The same was true of a threat of such aggression. The nuclear-armed permanent members would have a special duty to respond. The Council welcomed the stated intention of certain states to give prompt help. That help would go to any non-nuclear treaty party that was attacked or threatened. The right of self-defense under Article 51 was also reaffirmed.

Days after the guns fell silent over Cyprus in 1974, the Council set its next step. On 1 August, it adopted Resolution 355. Twelve members voted yes and none voted no. Two members held back. A truce had followed the Turkish intervention and the Greek junta's fall. The Council recalled its July call, Resolution 353, for a truce and talks.

The text notes that all states have voiced respect for Cyprus. Its freedom, self-rule, and land must stay whole. The Secretary-General must act in light of his statement to the Council. A full report is due from him. The truce counts as step one toward carrying out Resolution 353 in full.

Zambia complained in November 1979 about repeated Rhodesian attacks on its territory. The illegal minority regime in Southern Rhodesia was working with South Africa. Its raids violated Zambia's sovereignty, airspace, and territory. People were killed and property wrecked. Resolution 455 was adopted by consensus on 23 November 1979.

The Council strongly condemned the regime's aggression against Zambia. The attacks were continued, intensified, and unprovoked, the text says. South Africa's part in them was condemned as well. Zambia and the other front-line states were praised for backing Zimbabwe's struggle and for keeping their restraint. Britain, as the ruling power, was told to act promptly to stop the attacks. The text called for full compensation to Zambia and urgent aid for rebuilding. A small ad hoc committee was set up to help carry this out.

Talks on Indonesia's future had stalled by mid-1948. The Dutch and the young republic had signed a truce aboard the ship Renville. Its terms covered both arms and trade. A UN good offices team watched the deal and filed reports. One told of a trade squeeze. Resolution 55 passed on 29 July 1948 by nine votes to none.

Both sides were told to keep the truce in full. That meant its rules on arms and on goods alike. The twelve Renville points on politics had to be put into force, fast and whole. Six added points came with them. The Soviet bloc held back in the vote. The text shows the Council prodding a colonial power and a new-born republic toward a deal, step by grudging step.

Bosnia and Herzegovina was in far worse shape than its neighbors in spring 1992. It had declared independence from Yugoslavia. War erupted within weeks. Even so, the new state applied for UN membership. Resolution 755, adopted without a vote on 20 May 1992, answered that application.

The Council recommended that the General Assembly admit Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Assembly acted two days later. Membership did not stop the war. But it fixed Bosnia's status as a sovereign state in international law. That status mattered greatly in later debates. Arguments over intervention and borders returned to it again and again.
un-un-res-fourth-report-of-the-secretary:
Spring 2000 was the darkest hour of the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone, and the fourth report of the Secretary-General, document S/2000/455, covers that season. Rebel forces had attacked UN troops and taken hundreds hostage. The mission, UNAMSIL, faced collapse unless help arrived fast.

The report recounts the hostage crisis, rescue efforts, and the state of the ceasefire. It asks for a stronger, larger force with a tougher mandate. Britain's swift military move that May helped save the mission. The report shows the Council learning hard lessons about weak peacekeeping.
vesalius-de-humani-corporis-fabrica-1555:
Andreas Vesalius was a Flemish doctor who studied the human body by cutting open corpses himself, not just by reading old books. His great anatomy work first appeared in 1543. This Latin text is his own revised second edition, published in 1555. No public-domain English translation exists, so the work is presented here in Latin.

Inside, Vesalius describes bones, muscles, nerves, and organs in careful order, correcting many errors copied from Galen for over a thousand years. Detailed woodcut pictures showed the body layer by layer. The book founded modern anatomy because it trusted direct observation over ancient authority. Doctors and artists studied it for centuries.
warsaw-pact-1955:
The Soviet Union and seven Eastern European states signed the Warsaw Pact in May 1955. Its formal title was a treaty of friendship, cooperation, and mutual assistance. Moscow announced it days after West Germany joined NATO, presenting the new bloc as the East's answer to the Western alliance.

Members pledged to aid any member that came under armed attack, and they set up a joint military command under Soviet control. In practice the alliance served as Moscow's tool for holding its satellite states in line. Soviet-led forces used its framework to crush the Hungarian rising of 1956 and the Prague Spring of 1968. The pact dissolved in 1991 as the Cold War ended.
wathen-the-golden-colony-1855:
George Henry Wathen tours a gold mad land in The Golden Colony, his book of 1855. Wathen, a sage of stones, went to Victoria in its gold rush prime. He tells of mines, towns, roads, and the wild new wealth of the place. His eye is keen for both rock and man in a land turned upside down by greed and hope.

Midst the tour stands a rare scrap: a turf out line of a bunyip, cut in the soil at Challicum in late 1854. Wathen gauged it on site. That note is a key source on the beast.
whitman-leaves-of-grass-1855:
Walt Whitman published Leaves of Grass in Brooklyn in 1855, at his own cost. The slim first edition held twelve untitled poems and a bold prose preface. Whitman set the type himself and sent free copies to famed writers of the day.

The long lead poem, later called Song of Myself, praises body and soul alike. Whitman hails grass, labor, cities, and the vast American scene around him. His free verse broke the rules of meter that ruled his age's verse. Emerson praised the book while most critics scorned or ignored its new voice. All later editions of Whitman's life work grew from this seed.
zoist-vol-13-1855:
Volume thirteen of The Zoist, from April 1855 to January 1856, completes the journal's run. Elliotson founded the journal in 1843 and edited all thirteen volumes. Mesmerism and cerebral physiology shared its pages to the end. The final volume carries the usual reports of trance, cure, and somnambulist sight.

With it closes the most important English journal the mesmeric movement ever had. Surgical cases, debates, and wonders stand preserved across the whole set. The mesmerism to hypnotism debate found its archive here. Later ages dismissed much of it, yet the record endures. Readers can now follow the cause from first trumpet to last. Few movements documented themselves so fully.
